Preface




This textbook offers a friendly introduction to advanced microeconomic theory that
undergraduate and graduate students can use to transition into more technical topics.
Every chapter explicitly connects the materials of Intermediate microeconomics
courses with the topics taught in most Master’s programs (and some PhD courses) dur-
ing the first semester: preference relations, demand theory and applications, producer
theory, and choice under uncertainty; and some of the topics studied during the second
semester: partial and general equilibrium, monopoly, oligopoly models, externalities
and public goods, and contract theory.
   The presentation differs from current graduate-level textbooks—essentially,
Mas-Colell et al. (1995), Jehle and Reny (2011), and Varian (1992)—along several
dimensions: (1) it emphasizes the economic intuition behind mathematical properties
and assumptions, (2) it provides several step-by-step examples in every chapter in
order to help students to apply theoretical results using specific functional forms, and
(3) it includes several sections discussing topics on behavioral economics. Therefore,
while the presentation includes advanced materials covered in Master’s and PhD
programs, the economic interpretations and examples make the exposition easy to
understand for upper-level undergraduate students as well. This textbook should
therefore be especially attractive for students in Master’s programs—in disciplines
such as Economics, Finance, and Public Policy—as well as for PhD students in pro-
grams with a strong applied focus. Unfortunately, current graduate-level textbooks
provide limited intuition and applications, leaving many students with the impression
that their first year of graduate school is disconnected from the topics they learned
as undergraduates, ultimately discouraging students from finishing their graduate
studies. In contrast, this textbook seeks to provide a more explicit bridge to graduate-
level microeconomic theory, thus preparing students to easily apply theory to their
future research interests.
xii                                                                                     Preface



         The textbook is accompanied by a Workbook for Advanced Microeconomic Theory,
      which includes a complete set of exercises for every chapter with detailed answer keys
      (106 exercises in total). In particular, the Workbook offers step-by-step explanations so
      that students can better understand how to approach similar exercises on their own, and
      emphasizes the economic intuition behind mathematical results. As a consequence the
      Workbook is radically different from solution manuals currently in the market, which
      rarely provide detailed explanations, are difficult to read on their own, and are only
      distributed to instructors. The combination of textbook and workbook is hence the
      only combination of its kind in the market, and together, they seek to help graduate
      students improve both their theoretical and practical preparation in advanced micro-
      economics.

      Organization of the Book

      The first two chapters are dedicated to consumer theory, first describing preference
      relations and utility functions (chapter 1), and then presenting demand theory (chapter
      2). Chapter 3 provides a more applied perspective by using the tools learned in previ-
      ous chapters to evaluate the welfare change that results from a price change, and the
      setting of different types of taxes. Chapters 4 and 5 study topics on choice under un-
      certainty and production theory, respectively, and chapter 6 analyzes partial and gen-
      eral equilibrium. The last four chapters examine equilibrium behavior under market
      imperfections, namely monopoly (chapter 7), imperfect competition (chapter 8), exter-
      nalities and public goods (chapter 9), and contract theory (chapter 10), and these last
      chapters discuss how regulation can induce private agents to voluntarily produce
      socially optimal outcomes. Every chapter includes several parametric examples that
      apply the main theoretical results to specific functional forms, and further reading
      recommendations are noted throughout each chapter.

      How to Use This Textbook

      The writing style of the textbook, and the possibility of combining it with the Work-
      book, allows for flexible uses by instructors:
      Upper-undergraduate and Master’s programs Instructors in these courses can as-
      sign chapters of the textbook as required readings, since they are self-contained and
      their explanations should be easily accessible. Additionally instructors could assign
      the reading of specific exercises in the Workbook, which should help students better
Preface                                                                                           xiii



          understand the application of theoretical foundations, ultimately helping them to be-
          come better prepared for homework assignments and exams.
          PhD level—applied approach Instructors can assign this textbook as the main
          reading reference, complementing it with journal articles, and the reading of
          certain exercises of the Workbook. As mentioned above, this strategy could be
          particularly effective to ensure that students can more easily link theoretical topics
          with applications.
          PhD level—theoretical approach Instructors preferring a more theoretical focus
          can recommend chapters as an introduction to the more advanced topics covered in
          class. This strategy can prove especially useful, as it could allow instructors to dedicate
          more time to discussing theoretical foundations in class, such as detailed proofs and
          recent journal articles. Instructors could also assign the reading of a list of exercises
          from the Workbook, in order to facilitate the comprehension of the main theoretical
          results and its application to specific settings.

          Examples of Course Guidelines

          Master’s programs in Economics Schools offering two semesters in microeconomic
          theory could cover chapters 1 through 5 in the first semester, and chapters 6 through 10
          in the second semester. Schools only offering one-semester course could cover chap-
          ters 1 through 6 if their focus is on consumer and producer theory, or chapters 1, 2, 5,
          and 7 through 10 if their focus is on market imperfections and contract theory.
          Master’s programs in Finance If the program only offers a one-semester course in
          microeconomic theory, a natural list of tentative chapters (with a focus on optimal
          decision making, uncertainty, strategy, and contracts) would be chapters 1, 2, 5, 7,
          8, and 10.
          Master’s programs in Public Policy If the program only offers a one-semester
          course in microeconomic theory, a natural list of tentative chapters (with a focus on
          consumer and producer theory, market imperfections, and public policies addressing
          these market imperfections) would be chapters 1, 2, 3, and 7-10
          PhD programs in Economics or Finance Most programs require two semesters in
          microeconomic theory, and often focus on consumer and producer theory during the
          first semester (chapters 1 through 6, thus including partial and general equilibrium);
          and analyze game theory, market imperfections and contract theory during the second
          semester (chapters 7 through 10).
xiv                                                                                        Preface



      Undergraduate courses Courses such as a one-semester “Topics in Microeconom-
      ics” for seniors might include a subset of chapters from the textbook (about five chap-
      ters or less), depending on the topics that instructors plan to emphasize in the course:
      •  	Focus on consumer theory and uncertainty (chapters 1–5)
      •  	Focus on consumer and producer theory, including general equilibrium (chapters
          1–4, 6)
      •  	Focus on uncertainty, monopoly, game theory, imperfect competition, externalities
          and public goods (chapters 5, 7–9)
      •  	Focus on optimal decision making, uncertainty, strategy and contracts (chapters 1,
          2, 5, 8, 10)
      •  	Focus on strategy, market imperfections and regulation (chapters 7–10)

      Ancillary Materials

      Workbook for Advanced Microeconomic Theory The accompanying Workbook
      includes step-by-step answer keys with intuitive explanations to all odd-numbered
      end-of-chapter exercises (106 exercises). These exercises and their answer keys are
      intended to facilitate students’ preparation for their own homework assignments and
      exams (at both the Master’s and PhD levels) and to help students strengthen the core
      topics before transitioning into more challenging materials (at the PhD level). A set
      of exercises could be assigned as a required reading for every chapter during the
      semester, since they could effectively support students’ learning.
      Solutions Manual for Advanced Microeconomic Theory The accompanying
      Solutions Manual provides detailed answer keys to all chapter exercises (215 exercises
      in total). The Solutions Manual is only available to instructors.
      PowerPoint slides The accompanying PowerPoint slides cover the main topics in
      every chapter of the current textbook. They can be used by instructors, edited in order
      to elaborate on specific topics, and distributed to students as a first set of lecture notes
      they can complement with in-class explanations.

1 Preferences and Utility



    How can we formally describe an individual’s preference for different amounts of a
    good? And, how can we represent his preference for a particular list of goods (a bun-
    dle) over another? In this chapter we study preference relations over bundles, their
    mathematical representation, and different properties that preferences can satisfy. We
    seek, for instance, to formalize the notion of desirability (preferring more units of at
    least one good, and perhaps of all goods). We also explore other properties such as
    completeness (the individual’s ability to compare any two bundles we show at him),
    transitivity (by which his preferences cannot suffer from cycles), convexity (which
    implies that an individual is better off with balanced than unbalanced bundles), or
    monotonicity, which states that an individual is strictly better off when the amount of
    one good increases, while the amounts of all other goods are unaffected. We test which
    of these properties are satisfied/violated for different preference relations in the
    worked-out examples of the chapter.
       In our discussion we examine under which conditions an individual’s preference
    relation can be mathematically represented with a utility function. This is not just a
    mathematical curiosity. Rather, it provides several benefits: (1) utility functions allow
    for algebraic manipulation, (2) they can be graphically represented (i.e., we can depict
    their level sets, which we refer to as “indifference curves”), (3) their partial derivative
    helps us better understand whether utility increases/decreases when the consumption
    of one (or several) goods increases, and (4) in subsequent chapters we will differenti-
    ate them in order to find the bundle/s that maximizes an individual’s utility. We also
    explore how the properties of preference relations discussed in the first section of the
    chapter affect the utility function that represents them.
       We also provide a brief review of the behavioral economics literature. This literature
    has expanded significantly in the last two decades. In particular, it has offered utility
    functions that try to account for a recurrent observation in controlled experiments
2                                                                                   Chapter 1



    whereby individuals not only seem to value their own material well-being but also that
    of other individuals in the society, commonly referred to as “social preferences.” We
    also describe two other types of behavioral theories. The first assumes that the utility
    an individual obtains from consuming a certain bundle not only depends on the char-
    acteristics of that bundle but also on how such bundle compares to a reference bundle,
    often referred to as “reference-dependent” preferences. The second discusses hyper-
    bolic (and quasi-hyperbolic) discounting of future payoffs.
       The chapter then explores a different approach to preferences, the “choice-based”
    approach, which analyzes actual choices rather than preferences over potentially avail-
    able bundles. The chapter concludes with a mathematical description of constraints on
    the set of goods that the individual can feasibly consume, for instance, restricting the
    set of possible bundles to those that the individual can afford. The description on util-
    ity functions and constraints in this chapter will constitute the two main ingredients of
    the utility maximization problem in the next chapter, whereby the individual decision
    maker seeks to maximize his utility subject to a set of constraints.

    1.1   Preference and Choice: The Preference-Based Approach

    We begin our analysis of individual decision making in an abstract setting. We will
    first specify a set of possible alternatives (denoted by set X) for a decision maker.
    This set may include the consumption bundles that an individual is considering to
    buy, or any other general list of alternatives. For instance, X could be a subset of
     +N , implying that a bundle x would be an n-dimensional vector (x1, x2, ..., xN); a
    common assumption in many applications. Given this set, we will tackle the decision-
    making process in two ways, first, using the “preference-based approach” and, sec-
    ond, using the “choice-based approach.” The first approach explores how the
    individual uses his preferences to choose an element (or elements) from the set of
    alternatives X. We will therefore impose a rationality assumption on the individual’s
    preferences. The second approach observes instead the actual choices the individual
    makes when he is called to choose an element (or elements) from the set of possible
    alternatives. As in the preference-based approach, we will impose a consistency
    condition on the choices that the individual makes. These two approaches have their
    own advantages. For instance, the preference-based approach is based on unobserv-
    ables (the individual’s preferences), whereas the choice-based approach is based on
    observables (the actual choices made by the individual decision maker). The
    preference-based approach is more tractable than the choice-based approach, espe-
    cially when the set of alternatives X contains many elements, which is usually the
Preferences and Utility                                                                                              3



                    case in individual decision-making problems.1 After describing both approaches, and
                    the assumptions that we impose on each approach, we investigate the relationship
                    (and potential equivalence) between them. Hence we examine under which condi-
                    tions rational preferences imply a consistent choice behavior and under which condi-
                    tions the opposite relationship holds.

                    1.1.1      Preference-Based Approach
                    In the preference-based approach we understand the decision maker’s preferences as
                    his “attitudes” toward the elements in a set of possible alternatives X. These attitudes
                    could be obtained by presenting a questionnaire to the individual in which we ask: For
                    any pair of elements x and y in the set of alternatives X, namely for all x, y ∈ X, how
                    do you compare element x and y? Check one and only one box.

                    □ I prefer x to y (which we write as x ≻ y), or

                    □ I prefer y to x (which we write as y ≻ x), or

                    □ I am indifferent (which we write as x ~ y).

                    Note that we are asking the individual decision maker to check one box. This is related
                    with the completeness assumption on strict preferences, as we define next.2

                          Completeness (in strict preferences) A preference relation is complete if,
                          for any two alternatives x, y ∈ X, either: alternative x is preferred to y, x ≻ y; or
                          alternative y is preferred to x, y ≻ x; or the individual is indifferent between x and
                          y, which is expressed as x ~ y.


                      The completeness axiom suggests that the individual is capable of comparing
                    any pair of alternatives that we present to him. This might be a relatively strong as-
                    sumption if we think about goods that we have not consumed in the past, or goods that
                    we have not even seen before. Think, for instance, about the last time you were in a
                    new ethnic restaurant in which the descriptions in the menu did not help you decide
                    what to order. This assumption, hence, considers that the decision maker has had

                    1
                      This explains why the preference-based approach is presented in more detail in most micro­
                    economics textbooks.
                    2
                     We do not allow the individual to add a new box in which he writes “I love x but hate y.” In other
                    words, we do not allow him to specify the intensity of his preferences over two alternatives.
4                                                                                                  Chapter 1



    enough time to compare all alternatives, and that he is ready to express his preference
    for one (or indifference between the two alternatives) when we ask this individual to
    compare any two alternatives x and y.

    Remark about completeness A binary relation is a collection of ordered pairs (x, y)
    from a set x, y ∈ X, such as the two elements that the individual compared in the
    questionnaire shown above (e.g., two bundles of goods). If we consider a sufficiently
    large number of binary relations, it may be easy to find some of them not satisfying
    completeness. Indeed, the binary relation “is the brother of” does not satisfy com-
    pleteness for all elements (persons) in the set of available alternatives (set X in this
    case could be a given group of people). If we select John and Bob from this group X,
    we might observe that neither John is the brother of Bob nor Bob is the brother of
    John, meaning they are not related. That is, not all pairs of alternatives are compa-
    rable according to this binary relation, implying that the binary relation does not
    satisfy completeness. Similarly, the binary relation “to be the father of” does not
    satisfy completeness, since, from a group of people, we can select two individuals
    who are not related.

       Let us now turn to weak preferences. In order to learn the weak preferences of an
    individual, we can present a questionnaire to him worded as follows: For all alterna-
    tives x and y in the set of alternatives X (where x and y are not necessarily distinct),3 is
    alternative x at least as preferred as y?

    □ Yes, which we write as x ≿ y.

    □ No, which we write as y ≿ x.

    The respondents therefore must answer yes, no, or both, where checking both boxes
    reveals that the individual is indifferent between alternative x and y, x ~ y ∈ X.4 Our
    previous discussion did not explicitly define reflexivity. We do that next.

    3
      We do not assume that alternatives x and y are different. In the case that they coincide, the definition
    of completeness becomes the reflexivity assumption. We discuss this assumption below, but at this
    stage we can understand the reflexivity assumption as a condition on the preference relation
    guaranteeing that every alternative x is weakly preferred to, at least, one alternative: itself.
    4
      Note that this refers to the assumption of completeness again, since we ask the individual to be able
    to compare any pair of two alternatives, where now this comparison is done using the weak preference
    symbol, ≿, rather than the strict preference symbol, ≻.
Preferences and Utility                                                                                               5




                          Reflexivity A preference relation satisfies reflexivity if for any alternative x
                          in X, we have that x ≿ x, so that any bundle is weakly preferred to itself.

                    This property entails that
                          1. x ~ x, so that any bundle is indifferent to itself, and
                          2. x ⊁ x.
                    This assumption ensures that any bundle belongs to at least one indifference set5,
                    namely the set containing itself if nothing else. However, reflexivity is implied from
                    completeness. Indeed, if we replace alternative y for x, we can transform the assump-
                    tion of completeness into the assumption of reflexivity.

                    1.1.2      Rationality
                    We are now ready to define what we mean by a rational preference relation.

                          Rationality We say that a preference relation ≿ is rational if it satisfies the fol-
                          lowing two properties:
                          • Completeness For any pair of alternatives x, y ∈ X, either x ≿ y, or y ≿ x, or
                            both (x ~ y).
                          • Transitivity For any three alternatives x, y, z ∈ X, if x ≿ y and y ≿ z, then it
                            must be that x ≿ z.

    which entails that ∑ iN=1 xi ≥ ∑ iN=1 zi , thus implying x ≿ z, as required for transitivity. ■

    The assumption of transitivity is often understood as that individual preferences should
    not cycle. In order to understand this point, let us consider an example in which an
    individual’s preferences violate transitivity. James weakly prefers an apple to a ba-
    nana, and he weakly prefers a banana to an orange. However, he prefers an orange to
    an apple. (Note that according to transitivity, he should prefer an apple to an orange.)
    That is, this individual’s preferences are

                  Apple ≿ Banana and Banana ≿ Orange, but Orange ≻ Apple.

       What is the problem associated to this intransitive preference relation? James would
    be wiped out from the market. Indeed a businessman could approach James when he
    owns an orange and offer him a banana for one dollar.6 James will accept the deal,
    since he prefers a banana to an orange. Then the businessman could approach James
    again and offer him an apple for a dollar, something James will also accept, since he
    prefers an apple to a banana. Finally, the businessman could approach James again of-
    fering him an orange for the apple he now owns. Since James’ preferences are intransi-
    tive (and therefore he prefers an orange to an apple), he would accept this deal, paying
    another dollar. However, this makes James return to his original position, owning an
    orange but having spent three dollars in the process. Of course, this cycle could be
    repeated ad infinitum, extracting all of James’s wealth.7

    6
      The extraction of wealth we described is insensitive to the object the individual initially owns. As
    a practice, you can repeat the example considering that, instead, James initially owns an apple or a
    banana.
    7
      A famous example of intransitive preferences leading to such money extraction patterns is that in
    Dr. Seuss’ book The Sneetches where the character Sylvester McMonkey McBean uses his star-on
    and star-off machine to add or remove stars from the bellies of fictional characters. While the moral
    of this children’s book is that society should not discriminate against individuals who look different
    from them, it also teaches the dangerous consequences of intransitive preferences, as they lead to
    preference cycles!
Preferences and Utility                                                                                                      7



                       Despite the previous argument on the reasons why we should not observe individual
                    decision makers with intransitive preference relations, there are situations in which
                    intransitivities might arise. Here are some examples.8

                    Example 1.2: Comparing elements that are too close to be distinguishable
                    When alternatives are very similar, we are often unable to state which of them we pre-
                    fer. Consider the following example. Take the set of alternatives X to be the real num-
                    bers, say, a share of pie. An individual states that he prefers alternative x to y if x ≥ y
                    − 1 (x + 1 ≥ y), but he is indifferent between x and y if the two alternatives are very
                    close together, that is, if |x − y| < 1. Intuitively, he prefers x to y when alternative x is
                    larger than y by at least one unit. However, if the difference between the two alterna-
                    tives is smaller than one unit, he cannot tell them apart and becomes indifferent be-
                    tween them. Consider the following example between alternatives 1.5, 0.8 and 0.3:

                                     1.5 ~ 0.8, since their difference is 1.5 – 0.8 = 0.7 < 1, and

                                        0.8 ~ 0.3, since their difference is 0.8 – 0.3 = 0.5 < 1.

                    Therefore, by transitivity, we would have that 1.5 is indifferent to 0.3, but in fact this
                    preference relation tells us that 1.5 is preferred to 0.3 (since 1.5 is larger than 0.3 by
                    more than one unit). As a consequence this preference relation is intransitive.9 ■

                    Example 1.3: Framing effects In certain cases intransitivity might be violated be-
                    cause of the way in which alternatives are presented to the individual decision maker,
                    also referred as “framing effects.” Let us consider an example from Rubinstein (2012),
                    where the following holiday packages are shown to Master’s students, asking each
                    student: “Which holiday package do you prefer?”
                    a. A weekend in Paris for $574 at a four-star hotel.
                    b. A weekend in Paris at the four-star hotel for $574.
                    c. A weekend in Rome at the five-star hotel for $612.

                    8
                       Example 1.8 examines a preference relation that, despite satisfying transitivity, violates completeness.
                    In particular, the preference relation establishes that, for any two bundles x, y ∈ ℝN, x ≿ y if and only
                    if bundle x contains more units of every good than bundle y does, meaning xk ≥ yk for every good k. For
                    examples of preference relations violating transitivity, see exercise 1 at the end of the chapter.
                    9
                      This example could be applicable to milligrams of sugar in your coffee (very difficult to distinguish)
                    or to similar shades of gray paint on the wall of a room. You might not be able to distinguish one
                    milligram more of sugar in your coffee (a slightly darker gray color on your office walls, respectively),
                    but you can probably detect when your coffee is becoming too sweet (or your office is nearly pitch
                    black!).
8                                                                                              Chapter 1



       Alternatives a and b are, of course, the same. This is indeed detected by most
    students who claim to be indifferent between alternatives a and b (i.e., a ~ b), when
    they are asked to state their preference for one of two alternatives. Moreover most
    students strictly prefer alternative b to c (i.e., b ≻ c). By transitivity, we should there-
    fore expect the students who gave these responses to strictly prefer alternative a to c
    when asked to compare these two options. While most students exhibit transitive pref-
    erences in their choices, as they strictly prefer a to c, about 25 percent of students who
    respond that they strictly prefer alternative c to a show an intransitive preference rela-
    tion, as may be induced by the way in which the options were presented (framed) to
    them.10 ■

    Example 1.4: Aggregation of criteria In some cases several individual preferences
    may be aggregated into one. In these situations we might find that the resulting prefer-
    ence relation violates transitivity. Let us consider the set of possible alternatives X that
    contains three universities to which you were admitted: Massachusetts Institute of
    Technology (MIT), Washington State University (WSU), and your home state univer-
    sity. In considering which university to attend, you might compare them according
    to different criteria, which we can represent as different preference relations ≻1, ≻2,
    and ≻3, and which we will treat as strict preferences for simplicity. First, if you only
    consider academic prestige, some students could exhibit the following ranking:

                                    1: MIT 1 WSU 1 Home Univ.
    Second, in considering the city size or congestion, your comparison could be

                                   2 : WSU 2 Home Univ. 2 MIT .
    Third, in considering the proximity of the university to your family and friends, a rea-
    sonable comparison would be the following (unless you live in Boston!):

                                   3 : Home Univ. 3 MIT 3 WSU .
      We must now aggregate all of these considerations (e.g., using majority rule). We
    do so by making all possible pairwise comparisons and checking, for each pair, which
    university wins according to most of the criteria described above. When comparing

    have picked answers at random, and the intransitivities reported could not be necessarily attributed
    to a lack of consistency in a student’s preferences.

                    MIT and WSU, the former wins according to criteria 1 and 3, that is, MIT ≻1,3 WSU.
                    When comparing WSU and your home university, the former beats the latter accord-
                    ing to criteria 1 and 2, that is, WSU ≻1,2 Home Univ. Finally, comparing your home
                    university with MIT, the former wins against the latter according to criteria 2 and 3,
                    that is, Home Univ. ≻2,3 MIT. However, this resulting preference relation violates
                    transitivity. Indeed we created a cycle:

                                               MIT 1,3 WSU 1,2 Home Univ. 2,3 MIT .
                       A similar argument can be used for the aggregation of individual preferences in
                    group decision making, where every person in the group has a transitive preference
                    relation but the group preferences (aggregated from these individual preferences) are
                    not necessarily transitive. This is called the “Condorcet paradox,” and it is extensively
                    studied in social choice problems. For instance, for three government programs (e.g.,
                    building a bridge, a library, or a military plane) individual 1 prefers B ≻1 L ≻1 P, indi-
                    vidual 2 prefers L ≻2 P ≻2 B, and individual 3 prefers P ≻3 B ≻3 L. Aggregating their
                    preferences according to majority rule yields the cycle

                                                           B ≿1,3 L ≿1,2 P ≿2,3 B.

                      As a consequence the individual controlling the agenda (i.e., the order in which
                    options B, L, and P are pairwise voted) can guarantee that his preferred alternative
                    wins. For example, if individual 3 sets the agenda, he can design the voting agenda
                    so that alternative P wins.11 A similar argument applies for individual 1 (who could
                    guarantee that B wins by having an initial vote between L and P) and for individual
                    2 (who could ensure that L wins by having P and B confronted first). ■

                    goods that create a strong dependency or that become addictive. For instance, when an
                    individual starts smoking, his cigarette preferences might be: One cigarette ≻ No
                    smoking ≻ Smoking heavily. Hence, by the definition of transitivity, he should prefer
                    one cigarette to smoking heavily. However, after this individual has been smoking for

                    Since B emerges the winner in the first round of votes (when B competes against L), it is then

     1.2    Utility Function

     After describing the main assumptions behind a rational preference relation, we are
     ready to define a utility function.


          Utility function A function u : X → ℝ from the set of alternatives to the set
          of real numbers is a utility function representing a preference relation ≿ if, for
          every pair of alternatives x, y ∈ X,

                                      x ≿y is equivalent to u(x) ≥ u(y).

        Let us emphasize two points in this definition. First, only the ranking of
     alternatives matters. Indeed, a utility function u(x) yielding utility levels u(x) = 14
     and u(y) = 10 provides the same ranking of alternatives x and y as utility function
     u1(·), where u1(x) = 2000 and u1(y) = 3, since both utility functions rank alternative x
     above alternative y. Hence the individual does not care about cardinality (the number
     that the utility function associates with each alternative) but instead cares about ordi-
     nality (the ranking of utility values among alternatives). Second, if we apply any
     strictly increasing function f (∙) on the utility function u(x), that is, v(x) = f(u(x)), the
     new function keeps the ranking of alternatives intact, and therefore the new function
     still represents the same preference relation.13

     12
       This case has been criticized as a real form of intransitivity, since in each time period the individual
     decision maker could be regarded as a different individual who states his preferences over alternatives.
     Hence we will only refer to the first three types of intransitivity.
     13
        For instance, v(x) = 3u(x), or v(x) = 5u(x) + 8 are examples of strictly increasing functions applied
     to the original utility function u(x) and representing the same preference relation as u(x), since they
     all maintain the same ranking of utility values associated to every pair of alternatives x, y ∈ X. For
     more examples on transformations of an original utility function u(x), and testing whether they
     constitute monotonic transformations that represent the same preference relation as u(x) does, see
     exercise 8 at the end of the chapter.

                    1.3     Desirability

                    We can compare the desirability of two bundles in different ways, as we next describe.
                    In our subsequent definitions, we consider that x is an N-dimensional bundle, x ∈ ℝN,
                    that is, x = (x1, x2, … , xN), where its kth component represents the amount of good (or
                    service) k, xk ∈ ℝ.

                          Monotonicity A preference relation satisfies monotonicity if, for any two
                          bundles x, y ∈ X, where x ≠ y,
                          xk ≥ yk for every good k, implies x ≿ y, and
                          xk > yk for every good k, implies x ≻ y.


                    That is, increasing the amounts of some commodities (without reducing the amount of
                    any other commodity) cannot hurt, x ≿ y; and increasing the amounts of all commodi-
                    ties is strictly preferred, x ≻ y.


                          Strong monotonicity A preference relation satisfies strong monotonicity if,
                          for any two bundles x, y ∈X, where x ≠ y, and xk ≥ yk for every good k, we have
                          that x ≻ y.


                       In particular, under monotonic preferences, we can increase the amount of all
                    but one of the goods, making the consumer indifferent between his new and old
                    bundles. Only if we increase the amounts of all goods can we be sure that the indi-
                    vidual strictly prefers the new to the old bundle. However, under strongly monotonic
                    preferences, if we increase the amount of only one commodity, the individual is made
                    strictly better off. Note that this is not necessarily true if this individual’s preferences
                    satisfy monotonicity.
                       The two definitions above exhibit a connection between preference relations and the
                    utility function representing them. In particular, monotonicity in preferences implies
                    that the utility function is weakly increasing in its arguments. That is, if we increase
                    some of its arguments, the value of the utility function weakly increases, whereas if we
                    increase all of its arguments, the value of the utility function strictly increases. More
                    formally, for a common factor α > 1, monotonicity in preferences implies that

                                           u(αx1, x2) ≥ u(x1, x2)   and u(αx1, αx2) > u(x1, x2),
12                                                                                             Chapter 1



     where α >1 indicates that we increase the amount of each good by a common factor α.
     However, strong monotonicity in preferences implies that the utility function is strictly
     increasing in all its arguments. That is, if we increase some of its arguments (even only
     one argument), the value of the utility function strictly increases. More formally, strong
     monotonicity in preferences implies that for α > 1,
                                           u(αx1, x2) > u(x1, x2),

     where we have only increased the amount of one of the goods, x1. Let us check if the
     following utility functions represent an underlying preference relation that satisfies
     monotonicity alone or strong monotonicity.

     Example 1.5: u(x1, x2) = min{ax1, bx2}, where a, b > 0, representing that goods 1
     and 2 are regarded as perfect complements The preference relation represented
     by this utility function satisfies monotonicity, since, if we increase all arguments by a
     common factor δ > 0, we obtain min{ax1 + δ, bx2 + δ}, which is larger than min{ax1,
     bx2} for any positive δ. However, this result does not satisfy strong monotonicity,
     since, if we increase one argument alone (e.g., the amount of good 1 consumed), we
     obtain min{ax1 + δ, bx2}, which is not necessarily larger than min{ax1, bx2}. (This
     happens, for instance, when min{ax1, bx2} = bx2, since in this case the utility level is
     unaffected if we increase the amount of good 1 without simultaneously increasing
     the amount of good 2.) ■

     Example 1.6: u(x1, x2) = ax1 + bx2, where a, b > 0, which denotes that this indi-
     vidual regards good 1 and 2 as perfect substitutes The preference relation
     represented by this utility function satisfies monotonicity, since, if we increase all ar-
     guments, we obtain (ax1 + δ) + (bx2 + δ), which is larger than ax1 + bx2 for any positive
     δ. It also satisfies strong monotonicity, since, if we increase one argument alone (e.g.,
     the amount of good 1), we obtain (ax1 + δ) + bx2, which exceeds ax1 + bx2. ■

     Combining our results in examples 1.4 and 1.5, we can see that a preference relation
     that satisfies strong monotonicity, such as that in example 1.5, must also satisfy mono-
     tonicity, but the opposite is not necessarily true: a preference relation that satisfies
     monotonicity, such as that in example 1.4, does not necessarily satisfy strong monoto-
     nicity; that is,
                               Strong monotonicity →
                                                   / Monotonicity .
                                                   ←
                                                                    14



     14
        For more examples of preference relations satisfying or violating monotonicity, see exercise 1 at
     the end of this chapter.
Preferences and Utility                                                                                         13



                      In addition to monotonicity and strong monotonicity, we can express the desirability
                    of a consumption bundle using other measures, such as nonsatiation and local
                    nonsatiation, which we present below.

                          Nonsatiation A preference relation satisfies nonsatiation (NS) if, for every
                          bundle x ∈ X, we can find another bundle y ∈ X that is strictly preferred to x, and
                          we write this as y ≻ x.


                       Intuitively, NS implies that the individual never reaches a bliss point at bundle x
                    because he can find another consumption bundle y that he finds strictly preferred to his
                    current bundle x. This notion of desirability is, however, too general, since we could
                    think about a bundle y containing extremely larger amounts of some goods than x. For
                    a more restricted version, the following definition bounds this “search” for a strictly
                    preferred bundle y to those bundles that lie relatively close to our initial bundle x. In
                    particular, bundle y must be an ε away from bundle x, for every value of ε. Graphi-
                    cally, this entails that we find a bundle preferred to x, regardless of how close we need
                    to search around x.

                          Local nonsatiation A preference relation satisfies local nonsatiation (LNS) if,
                          for every bundle x ∈ X, we can find another bundle y ∈ X that is strictly preferred
                          to x, y ≻ x, and where y is less than ε-away from x, ||y − x|| < ε for every ε > 0.


                       First note that, as figure 1.1 illustrates, ||y − x|| represents the Euclidean distance
                    between x and y when bundles x and y are in ℝ2. Therefore LNS implies that, for
                    every bundle x, and for every distance ε > 0 from x, we can find a more preferred
                    bundle y.
                       In figure 1.1 the individual decision maker prefers bundle y to x even if bundle
                    y contains less of good 2 (but more of good 1) than bundle x. Also LNS allows
                    for the possibility that an individual decision maker with an initial bundle x might
                    prefer a bundle y that contains less of both good 1 and 2 than x does, as figure 1.2
                    depicts.
                       LNS, however, rules out that the possibility that the decision maker regards all goods
                    as bad for the whole range of x1 and x2. If, in contrast, the decision maker regarded
                    goods 1 and 2 as bads regardless of their level at bundle x, then we could have a situa-
                    tion like that represented in figure 1.3, where bundle y is strictly preferred to x but y is
                    unfeasible given that it lies outside the consumption set, meaning y ∉  2+ . In such a

                       Furthermore LNS rules out “thick” indifference sets, as figure 1.4 illustrates. In such

     1.4     Indifference Sets, Upper Contour Sets, and Lower Contour Sets

     1.4.1    Indifference Set
     While describing different notions of desirability, we made use of the concept of
     “indifference set.” Let us next define this set more formally. The indifference set of a
     bundle x ∈ X is the collection of all other bundles in set X, y ∈ X, such that y ~ x. More
     formally, we can write the indifference set of bundle x as
                                     IND( x ) = { y ∈ X : y ~ x} .

     The upper contour set of bundle x is the set of all bundles y ∈ X that are weakly
     preferred to bundle x, that is,
                                    UCS ( x ) = { y ∈ X : y  x}.

     The lower contour set of bundle x is the set of all bundles y ∈ X for which bundle x is
     weakly preferred to all other bundles, which we write as

                                    LCS ( x ) = { y ∈ X : x  y}.
     Figure 1.5 depicts examples of IND, UCS, and LCS sets where bundle x lies in  2+ .

     1.4.2   Strong Monotonicity and IND
     Connecting our current discussion of indifference sets with our previous analysis of
     desirability, we next show that if a preference relation satisfies strong monotonicity, its




     Figure 1.5
     UCS, LCS, and LCS sets
Preferences and Utility                                                                                      17



                    indifference curves must be downward sloping. To see this, consider a bundle x ∈X. By
                    strong monotonicity, other bundles y ∈X, where y ≠ x, that contain strictly more of all
                    goods than bundle x does, that is, y >> x, must be strictly preferred to x, y ≻ x, thus
                    implying that y ∉IND(x). Similarly bundles z ∈X, where z ≠ x, containing strictly less
                    of every good than bundle x does, that is, z << x, must satisfy z ≺ x, thus entailing that
                    z ∉IND(x). As depicted in figure 1.6 for a given bundle x ∈  2+ , bundles satisfying y >>
                    x lie to the northeast of x and bundles satisfying z << x lie to the southwest of x. Since
                    the indifference set IND(x) cannot lie on either of these regions by strong monotonic-
                    ity, the only regions where IND(x) can lie are regions A and B, which yield a downward-
                    sloping indifference curve passing through x. Alternatively, for indifference curves to
                    be upward sloping, the preferences cannot satisfy strong monotonicity, but they can
                    satisfy a milder form of desirability such as local nonsatiation.

                    1.5     Convexity of Preferences

                    Let us next define convexity in a preference relation. We use two equivalent definitions.


                          Convexity 1 A preference relation satisfies convexity if, for any two bundles x,
                          y ∈ X,

                                       x ≿ y implies that αx + (1 − α) y ≿ y for all α ∈ (0, 1).




                    Figure 1.6
                    Strong monotonicity and IND(x)
18                                                                                                 Chapter 1



     Intuitively, the convex combination of bundles x and y is weakly preferred to bundle
     y alone. Figure 1.7a depicts a convex preference relation where, for simplicity, bundle
     x lies in the upper-contour set of bundle y, x ∈ UCS(y).15


          Convexity 2 A preference relation satisfies convexity if, for every bundle x, its
          upper contour set, UCS(x) = {y ∈ X : y}≿ x}, is convex.


     In words, for every two bundles y and z weakly preferred to x, y ≿ x and z ≿ x
     (which then belong to the UCS of x, as figure 1.7b illustrates), their convex combina-
     tion αy + (1− α)z is also weakly preferred to x:

                                  αy + (1− α)z  x       for any α ∈(0, 1) .

     As a consequence the convex combination of bundles y and z also belongs to UCS(x).
     Graphically, convexity in the preference relation implies that the UCS is a convex set,
     and that indifference curves are bowed in toward the origin. If, in contrast, a preference
     relation violates convexity, the indifference curves are bowed away from the origin.

          Strict convexity A preference relation satisfies strict convexity if, for every
          two bundles x and y weakly preferred to z, that is, for all x, y ∈ X, where x ≠ y such
          that x ≿ z and y ≿ z, their convex combination αx + (1 − α)y, where α ∈ (0, 1), is
          strictly preferred to bundle z.


        Figure 1.8 illustrates a preference relation that satisfies strict convexity. Note that
     when bundles x and y lie on both the UCS and the IND, the definition of strict convex-
     ity is satisfied because the convex combination of these two bundles lies strictly inside
     the UCS, thus implying αx + (1 − α)y ≻ z.
        Figure 1.9, in contrast, illustrates a preference relation that satisfies convexity but
     not strict convexity. Since the convex combination of bundles x and y lies strictly on
     the indifference curve, their convex combination therefore produces a bundle αx +
     (1 − α)y that the consumer regards as indifferent to bundle z. (This preference relation

     Convexity can be intuitively understood according to two different interpretations.

                    the consumer needs to receive increasingly larger amounts of good 1 in order to accept
                    further reductions of good 2. Figure 1.10b depicts this property. Note that, starting
                    from point A where the individual consumes a large amount of good 2, a given reduc-

                    amount of good 1 (point B). When the individual consumes small amounts of good 2
                    (point C), however, the same one unit reduction in the amount of good 2 leaves this
                    consumer’s utility unaffected provided that the amount of good 1 is significantly in-
                    creased (point D). Alternatively, since the MRS represents the slope of the indifference
                    curve, a diminishing MRS implies a diminishing slope of the indifference curve, as
                    illustrated in figure 1.10b.

                    1.7   Quasi-Concavity

                    A utility function u(·) is quasi-concave if, for every bundle x, the set of all bundles for
                    which the consumer experiences a higher utility, that is, UCS(x) = {y ∈ X | u(y) ≥ u(x)},
                    is convex. Hence the following three properties are equivalent:

                           Convexity of preferences ⇔ UCS(x) is convex ⇔ u(·) is quasi-concave.

                       Alternatively, quasi-concavity can be understood as follows: for every two bundles
                    x, y ∈X, the utility of consuming the convex combination of these two bundles, u(αx +
24                                                                                     Chapter 1



     (1 − α)y), is weakly higher than the minimal utility from consuming each bundle
     separately, min{u(x), u(y)}; or more compactly,

                               u(αx + (1 −α)y) ≥ min{u ( x ) , u( y )}.
        Figure 1.11 illustrates the definition above. In particular, starting from bundles x and
     y, with associated utility levels u(x) and u(y), respectively, we can construct a convex
     combination of the two bundles. If the utility that the consumer derives from consum-
     ing this convex combination is larger than from consuming the bundle associated to
     the lowest utility level (which in this case is bundle y), we say that this individual’s
     utility function satisfies quasi-concavity.

     1.7.1   Strict Quasi-Concavity
     A utility function u(·) satisfies strict quasi-concavity if, for every two bundles x, y ∈X,
     the utility of consuming its convex combination, u(αx + (1 − α)y), where 0 < α < 1,
     is strictly higher than the minimal utility from consuming each bundle separately,
     min{u(x), u(y)}.
        Hence the utility function that yields the indifference curves in figure 1.11 satisfies
     strict quasi-concavity. A natural question at this point is whether we can check for the
     presence of quasi-concavity by selecting a bundle x that lies on the same indifference

                    curves are strictly convex (i.e., bowed-in toward the origin), a convex combination of

                    1.7.2     Concavity and Quasi-Concavity
                    Let us now examine the relationship between concavity and quasi-concavity of a util-
                    ity function. Interestingly, concavity implies quasi-concavity, as we show next, but the
                    converse relation is not necessarily true. That is,
                                                        Concavity →
                                                                  / Quasi-concavity
                                                                  ←

                       Hence quasi-concavity is a weaker condition than concavity. In particular, if a func-
                    tion f is concave, it must also be quasi-concave, that is, for any two points x, y ∈X,

                          f (α x + (1 − α ) y ) ≥ α f ( x ) + (1 − α ) f ( y ) ≥ min { f ( x ) , f ( y )} for all α ∈( 0, 1) ,
                    where the first inequality follows from the definition of concavity, and the second
                    holds true for all concave functions, as depicted in figure 1.13. From the first and third
                    element in the above inequality, we obtain that f(αx + (1 − α)y) ≥ min{f(x), f(y)}, which

     coincides with the definition of quasi-concavity. As a consequence concavity implies
     quasi-concavity.
        Let us next elaborate on the distinction between the two properties. In particular, a
     concave utility function implies that, for an increase in the consumption bundle, the
     increase in utility is smaller as we move away from the origin, meaning it exhibits
     diminishing marginal utility. Graphically, an increase in the amount of goods 1 and 2
     implies that the “jump” from one indifference curve to another is initially achieved by
     slightly increasing x1 and x2 (when we are close to the origin), but this becomes more
     difficult (i.e., requires more significant increases in the amount of goods 1 and 2) as we
     get further away from the origin. Figure 1.14a represents in 3D a Cobb–Douglas util-
     ity function u( x1 , x2 ) = x11 4 x12 4 that increases in both arguments but at a decreasing rate
     (i.e., satisfying the definition of concavity).
        Figure 1.14b shows the level sets of this utility function (2D projection of figure
     1.14a) where the regions of goods 1 and 2 reach the same height in figure 1.14a as the
     contour lines in a topographic map, and shows that bundles reach the same height.
     Hence these level sets represent the individual’s indifference curves, since they are
     combinations of (x1, x2) that yield the same utility level. As we see, for any given
     bundle x on an indifference curve, the associated UCS(x) of this bundle is a convex set,

     their different mathematical properties. Importantly, both utility functions are quasi-
     concave, although one of them is concave and the other is convex. For this reason we
     normally require utility functions to satisfy quasi-concavity alone.19

                    units of good 1, whereas the opposite argument applies to region B, which contains
                    bundles with more units of good 1 but fewer units of good 2. Importantly, according
                    to this preference relation, the consumer cannot compare bundles in either of these
                    regions against bundle (2, 1), since, for him to be able to rank one bundle against
                    another, one of the bundles must contain weakly more units of all goods.

                    The preference relation is not complete. Recall that completeness requires that, for
                    every pair x and y, either x ≿ y or y ≿ x (or both). To see why this property does not
                    hold, consider two bundles x, y ∈  2+ with bundle x containing more units of good 1
                    than bundle y but fewer units of good 2, meaning x1 > y1 for good 1 but x2 < y2 for
                    good 2 as in region B of figure 1.16. Then we have neither that x ≿ y (since for that
                    we would need x1 ≥ y1 and x2 ≥ y2, as in the UCS region of figure 1.16) nor y ≿ x (for
                    that we would need y1 ≥ x1 and y2 ≥ x2, as in the LCS region of figure 1.16). In words,
                    this preference relation does not help us compare bundle (2, 1) against any bundle in
                    region B.

                    The preference relation is transitive. Recall that transitivity requires that, for any three
                    bundles x, y, and z, if x ≿ y and y ≿ z, then x ≿ z. Now x ≿ y and y ≿ z means that
32                                                                                                Chapter 1



     xk ≥ yk and yk ≥ zk, for every good k.21 By transitivity of the “greater or equal than”
     symbol ≥ we thus have xk ≥ zk for every good k, and so x ≥ z (i.e., bundle x is weakly
     larger than bundle z in every component). As a consequence, x ≿ z holds, as required.

     The preference relation is strongly monotone. Recall that the property of strong mono-
     tonicity requires that, if we increase one of the goods in a given bundle, then the
     newly created bundle must be strictly preferred to the original bundle. More com-
     pactly, for a given bundle y, if bundle x satisfies
                                       x ≥ y and x ≠ y, then x  y .

     Recall that x ≥ y denotes, in vector notation, that bundle x contains weakly larger
     amounts than bundle y in every component. Hence x ≥ y and x ≠ y imply that xk ≥ yk for
     every good k and that xl > yl for at least one good l (otherwise, the two bundles would
     be the same). Thus x ≥ y, and x ≠ y implies, for this preference relation, that
                                            x  y and not y  x .

     In words, bundle x being weakly larger than y in all components (but being strictly
     larger in at least one component) implies that bundle x is weakly preferred to y, and
     that bundle y is not weakly preferred to bundle x. We can therefore conclude that x is
     strictly preferred to y, x ≻ y, as required for strong monotonicity.

     The preference relation is strictly convex. Recall that strict convexity requires that if x
     ≿ z and y ≿ z and x ≠ z, then the convex combination of bundles x and y, αx + (1 − α)y
     is strictly preferred to z,

                    1.8     Common Utility Functions in Economics

                    In this section we briefly list some of the typical utility functions used in economic
                    applications and their functional form.

                    1.8.1   Cobb–Douglas Utility Functions
                    In the case of two goods, x1 and x2, u ( x1, x2 ) = Ax1α x2β , where A, α, β > 0. Alternatively,
                    we can apply logs on both sides, and obtain log u = log A + α log x1 + β log x2. Hence
                    the exponents in the original utility function can be interpreted as elasticities, since,
                                                     ∂u ( x1 , x2 )      x1                        x
                                        ε u , x1 =                                = α Ax1α −1 x2β α1 β = α .
                                                         ∂x1        u ( x1 , x2 )                Ax1 x2
34                                                                                         Chapter 1



        Intuitively, an increase of 1 percent in the amount of good x1 increases individual
     utility by α percent. A similar interpretation applies to ε u, x2 = β . Special cases are those
     in which α + β = 1, such as u ( x1, x2 ) = Ax1α x21−α , or those in which A = 1, such as
     u ( x1, x2 ) = x1α x2β . (The case where A = α = β = 1 can also be interpreted as a special case
     of a Cobb–Douglas utility function where u(x1, x2) = x1x2) Besides yielding positive
     marginal utilities for all goods, whereby ∂u/∂x1 > 0 and ∂u/∂x2 > 0, and thus satisfying
     strong monotonicity, the Cobb–Douglas utility function yields a diminishing MRS,
     since
                                                     α Ax1α −1 x2β       α x2
                                     MRS x1 , x2 =                   =
                                                     β Ax1α x2β −1       β x1

     is clearly decreasing in x1. Hence indifference curves become flatter as x1 increases
     (i.e., as we move rightward on the horizontal axis). Graphically, indifference curves
     are therefore bowed in toward the origin, as figure 1.17 shows.
        As previously described, individuals with Cobb–Douglas preferences are willing to
     give up many units of x2 in order to increase their consumption of x1 by one unit when
     they do not enjoy many units of x1 (movement from point A to B in the figure), but such
     willingness to give up units of x2 to obtain one more unit of x1 decreases as x1 becomes
     relatively abundant (movement from point C to D).

     1.8.2   Perfect Substitutes
     This utility function is strictly linear in both goods u(x1, x2) = ax1 + bx2, where a,
     b > 0. As a consequence the marginal utility of every good is constant, that is, ∂u/∂x1 =




     Figure 1.17
     Cobb–Douglas preference
Preferences and Utility                                                                                    35

                    Perfect substitutes


                    a for all x1, and similarly ∂u/∂x2 = b for all x2. The MRS is also constant, since
                    MRS x1 , x2 = a b does not depend on the amount of goods 1 or 2. Therefore indifference
                    curves are straight lines with a slope of −a/b, as depicted in figure 1.18.
                      Intuitively, the individual is willing to give up a/b units of x2 in order to obtain one
                    more unit of x1 and keep his utility level unaffected. Such willingness is, unlike in the
                    Cobb–Douglas case, independent in the relative abundance of the two goods. Typical
                    examples include goods such as butter and margarine, coffee, and black tea, or two
                    brands of unflavored mineral water.

                    1.8.3   Perfect Complements
                    In this case the utility function is u(x1, x2) = A min{αx1, βx2}, where A, α, B > 0.
                    Intuitively, increasing one of the goods without increasing the amount of the other good
                    entails no increase in utility, which only goes up if the amounts of both goods increase
                    (although they do not need to increase by the same amount). In addition the indifference
                    curves of this utility function form right angles with a kink at αx1 = βx2, which, after
                    rearranging, yields ray x2 = αx1/β from the origin, as depicted in figure 1.19.
                       The slope of such a ray, α/β, indicates the rate at which goods x1 and x2 must be
                    consumed in order to achieve utility gains. For instance, if α = 2 and β = 1, the indi-
                    vidual must consume two units of x1 for every unit of x2. Note that some applications
                    assume that both goods are consumed in the same proportion, meaning α = β, thus
                    yielding u(x1, x2) = A·min{αx1, αx2}, which simplifies to u(x1, x2) = Aα min{x1, x2}, or
                    B min{x1, x2} if we define B ≡ Aα. Typical examples of goods regarded as comple-
                    ments include those that are consumed in fixed proportions, such as cars and gasoline,
                    or peanut butter and jelly.

                    1.8.5   Quasi-linear Utility Function
                    This utility function has some goods entering linearly while others enter nonlinearly.
                    In the case of two goods, x1 and x2, u(x1, x2) = v(x1) + bx2, where x2 enters linearly, b >
                    0, and v(x1) is a nonlinear function of x1. For instance, v(x1) = a ln x1 or v ( x1 ) = ax1α ,
                    where a > 0 and α ≠ 1 (e.g., v ( x1 ) = 5 x1 , v(x1) = lnx1, or v ( x1 ) = 3x12 ).
                       The MRS of such functions is constant in the good that enters linearly in the utility
                    function. In other words, for a given level of good 1, an increase in the amounts of
                    good 2 (the desirable good that enters linearly) does not affect the slope of the indiffer-

                    1.9     Properties of Preference Relations

                    1.9.1     Homogeneity


                          Homogeneity A utility function is homogeneous of degree k if varying the
                          amounts of all goods by a common factor α > 0 produces an increase in the util-
                          ity level by αk.


                    That is, for the case of two goods,

                                                        u(αx1, αx2) = αku(x1, x2),

                    where α > 0 allows for a common increase in all goods (if α > 1), or a common de-
                    crease (if 0 < α < 1). This function exhibits three properties that we often use:
                    1. First, the first-order derivative of a function u(x1, x2), which is homogeneous of
                       degree k, is homogeneous of degree k − 1. In particular, by homogeneity of degree
                       k, u(αx1, αx2) = αku(x1, x2). Differentiating with respect to xi for i = {1, 2} yields
                                                   ∂u (α x1, α x2 )           ∂u ( x1, x2 )
                                                                    ⋅α = αk ⋅               ,
                                                        ∂xi                       ∂xi

                          and after rearranging,

                                                     u ′ (α x1, α x2 ) = α k −1u ′ ( x1, x2 ) .
                          Therefore u′(x1, x2) is homogeneous of degree k − 1.
                    2. Indifference curves of a homogeneous utility function are radial expansions of
                       one another. That is, if two bundles y and z lie on the same indifference curve, that
                       is, u(y) = u(z), bundles αy and αz also lie on the same indifference curve, that is,
                       u(αy) = u(αz), as depicted in figure 1.22. For bundle y, we have u(αy) = αku(y), and
                       similarly for bundle z, which yields u(αy) = αku(y) = u(αz) = αku(z), meaning u(αy)
                       = u(αz), as required.

                    3. The MRS of a homogeneous function is constant for all points along each ray from

                       slope at the “scaled-up version” of x, αx. Since the MRS at bundle x = (x1, x2) is

      We can alternatively define homotheticity in the preference relation as we do next,
     which is a corollary of the definition of homotheticity.

     Homotheticity (a graphical interpretation) A preference relation on X =  +N is ho-
     mothetic if all indifference sets are related to proportional expansions along the rays.
     That is, if the consumer is indifferent between bundles x and y, meaning x ~ y, he must
     also be indifferent between a common scaling in these two bundles, meaning αx ~
     αy, for every scalar α ≥ 0. Figure 1.22 illustrates this property. Starting from bundles x
     and y on the same indifference curve u1 (where, by definition, the consumer is indiffer-
     ent between them), the scaling up of bundle x, αx, and of bundle y, αy, lie on a indif-
     ference curve associated to a higher utility level, and both points still lie on the same
     indifference curve, u2, entailing that the consumer is indifferent between αx and αy.
     Hence, for a given ratio of x1 and x2, x1/x2, the slope of the indifference curve (i.e., the
     MRS) is constant. Graphically, for a given ray from the origin—where the ratio be-
     tween the two goods x1/x2 remains constant along all points in the ray—the slope of the
     indifference curves that the ray crosses coincides. Intuitively, the rate at which a con-
     sumer is willing to substitute one good for another (his MRS) only depends on the rate
     at which he consumes the two goods, namely x1/x2, but does not depend on the volume
     of goods he consumes, nor on the utility level he obtains (the indifference curve he
     reaches).

     1.9.3   Relationship between Homogeneity and Homotheticity
     Homogeneous utility functions represent homothetic preference relations; that is, we
     only need to apply a monotonic transformation g(·) on v(x1, x2), which we write as u(x1,
     x2) = g(v(x1, x2)). In contrast, homothetic preference relations are not necessarily repre-
     sented with homogeneous utility functions. In short, homogeneity implies homothetic
     preferences, but the converse is not necessarily true. We next show that homotheticity
     does not imply homogeneity.

     Proof We only need to find an example of a function that, despite being homothetic,
     is not homogeneous. Consider a homothetic function such as v(x1, x2) = x1, x2. This is a
     Cobb–Douglas utility function, and it is homogeneous of degree 2, since
Preferences and Utility                                                                                                  43




                                         v (α x1, α x2 ) = (α x1 )(α x2 ) = α 2 ( x1 x2 ) = α 2 v ( x1, x2 ) .
                      Consider a monotonic transformation g(y) = y + a, where a > 0, which together with
                    the homogeneous function v(x1, x2) = x1x2 yields u(x1, x2) = x1x2 + a. Such a function is
                    not homogeneous, since a scaling of all its arguments by α produces

                                           u (α x1, α x2 ) = (α x1 )(α x2 ) + a = α 2 v ( x1, x2 ) + a.
                    That is, u(αx1, αx2) cannot be reduced to a product of αk times u(x1, x2), as required for
                    homogeneity to hold. We can easily find other monotonic transformations yielding
                    similar (nonhomogeneous) utility functions, such as g(y) = αxγ + by, where a, b, γ > 0,
                    or g(y) = α ln y, where a > 0. ■

                    You can easily check that linear utility functions u(x1, x2) = αx1 + bx2, where a, b > 0,
                    meaning goods x1 and x2 are perfect substitutes, and the Leontief utility function u(x1,
                    x2) = A min{αx1 + bx2}, where A > 0, meaning goods x1 and x2 are perfect complements,
                    both satisfy homotheticity, and their MRS(x1, x2) coincide with MRS(αx1, αx2). In par-
                    ticular, for perfect substitutes we have that
                                                               a                                       aα a
                                         MRS ( x1. x2 ) =            and      MRS (tx1, tx2 ) =          = .
                                                               b                                       bα b

                    And for perfect complements, while we cannot define the MRS along all the points of
                    the indifference curves, we can check that their slopes at the point in which they are
                    crossed by a ray from the origin coincides, as depicted in figure 1.23.
                      The next example checks whether Cobb–Douglas utility satisfies homotheticity and
                    quasi-concavity.

     1.9.4   Quasi-linear Preference Relations
     The preference relation on X = (−∞, ∞) ×  +L−1 is quasi-linear with respect to good 1
     (often referred to as the numeraire) if
     1. all indifference sets are parallel displacements of each other along the axis of good
        1, that is,

                 if x ~ y, then (x + αe1) ~ (y + αe1), where e1 = (1, 0, ..., 0); and

     2. good 1 is desirable, that is, x + αe1 ≻ x for all x and α > 0.
        Intuitively, the first condition simply states that if two bundles lie on the same in-
     difference curve, then, if we increase the amount of the first good contained in both
     bundles, the newly created bundles must also lie on the same indifference curve (e.g.,
     if α = 1, we would be adding one unit of good 1 to both bundles). The second condi-
     tion states that if we increase the amount of the first good in bundle x, the newly
Preferences and Utility                                                                                                   45



                    created bundle must be strictly preferred to the original bundle x. These conditions
                    are illustrated in figure 1.24a.24
                       Last, note an implication of the two conditions above. In particular, if bundle x is
                    strictly preferred to bundle y, x ≻ y, and we increase the amount of good 1 in both
                    bundles x and y, it must be that the enlarged bundle x, x + αe1, is still preferred to the
                    enlarged bundle y, y + αe1, meaning x + αe1 ≻ y + αe1. This property is depicted in
                    figure 1.24b.25
                       Recall that a quasi-linear utility functions are given by u(x, y) = v(x) + by, where y
                    denotes the desirable good (which enters linearly), b > 0, and v(x) is a nonlinear func-
                    tion of x, such as v(x) = x2 or v(x) = x1/2 or v(x) = ln x. This quasi-linear utility function
                    is easily generalizable to N > 2 goods. For instance, for three goods, x, y, and z, we
                    would write u(x, y, z) = v(x, y) + bz, where z denotes the desirable good, and v(x, y) is
                    a nonlinear function of goods x and y.

                    1.9.5    Lexicographic Preferences
                    Thus far we examined properties behind preference relations and particular types of
                    utility functions. However, we have not analyzed under which conditions we can guar-
                    antee that a preference relation can be represented with a utility function. Specifically,
                    the assumptions considered so far are not enough to guarantee that a preference
                    relation can be represented with a utility function. A classic example of a preference
                    relation that cannot be represented by a utility function is the so-called lexicographic
                    preference relation, which we discuss next.

                    Lexicographic preferences A bundle x = (x1, x2) is weakly preferred to another bun-
                    dle y = (y1, y2) which we write as (x1, x2) ≿ (y1, y2), if and only if,

                                                                x1 > y1 , or if
                                                           
                                                            x1 = y1 and x2 > y2 .

                      Intuitively, this preference relation works like alphabetizing a dictionary. First the
                    individual prefers bundle x if it contains more units of good 1 than bundle y, that is,

                    reach a higher/lower utility level than the original bundle x, as long as it reaches a strictly lower
                    utility level than the enlarged bundle x + αe1.

                    x1 > y1. If, however, both bundles contain the same amount of good 1, x1 = y1, then the
                    individual prefers the bundle that contains more units of the second good, x2 > y2.
                       One important characteristic of this preference relation is that its indifference set
                    cannot be drawn as an indifference curve. That is, for a given bundle x′, there are no
                    more bundles for which the consumer is indifferent, since each indifference set con-
                    tains a single bundle (it is singleton). Let us examine this property by identifying the
                    upper contour set, lower contour set, and the indifference set of a given bundle x′, as
                    figure 1.25 depicts.
                       First, the upper contour set of bundle x′, UCS(x′), is the set of bundles containing
                    more of good 1 and those bundles that, containing the same amount of good 1, have
                    more of good 2. Graphically, UCS(x′) includes those bundles strictly to the right-hand
                    side of x′ (with strictly larger amounts of good 1), and those that lie in the shaded ver-
                    tical line above x′ (which contain the same amount of good 1 as x′ does, but more of
                    good 2). Similarly the lower contour set, LCS(x′), is defined by those bundles that con-
                    tain less of good 1 and those that, containing the same amount of good 1, have less of
                    good 2. Graphically, LCS(x′) includes those bundles strictly to the left-hand side of x′
                    and those that lie in the dashed vertical line below x′ (which contains the same amount
                    of good 1 as x′ does, but less of good 2). Hence the UCS(x′) and LCS(x′) span all the
                    positive quadrant, leaving no room for the indifference set of bundle x′, other than
