     bundle x′ itself. As a consequence we say that the indifference set for bundle x′, IND(x′)
     is bundle x′ itself, or in other words, that IND(x′) is a singleton in that it contains a
     single element.26

     1.10     Continuous Preferences

     The previous discussion about lexicographic preferences suggests that we need to im-
     pose an additional condition on preference relations in order to guarantee that they can
     be represented with a utility function. This property is continuity, as we define below.

          Continuity A preference relation defined on X is continuous if it is preserved
          under limits. That is, for any sequence of pairs {( x n , y n )}n=1 with x n  y n for all n
                                                                          ∞


          and lim x n = x and lim y n = y , the preference relation is maintained in the limit-
              n→∞              n→∞
          ing points, meaning x ≿ y.

        Intuitively, this property states that there are no sudden jumps in an individual pref-
     erence over a sequence of bundles. In other words, there are no sudden preference re-
     versals. Figure 1.26 illustrates preferences that satisfy continuity, where the individual
     decision maker prefers bundle x1 to y1, x2 to y2, and similarly at the limiting points of
     the sequence, where he still prefers bundle x to y.
        Let us next show why a lexicographic preference relation does not satisfy continuity.
     Consider the sequence xn = (1/n, 0) and yn = (0, 1), where n = {0, 1, 2, 3, …}. Therefore,
     while yn = (0, 1) is constant in n, as depicted in the upper left-hand corner of
     figure 1.27, xn = (1/n, 0) starts at x1 = (1, 0) at the lower right-hand corner of figure
     1.27, and moves leftward to x2 = (1/2, 0), then to x3 = (1/3, 0), and so on.
        Intuitively, the individual prefers bundle x1 to y1 since the former contains more of
     good 1 that the latter. Similarly the individual prefers bundle x2 to y2 given that the
     former still contains more of good 1 than the latter. However, at the limiting points of
     the sequence, bundle x becomes (0, 0), such that lim xnn→∞ = (0, 0) while bundle y is
     still (0, 1). Therefore both bundles contain the same amount of good 1 (zero units), and
     the individual ranks them according to the content of good 2, leading him to strictly
     prefer bundle y, since bundle y contains one unit of good 2 while bundle x has zero

     1.11    Existence of a Utility Function

     If a preference relation satisfies monotonicity and continuity, then there exists a utility
     function u(∙) representing such preference relation.

     Proof For presentation purposes, this proof, based in Rubinstein (2012), makes ex-
     tensive use of figure 1.28. Let us start by taking a bundle x ≠ 0:
     1. By monotonicity, x ≿ 0, where 0 = (0, 0, …, 0). Indeed, if bundle x ≠ 0, then it con-
        tains positive amounts of at least one good, and, by monotonicity, it is preferred to
        bundle 0.
     2. Let m ≡ max{x1, x2, ..., xN} be the number of units of the most abundant good in
        bundle x. Define bundle M as the bundle where all components coincide with the
        highest component of bundle x. That is,




     Figure 1.28
     Existence of a utility function
Preferences and Utility                                                                                     51




                                                          M ≡ ( m, m, ..., m ) .
                          Bundle M hence increases the amounts of all goods in bundle x (except for the most
                          abundant commodity, good 1 in figure 1.28). And hence, by monotonicity, we have
                          that the consumer prefers M to x, M ≿ x.
                    3. Bundles 0 and M are both on the main diagonal (45-degree line), since each of them
                       contains the same amount of good x1 and x2.
                       By continuity and monotonicity, there exists a bundle that is indifferent to x and lies
                    on the main diagonal. By monotonicity, this bundle is unique. Otherwise, modifying
                    any of its components would lead to indifference curves associated to higher/lower
                    utility levels, different from that associated with bundle x. We denote this bundle as
                    (t(x), t(x), … , t(x)). For compactness, let us define u(x) = t(x), which is a real number.
                       Applying the same steps for another bundle y ≠ x (see this bundle in figure 1.28), we
                    obtain a similar bundle on the main diagonal, (t(y), t(y), … , t(y)), which lies on the
                    same indifference curve as bundle y. For completeness, let u(y) = t(y), which is also a
                    real number. We know that

                                        x ~ ((t(x), t(x), …, t(x)), y ~ (t(y), t(y), …, t(y)), and
                                                                    x≿y

                    Hence, by transitivity of the preference relation x ≿ y, if and only if

                                         x ~ ((t(x), t(x), …, t(x))  (t(y), t(y), …, t(y)) ~ y,

                    and, by monotonicity, this is true as long as the real number t(x) exceeds t(y), meaning
                    t(x) ≥ t(y),

                                                 x  y ⇔ t(x) ≥ t(y) ⇔ u(x) ≥ u(y),

                    as required for our representability result. ■

                    As an aside, note that a utility function can satisfy continuity but still be nondifferen-
                    tiable. For instance, the Leontief utility function, A min{ax1, bx2}, is continuous but
                    cannot be differentiated at the kink.

                    1.12      Behavioral Economics—Two Utility Functions

                    While standard models consider that the individual decision maker has unbounded
                    rationality, willpower and selfishness, many of the models suggested in the field
                    of behavioral economics relax some of these assumptions. (For an introduction to
52                                                                                                Chapter 1



     the field, see Camerer et al. 2004.) In the following two sections, we briefly explore
     two models that consider specific utility functions under settings of certainty. In subse-
     quent chapters, we describe models and results of this literature in contexts such as
     choice under uncertainty, game theory, market competition, and the provision of
     public goods.

     1.12.1    Introducing Social Preferences in the Utility Function
     Over the last two decades a large number of articles tested the existence of social, as
     opposed to individual, preferences and analyzed their effects on strategic settings
     through the use of experiments. In particular, while these articles generally use differ-
     ent functional forms to account for distributional concerns, they all use additively
     separable utility functions of the form

                                         ui ( xi , x ) = f ( xi ) + gi ( x ),
     where f(xi) captures individual i’s utility from the monetary amount that he receives, xi,
     whereas gi(x) measures the utility or disutility he derives from the distribution of
     payoffs x = (x1, x2, … xI) among all I individuals. (Note that this specification can be
     generalized to measure utility from bundles of goods rather than from monetary
     amounts.) We next describe some of the most common functional forms found in the
     literature.

     Fehr–Schmidt Preferences
     For the case of two individuals, Fehr and Schmidt’s (1999) utility function reduces to

                        ui(xi, xj) = xi − αi max{xj − xi,0} − xiβi max{xi − xj,0},

     where xi is individual i’s payoff and j ≠ i. Parameter αi represents individual i’s disutil-
     ity from envy, which occurs when he earns less than individual j, that is, xi < xj. In this
     context, the second term becomes max {xj − xi,0} = xj − xi > 0 whereas the third term
     is null as max {xi − xj,0} = 0, thus yielding an overall utility of xi − αi(xj − xi). In con-
     trast, parameter βi captures individual i’s disutility from guilt when he earns a higher
     payoff than individual j. Indeed, when xi > xj, the second term cancels out, while the
     third term is positive, entailing an overall utility of xi − βi(xi − xj). Additionally Fehr and
     Schmidt (1999) assume that individuals’ envy is stronger than their guilt, which is
     captured by assuming that αi ≥ βi and 1 > βi ≥ 0.27

     27
        Intuitively, αi ≥ βi implies that individuals (weakly) suffer more from inequality directed at them
     than inequality directed at others. In contrast, βi ≥ 0 means that individuals dislike being better off
     than others (this assumption rules out cases in which individuals are status seekers but serves to
Preferences and Utility                                                                                                  53



                       Players hence exhibit what the literature refers as “concerns for fairness” in the
                    distribution of payoffs, or more compactly, “social preferences.” Note that if αi = βi =
                    0 for every individual i, agents only care about their material payoff xi (the first term in
                    the utility function above), and their preferences coincide with the more standard,
                    self-regarding preferences. Figure 1.29 depicts an indifference map in the Fehr and
                    Schmidt’s (1999) preferences. In particular, if u = u and xi > xj, solving for xj yields
                    x j = (u β ) − ((1 − β ) β ) xi , but if xi < xj, we obtain x j = ( u α ) − ((1 − α ) α ) xi , thus giv-
                    ing rise to two segments in each indifference curve: one with slope (1 − β)/β above the
                    45-degree line, and another with slope (1 − α)/α for points below that line. In addition
                    note that (xi, xj) pairs to the northeast yield larger utility levels for individual i, as both
                    individuals receive a large monetary payoff.
                       Importantly, if we allow for parameters αi and βi to take more general values, the
                    model above accounts for other behavioral motives. First, if the disutility of envy is
                    positive, αi ∈[0,1], but that from guilt is negative, βi ∈ (−1, 0] (and the former domi-
                    nates the latter, |αi| ≥ |βi|), Fehr and Schmidt’s (1999) specification would capture

                    simplify the analysis). Last, βi < 1 suggests that when i’s payoff is higher than that of j by one unit
                    (e.g., a dollar), individual i. will never be willing to give up more than one unit in order to

     concerns for status acquisition. Second, if the disutility from envy is negative, αi ∈

     preference for efficiency. Intuitively, it reveals that a reduction in my own payoff is
     only acceptable if the payoff of other individuals is increased by a larger amount.

     Charness–Rabin Preferences
     Fehr and Schmidt’s (1999) preferences might not be able to explain individuals’ reac-
     tions in strategic settings, where they may infer certain intentions from individuals
     who acted before them. In order to rationalize observed behavior in controlled experi-
     ments, Charness and Rabin (2002) modified Fehr and Schmidt’s (1999) preferences as
     follows:
             ui ( xi , x j ) = xi − (α i − θγ j ) max { x j − xi , 0} − ( βi + θγ j ) max { xi − x j , 0} .

                       In particular, parameter γj only takes two possible values, namely γj ∈ {−1, 0}, being
                    γj = −1 when individual i interprets that j misbehaved, and thus increases its envy
                    parameter by θ, or reduces his guilt parameter by θ. If instead individual i interprets
                    that j behaved, γj = 0, the utility function coincides with that in Fehr and Schmidt’s
                    (1999) specification. Intuitively, when individuals interpret that others misbehaved,
                    the envy (guilt) concerns analyzed above are emphasized (attenuated, respectively).

                       Note that, when individuals are completely selfish, α = 1, this utility function col-

                    substitution between individual i’s and j’s payoffs. That is, if xj decreases by 1 percent,
                    xi needs to be increased by ρ percent for individual i to maintain his utility level
                    unaffected.

                    1.12.2    Hyperbolic and Quasi-hyperbolic Discounting
                    Most individuals prefer a monetary amount $x today rather than in the future (i.e.,
                    t ≥ 1 periods from today). As a result many economic models assume that individuals
                    discount future payoffs. We next present three of the most common approaches to
                    model such discounting in the literature.

                    Exponential Discounting
                    According to this approach, the discounted value of a monetary amount $x received at
                    time t ≥ 1 is
                                                                    1
                                                                           x
                                                                 (1 + r )t
56                                                                                                   Chapter 1



     in today’s terms, which is exponentially decreasing in time t, where 0 ≤ r ≤ 1 denotes
     the interest rate. Allowing for continuous time, we can find the subjective discount rate
     of $x, which measures how (1/(1 + r)t)x varies along time relative to its initial value,
     that is,

                      ∂ [(1 (1 + r )t ) x ∂t ] −ln(1 + r ) 1 (1 + r ) x 
                                                                        t

                                              =                              = −ln(1+ r ),
                          (1 (1 + r )t ) x          (1 (1 + r )t ) x
     which is constant in the time period t when the individual makes the comparison. In
     other words, exponential discounting assumes that individuals’ comparison of payoff
     $x between period 0 and k coincides with that between period t and t + k, since in both
     cases k periods mediated.
        Several controlled experiments, however, report that individuals’ willingness to
     substitute consumption between period t and t + k depends on the specific moment
     at which the individual makes the comparison. For instance, when asked to choose
     between $100 today and $110 tomorrow, most individuals prefer to receive $100
     today, but when asked between $100 in, for instance, 60 days and $110 in 61 days,
     some individuals reveal a preference for $110 in 61 days. This present bias is rather
     troubling, as an individual who reveals today that he prefers $110 in 61 days, would
     re-evaluate his decision when day 60 arrives, informing us that he would rather
     prefer $100 in day 60 than waiting to receive $10 more the following day. In short, his
     preferences are time inconsistent. In order to account for this anomaly, hyperbolic
     and quasi-hyperbolic discounting assumes that individuals do not use the exponential
     discounting described above but a different format. Let us next examine each of them
     separately.

     Hyperbolic Discounting
     According to this theory, individuals discount a future payoff $x received in period t by
                                                      1
                                                              x,
                                                 (1 + rt )γ α
     where α , γ > 0 . In this setting, the subjective discount rate is

                 ∂ [(1 (1 + rt )γ α ) x ∂t ] − [γ r (1 (1 + rt )(α +γ ) α ) x ] α        γr
                                            =                                     =−             ,
                     (1 (1 + rt )γ α

     which is decreasing in t. For simplicity, a common assumption is that α = γ, yielding
     a subjective discounting of −r/(1 + rt). Figure 1.30 compares exponential (standard)
Preferences and Utility                                                                                          57




                    Figure 1.30
                    Hyperbolic discounting


                    discounting and hyperbolic discounting, as a function of the time period in which pay-
                    offs are received, t. Intuitively, individuals with hyperbolic discounting exhibit present
                    bias: on one hand, they strongly discount payoffs that will be received in the nearby
                    future, so that hyperbolic discounting lies below exponential discounting for small
                    values of t; on the other hand, individuals do not significantly discount two future pay-
                    offs that, despite being close to each other, are both received in the distant future, so
                    that hyperbolic discounting becomes almost flat for large values of t and lies above
                    exponential discounting.

                    Quasi-hyperbolic Discounting
                    Laibson (1997) presented a discounting approach that also yields present bias under
                    discrete time, whereby t = {0, 1, 2, …}. In particular, under “quasi-hyperbolic” dis-
                    counting, individuals assign a discount rate of 1 to current payoffs, t = 0, but a discount
                    of βδ t, to all future payoffs, t ≥ 1, where β ≤ 1. That is,

                                                           1      if t = 0,
                                                            t
                                                           βδ     if t ≥ 1.
                      Note that when β = 1, the model collapses to standard (exponential) discounting;
                    but otherwise its discounting pattern differs.28 When β ≤ 1, the subjective discount rate
                    for t ≥ 1 is



                    28
                       For instance, if δ = 1 and β = 0.6,then the stream of discounting is {1, 0.6, 0.6, …} and, if
                    δ = 0.9 and β = 0.6, this stream becomes {1, 0.54, 0.486, …}.
58                                                                                               Chapter 1




               ∆ ( βδ t x ) ∆t βδ t +1 x − βδ t x (δ t +1 − δ t ) β x (δ − 1) δ t β x

     where we used increments since time is discrete. Subjective discount rate under quasi-
     hyperbolic discounting is, thus, constant in t; as opposed to that under hyperbolic
     discounting which was decreasing in t. However, present bias can still arise under
     quasi-hyperbolic discounting. In order to see this, consider an individual evaluating
     today whether to invest c > 0 in period t, and obtain a benefit b > 0 with certainty n
     periods into the future (in period t + n). If he discounts future payoffs according to
     discount factor δ ∈(0,1), he would invest as long as δ tc < δ t+nb, or c < δ nb. Given his
     time preferences, if this individual is given the opportunity to reconsider his invest-
     ment when period t arrives, he will not need to reconsider it since c < δ nb still holds.
        What if instead this individual discounts future payoffs according to quasi-
     hyperbolic discounting, with βδ t? In this setting, the consumer will still invest as long
     as βδ tc < βδ t+nb, which simplifies into c < δ nb. This is the same decision rule as in the
     case above of the time-consistent individual. However, when at time t we ask him to
     submit his c dollars, he will want to reconsider his investment decision. In particular,
     he will compare the cost c today against the discounted benefit b that he will receive n
     periods into the future, thus investing if only if c < βδ nb, which does not coincide with
     his decision rule t periods ago. As a consequence this individual’s decision could be
     time inconsistent, since he could initially accept to make the investment in period t,
     whereby c < δ nb, but renege from his promise once period t arrives if c < βδ nb, which
     occurs if c satisfies βδ nb < c < δ nb, that is, as long as β < 1.
        Importantly, the emergence of time-inconsistencies in the (β, δ)-model is not due to
     changes in the decision maker’s discount factor as time progresses. Specifically, if an
     individual uses δj to discount at period j, the stream of payoffs he will receive in period
     j + 1 (where we allow his discount factor to change from one period to the next), he
     will invest as long as the discounted value of its cost in period t, δ1δ2 … δtc is smaller
     than the discounted value of the benefit, δ1δ2 … δt … δt+nb, that is, if δ1δ2 … δtc < δ1δ2
     … δt … δt+nb, which simplifies to c < δt+1 … δt+nb. This individual, if asked at period t
     whether he is still interested in the investment, might then invest provided that c < δt+1
     … δt+nb, which gives rise to the same decision rule as in period 0.

     Further reading Hyperbolic discounting has been used to explain many problems
     of addiction and self-control, as individuals displaying such type of discounting ex-
     hibit patience in the long run (joining a gym, starting a diet), but are impatient in the
     short run (skipping the gym and eating chocolate cake after dinner). Similar patterns
Preferences and Utility                                                                                              59



                    have been used to rationalize how many individuals simultaneously have large credit
                    card debts (as their impatience leads them to not resist the temptation of something
                    today) but retirement accounts earning low interest rates (since their long-term pa-
                    tience implies that they do not significantly discount future payoffs). Additionally
                    hyperbolic discounting has been shown to vary depending on the context in which
                    options are presented, and the characteristics of the individual. For instance, hyper-
                    bolic discounting tends to decrease with age, and in social groups with favorable com-
                    parisons. For an excellent review of the literature on hyperbolic discounting, see
                    O’Donaghue and Rabin (1999) and Frederick et al. (2002) and references therein; see
                    also Rubinstein (2005).

                    1.13      Choice-Based Approach

                    In the choice-based approach, we consider the actual choices made by the individual,
                    rather than on the process of introspection by which the individual discovers his own
                    preferences by systematically comparing different alternatives. In the choice-based
                    approach we use a “choice structure,” which contains two elements:
                    1. ℬ is a family of nonempty subsets of X, so that every element B ∈ ℬ is a set B ⊂ X.
                       Let us provide some examples of sets B:
                          a. In consumer theory, set B can be understood as a particular set of all the afford-
                             able bundles for a consumer, given his wealth and market prices. (We refer to this
                             set of affordable bundles as the consumer’s budget set.) Note that many applica-
                             tions consider the budget set to be a subset of the real numbers.29
                          b. Set B can represent the list of all the universities where you were admitted for
                             graduate school, among all universities in the scope of your imagination X, that
                             is, B ⊂ X.

                    2. c(∙) is a choice rule that selects, for each budget set B, a subset of elements in B, with
                       the interpretation that c(B) are the chosen elements from B:

                          a. Following with our example of consumer theory, c(B) would be the bundle (or
                             bundles) that the consumer chooses to buy, among all bundles he can afford in
                             budget set B.
                          b. In the example of the universities you were admitted to, c(B) would contain the
                             university that you choose to attend.

                    29
                      In the case of only consuming two goods, the set of affordable bundles B (budget set) becomes a
                    subset of  2+ , namely a subset of the positive quadrant, and thus represents all possible bundles.
60                                                                                          Chapter 1



     Note that c(B) might contain a single element, in which case the choice rule is a
     function, or it might contain more than one element, in which case the choice rule is a
     correspondence.30

     Example 1.11: Choice structures Let us now see two examples of choice struc-
     tures. Define the set of alternatives as X = {x, y, z}, thus containing only three ele-
     ments. Consider two different budget sets (both of them being subsets of the set of
     alternatives X), budget set B1 ={x, y} and budget set B2 ={x, y, z}. In choice structure
     one, c1(∙), the individual chooses element x, and only x, regardless of which budget set
     is presented to him. That is,
                               c1({x, y}) = {x} and c1({x, y, z}) = {x}.

        In choice structure two, c2(∙), the individual still selects only alternative x when he is
     confronted with budget set B1, that is, c2 ({x, y}) = {x}. However, when the budget set
     is enlarged to contain alternative z as well, as it does in B2, his choice reverts to only
     alternative y, that is, c2 ({x, y, z}) = {y}. (You probably suspect that such a choice rule
     is inconsistent, and you are right; we show this result below after defining what we
     mean by consistency in choices.) ■

     1.14     Consistency on Choices: The Weak Axiom of Revealed Preference (WARP)

     Paralleling the rationality assumption on the preference-based approach, we now im-
     pose a consistency requirement on the choice-based approach. Specifically, we con-
     sider that the actual choices of an individual are consistent if they satisfy the following
     weak axiom of revealed preference (WARP).


          WARP Consider a budget set B ∈ ℬ with x, y ∈ B, where element x is chosen,
          x ∈ c(B). Then the choice structure (ℬ, c(∙)) satisfies WARP if, for any other
          budget set B′ ∈ ℬ, where alternatives x and y are still available, x, y ∈ B′, and
          where alternative y is chosen, y ∈ c(B′), alternative x is also chosen, x ∈ c(B′).


     30
        Informally, we may understand a function to be a mathematical mapping that provides a single
     element in the range to each element in the domain, whereas a correspondence may be understood as
     a mapping providing more than one element in the range to each element in the domain.
Preferences and Utility                                                                                     61



                    Example 1.12: Checking WARP in choice structures When the individual deci-
                    sion maker faces budget set B = {x, y}, he chooses only alternative x. When he faces an
                    enlarged budget set B′ (which contains the same alternatives as budget set B, x and y,
                    but also alternative z), meaning B′ = {x, y, z}, then his “legal” choices according to the
                    WARP are
                    1. x, which can be rationalized because alternative x is still the best alternative even
                       after including z as an additional alternative;
                    2. z, which can be explained because the new option z is better than the previous alter-
                       natives x and y; or
                    3. x and z, which can be justified because new option z is very similar to alternative
                       x, and as a consequence the decision maker is indifferent between x and z, and
                       chooses both.
                       This implies that the decision maker cannot select alternative y alone, that is, c({x,
                    y, z}) ≠ {y}. Indeed this alternative was available under budget set B but the individual
                    did not select it. Hence the fact that a new option z is now available under B′ should not
                    cause alternative y to be selected under the newly (enlarged) budget set B′. Addition-
                    ally this means that the individual cannot choose c({x, y, z}) = {x, y} when facing
                    budget set B′, since alternative y is contained in this choice. As suggested in the previ-
                    ous argument, y was not selected under budget set B, and therefore cannot be part of
                    the choices made by the individual under budget set B′. ■

                    Example 1.13: More on choice structures satisfying/violating WARP Let us
                    consider now that the decision maker selects both alternatives x and y when facing
                    budget B, so that c({x, y}) = {x, y}. In this case, when facing the enlarged budget set
                    B′, his “legal” choices according to WARP are c({x, y, z}) = {x, y} or c({x, y, z}) = {x,
                    y, z}, or c({x, y, z}) = {z}. Note that this example illustrates the definition of WARP for
                    cases in which not only x but also y was selected under budget B. Importantly, when
                    facing the enlarged budget set B′, if the decision maker selects y, he must also be
                    choosing x, as stated in the definition of WARP above. ■

                    Figure 1.31a illustrates a choice rule that satisfies the WARP. Indeed the individual
                    decision maker selects alternatives x and y, whether facing budget set B or B′. In con-
                    trast, Figure 1.31b represents a choice rule violating WARP, since the individual
                    chooses x (and not y) when facing budget set B, but switches to y (and not x) when
                    facing budget set B′, despite the fact that both alternatives x and y were available
                    under budget set B. This choice rule is similar to choice rule 2 in example 1.11, where
62                                                                     Chapter 1




     Figure 1.31
     (a) Choice rule satisfying WARP. (b) Choice rule violating WARP
Preferences and Utility                                                                                            63



                    the individual decision maker chooses only x when confronted with budget set B, and
                    only y when facing budget set B′, where both x and y belong to both budget sets B and
                    B′. For this reason we can conclude that choice rule 2 violated the WARP. 31

                    Further reading For more details on the WARP, its origins and applications in eco-
                    nomics, see Hal Varian’s (2012) review. For a more empirical approach, see Beatty and

                    1.15     Consumption Sets

                    In this part of the chapter we start considering the set of feasible bundles for the con-
                    sumer. The consumption set is the set of affordable bundles. While consumption sets
                    can be limited by market prices and wealth, they can also be defined by some other
                    restrictions (such as institutional and historical) that limit the variety, and quantities, of
                    available goods. We hence understand a consumption set as a subset of the commodity
                    space ℝN denoted by x ⊂ ℝN whose elements are the consumption bundles that the in-
                    dividual can conceivably consume, given the physical constrains imposed by his envi-
                    ronment. Let us denote a commodity bundle x as a vector of N components.

                    1.15.1    Physical Constraints
                    Let us first examine the effect of imposing physical constraints on a consumption set.
                    For simplicity, we assume that the consumption set is defined in the set of positive real
                    numbers. Figure 1.32a illustrates a physical constraint in the labor market. Specifical-
                    ly, a worker cannot work more than 24 hours a day, and therefore an individual’s
                    maximum amount of leisure is 24 hours. If a law establishes a maximum working day
                    of 16 hours, that consumption set would shrink, and would be represented by the area
                    from 8 to 24 hours of leisure per day.
                       Figure 1.32b represents the consumption of two goods that cannot be enjoyed
                    simultaneously in the same consumption bundle. In particular, good 1 denotes the
                    consumption of beer in Seattle at noon, while good 2 denotes the consumption of
                    beer in Barcelona (Spain) at noon of the same day. Therefore the consumption set co-
                    incides with the two axes. Indeed the consumer can choose to consume any amount
                    of beer in Seattle, or any in Barcelona, but not a combination of the two (unless you
                    teletransport). We can now define convexity in consumption sets.

     1.15.2    Economic Constraints
     These constraints describe the set of goods and services an individual can afford given
     that individual’s wealth and current market prices. Before we formally define the eco-

     assumptions we make on the price vector:
     1. Completeness of markets We assume that all commodities can be traded in
        a market, at prices that are publicly observable. This is the so-called principle
        of completeness of markets (or universality of markets), since all goods can be

                    3. Price-taking assumption A consumer’s demand represents a small fraction of the

     Appendix: Rational Preference Relations Satisfy the WARP

     In this appendix we show that every rational preference relation induces a choice rule
     that satisfies WARP. First, we can construct the preferences that the individual reveals
     in making actual choices when confronted to choose an element (or elements) from
     different budget sets.
     1. If there is some budget set B for which the individual chooses x, where x, y ∈ B, we
        can say that alternative x is revealed at least as good as alternative y, and denote it
        as x ≿* y; where the superscript * denotes that we infer the individual’s weak prefer-
        ence for x over y by observing his actual choice.
     2. If there is some budget set B for which the individual chooses x but does not select
        y, where x, y ∈ B, then we can say that alternative x is revealed preferred to alterna-
        tive y, and denote it as x ≻* y.36
      Let C *(B, ≿) be the set of optimal choices generated by the preference relation ≿
     when facing a budget set B. Using this notation, we can restate the WARP as follows:
     • If alternative x is revealed at least as good as y, then y cannot be revealed preferred
       to x, that is, if x ≿* y, then we cannot have y ≻* x.
        Intuitively, note the connection with WARP: when x and y were presented to this
     individual, x ≿* y implies that the individual chooses x for sure, whereas we don’t
     know whether he also selected y. If he did, it cannot be that y ≻* x because this would
     imply he should not have selected x, violating x ≿* y. If he did not, then it cannot be
     that y ≻* x either.
        We next examine the relationship between the preference-based approach and the
     choice based approach. In particular, we want to investigate under which conditions a
     rational preference relation implies that the choice structure satisfies the WARP, and
     under which conditions the opposite relationship holds. Let us next show that a ratio-
     nal preference relation implies that the choice structure satisfies the WARP.

     36
          Note that when x ≿* y in point (a), the individual decision maker is allowed to choose both
     alternatives x and y. However, when x ≻* y as in point (b), the individual is only allowed to choose x.
Preferences and Utility                                                                                            69



                    Proof
                    • First, suppose that for some budget set B ∈ ℬ, we have that x, y ∈ B and x ∈ C *(B,
                      ≿), that is, x belongs to the set of optimal choices given the individual’s underlying
                      preference relation ≿. This implies that x ≿ y for any available y ∈ B, that is,
                                                x ∈C * ( B, ) ⇒ x  y       for all y ∈ B.

                    • In order to check WARP, assume some other budget set B′∈ ℬ in which alternatives
                      x and y are still available, x, y ∈ B′ and y ∈ C *(B′, ≿). This implies that y belongs to
                      the set of optimal choices given the preference relation ≿ when the decision maker
                      faces budget set B′. Hence y ≿ z for any available element z ∈ B′, that is,

                                                y ∈C * ( B ′, ) ⇒ y  z    for all z ∈ B ′.

                    • Combining the conclusions from the previous two points, x ≿ y and y ≿ z, we can
                      apply transitivity (because the preference relation is rational), and obtain x ≿ z.
                      Then the individual also selects x when facing budget set B′, namely x ∈ C *(B′, ≿),
                      and we find that both x and y are chosen when the decision maker faces the budget
                      set B′, namely x, y ∈ C *(B′, ≿), which proves that WARP is satisfied. ■

                    The opposite relationship (that a choice structure satisfying WARP implies a rational
                    preference relation) only holds if the budget set B contains three or fewer elements.
                    Mas-Colell et al. (1995) describes a proof of this result based in Arrow (1959).

2 Demand Theory



   This chapter expands on two elements analyzed in chapter 1—utility functions and
   feasibility constraints—as the ingredients of the consumer’s utility maximization
   problem (UMP). Recall that the consumer chooses a bundle that maximizes his utility
   given the economic and physical constraints he faces. The bundle that emerges from
   such maximization problem constitutes the demand function of the individual (in par-
   ticular, the Walrasian demand), which we study in section 2.2. The Walrasian demand
   describes how optimal purchases of a certain good by an individual are affected by
   variations in the price of this good, changes in the prices of other goods, and changes
   in his income. In addition we can evaluate the individual’s utility function at the Wal-
   rasian demand (i.e., at the bundle that maximizes the individual’s utility) in order to
   identify the height that his utility reaches at the optimum. This utility evaluation is
   often referred to as the individual’s “indirect utility function,” which is the content of
   section 2.3. In sections 2.4 and 2.5 we switch our attention to the consistency require-
   ment on individual choices that we explored in chapter 1, the WARP, but present it in
   terms of the Walrasian demand functions, along with the implications that WARP has
   in terms of comparative statics, namely when the price of a good changes. Section 2.6
   further analyzes the comparative statics of varying the price of one good, and how such
   effect can be divided into two separate effects: the income and substitution effects, as
   captured by the Slutsky equation.
      Sections 2.7 and 2.8 examine the dual of the UMP, the expenditure minimization
   problem (EMP), in which the individual seeks to minimize his total expenditure
   on goods and services conditional on reaching a specific utility level. The bundle
   resulting from the EMP is the so-called Hicksian demand, whereas the minimal
   expenditure required to purchase such a bundle is commonly referred to as the expen-
   diture function. Last, in the remaining sections of the chapter we explore the relation-
   ships between the different results of the UMP and the EMP, such as the connection
   between the Walrasian and the Hicksian demands, and the relationship between the
78                                                                                               Chapter 2



     indirect utility function and the expenditure function. These connections can be useful
     in applications where we have information about elements of, for instance, the EMP,
     but seek to infer elements from the UMP. The appendices to this chapter elaborate on
     these connections by analyzing under which conditions the UMP is the dual of the EMP.

     2.1     The Utility Maximization Problem

     We are now ready to combine individual preferences, embodied in a consumer’s util-
     ity function, and his budget set, which represents the set of bundles he can afford. In
     particular, the consumer maximizes his utility level by selecting a bundle x (the choice
     variable of his maximization problem, where x can be a vector) subject to his budget
     constraint p · x ≤ w. Formally, his UMP can be represented as follows:

                                        max u( x ) subject to p ⋅ x ≤ w                          (UMP).
                                         x ≥0


        For compactness, we denote the solution/s to the UMP as the argmax of UMP,1 and
     represent it as x(p, w): the Walrasian demand that, for a given price vector and wealth
     level, specifies a bundle of goods that maximizes the consumer’s utility.2
        Figure 2.1 depicts the Walrasian demand x(p, w) at bundle A, where the consumer
     reaches a utility level of u2 by exhausting all his wealth. Notice that bundle B and C are
     not optimal because, despite exhausting the consumer’s wealth, they yield a lower util-
     ity level u1, where u1 < u2. Bundle D is unaffordable, and hence it cannot be the argmax
     of the UMP given a wealth level of w.

     2.1.1     Existence
     One important point is whether the maximization problem above has a solution. The
     Weierstrass theorem provides us with a positive answer (see the mathematical appen-
     dix for more details on this theorem): if the objective function we maximize (utility
     function) is continuous and the budget constraint defines a closed and bounded set
     (given that p >> 0 and w > 0), the problem has a solution. In addition, the solution is
     unique if preferences are strictly convex. We return to this issue below. Interestingly, if
     the utility function is continuous and preferences satisfy LNS over the consumption set
     X =  +N , then the Walrasian demand x(p, w) satisfies:

     1
         Recall that the argmax refers to the argument, x, that solves a given maximization problem.
     2
      Some textbooks refer to the solution/s of the UMP as the “Marshallian demand,” which coincides
     with the Walrasian demand identified above.

                   α > 0.
                2. Walras’s law      p·x(p, w) = w.
                3. Convexity/uniqueness If preferences are convex, then the Walrasian demand x(p,
                   w) defines a convex set. If preferences are strictly convex, then the Walrasian de-
                   mand x(p, w) contains a single element.
                    We next elaborate on each of these three properties.

                an increase in both the price vector and wealth level does not change the consumer’s
                budget set.3 In particular, the budget set satisfies

     2.1.3   Walras’s Law
     Walras’s law follows from LNS. Indeed, if the consumer were to select a bundle that
     lies strictly inside the budget set (so that he is not exhausting his wealth, as in bundle
     x in figure 2.3), we could find another bundle y at ε-distance from bundle x that is
     strictly preferred by the individual to bundle x. In this case, however, the initial bundle
     x would not be utility maximizing because there are other bundles that are still

     4
       Note that Walrasian demand x(p, w) satisfies homogeneity of degree zero even when preferences
     are linear (goods are regarded as substitutes), yielding a unique (or a continuum) of optimal
     consumption bundles that would be unaffected by a common change in both prices and wealth. A
     similar argument applies for preferences for complements.

                Walras’s law


                affordable and which are strictly preferred by the consumer. If the bundle the con-
                sumer chooses lies, in contrast, on the budget line (as bundle x′ in figure 2.3), we could
                still identify bundles that are strictly preferred to x′, such as those to the northeast of
                the budget line. However, these bundles would be unaffordable to the consumer, and
                thus cannot be utility maximizing. In summary, utility-maximizing bundles, such as x′,
                must lie on the budget line, thus exhausting all wealth.

                2.1.4    Convexity
                If preferences are convex (but not strictly convex), a continuum of bundles can be util-
                ity maximizing. In particular, the budget line and the indifference curve can become
                tangent along several bundles (see left-hand panel of figure 2.4), forming a convex set.
                Indeed, if we construct the convex combination of any two bundles in this set, the re-
                sulting bundle also lies within the set. If, in contrast, the consumer’s preferences are
                strictly convex, he selects a unique bundle as his Walrasian demand (unique tangency
                point between the budget line and the indifference curve, as depicted in the right-hand
                panel of figure 2.4).
                   Having described the UMP, we can now examine the first-order (necessary) condi-

                                                      =              .

       Intuitively, this optimality condition can be understood as that the consumer allo-
     cates his consumption among goods l and k until the point where the marginal utility
     per dollar spent on good l, MUl / pl, coincides with that of good k, MUk / pk. Informally,
     the consumer distributes his consumption to achieve the same “bang for the buck”
     across goods.

                    Rearranging, the above optimality condition can be alternatively expressed as

                  In words, the consumer allocates consumption among goods l and k until the point
                where his willingness to substitute across goods (his MRS) coincides with the rate at
                which he can substitute goods in the market (as captured by the price ratio). Graphi-
                cally, optimality implies that the slope of the consumer’s indifference curve coincides
                with that of the budget line.

                2.1.5    Sufficiency
                A natural question at this point is whether the necessary conditions above are also suf-
                ficient. In other words, under which conditions can we guarantee that the Walrasian
                demand is the maximum of the UMP (and not the minimum!). In particular, this is the
                case when (1) the utility function is quasi-concave and monotone, and (2) the vector of
                first-order derivatives is different from zero for all x, that is, ∇u ≠ 0 for all x. Let us
                briefly analyze these conditions. First, the condition stating that the utility function
                should be monotone only implies that, if we increase both goods simultaneously, we
                reach a higher utility level, and that if we increase the amount of some (but not all)
                goods, the consumer is not made worse off, which is expected in most economic ap-
                plications. If, instead, the utility function does not satisfy monotonicity, the consum-
                er’s indifference map could look like that in figure 2.5. In this setting, the consumer
                would choose bundle A (at the corner), since it yields the largest utility level, u3, given
                his budget. At point A, however, the tangency condition MRS1,2 = p1 / p2 does not hold,
                since the consumer would like to further decrease his consumption of x1.6
                   Second, the condition that the first-order derivatives are different from zero simply
                guarantees that there are no bliss points. Intuitively, if the vector of first-order deriva-
                tives was zero, we would have reached the “peak” of utility, which is the highest point
                of the “utility mountain” in our 3D representation in chapter 1. At this point, however,
                the individual would not be able to find any other more preferred bundle, thus violating
                LNS (and we know that monotone utility functions must satisfy LNS). Finally, the
                condition that the utility function satisfies quasi-concavity is also easy to justify. Fig-
                ure 2.6 represents an indifference map of an individual whose preferences violate
                quasi-concavity.

                6
                  At point A, the indifference curve is flatter than the budget line, implying that (MU1/MU2) < (p1/p2),
                or (MU1/p1) < (MU2/p2). Hence the marginal utility per dollar spent on good 2 is larger than that on
                good 1, inducing the consumer to purchase units of good 2 alone.
84                                                 Chapter 2




     Figure 2.5
     Corner solution




     Figure 2.6
     UMP with non–quasi-concave utility function
Demand Theory                                                                                            85



                   As the figure shows, the UCS of bundle C is not convex. This implies that the tan-
                gency condition between the indifference curves and the budget line is not a sufficient
                condition for a utility-maximizing bundle. Specifically, a point of tangency such as
                bundle C gives a lower utility level than a point of nontangency such as bundle B.
                Therefore, if preferences do not satisfy quasi-concavity, the Kuhn–Tucker conditions
                (graphically represented by the tangency condition) are not sufficient for a maximum.
                The true maximum in this case is actually bundle A. Because the three requirements for
                the necessary conditions to become sufficient are relatively mild (utility function being
                quasi-concave, monotonic, and ∇u ≠ 0), we can then expect Kuhn–Tucker conditions
                to be sufficient in many economic applications.
                   Figure 2.7 represents an interior solution where the utility maximizing bundle satis-
                fies MRSl,k / pl / pk, graphically implying that the slope of the budget line coincides with
                the slope of the indifference curve evaluated at the optimum.

     2.1.6   Corner Solutions
     We have so far analyzed interior solutions. If, however, the individual prefers to con-
     sume zero amounts of some of the goods, the preceding tangency condition will not be
     satisfied. In particular, at a corner solution we find that, after taking first-order condi-
     tions, MRSl,k > pl / pk, or alternatively,

                                      ∂u( x * ) ∂xl ∂u( x * ) ∂xk
                                                   >
                                           pl            pk

     Intuitively, the marginal utility per dollar spent on good l is larger than that on good k.
     As a consequence, even after spending all his income on good l (at the corner), the
     consumer would still like to consume more units of good l. In the first-order condi-
     tions, this entails that ∂u(x*)/∂xk ≤ λpk for those goods whose consumption is zero,
     xk* = 0, that is, ∂u(x*)/∂xk/pk ≤ λ; and ∂u(x*)/∂xl = λpl for the good whose consumption
     is positive, xl > 0, that is, ∂u(x*)/∂xl/pl = λ. That is,

                2.2     Walrasian Demand—Comparative Statics

                2.2.1    Wealth Changes
                Let us now analyze how the Walrasian demand is affected by changes in the individu-
                al’s wealth level. When demand increases in wealth, we say that good is a “normal”
                good, while when it decreases in wealth we refer to those goods as “inferior.” Exam-
                ples of the former are computers and iPads. Examples of the latter are Two-Buck
                Chuck (a really cheap wine) and Walmart shopping during the economic crisis.8
                   Graphically, an increase in the wealth level produces an outward shift in the budget
                line, as figure 2.10 illustrates. In addition, at a given wealth level, the consumer choos-
                es an optimal consumption bundle. We can connect all these optimal consumption




                Figure 2.10
                Wealth effects

                8
                  Several reports suggest that a decrease in the average wealth during the 2009 economic crisis
                produced an increase in the sales of certain discount supermarkets, such as Costco, Walmart, and
                dollar stores.
90                                                                                    Chapter 2




     Figure 2.11
     Engel curves


     bundles for different levels of wealth, w, w′, and w″, forming what we refer to as the
     “wealth expansion path.” When the wealth expansion path indicates an increase (de-
     crease) in the consumption of good j as a consequence of further increments in the
     wealth level, we say that that good j is normal (inferior, respectively). Figure 2.10 il-
     lustrates an example in which x1, in the horizontal axis, is initially normal but becomes
     inferior, while x2 is normal for all wealth levels.
        We can alternatively measure how consumption is affected by wealth changes by
     using Engel curves, which depict the consumption of a particular good in the horizon-
     tal axis and wealth on the vertical axis. When the slope of the Engel curve is positive
     (negative), it indicates that the good is normal (inferior). Of course, an Engel curve can
     be positively sloped for low wealth levels but become negatively sloped afterward.
     Figure 2.11 illustrates an Engel curve for a normal good (positive slope for all wealth
     levels), and an Engel curve for a good whose demand is normal for relatively low
     wealth levels, w < wˆ , but becomes inferior beyond ŵ.

                2.2.2   Price Changes
                Let us now analyze how demand reacts to price changes. When the demand for good k
                decreases as a result of an increase in the price of good k, we regard that good as a
                usual good, since its quantity demanded reacts negatively to its own price. If, in con-
                trast, quantity demanded increases as a result of an increase in its own price, we regard
                it as a Giffen good.9 We illustrate these negative and positive relationships in figure
                2.12, which represents the quantity demanded of good k in the horizontal axis and its
                own price in the vertical axis.
                   Besides analyzing the effect of a change in prices on its own quantity demanded
                (referred to as “own-price effects”), we are interested in examining the effect of a
                change in the price of good l on the quantity demanded for a different good k (referred
                to as “cross-price effects”). We can either find that this relationship is positive, when
                goods are regarded as substitutable (e.g., two brands of mineral water); or negative, for
                two goods regarded as complementary in consumption (e.g., cars and gasoline). We
                can use a similar graphical presentation as the one employed above in order to repre-
                sent these cross-price effects (see figure 2.13).
                   In the left panel of figure 2.13, an increase in the price of one brand of mineral water,
                from pl0 to p1l , increases the demand of the other brand of water (shifting its demand

     curve outward), since the consumer regards them as close substitutes. Intuitively, the
     consumer reduces his demand of good l, as it became relatively more expensive, and
     increases his demand of good k. In the right panel, we observe how an increase in the
     price of gasoline from pl0 to p1l reduces the demand for cars, shifting it inward. This

     2.3   Indirect Utility Function

     Besides the set of properties of the optimal consumption bundle that solves the UMP
     (Walrasian demand), there are some important points about the UMP that we should
     consider. First, when we insert the optimal consumption bundle into the individual’s
     utility function, we obtain the highest utility level that the individual can achieve by
     solving his UMP, u(x(p, w)), or compactly referred to as the indirect utility function,
     and denoted by v(p, w).10 Function v(p, w) satisfies several properties:

     Homogeneity of Degree Zero
     This property states that increasing market prices and wealth by the same proportion
     does not modify the consumer’s budget set (see figure 2.14). As a consequence, such
     an increase does not modify the consumer’s optimal consumption bundle, x(p, w), nor
     does it affect the maximal utility level that the individual reaches in his UMP, as mea-
     sured by v(p, w), meaning v(αp, αw) = v(p, w).

     Strictly Increasing in w, and Nonincreasing in pk for Every Good k
     This property states that if we increase the wealth of the individual, we enlarge the set
     of feasible bundles he can afford and, as a consequence, we allow him to reach an in-
     difference curve associated with a higher utility level. Therefore the maximal utility
     level that he can obtain is strictly increasing in his wealth, as depicted in figure 2.15
     where v(p, w′ ) > v(p, w) because w′ > w.
        In contrast, with an increase in the price of any good, the set of affordable bundles
     shrinks, so the individual can only reach indifference curves associated with weakly
     lower utility levels. Hence, an increase in the price of any good k produces a weak
     reduction in the maximal utility level that the individual can obtain by solving this
     UMP (see figure 2.16).

     Remark By the property above, v(p, w) is nonincreasing in pk, thus allowing v(p, w)
     to remain unaffected as the consumer experiences an increase in the price of the good.
     This can occur when he is initially at a corner solution, and a change in pk does not
     modify his optimal consumption bundle, thus not affecting v(p, w) either. Nonetheless,
     if pk changes sufficiently, even a consumer who is initially at a corner solution will

     10
         More generally, we refer to the objective function of an optimization problem evaluated at the
     solution of such optimization problem as the “value function.” Hence, the value function of the UMP
     is the indirect utility function.
Demand Theory                                        95




                Figure 2.14
                v(p, w) homogeneous of degree zero




                Figure 2.15
                v(p, w) strictly increasing in w
96                                                                                         Chapter 2




     Figure 2.16
     v(p, w) is nonincreasing in pk


     change his optimal consumption bundle by potentially moving to a different corner
     solution, ultimately lowering his utility level as measured by v(p, w).

     Quasi-Convexity
     The set {( p, w ) : v( p, w ) ≤ v } is convex for any v ∈  + . An intuitive explanation of this
     property is provided in figure 2.17. First, the figure depicts the indirect utility function
     with the price of good 1 on the horizontal axis and the wealth level on the vertical axis.
     Hence, when the price of good 1 increases from p11 to p12 , this individual’s wealth
     must also increase in order to keep his utility level unaffected. In contrast, lower prices
     and higher wealth levels are associated with higher maximal utilities. Graphically,
     moving to the northwest in figure 2.17 entails a higher utility level, v(p*, w*) > v(p, w),
     where p* < p and w* > w.
        Let us now examine the quasi-convexity of v(p, w). Specifically, this property im-
     plies that, if the maximum utility associated with a given pair of prices and wealth
     (point A in figure 2.17) is weakly higher than the maximum utility associated with
     another pair of prices and wealth (point B), then the convex combination of points A
     and B (point C) yields a maximum utility that is weakly lower than that associated with
     A. That is, if the consumer faces an intermediate price level λ p11 + (1 − λ ) p12 and an
Demand Theory                                                                                           97




                Figure 2.17
                Quasi-convexity of v(p, w)—I


                intermediate wealth level λw1 + (1 − λ)w2, the maximum utility level that he will be able
                to reach by solving his UMP is lower than that at point A ≡ ( p11 , w1 ) .
                   An alternative interpretation of quasi-convexity simply states that the pairs of prices
                and wealth for which the consumer reaches a lower utility level than that under pair
                (p*,w*) defines a convex set. More compactly, v(p, w) is quasi-convex if the set of
                (p, w) pairs for which v(p, w) < v(p*, w*) is convex, meaning {(p, w) : v(p, w) < (p*, w*)}
                is convex. Figure 2.18 illustrates this property by first depicting the utility level
                associated with the price-wealth pair (p*, w*), v(p*, w*), and then shading the set of
                price-wealth pairs that yield a lower utility level than v(p*, w*) does, thus yielding a
                convex set.
                   Another common illustration of quasi-convexity uses goods 1 and 2 on the axis (see
                figure 2.19). First, when the individual faces budget set Bp,w, his optimal consumption
                bundle is x(p, w). Second, when prices and wealth change to p′ and w′, he faces budget
                set Bp′,w′, and selects bundle x(p′, w′). Third, both bundles x(p, w) and x(p′, w′) induce
                the same utility u because they lie on the same indifference curve, so the indirect util-
                ity function satisfies v(p, w) = v(p′, w′) = u . We can now construct a convex combina-
                tion of prices and wealth:

                                     p′′ = α p + (1 − α ) p′ and w ′′ = α w + (1 − α )w ′,

                nally, note that any solution to the UMP when the consumer faces budget set Bp″,w″ must
                provide an optimal consumption bundle that lies on a lower indifference curve (associ-

                2.4     WARP and Demand

                Having explored the different properties of the UMP, its solution, x(p, w), and its value
                function, v(p, w), we can now connect the optimal consumption bundle and the WARP.
                In particular, we want to learn if the consistency requirement imposed by WARP limits
100                                                                                                    Chapter 2



      the set of optimal consumption bundles that the individual decision maker can select
      when solving the UMP.
        Consider two different consumption bundles x(p, w) and x(p′, w′), both being afford-
      able under (p, w), that is, p · x(p, w) ≤ w and p · x(p′, w′) ≤ w. When prices and wealth are
      (p, w), the consumer chooses x(p, w) despite x(p′, w′) also being affordable. Therefore
      the consumer “reveals” a preference for x(p, w) over x(p′, w′), though both are afford-
      able (consistency). However, bundle x(p, w) may not be affordable at (p′, w′), since the
      consumer chose x(p′, w′). That is, p′ · x(p, w) > w′. We can summarize these properties
      as follows:

           WARP Walrasian demand satisfies WARP if, for two different consumption
           bundles, x(p, w) ≠ x(p′, w′):
                                      p ⋅ x( p′, w ′) ≤ w ⇒ p′ ⋅ x( p, w ) > w ′.


      In words, if bundle x(p, w) and x(p′, w′) are affordable under budget set Bp,w, and the
      consumer selects x(p, w) rather than x(p′, w′), then bundle x(p, w) must not be afford-
      able under budget set Bp′,w′, since the consumer selected bundle x(p′, w′).
         Let us begin by presenting optimal consumption bundles that satisfy WARP. In fig-
      ure 2.20, bundles x(p, w) and x(p′, w′) are both affordable under (p, w), since they both
      lie on or below budget line Bp,w. In contrast, bundle x(p, w) is not affordable under
      (p′, w′) because it lies above budget line Bp′,w′. Therefore WARP is satisfied.11
         Let us next examine the case in figure 2.21, where demand under final prices and
      wealth, x(p′, w′), is not affordable under initial prices and wealth because it lies above
      budget line Bp,w. In this case we cannot check if WARP applies, since the premise of
      WARP is not satisfied in the first place given that bundle x(p′, w′) is not affordable
      under (p, w). Hence WARP is not violated. A similar argument applies to the bundles in
      figure 2.22, since x(p′, w′) is not affordable under initial prices and wealth (p, w).

      2.4.1    Testing WARP
      The procedure that we have been using to test whether two particular bundles satisfy
      WARP can be sequentially described as follows:

      11
         Note that we first checked whether the premise of WARP holds, that is, whether both bundles
      x(p, w) and x(p′, w′) are affordable under (p, w), thus lying on or below budget line Bp,w. We then
      checked whether the conclusion of WARP is satisfied, that is, whether bundle x(p, w) is unaffordable
      under (p′, w′), thus lying above budget line B p′ ,w ′ . In this example, the premise was satisfied, as well
      as its conclusion.

      1. We check if bundles x(p, w) and x(p′, w′) are both affordable under the initial prices
         and wealth. Graphically, both bundles must lie on or below budget set Bp,w:
         •  	If step 1 is satisfied, then we can move to step 2.
         •  	Otherwise, the premise of WARP is not satisfied, not allowing us to continue
             checking whether it is violated. In such cases we say that the WARP is “not vio-
             lated.” (Recall that for us to be able to claim that WARP is violated, we must find
             that its premise holds, namely that p · x(p′, w′) ≤ w, but its conclusion does not,
             that is p′ · x(p, w) < w′.)
      2. We check if bundle x(p, w) is not affordable under final prices and wealth. Graphi-
         cally, bundle x(p, w) must lie on or above budget line Bp′,w′.
         •  	If this condition is satisfied, then the Walrasian demand satisfies WARP.
         •  	If, in contrast, this condition does not hold, then the Walrasian demand violates
             WARP.
         Figure 2.23 represents a similar case to those previously analyzed. Bundle x(p′, w′)
      is not affordable under the price-wealth pair (p, w) because x(p′, w′) lies above Bp,w.
      Hence the premise of WARP does not hold, which, as in our previous examples, means
      that WARP is not violated.

                   Suppose that, as shown in figure 2.24, the optimal consumption bundle under final
                prices and wealth, x(p′, w′), is affordable at initial prices and wealth, since it lies below
                the budget line Bp,w. Similarly bundle x(p, w) is affordable under Bp,w, and hence the
                premise of WARP is satisfied. Applying the second step of the WARP procedure, we
                can see that the optimal consumption bundle x(p, w) is unaffordable under the new
                prices and wealth, given that it lies above budget line Bp′,w′.. Hence WARP is satisfied.
                   Our last example in figure 2.25 exhibits a similar pattern. Specifically, the optimal
                consumption bundle with final prices and wealth, x(p′, w′), is affordable under (p, w),
                since it lies below budget line Bp,w. A similar argument applies to bundle x(p, w), which
                lies on Bp,w, thus being affordable as well, so the premise of WARP holds. Furthermore,
                upon applying the second step of the WARP procedure, we learn that although the
                demand x(p, w) is affordable under the new prices and wealth, it lies below budget set
                B p′ ,w ′ . Therefore WARP is not satisfied.12

                2.4.2   Implications of WARP
                WARP has some important implications for the set of admissible consumption
                bundles that a consumer may choose before and after a price change. Let us begin by

                considering a reduction in the price of good 1, as figure 2.26 illustrates with an upward
                pivot on the budget line.
                   After the price change, we adjust the consumer’s wealth so that he can consume his
                initial demand x(p, w) at the new (lower) prices. Therefore we shift the final budget line
                Bp′,w inward (reducing this consumer’s wealth) until the point at which we reach the
                initial consumption bundle x(p, w). Importantly, the budget line after the shift (after the
                reduction in wealth) is parallel to budget line Bp′,w, reflecting the final price ratio.
                   What is the precise reduction in wealth that we must apply to this consumer in order
                for him to exactly afford bundle x(p, w)? To find this wealth adjustment, the individual
                must spend p · w(p, w) = w in order to buy bundle x(p, w) at price p but must spend
                p′ · x(p, w) = w′ when the market price is p′. The difference in his expenditure is

                                             w ′ − w = p′ ⋅ x ( p, w ) − p ⋅ x ( p, w ) ,

                                                    or ∆w = ∆p ⋅ x( p, w ),

                where Δw = w′ − w and Δp = p′ − p. This wealth adjustment is the Slutsky wealth com-
                pensation. Intuitively, it represents the increase (decrease) in wealth, measured by Δw,
                that must be provided to the consumer in order for him to afford the original bundle
                x(p, w) after experiencing a price increase (decrease, respectively). In figure 2.27 the
106                                                                                              Chapter 2




      Figure 2.27
      Uncompensated and compensated price change


      Slutsky wealth compensation is illustrated by the reduction in the consumer’s wealth
      that affords him the same consumption bundle as before the price decrease.13 Given
      this interpretation of Slutsky wealth compensation, we are ready to establish a relation-
      ship between the law of demand and WARP. Suppose that the Walrasian demand
      x(p, w) satisfies homogeneity of degree zero and Walras’s law. Then x(p, w) satisfies
      WARP if and only if Δp·Δx ≤ 0, where Δx = x(p′, w′) − x(p, w) and where x(p′, w′) is eval-
      uated at w′, which is the wealth level that allows the consumer to buy his initial de-
      mand at the new prices, w′ = p′ · x(p, w)
         This result establishes that if, after the price change, the consumer’s wealth is com-
      pensated “à la Slutsky,” as described above, then the WARP becomes equivalent to the
      law of demand (i.e., quantity demanded and price move in different directions). That
      is, in the case of a price decrease, the WARP implies that quantity demanded must in-
      crease, provided that the consumer’s wealth is adjusted “à la Slutsky.”
         Figure 2.28 depicts another example in which the WARP restricts behavior when the
      Slutsky wealth compensation is applied. In the figure the price change is similar to that

      consumption). We comment on this type of wealth compensation in subsequent sections of this
      chapter.

                2.5   Slutsky Matrix

                The Walrasian demand function is differentiable in both prices and wealth under rela-
                tively general conditions. We next further examine the relationship between the CLD
                and the WARP. In order to do so, let us first totally differentiate the Walrasian demand
                function, as follows:

                                            dx = D p x( p, w )dp + Dw x( p, w )dw.
                And since the consumer’s wealth is compensated, dw = x(p, w) · dp (this is the differen-
                tial analogue of Δw = Δp · x(p, w) in the Slutsky wealth compensation described in the
                previous section). Substituting dw = x(p, w) · dp in the expression above obtains

                                     dx = D p x( p, w )dp + Dw x( p, w )[ x( p, w ) ⋅ dp],
                                                                                 
                                                                                     dw


                or equivalently,

                                       dx = [ D p x( p, w ) + Dw x( p, w ) x( p, w )T ] dp,
                where the subscript T denotes the transposed vector x(p, w). Hence the CLD,
                dp·dx ≤ 0, can be also expressed as

                                       dp ⋅ [ D p x( p, w ) + Dw x( p, w ) x( p, w )T ] dp ≤ 0,
                where the term in brackets is the so-called Slutsky (or substitution) matrix, S(p, w). In
                particular,

                                                       s11 ( p, w ) ... s1N ( p, w ) 
                                         S ( p, w ) =                                ,

                where each term of the matrix is

      for every two goods l and k.
         We next examine under which conditions the own-price effects, as represented by
      the elements in the main diagonal of the matrix, sll(p, w), are negative. If sll(p, w) ≤ 0
      for all goods, then the Slutsky matrix would be negative semidefinite. In particular, if
      x(p, w) is differentiable, satisfies Walras’s law, homogeneity of degree zero and WARP,
      then the Slutsky matrix S(p, w) is negative semidefinite. That is, v · S(p, w) · v ≤ 0 for
      any vector v ∈ ℝN and all terms in the main diagonal of the matrix must be weakly
      negative, meaning own-price effects satisfy sll(p, w) ≤ 0.15 As described above, the sub-
      stitution effect sll(p, w) embodies two effects:
                                                             ∂ xl ( p , w )  ∂ x ( p, w )

                                                           (+) for Giffen goods    ( − ) for inferior goods


          We can rearrange this expression to state that the total effect is equal to the substitu-
      tion effect minus the income effect, TE = SE – IE.16 Let us describe each of the terms in
      the expression above. First, from our previous discussion on Slutsky compensation and
      the CLD, we know that the substitution effect is negative for all types of goods because
      sll(p, w) ≤ 0. Second, the total effect measures the change in the quantity demanded for
      good l as a result of a change in the price of good l. Hence it considers an uncompen-
      sated price effect, given that it reflects a change in the price of good l without adjusting
      the wealth of the individual. Third, the income effect describes the change in demand
      due to the adjustment in wealth as a result of a Slutsky wealth compensation.17

      15
         The fact that the substitution matrix is negative semidefinite does not imply that this matrix is
      symmetric. Nevertheless if the utility function is continuous and represents a strictly convex
      preference relation that satisfies LNS, then the substitution matrix is symmetric. In many applications,
      these conditions hold and therefore the substitution matrix is symmetric. However, in the case of
      preferences for perfect substitutes, indifference curves do not satisfy strict convexity and, hence, we
      cannot use the above result to guarantee that the substitution matrix is symmetric.
      16
         Recall that when the quantity demanded of good l decreases (increases) in the price of good l, we
      refer to that good as usual (Giffen, respectively). Similarly, when the quantity demanded of good l
      increases (decreases) in wealth, we refer to that good as normal (inferior, respectively).
      17
         Recall the difference between a Slutsky and a Hicksian wealth compensation. The former adjusts
      the consumer’s wealth so that he can still afford the same bundle that he purchased before the price
      change, whereas the latter adjusts wealth so that the consumer can still reach the same utility level as
      before the price change (graphically reaching the same indifference curve).

                demand curve or the CPP demand curve). This increase is smaller than the increase in
