      3.7 Application of Income and Substitution Effects—III: Income and Substitution
      Effects among Different Goods

      In previous sections we focused on the substitution and income effects of varying the
      price of good k on the demand for that same good. In this section, however, we analyze
      the substitution and income effects of varying the price of good k on the demand for
      other good j. In terms of the Slutsky matrix, we paid close attention to the elements
      along the main diagonal of the matrix, whereas we now turn to the elements away from
      the main diagonal. For simplicity, let us start our analysis using only two goods, x and
      y. The types of relationships that can occur between only two goods are, of course,
      relatively limited, but this will help us graphically illustrate their main intuitions. Be-
      low we generalize our analysis to N > 2 goods. Let us start defining goods that are
      gross complements or substitutes in consumption. In particular, when py falls, the sub-
      stitution effect can be so small that the consumer purchases a larger amount of both
      goods x and y. In this case we denote good x and y as gross complements. Figure 3.19
      illustrates this case. Specifically, the consumer starts purchasing bundle A. Afterward,
Demand Theory—Applications                                                                                       195




                 Figure 3.19
                 Gross complements, ∂x / ∂py < 0


                 py decreases, producing an upward-pivoting effect on the consumer’s budget line. We
                 then apply a Hicksian wealth compensation so the consumer can maintain his utility
                 level intact after the price change. The reduction in consumption of good x from bun-
                 dle A to B reflects the substitution effect,24 and the increase in consumption of good x
                 from B to C illustrates the income effect. Intuitively, the substitution effect measures
                 the change in the consumption of the good that became relatively more expensive
                 (good x, and for this reason its substitution effect is negative), and the income effect
                 captures the increase in consumption due to an expansion in the consumer’s purchas-
                 ing power after the price decrease. Indeed the total effect on the consumption of good
                 x is positive, since the demand for x increases from x0 to x1. Nonetheless, the total ef-
                 fect on the consumption of good y is also positive, since the consumer increases his
                 consumption of good y from y0 to y1. We can therefore conclude that a reduction in py
                 produces an increase in the consumption of good x and that these two goods can be
                 regarded as gross complements.

                 24
                    The substitution and income effects discussed in this section measure the change in the consump-
                 tion good x that results from a reduction in the price of good y. In previous chapters, in contrast,
                 substitution and income effects measured how a change in the price of one good (e.g., x) affects its
                 own consumption.
196                                                                                               Chapter 3



         Let us now describe the opposite case. As in figure 3.19, py decreases, rotating the
      consumer’s budget line. The reduction in consumption of good x from A to B illustrates
      the (large) substitution effect, while the increase in consumption of good x from B to C
      reflects the (small) income effect. The total effect is negative, implying that a decrease
      in py leads to a reduction in the consumption of good x, since it became relatively more
      expensive than good y. Hence goods x and y can be regarded as gross substitutes.
         After providing a graphical representation of gross substitutes and complements, let
      us next mathematically analyze the relationship between these two goods. In particu-
      lar, the change in the consumption of good x caused by changes in py is captured by the
      Slutsky equation, as follows:

         First, note that the substitution effect is positive. Intuitively, a decrease in py induces

      utility he must reach. Indeed good y became relatively cheaper and good x relatively
      more expensive, inducing the consumer to shift his consumption toward the cheaper
      good. Second, the derivative ∂x / ∂w from the second term of the Slutsky equation is
      positive when good x is normal but negative if it is inferior.25 Intuitively, the income
      effect in this case represents that a decrease in py increases the consumer’s real purchas-
      ing power—making him “richer”—leading him to increase his consumption of good x.
      As a consequence a decrease in py increases (decreases) the consumption of good x due
      to the income effect if good x is normal (inferior, respectively). Overall, the total effect
      of a decrease in py is therefore ambiguous, and depends on the relative size of the sub-
      stitution and income effects. The previous Slutsky equation can also be represented

      3.7.1   Asymmetry of the Gross Substitute and Complement Definitions
      Importantly, the definitions of gross substitutes and complements are not necessarily
      symmetric. In particular, it is possible for good x1 to be a gross substitute for x2, and
      simultaneously for good x2 to be a gross complement of x1. Let us next see this poten-
      tial asymmetry with an example.

      Example 3.5: Gross and net substitutability Suppose that the utility function
      for two goods, x and y, is given by u(x, y) = ln x + y. Setting up the Lagrangian of the
      UMP as

                                    L = ln x + y + λ ( w − px x − py y )
Demand Theory—Applications                                                                               199



                 obtains the following first-order conditions:

                                                      ∂L
                                                         = 1 − λ py = 0,
                                                      ∂y
                                                  ∂L
                                                     = w − px x − py y = 0.
                                                  ∂λ
                    Manipulating the first two equations we obtain pxx = py. Inserting this information
                 into the budget constraint, we find the Walrasian demand for good y as y = (w − py) / py.
                 We can observe that an increase in py causes a decline in spending on y, namely
                 ∂y ∂p y = − w p 2y . Therefore we can conclude that the spending on good x must rise,
                 since px and w are unchanged. That is, ∂x / ∂py > 0. Hence good y is a gross substitute of
                 good x. However, spending on good y is independent on px (given that the demand for
                 x and y are independent on one another). Therefore ∂x / ∂py = 0, indicating that good x
                 is neither a gross substitute nor a gross complement of good y. This shows the asym-
                 metry of gross substitute and complement definitions: while good y is a gross substi-
                 tute of x, ∂x / ∂py > 0, good x is neither a gross substitute or complement of y, that is
                 ∂x / ∂py = 0. ■

                 This conclusion suggests that, depending on how we check for gross substitutability or
                 complementarity between two goods, there is potential to obtain different results. A
                 natural question, of course, is whether we can use an alternative approach to check if
                 two goods are complements or substitutes that is unaffected by this asymmetry. We
                 next present such an approach.

                 3.7.2   Net Substitutes and Net Complements
                 The concept of net substitutes and net complements focuses solely on the substitution
                 effect. In particular, using the Hicksian demand of good i, hi(pi, pj, u), we claim that two
                 goods i and j are regarded as net substitutes if ∂hi / ∂pj > 0, while two goods are net
                 complements if ∂hi / ∂pj < 0. Graphically, this condition looks only at the shape of the
                 indifference curve. We analyze how an increase in the price of one good affects the
                 demand for another good when the consumer remains at the same indifference curve.
                 Indeed recall that, when we examine a consumer’s Hicksian demand, we apply a
                 wealth compensation in order to guarantee that the consumer is still reaching his initial
                 utility level. As a consequence a compensated price change maintains the consumer on
                 the same indifference curve but induces him to move to a different point along this
                 curve, thus increasing (decreasing) his consumption of the good that became relatively
                 cheaper (more expensive, respectively).
200                                                                                                  Chapter 3



         In contrast to our definition of gross substitutes and gross complements, this defini-
      tion is symmetric across two goods. This means that, if we determine that two goods i
      and j are net substitutes or complements in consumption, their relationship is unaf-
      fected by the direction in which the definition is applied. Specifically,

                                                    ∂hi ∂h j
                                                        =    .
                                                    ∂p j ∂pi

      above the main diagonal is symmetric with respect to the corresponding element below

                    Since our definition of net complements and net substitutes focuses solely on the
                 substitution effect, two goods can be regarded as gross complements even if they are
                 net substitutes. Let us see an example of this surprising result. Figure 3.21 illustrates
                 a decrease in py that reduces the consumption of good x due to the substitution effect
                 (so goods x and y are regarded as net substitutes) but increases the overall consumption
                 of good x measured by the total effect (so goods x and y are regarded as gross
                 complements).
                    More generally, a diminishing MRS between two goods implies that the indifference
                 curves are bowed in toward the origin, ultimately indicating that the substitution effect
                 must be negative. Indeed, if good y becomes cheaper, and the consumer remains at the
                 same indifference curve, the budget line (after the wealth compensation) must become
                 steeper, as depicted in figure 3.21. As a consequence the consumer reduces his con-
                 sumption of good x (since this good became relatively more expensive) but increases
                 his purchases of good y (since this good is now relatively cheaper). Therefore, while
                 convex preferences (as that depicted in figure 3.21) imply that goods must be net
                 substitutes, they are not necessarily gross substitutes (in the example illustrated in

      3.8   Aggregate Demand

      consumers. Note that, for generality, we still allow individual i’s demand xi(p, wi) to
      represent a vector of N components, describing his demand for N different goods. In

      any fixed price vector p, for any good k, and for any wealth level of any two individu-
      als i and j, the income effect of a redistribution of wealth is the same across individuals.
         Graphically, this condition entails that all consumers exhibit parallel, straight wealth
      expansion paths. First, note that straight wealth expansion paths imply that income
      effects do not depend on the individual’s wealth level at which they are evaluated. That
      is, a given increase in wealth produces the same change in the consumption of good k,
      regardless of the initial wealth of the individual. Figure 3.22 illustrates a straight wealth
      expansion path where an increase in the wealth of an individual from w to w′ produces
      an increase in consumption of the same size as when his wealth increases from w′ to
      w″. (This property holds for all goods, x1 and x2, in figure 3.22.) In contrast, a non-
      straight (curvy) wealth expansion path, as the one depicted in the right-hand panel of
      figure 3.22, implies that a given increase in wealth can lead to changes in the consump-
      tion of good k that are dependent on the individual’s wealth level. This is illustrated in

                    Second, note that a parallel wealth expansion path across individuals implies that
                 individuals’ wealth effects must coincide. We illustrate this property in figure 3.23
                 where the wealth expansion path for consumers 1 and 2 are parallel to each other, in-
                 dicating that both individuals’ demands change by the same amount as they become
                 richer.
                    Recall that in the previous two chapters we saw several examples of preference rela-
                 tions that imply straight and parallel wealth expansion paths, such as homothetic pref-
                 erences and quasi-linear preferences. Hence, if both individuals exhibit either of these
                 preference relations, we can guarantee that their wealth expansion paths will be straight
                 and parallel to each other. As a consequence, income effects cancel out across consum-
                 ers, and ultimately demand can be expressed as a function of market prices and aggre-
                 gate wealth.
                    A question at this stage is whether we can group all these types of preference rela-
                 tions (e.g., homothetic and quasi-linear) as special cases of a more general family of
                 preference relations. In particular, a necessary and sufficient condition for consumers
                 to exhibit parallel, straight wealth expansion paths is that every individual i’s indirect
                 utility function can be expressed as

      Appendix: Applying Euler’s Theorem to the Hicksian Demand

      Let us recall the definition of homogeneity. We say that a function f (x1, x2) is homoge-
      neous of degree k if, when increasing all its arguments by a common factor t > 0, we
      obtain that the value of the function is increased by t k. That is,

                                            f (tx1 , tx2 ) = t k ⋅ f ( x1 , x2 ).                (3A.1)

      31
         The condition that all individuals’ indirect utility function can be represented with the Gorman
      form, however, might be somewhat restrictive. One might wonder, hence, if we can obtain the same
      results using weaker conditions. The literature has shown that we can indeed use weaker conditions
      by assuming that aggregate demand depends on a wider set of variables, such as average wealth
      level, or the variance of the wealth distribution, as shown in Deaton and Muellbauer (1980).
Demand Theory—Applications                                                                                    209



                 Differentiating this expression with respect to x1, we obtain

                                                  ∂f (tx1 , tx2 )           ∂f ( x1 , x2 )
                                                                  ⋅t = tk ⋅                .
                                                      ∂x1                       ∂x1

                 Rearranging and denoting f1(x1, x2) ≡ ∂f(x1, x2) / ∂x1 yields

                                                    f1 ( tx1 , tx2 ) = t k −1 ⋅ f1 ( x1 , x2 ).

                    Hence, if a function is homogeneous of degree k, its first-order derivative must be
                 homogeneous of degree k − 1. This is a useful result that we draw on below. Differen-
                 tiating the left-hand side of expression (3A.1) with respect to the proportionality factor
                 t, we obtain

                                         ∂f (tx1 , tx2 )
                                                         = f1 (tx1 , tx2 ) x1 + f 2 (tx1 , tx2 ) x2 .
                                              ∂t
                 And differentiating the right-hand side yields

                                                ∂(t k ⋅ f ( x1 , x2 ))
                                                                       = k ⋅ t k −1 f ( x1 , x2 ).
                                                         ∂t
                 Therefore we can rewrite expression (3A.1) as
                                       f1 (tx1 , tx2 ) x1 + f 2 (tx1 , tx2 ) x2 = k ⋅ t k −1 f ( x1 , x2 ).

                 And making the proportionality factor t = 1, we obtain

                                          f1 ( x1 , x2 ) x1 + f 2 ( x1 , x2 ) x2 = k ⋅ f ( x1 , x2 ),
                 where k is the degree of homogeneity of the original function f(x1, x2). From this result
                 we can conclude two useful properties:
                 1. If the original function is homogeneous of degree zero, k = 0, the right-hand side of
                    the expression above becomes zero. This result is intuitive: it says that if a function
                    is homogeneous of degree zero, increasing the proportionality factor t will not affect
                    its value.
                 2. If the original function is homogeneous of degree one, k = 1, we obtain that the
                    right-hand side of the expression above is f(x1, x2). Intuitively, if we marginally in-
                    crease the proportionality factor t, the function increases by exactly its initial value
                    f(x1, x2).
210                                                                                       Chapter 3



         We can now apply this result to the Hicksian demand function. We know that the
      Hicksian demand h(p1, p2, … u) is homogeneous of degree zero in prices, meaning k =
      0. That is, h(tp1, tp2, … , u) = h(p1, p2, … , u). Hence

                                   ∂h       ∂h          ∂h
                                       p1 +     p2 + …+     pL = 0.
                                   ∂p1      ∂p2         ∂pL

      Therefore increasing the proportionality factor t by which we multiply all prices does
      not affect the value of the Hicksian demand.

4 Production Theory



    In this chapter we switch our focus from consumer theory (the main topic in previous
    chapters) to production theory. In section 4.1 we define production sets, namely the
    combination of inputs and outputs that are feasible according to a certain technology,
    and in section 4.2 we discuss the properties of production sets. In section 4.3 we
    describe a common measure of how easily firms can modify their input usage (e.g.,
    from labor intensive to capital intensive combinations) and still maintain their current
    production level, namely the elasticity of substitution. We then evaluate such elasticity
    for different types of production functions.
       Section 4.4 presents the firm’s profit-maximization problem (PMP), its result, the
    profit-maximizing production plan (also referred to as the “supply correspondence”),
    and evaluates its properties and comparative statics. Section 4.5 then explores the dual
    of the PMP, the cost-minimization problem (CMP), whereby the firm chooses its input
    combination in order to minimize its costs subject to reaching a certain output level q.
    We analyze the comparative statics of modifying input prices on the firm’s factor de-
    mand. In particular, altering input prices yields a more intensive use of the input that
    became relatively cheaper. However, this describes an overall effect which can be
    separated into a substitution effect (whereby the firm changes its input usage toward
    the relatively cheaper input, while maintaining its output level) and an output effect
    (where the firm increases its output level after the price of one input decreased, and
    still incurs the same total costs as before the input price changed). Sections 4.6 and 4.7
    list some interesting properties of the factor demand function and the cost function,
    such as homogeneity and Shephard’s lemma. Section 4.8 describes the production
    function, section 4.9 presents an alternative approach to the PMP often used by the
    literature, and section 4.10 discusses the firm’s expansion path, that is, how the cost-
    minimizing combination of inputs changes as the firm seeks to produce larger levels of
    output.
       In section 4.11 we focus on the specific case in which the firm produces a single
    output (but can still use different inputs), a common assumption in economic
222                                                                                                   Chapter 4



      applications. Section 4.12 then examines aggregate supply—the sum of the individual
      supply curves of all firms in an industry—and analyzes under which conditions we can
      guarantee that the “law of supply” holds at the aggregate level.1 Finally, section 4.13
      investigates whether a profit-maximizing production plan is necessarily efficient in the
      sense of lying on the frontier of the firm’s production plan, and its converse: whether
      efficient production plans are necessarily profit maximizing. These two results are an
      application to production theory of the first and fundamental theorem of welfare eco-
      nomics. A graphical analysis of total and marginal costs, allowing for fixed, sunk and
      non-sunk costs, is provided in the appendix at the end of the chapter.

      4.1    Production Sets

      Let us define a production plan y = (y1, y2, …, yL) as a vector with L components. If a
      particular component of the vector is positive, it denotes that the firm produces posi-
      tive amounts of that good; for instance, y2 > 0. If instead a component of the y vector
      is negative, it denotes that the firm uses good 2 as an input in its production process.
      We are especially interested in production plans that are technologically feasible, rep-
      resented as part of the production set Y, as follows:

                                            Y = { y ∈  L : F ( y ) ≤ 0}
                                                                 ,
      where F(y) is the transformation function. This function can be intuitively understood
      as a production function, as figure 4.1 illustrates.
         In the production process depicted in figure 4.1, the firm uses units of y1 as input in
      order to produce units of y2 as output. For this reason, in the left-hand side of the figure,
      we observe that y1 < 0 (input) and y2 > 0 (output).2 On the one hand, the boundary of
      the production function indicates production plans for which F(y) = 0. (We also refer
      to this boundary as the “transformation frontier.”) On the other hand, points strictly
      below the transformation frontier indicate (strictly) feasible production plans, since
      F(y) < 0. Therefore we can totally differentiate F(y), as follows:

                    4.2   Properties of Production Sets

                    Let us next describe different properties of production sets. Note that the following
                    properties are not necessarily mutually exclusive.
                    1. Y is nonempty That is, we have inputs and/or outputs. This property is relatively
                       general. For instance, if a firm, despite using large quantities of inputs produces
                       no output, our production set would still be nonempty. This case is illustrated in
                       figure 4.5 where the production set Y is nonempty, despite producing no units of
                       output. (Recall that empty sets contain no elements, so if set Y contains point (0, 0),
                       it is nonempty.)
                    2. Y is closed Hence the production set Y includes its boundary points5.
                    3. No free lunch This property states that the firm must use inputs in order to produce
                       output. In other words, the firm cannot produce outputs without using any inputs.
                       The top panel of figure 4.6 represents a production set that satisfies the “no free
                       lunch” property, since the firm is using amounts of input y1 in order to produce
                       positive amounts of output y2. In contrast, the bottom panels of figure 4.6 illustrate
                       production plans that violate the “no free lunch” property. Note that the firm: (1)

                    4. Possibility of inaction This property states that the firm can choose to be inactive,
                       using no inputs, and obtaining no output as a consequence. In other words, the
                       input–output vector 0 (at the origin of figure 4.7) is part of the production set. At
                       first glance, a firm’s possibility of inaction may seem applicable to many production
                       processes, such as the production set depicted in figure 4.7. However, when firms
                       face sunk costs, this property might be violated, meaning 0 ∉ Y. In particular, if the
                       firm experiences a setup (fixed) cost, as the top panel of figure 4.8 depicts, the firm
                       needs to use an amount of input y1 without obtaining any output y2 in return. Inac-
                       tion, however, is still possible since the origin belongs to the production set, 0 ∈ Y.
                       If the fixed costs that the firm must incur (e.g., setup costs) are sunk, then the firm
                       cannot move toward the origin. For instance, if the firm already signed the purchase
                       of y1 units of input, and cannot renege from such a contract, inaction is not possi-
                       ble, 0 ∉ Y, as the bottom panel of figure 4.8 illustrates.6

      9. Constant returns to scale Take production plan y ∈Y. Then production plan αy
         also belongs to production set Y, for any α ≥ 0. Hence both scaling down an original
         production plan y (when α ∈ [0, 1]) and scaling it up (when α > 1) yields a new
         production plan that still belongs to production set Y. This point is illustrated in
         figure 4.15. Graphically, for a production set Y to satisfy constant returns to scale,
         we need the transformation frontier to be a straight line.13 Another way to interpret
         constant returns to scale is by noticing that production set Y simultaneously satisfies
         both nonincreasing and nondecreasing returns to scale.14

                       Therefore, when α + β = 1, we have constant returns to scale. Importantly, note
                    the strong relationship between returns to scale and homogeneity of the production
                    function. The definition of homogeneity of degree one states that, if we increase all
                    inputs in the same proportion, total output increases by the same proportion. This is
                    exactly what occurs when constant returns to scale are satisfied, α + β = 1. When α +
                    β > 1, we have increasing returns to scale and the production function is homogeneous
                    in a degree larger than one. Finally, when α + β < 1, we have decreasing returns to scale
                    and the production function is homogeneous of degree less than one. Several empirical
                    applications use the Cobb–Douglas production function to test for the presence of in-
                    creasing, decreasing, or constant returns to scale. Table 4.1 presents the sum of expo-
                    nents α + β, separating industries in three groups: those with increasing returns to scale
                    (α + β > 1), constant returns to scale (α + β = 1), and decreasing returns to scale (α + β
                    < 1). For example, doubling all inputs in the tobacco industry implies that output grows
                    less than proportionally (in 1.42), while increasing inputs in a similar fashion in the
                    primary metal industry produces a more-than-proportional increase in output (of
                    2.36).16 ■


                    producing half as much output. In such a context, a market would be more efficiently served by a
                    large firm than by several small firms, thus inducing the regulator to favor mergers between firms. If,
                    in contrast, firms in an industry exhibit decreasing returns to scale, an opposite argument applies, and
                    a market would be more efficiently served by several firms rather than by a large firm.

      Example 4.4: Returns to scale and transformations The linear production func-
      tion exhibits constant returns to scale. Indeed increasing all inputs by a common factor
      t yields f(tK, tL) = atK + btL = t(aK + bL) = t ∙ f(K, L). Similarly the fixed proportion
      production function f(K, L) = min{aK, bL} exhibits constant returns to scale, since
      f(tK, tL) = min{atK, btL} = t ∙ min{aK, bL} = t ∙ f(K, L).
         One interesting property of a production function f (K, L) that exhibits constant
      returns to scale is that we can incorporate increasing or decreasing returns to scale by
      simply using a monotone increasing transformation T( · ) : [0, +∞) → [0, +∞) defined by
      T(x) = xγ, where γ > 0. In particular, let us define

                                         F ( K , L ) = T ( f ( K , L )) = [ f ( K , L) ] .
                                                                                           γ



      Indeed, if we increase all inputs by t, we obtain

                      F(tK, tL) = [f(tK, tL)]γ = [t ∙ f(K, L)]γ = tγ∙ f(tK, tL) = tγ∙F(K, L),

      where the second equality is due to the constant return to scale property of our initial
      production function f(K, L). Then, if γ > 1, the (transformed) production function
      F(K, L) exhibits increasing returns to scale; if γ = 1, it exhibits constant returns to
      scale; and if γ < 1, it exhibits decreasing returns to scale. (The following section pro-
      vides a detailed explanation about the relationship between returns to scale and output
      elasticity.17) ■

      (labor, respectively).

                    Let us now continue with our discussion of the properties that production set Y can
                    satisfy.
                    10. Additivity (or free entry) If production plans y and y′ belong to production set Y,
                        meaning y, y′ ∈ Y, then its sum y + y′ must also belong to Y. That is, if one plant
                        produces y and another plant enters the industry producing y′, then the aggregate
                        production plan y + y′ must be feasible.
                    11. Convexity If two production plans y and y′ belong to production set Y, then
                        their convex combination must also belong to Y. More compactly, if y, y′ ∈ Y,
                        then

                                                           αy + (1 − α)y′ ∈ Y,

                         where α ∈ [0, 1]. The left panel of figure 4.17 illustrates a production set that
                         satisfies convexity. In particular, the convex combination of two production
                         plans y and y′ on the production frontier belongs to production set Y, and so does
                         the convex combination or two production plans that do not belong to the pro-
                         duction frontier. In contrast, the panel on the right reflects a production set that
                         violates convexity. Specifically, the convex combination of two production plans
                         does not necessarily lie within production set Y. The interpretation of convexity
                         is that balanced input–output combinations also belong to the production set Y.
                         Indeed, note that the convex combination of y and y′, αy + (1 − α)y′, produces
                         more output than y′ but less than y, and uses fewer inputs than y but more than

      Convex for production sets with fixed (a) and sunk costs (b)


           y′, namely αy + (1 − α)y′ is a more balanced input–output vector than y and y′
           alone.18
         Figure 4.18 examines convexity for production sets in which the firm incurs
      fixed costs (left figure) or sunk costs (right figure). When the firm incurs fixed costs, a
      convex combination of two production plans yields a new production plan that does
      not necessarily lie in Y. In contrast, when the firm incurs sunk costs, any convex com-
      bination between two production plans lies within production set Y, thus satisfying
      convexity.

      4.2.1    Constant Returns to Scale
      When a production function exhibits constant returns to scale (CRS), an increase in all
      inputs by the same proportion t produces an increase in the firm’s output by the same
      proportion. That is, f(tk, tl) = t∙f(k, l). In words, if the production function exhibits CRS,
      then it must be homogeneous of degree one. In addition we know that if a function is
      homogeneous of degree one, its derivative must be homogeneous of degree zero.
      Hence the marginal product of labor must be homogeneous of degree zero. That is,
                                                ∂f ( k , l ) ∂f (tk , tl )
                                        MPl =               =
                                                   ∂l            ∂l
                                              = fl(k, l) = fl(tk, tl),
      18
         The convexity of the production set maintains a close relationship with the concavity of the pro-
      duction function. Indeed a concave production function yields a production frontier similar to that in
      the left panel of figure 4.18, implying a convex production set Y.
Production Theory                                                                                                      243




                    Figure 4.19
                    Homothetic production function


                    and if we set the productivity factor t, so that t =1 / l, we obtain MPl = fl(k, l) = fl(k / l, 1).
                    Therefore, when the firm’s production function exhibits CRS, the marginal product of
                    labor only depends on the ratio of capital to labor, but not on the absolute levels of
                    capital and labor used by the firm. A similar argument can be extended to the marginal
                    product of capital. Likewise the ratio of the marginal products MRTSl,k = MPl/MPk only
                    depends on the ratio of capital to labor, and not on the absolute levels of capital and
                    labor. Graphically, this implies that the slope of a firm’s isoquants coincides at any
                    point along a ray from the origin.19 This occurs, in particular, when the firm’s produc-
                    tion function is homothetic.20 We illustrate this property in figure 4.19.

      4.3     Elasticity of Substitution

      4.3.1     Motivation and Definition


         Elasticity of substitution The elasticity of substitution measures the propor-
         tionate change in the k/l ratio relative to the proportionate change in the MRTSl,k
         along an isoquant. That is,

                                     σ =  %∆  (%∆MRTSl ,k )
                                              k
                                             l
Production Theory                                                                                         245



                    For convex isoquants, the value of the elasticity of substitution is positive because a
                    decrease (increase) in the k/l ratio decreases (increases) the slope of the isoquant. In-
                    deed, if we move rightward along an isoquant toward higher amounts of labor, the ratio
                    k/l decreases and the isoquant becomes flatter (reducing MRTSl,k). The opposite argu-
                    ment applies when we move toward higher amounts of capital. This is illustrated in
                    figure 4.20, whereby a movement from point A to B reduces the ratio k/l and also the
                    slope of the isoquant, measured by MRTSl,k. Therefore the elasticity of substitution
                    provides a measure about which magnitude (k/l ratio or MRTSl,k) changes the most in
                    percentage terms.
                       If, as depicted in the figure, the elasticity of substitution is high, the MRTSl,k does
                    not substantially changes relative to k/l, that is, the denominator σ is a number close
                    to zero whereas the numerator significantly changes. This occurs when the isoquants
                    are relatively flat, implying that capital and labor are easily interchangeable in the
                    production process. While the ratio k/l changes, the slope of the isoquant remains
                    almost unaffected.
                       Conversely, if the elasticity of substitution is low, the MRTSl,k substantially changes
                    relative to k/l. This occurs when the slope of the isoquant changes significantly when
                    we alter the input combination. Figure 4.21 illustrates an isoquant with a low elasticity
                    of substitution.




                    Figure 4.20
                    High elasticity of substitution

      Low elasticity of substitution


      Example 4.5: Elasticity of substitution for different production functions Let us
      evaluate the elasticity of substitution in a few parametric examples. Starting with the
      linear production function q = f(k, l) = ak + bl, note that its isoquants are straight lines
      (so their slope is constant for all amounts of labor, and hence, for all k/l ratios). Indeed,
      solving for k in production function q = ak+ bl yields an isoquant k = (q / a) − (b / a) / l,
      with slope, −b / a, which is constant in labor. Figure 4.22a illustrates a linear production
      function in which labor and capital are perfect substitutes in the production process.
      Importantly, this implies that the MRTSl,k is constant in k/l, and hence the elasticity of
      substitution yields an infinitely large number, σ = ∞.21
         Let us next examine the other polar case in which both inputs must be used in
      fixed proportions, as q = min{ak, bl}, where a, b > 0. In this case the MRTSl,k changes
      dramatically from infinite (for labor amounts below the kink of the isoquant, as de-
      picted in figure 4.22b) to zero (for labor amounts beyond the kink). This implies that
      the change in the MRTSl,k is infinite, yielding as a consequence a zero elasticity of
      substitution, namely σ = 0.22

                    4.4   Profit Maximization

                    Let us now analyze the profit-maximization problem and its dual, the cost-minimization
                    problem. We will henceforth assume that firms are price takers, implying that the pro-
                    duction plans of every individual firm do not alter market prices p. (This assumption
                    holds for both output and inputs, implying that the firm’s share in the product and input
                    market is negligible.) In addition, we will assume that the production set is nonempty
                    and closed, and satisfies free disposal. (For generality, we do not impose specific con-
                    ditions on convexity or returns to scale, but we comment on these properties later.) In
                    particular, the profit-maximization problem (PMP) for the firm is to choose a produc-
                    tion plan y that solves

                                                       max p ⋅ y subject to y∈Y,
                                                         y

                                                  or alternatively, subject to F(y) ≤ 0,

                    where F(y) is the transformation function describing the set of feasible production
                    plans that the firm can produce given its technology.25 The production plan that solves
                    this PMP is the firm’s “supply correspondence” y(p). The value function resulting from
                    24
                       For instance, Kemfert (1998) estimates the elasticity of substitution for different German indus-
                    tries and observes that inputs cannot be easily substituted in the chemical industry (while maintaining
                    constant output), but they can be in other sectors, such as the food industry.
                    25
                      Recall that, since we consider production plans that embody output and inputs, we can express the
                    overall profits of the firm as py, without the need to explicitly include a cost function.

                    this maximization problem, π(p), denoted as the “profit function” of the firm, describes
                    for every price p the highest amount of profits, chosen by the profit-maximizing pro-
                    duction plan y(p). More formally, we can define the profit function as

                                                         Pi(p) = p ⋅ y ( p ) ,
                    that is, the firm’s profit evaluated at y = y(p).
                       Hence, the supply correspondence y(p) can be represented with the help of the
                    profit function as follows: y(p) = {y ∈ Y : p · y = π(p)}. In words, a supply correspon-
                    dence is the set of feasible production plans that yield the same profits as Pi(p) does.
                       Positive components in the supply correspondence y(p) reflect the outputs that this
                    firm supplies to the market, while negative components are inputs in its production
                    process. Figure 4.24 illustrates the profit-maximization problem.
                       First, in addition to the firm’s production set Y, we depict the firm’s isoprofit lines.
                    Intuitively, an isoprofit line represents the combinations of inputs and output for which
                    the firm obtains a given level of profits, for instance, 1 million dollars, for a given price
                    vector p. If the firm uses a larger amount of inputs, it should also obtain a larger
                    amount of output to be sold in the market in order to maintain its profit level. Graphi-
                    cally, this implies that isoprofit lines have a negative slope. For an amount of input
                    y1 and an output y2, the isoprofit line that reaches a profit of π0 dollars is π0 = p2 y2 − p1
                    y1. Solving for y2 yields

         Hence the slope of the isoprofit line is given by the price ratio −p1 / p2.26 Because
      larger profits are associated to higher isoprofit lines, that is, an increase in π0 raises the
      vertical intercept of the isoprofit line, π0 / p2, graphically the isoprofit lines shift in the
      northeast direction. Therefore the firm increases its isoprofit line as far as possible
      (maximizing profits) by moving it in the northeast direction, and selects the production
      plan that is technologically feasible according to production set Y. In the example
      above, this occurs at point y(p), where the upper boundary of the production set Y is
      tangent to the isoprofit line associated to profit level π(p). Hence the firm chooses sup-
      ply correspondence y(p), which reaches a profit level of π(p).27

      4.4.1   Unconditional Factor Demand
      Recall that the argmax of the PMP above is a vector of inputs (z1, z2) that maximize the
      firm’s profits for a given price vector (p, w), that is,

                                          z ( w , p ) = ( z1 ( w , p ) , z2 ( w , p) ) .
      Importantly, this vector is independent of output q because the firm’s output in the
      PMP can be immediately found by plugging z(w, p) in production function q = f(z),
      which yields f(z(w, p)). Hence, since input demand z(w, p) is not a function of a
      specific production level y, we refer to it as “unconditional factor demand.” In sum-
      mary, the supply correspondence y(p) lists both the firm’s demand for inputs at the
      PMP and the resulting output, y(p) = (z(w, p), f(z(w, p))), as the following example
      illustrates:

      Example 4.7: Comparative statics on factor demand and the supply correspon-
      dence Consider a firm with production function y = f(z, e), where z denotes units of
      input, and e represents any external element that negatively impacts the firm’s produc-
      tion (e.g., pollution), where the first-order derivatives of f with respect to z and e are
      fz ≥ 0 and fe ≤ 0. The firm’s PMP is

                                                  max pf ( z , e ) − wz .
                                                      z ≥0

      Taking the first-order condition with respect to input z yields

                                    pf z − w ≤ 0             (= 0 in interior solutions).
Production Theory                                                                                             257



                       For this first-order condition to be sufficient, we need pfzz ≤ 0. Since p > 0 by defini-
                    tion, we require that fzz ≤ 0, that is, a diminishing marginal product of input z. From this
                    first-order condition, we obtain the unconditional input demand z(w, p, e), which de-
                    pends on input and output prices as well as the external effect e.
                       In order to analyze conditions under which the unconditional factor demand
                    z(w, p, e) decreases in e, let us differentiate again the first-order condition above with
                    respect to z :

                                                          ( pf zz ) dz + ( pf ze ) de = 0.
                    We can finally rearrange, (fzz)dz = −(fze)de, and solve for ∂z(w, p, e) / ∂e, as follows:

                                                            ∂z ( w , p, e)     f
                                                                           = − ze .
                                                                  ∂e           f zz

                      Therefore, since fzz ≤ 0 for sufficiency (i.e., for profits to be concave in z), the sign
                    of ∂z(w, p, e) / ∂e coincides with that of fze. For instance, if fze < 0 (which occurs when
                    the firm’s marginal product fz is decreasing in e, such as pollution), the profit-
                    maximizing z(w, p, e) decreases in e. (An opposite argument applies if fze > 0, but that
                    case is more difficult to justify, since it would indicate that marginal product
                    increases in pollution.)

      4.4.2  Profit Function
      Let us next describe some properties of the profit function, π(p). Assume for the
      remainder of this section that the production set Y is closed and satisfies the free
      disposal property:
      1. Homogeneity The profit function π(p) is homogeneous of degree one in prices.
         That is, increasing the prices of all inputs and outputs by the same factor λ pro-
         duces a proportional increase in the firm’s profits, π(λp) = λπ(p). To see this result,
         recall that the profit function can be expressed as π(p) = p · q − w · z, where all L in-
         puts (in vector z) and the output q are evaluated at their profit-maximizing amounts.
         Scaling all prices by a common factor λ, we obtain
                                      λp · q − λw · z = λ(p · q − w · z) = λ · π(p),
           which shows that the firm’s profit increases in the same proportion (λ) as input and
           output prices, thus implying that homogeneity of degree one holds.30
      2. Convex in price The profit function π(p) is convex. Figure 4.26 describes
         this property. For a price vector p, the profit-maximizing production plan is y(p),
         yielding an associated profit function π(p). Similarly, for a price vector p′, the profit-
         maximizing production plan is y(p′), with associated profits of π(p′).31 An interme-
         diate price vector p=αp+(1− α)p′ entails y( p) and profits π( p).32
      30
         In most of the presentation, we use p to denote the vector of input–output prices. In a slight abuse
      of notation, however, we sometimes use p to denote the output price.
      31
         Since the slope of the isoprofit lines is w / p, a steeper isoprofit line (e.g., that associated with price
      vector p) indicates more expensive inputs, relative to the price of output, while vector p′ illustrates
      the opposite.
      32
         As a practice, take a Cobb–Douglas production function with only one input (labor), q = l , and
      consider two price vectors, p = (pl, pq) = (8, 6) and p′ = (8, 12). Find y(p) and its associated profit
      function π(p); then find y(p′) and π(p′). Finally, construct a convex combination of the previous
      prices, p = α p + (1 − α ) p ′ , find the supply correspondence y( p ), and show that the resulting profit
      function π ( p ) satisfies π ( p ) > max{π ( p), π ( p′)}. An alternative, more direct, proof just requires you
      to show that δ2π(p)/δp2 > 0. Graphically, profits must increase in p at an increasing rate.

                    Figure 4.26
                    Convexity in output price


                    3. Alternative representation If the production set Y is convex, then

                                                Y = { y ∈  L : py ≤ π ( p ) for all p  0}
                    Intuitively, the production set Y can be alternatively represented by this “dual” set. It
                    specifies that, for any given price vector p, all production vectors y generate less profit
                    p·y than the profit-maximizing production plan y(p), which entails a profit function
                    π(p) = py(p). A graphical representation of this property is provided in figure 4.27. As
                    the figure shows, in a convex production set Y, the supply correspondence y(p) maxi-
                    mizes profits, and the associated isoprofit line is π = pq − wz. Since all production plans
                    (z, q) below this isoprofit line yield a lower profit level for the firm, pq – wz ≤ π(p).
                    Alternatively, the isoprofit line π = pq – wz can be represented by
                                                                     π       w
                                                                q=       −     z.
                                                                     p       p

                    If the price vector w/p is constant, meaning input (output) price are unaffected by dif-
                    ferent levels of input usage (or different levels of output sales, respectively), then the
                    slope of the isoprofit line is constant in z. Therefore the set of (z, q)-pairs below profit
                    function π(p) define a convex set. (The convex combination of any two points (z, q)
                    and (z′, q′) is on or below the isoprofit line, i.e., lies within the set.33)

                    33
                      If, however, input prices (w) and/or output prices (p) are not constant, we might have that the price
                    vector is not constant, implying a nonconvex set of (z, q)-pairs for which pq – wz ≤ π(q).

        The profit function can be understood as a support function. In particular, let us first
      take the negative of the production set Y, –Y. We can define the support function of this
      –Y set as

                                        μ–Y(p)= min { p ⋅ ( − y ) : y ∈Y } .
                                                     y
         The support function first evaluates the profits resulting from all production vectors
      y ∈Y, py; second, it takes the negative of this list of profits, p(−y), one for each produc-
      tion vector y; and finally, the support function chooses the lowest of this negative
      profits. Of course, this procedure yields the same result as maximizing the positive
      value of the profits from all possible production vectors y ∈ Y, py.34 Therefore the
      profit function π(p) is the support function of the negative production set –Y, that is,
      π(p) = μ-Y(p). The representation of the profit function as a support function allows us
      to “equivalently” represent the production set using the support function. We do
      that in figure 4.28. First, note that production set Y is convex. Therefore, for a given

      ment that minimizes –f(x), then x*1= x*2.

                    price vector p, we find the supply correspondence y(p) resulting from solving the PMP
                    at prices p. We obtain an associated profit function π(p). We can then take all produc-
                    tion plans y for which profits are lower, that is, {y : p · y ≤ π(p)}.
                       Graphically, this set includes all production plans below the isoprofit line associated
                    with y(p) in figure 4.28. For a different price vector p′, we can similarly find the supply
                    correspondence y(p′) resulting from solving the PMP, which yields a profit function
                    π(p′). We can now take all production plans y yielding a lower profit {y : p′ · y ≤ π(p′)}.
                    Graphically, the set considers all production plans below the isoprofit line associated
                    with y(p′), which contains an overlap region with the set described above for price vec-
                    tor p. If we repeat this process for any other price vector p, we can define infinitely
                    many sets whose overlap exactly coincides with the area of production set Y, since Y is
                    a convex set. The representation of the profit function as a support function therefore
                    allows us to “equivalently describe” production set Y.

                    4.4.3   Supply Correspondence
                    Let us now describe the properties of the supply correspondence y(p).
                    1. Convex production set Y If the production set Y is weakly convex, then the supply
                       correspondence y(p) is a convex set for all p. If Y is strictly convex, then the supply
                       correspondence y(p) is single valued (if nonempty).
                         In figure 4.29a the production set is weakly convex, thus exhibiting a flat surface
                       of tangency with the isoprofit line associated to the highest profit level. Therefore
                       we can identify the set of supply correspondences that generate the highest profit for
262                                                                   Chapter 4



      a.




      b.




      Figure 4.29
      Production set Y is weakly convex (a) and strictly convex (b)
Production Theory                                                                                                        263



                         the firm. Intuitively, the firm manager is indifferent along the input–output combi-
                         nations within the y(p) region of tangency between the isoprofit line and the produc-
                         tion set, since all these combinations yield the same profit. Such a set of supply
                         correspondences is, of course, convex, since a convex combination between any
                         two production plans in the y(p)-region also lies within that region.
                            If the production set Y is strictly convex, as figure 4.29b illustrates, then the tan-
                         gency condition between the isoprofit line and the production set is a single point.
                         Therefore, in this case, the supply correspondence y(p) is single-valued.
                    2. Hotelling’s lemma If the supply correspondence y( p) consists of a single point,
                       then the profit function π(·) is differentiable at p. Moreover such a derivative yields
                       ∇ pπ ( p ) = y ( p ) .
                         This lemma is an immediate application of the duality theorem that we described
                       in consumer theory. (Exercise 8 at the end of the chapter asks you to prove
                       Hotelling’s lemma using duality.35)
                       If the supply correspondence y(p) is differentiable at p , then its derivative Dy( p) =
                    D2π( p) is a symmetric and positive semidefinite matrix with Dy( p) p = 0. This prop-
                    erty has two immediate consequences. First, since matrix Dy( p) is symmetric, the
                    cross-substitution effects (the elements outside the matrix diagonal) are symmetric.
                    That is,
                                                    ∂yl ( p ) ∂yk ( p )
                                                             =              for all l and k.
                                                     ∂pk        ∂pl

                    Second, Dy( p) p = 0 implies that the elements in the main diagonal of matrix Dy( p)
                    are nonnegative. Recall that the elements in the main diagonal of this matrix describe
                    own substitution effects. We therefore have
                                                           ∂yk ( p )
                                                                     ≥0     for all k.
                                                            ∂pk

                    Importantly, nonnegative own substitution effects imply that quantities and prices
                    move in the same direction, that is,
                                                            (p − p′)(y − y′) ≥ 0.

                    35
                       Exercise 6 at the end of the chapter provides a functional form for the profit function π(p), and asks

      Figure 4.30
      Law of supply


      This implies that the supply function of the firm is positively sloped, as figure 4.30
      indicates. That is, the “law of supply” holds.
        In particular, since in the PMP there is no budget constraint, there are no wealth
      compensation requirements, as opposed to demand theory. This implies that there are
      no income effects, only substitution effects.36 Alternatively, from a revealed preference
      perspective, the law of supply can be expressed as

                           ( p − p′ ) ⋅ ( y − y ′ ) = ( py − py ′ ) + ( p′y ′ − p′y ) ≥ 0,
      where the first term in parentheses, (py− py′), is positive, since, for a given price
      vector p, production plan y is profit maximizing, and thus py ≥ py′ for any y′ ≠ y.
      Similarly, the second term in parenthesis, (p′y′−p′y), is also positive because, for a
      given price vector p′, production plan y′ is profit maximizing, entailing that p′y′ ≥ p′y
      for any y ≠ y′. Since the terms in both sets of parentheses are positive, their sum must
      be also positive, and hence(p − p′) · (y − y′) > 0.

      4.5   Cost Minimization

      We now turn to analyze the combination of inputs (vector z) that the firm selects in
      order to minimize its total cost of production, conditional on reaching a particular

      36
         We return to this issue when analyzing the cost-minimizing problem for the firm, where we de-
      scribe it in more detail.
Production Theory                                                                                                 265




                    Figure 4.31
                    Cost minimization


                    output level q. For simplicity, we focus on the single output case, where z is the input
                    vector, q = f(z) reflects the production function, and w >> 0 is the vector of input prices
                    (positive in all components). The cost-minimization problem (CMP) can therefore be
                    stated as follows (we assume free disposal of output):

                                                     min wz subject to f ( z ) ≥ q.
                                                      z ≥0

                    In words, the firm selects a vector of inputs, z, that minimizes total costs, wz, subject
                    to the production of at least q units of output, f(z) ≥ q. The cost-minimizing vector
                    of inputs is denoted z(w, q), and it is usually referred to as the conditional factor de-
                    mand correspondence (or conditional factor demand function if it is single valued).37
                    Intuitively, z(w, q) reflects the optimal demand of inputs when the firm faces input
                    prices w and seeks to reach a production level q, that is, a given isoquant. Figure 4.31
                    provides a graphical representation of the CMP for a firm producing output using two
                    inputs, z1 and z2.
                       First, the input combinations on or above isoquant f (z) = q are technologically
                    feasible, since they satisfy the output constraint, f(z) ≥ q; however, those below the
                    isoquant are not, since they reach a lower output level, f(z) < q. Therefore the CMP can
                    be summarized as: “for input combinations along a given isoquant f(z) = q, choose the
                    input combination associated to the lowest cost, wz, that is, in the isocost line closest

                    37
                      The term “conditional” in this expression emphasizes the fact that z(w, q) represents the firm’s

      to the origin.” At input combination z(w, q) the firm cannot reduce its costs any further
      and still produce output level q. At this input combination, the firm’s costs are wz =
      c(w, q), as depicted in figure 4.31.38 Therefore the input combination that minimizes
      costs is z(w, q), and the isocost line associated with that combination of inputs is {z: wz
      = c(w, q)}, where c(w, q) represents the lowest cost of producing output level q when
      input prices are w, and it is usually referred to as the cost function.39 Graphically, at
      the cost-minimizing input combination z(w, q), the firm’s isoquant curve is tangent to
      the isocost line.

      Note that the Lagrange multiplier λ can be interpreted as the cost increase that the firm

      multiplier is the marginal cost of production; the marginal increase in the firm’s mini-
      mal costs from producing an additional unit of output.

      4.5.1    Comparative Statics of z(w, q)
      In minimizing production costs, we are also interested in examining how the condi-
      tional factor demand correspondence z(w, q) is affected by changes in input prices. For
      simplicity, we consider two inputs, labor and capital. When the price of labor, w, falls,
      two effects occur:
      1. A substitution effect If output is held constant (the firm produces along the same
         isoquant), there will be a tendency for the firm to substitute labor for capital in the
         production process, since labor became relatively cheaper.
      2. An output effect A change in the price of labor, w, reduces firm’s costs, allowing
         it to produce larger amounts of output, which entails the use of more units of both
         labor and capital.
        Let us first provide a graphical intuition behind these two effects and subsequently
      describe them mathematically. Figure 4.33 sequentially illustrates the substitution ef-
      fect associated to a wage decrease.
           First step: Starting from an initial cost-minimizing input combination z0(w, q), a
              reduction in wages produces an outward pivoting effect on the firm’s isocost line
              associated with cost level c(w, q).43
           Second step: The firm is not cost minimizing if it selects a point along the new
             isocost. It can then reduce its total costs (graphically, pushing the new isocost
             inward in a parallel fashion) until it reaches a tangency point with the isoquant
             (recall that producing f(z) = q is the constraint of the CMP).

      42
         Recall that, generally, the Lagrange multiplier represents the change in the value function of a
      given optimization problem if we relax the constraint, such as the change of wealth level in the UMP,
      the utility level that must be reached in the EMP, or the quantity level q that the firm must reach in
      the CMP that we study in this chapter.
      43
         The isocost associated to the cost-minimizing input combination z(w, q) = (l(w, q), k(w, q)) must
      incur a cost level c(w, q) = wl(w, q) + rk(w, q), where l(w, q) denotes the cost-minimizing amount of
      labor and k(w, q) that of capital. A reduction in w therefore pivots the isocost line outward, as de-
      picted in figure 4.34.
Production Theory                                                                                                         269




                    Figure 4.33
                    Substitution effect in production


                       At the new cost-minimizing input combination z1(w, q) the firm is selecting the input
                    combination that minimizes total costs (at the new input prices), but the firm still
                    reaches output level q. That is, z1(w, q) solves the new CMP for the firm after the
                    change in input prices. Comparing the cost-minimizing input combinations before and
                    after the fall in w, z0(w, q) and z1(w, q), we can observe that the firm uses more labor
                    (the factor of production that became relatively cheaper) and less capital (the input that
                    became relatively more expensive).
                       We can therefore conclude that the substitution effect is negative: a decrease in the
                    price of one input increases the firm’s demand (use) of precisely that input.44 There is,
                    however, another effect associated to a decrease in the price of labor: the firm can now
                    reach a higher output level incurring the same total costs as before the change in input
                    prices. We refer to this effect as the “output effect,” and figure 4.34 represents it.
                       Starting from the cost-minimizing input combination after the price change (denoted
                    as C in the figure), we can observe that the firm is able to reach a higher isoquant
                    f(z) = q1 incurring the same total costs as before the price change. Specifically, the
                    isocost passing through input combination A (at old input prices) and that passing
                    through C (at new input prices) are equally costly. We can hence decompose the

                    44
                       As in the substitution effect in consumer theory, this negative substitution effect is a consequence of
                    the diminishing MRTS (isoquants become flatter as we increase labor in figure 4.34).
270                                                                                    Chapter 4




      Figure 4.34
      Output effect


      increase in labor demand associated to a reduction in labor prices into two effects. On
      one hand, a “substitution effect” (measured by the increase in labor demand from LA to
      LB in the horizontal axis), which occurs if the firm still produces the same amount as
      before the price change (in isoquant q0); on the other hand, an “output effect” (mea-
      sured by the increase in labor demand from LB to LC) occurs if the firm increases its
      output level while incurring the same total costs as before the price change. The sum
      of these two effects reflects the total effect of a decrease in wages on labor demand. Let
      us now mathematically represent substitution and output effects, first for own-price
      effects, and second for cross-price effects across different inputs.

      4.5.2   Own-Price Effects
      Let zl(w, q) denote the conditional demand for labor (where “conditional” refers to the
      fact that the firm reaches output q), and let zl(w) denote the “unconditional” demand for
      labor (which depends on the market price for output and on input prices but does not
      depend on a particular output level q). Recall that, while zl(w, q) solves the CMP where
      the firm targets an output level q, zl(w) solves the PMP. We know that at the
Production Theory                                                                                          271



                    profit-maximizing output level, q = q(p, w), both the conditional and unconditional
                    demand for labor must coincide. That is,

                                                       zl(w) = zl(w, q(p, w)).

                    Differentiating with respect to w yields
                                              ∂zl ( w ) ∂zl ( w , q ) ∂zl ( w , q ) ∂q
                                                       =             +             ⋅    .
                                                ∂w         ∂w             ∂q         ∂w
                                                                          
                                                        Substitution effect   Output effect


                       As indicated above, a reduction in wages produces an increase in the demand for
                    labor when the firm maintains its production level unaffected. This increase in labor
                    demand is captured by the substitution effect. Nonetheless, a reduction in the price of
                    labor allows the firm to increase production (reach a higher isoquant), dq/dw < 0, and
                    in turn, an increase in production is associated to an increase in the demand for labor,
                    dzl(w, q)/dq > 0. As a result the output effect is also negative, reinforcing the substitu-
                    tion effect. Hence the unconditional labor demand zl(w) must be negatively sloped.
                    Figure 4.35 illustrates the conditional and unconditional labor demands. The reduction
                    in wages produces a relatively small increase in labor demand if output is held fixed at
                    q1, moving from A to B along the conditional labor demand zl(w, q1), as measured by




                    Figure 4.35
                    Conditional and unconditional labor demand
272                                                                                                      Chapter 4



      the substitution effect. This increase is reinforced by the output effect, since the firm is
      now capable of reaching a higher production level q2. The total effect, moving from A
      to C, is hence captured by the unconditional labor demand zl(w). Note that, because the
      total effect is larger than the substitution effect, the unconditional labor demand must
      be flatter (more responsive to a given change in wages) than the conditional labor
      demand.
         Hence not only the substitution effect but also the output effect is negative.45 As
      a consequence the so-called Giffen paradox we described in consumer theory cannot
      arise in production theory. The total effect of a given decrease in input prices will result
      in an unambiguous increase in input usage, and graphically in a positively sloped
      supply curve.

      4.5.3    Cross-Price Effects
      Let us now turn into the cross-price effects associated to a reduction in the price of one
      input. In particular, the cross-price total effect of a variation in w on the firm’s demand
      for capital, zk(w), can be measured as follows:
                                      ∂z k ( w ) ∂z k ( w , q ) ∂z k ( w , q ) ∂q
                                                =              +              ⋅    .
                                        ∂w           ∂w              ∂q         ∂w

        Unlike in the case of own-price effects, we cannot make a precise prediction about
      the overall sign of cross-price effects. On one hand, after a fall in wages the firm will
      substitute labor for capital (since the latter became relatively more expensive). As a
      consequence the cross-price substitution effect is positive, ∂zk(w, q) / ∂w > 0. On the
      other hand, the output effect we described above induces the firm to demand more
      capital as it expands production. This implies that the cross-price effect of output is
      negative, since δq / δw < 0,
                                                 ∂z k ( w , q ) ∂q
                                                               ⋅    < 0.
                                                      ∂q         ∂w

      45
          In particular, the output effect (∂zl(w, q) / ∂q) · (∂q / ∂w) can be expressed as (∂zl(w,
      q) / ∂q) · (∂2π(p) / ∂w∂p), which in turn can be alternatively represented as (∂zl(w, q) / ∂q) · (−∂z(w) / ∂p)
      by Hotelling’s lemma. This expression can also be rewritten as −(∂zl(w, q) / ∂q)2(∂q / ∂p) from the fact
      that zl(w) = zl(w, q(p, w)) at the profit-maximizing output level q(p, w). Finally, this expression can
      also be represented as −(∂zl(w, q) / ∂q)2(∂2π(p) / ∂p2) from Hotelling’s lemma. Since the first term,
      −(∂zl(w, q) / ∂q)2 is clearly negative, and the second term, ∂2π(p) / ∂q2, is negative by the convexity of
      the profit function in output prices, the overall sign of the output effect becomes negative.
Production Theory                                                                                                    273




                    Figure 4.36
                    Cross-price substitution and output effects in production


                       Therefore we cannot conclude whether the positive cross-price substitution effect
                    dominates the negative output effect (implying that the cross-price total effect is posi-
                    tive) or whether, instead, the cross-price output effect dominates the substitution effect
                    (in which case the cross-price total effect is negative).46
                       Figure 4.36 illustrates these results: first, the compensated capital demand zk(w, q)
                    is positively sloped (increases in w) for any given output level q1 or q2. Intuitively,
                    a decrease in wages induces the firm to use more labor and less capital, for a given
                    output level q, implying a movement from point A to B along the compensated capital
                    demand curve zk(w, q1). After the reduction in wages, however, the firm decides
                    to increase output, from q1 to q2, thereby increasing the demand for capital from
                    zk(w, q1) to zk(w, q2). That is, the movement from B to C illustrates the cross-price
                    output effect. In the left panel, the positive cross-price output effect completely offsets
                    the negative cross-price substitution effect, leading to a positive cross-price total
                    effect. As a consequence the unconditional factor demand for capital, zk(w), is
                    negatively sloped in the price of labor, w. In contrast, in the right panel, the (positive)
                    cross-price output effect only partially offsets the (negative) cross-price substitution
                    effect, entailing a negative cross-price total effect. Ultimately, this implies an uncondi-
                    tional demand for capital that increases in w (positively slopped).

                    46
                       For a parametric example of the substitution and output effects, see Nicholson and Snyder (2012:
                    379–80). In particular, the example considers a firm experiencing an increase in wages that produces
                    a reduction in labor demand, but also a decrease in capital demand due to a substantial negative out-
                    put effect that totally offsets the positive cross-price substitution effect.
