      4.6   Cost Function

      Let us next examine the properties of the cost function c(w, q), which is the value func-
      tion of the CMP. If the production set Y is closed and satisfies the free disposal prop-
      erty, then:
      1. Cost function c(w, q) is homogeneous of degree one in input prices w, c(λw, q) =
         λc(w, q) for any λ > 0. That is, increasing all input prices by a common factor λ
         induces a proportional increase in the minimal cost of production. As figure 4.37
         illustrates, an increase in all input prices (w1, w2) by the same proportion λ produces
         a parallel downward shift in the firm’s isocost line. Since the firm seeks to reach
         isoquant f(z) = q (it must still satisfy the constraint of the CMP), it needs to incur
         larger costs (shifting its isocost upward) until it reaches f(z) = q.47
      2. Cost function c(w, q) is nondecreasing in output. Intuitively, producing higher out-
         put levels entails a weakly higher minimal cost of production. Figure 4.38 illustrates
         this property, where the firm incurs a minimal cost c(w, q0) when producing output
         level q0, but needs to incur a higher cost c(w, q1) when producing q1, where q1 > q0,
         that is, c(w, q1) > c(w, q0).48

      47
        This property is analogous to homogeneity of degree zero of the expenditure function e(p, u) in the
      consumer’s expenditure-minimization problem (EMP).
      48
         This property also resembles the fact that the expenditure function e(p,u) resulting from the EMP
      in consumer theory increases in the utility level that the consumer seeks to reach, u.
Production Theory                                                                                          275




                    Figure 4.38
                    Cost function c(w, q) that is nondecreasing in output


                    3. Set {z: f(z) ≥ q} is convex for every output level q. The production set can then be
                       equivalently described as

                                            Y = {(−z, q): wz ≥ c(w, q) for every w ≫ 0}.

                      Figure 4.39 illustrates this property. First, consider a given isoquant f(z) = q. Next,
                    for input prices w = (w1, w2), we find the cost function c(w, q) by solving the CMP.
                    We do that at input combination z(w, q) in the left of the figure, with associated cost
                    function c(w, q). For completeness, we also depict input combinations that are more
                    costly than z(w, q), wz ≥ c(w, q), lying above the isocost line {z : wz = (w, q)}. We can
                    now repeat this process for other input prices w′ = (w1′, w2′): first finding the cost-
                    minimizing input vector z(w′, q) and then its associated cost function c(w′, q). If we
                    repeat this process for infinitely many vectors of input prices, the intersection of the
                    sets of “more costly” input combinations, wz ≥ c(w, q), for every input price vector
                    w >> 0, would coincide with (equivalently describe) set f(z) ≥ q.

                    4.7   Conditional Factor Demand Correspondence, z(w, q)

                    If the production set Y is closed and satisfies the free disposal property, then the condi-
                    tional factor of demand correspondence, z(w, q), satisfies the following properties:
276                                                                                              Chapter 4




      Figure 4.39
      Duality in cost minimization


      1. The conditional factor demand correspondence z(w, q) is homogeneous of degree
         zero in input prices, w, z(λw, q) = z(w, q).
         In words, an increase in all input prices by the same factor λ does not alter the firm’s
         demand for inputs. We provide a graphical representation of this property in figure
         4.40. In particular, the firm initially chooses the cost-minimizing input vector z(w,
         q). When all inputs become more expensive, the firm’s isocost line shifts downward
         (in a parallel fashion, since the ratio of input prices has not been modified). How-
         ever, since the firm still needs to reach output level q, it must shift the isocost line
         upward until reaching isoquant f(z) = q again. This, however, implies incurring larg-
         er costs, as described in our discussion of the cost function. Importantly, since the
         relative input prices have not changed, the tangency between the isoquant and iso-
         cost occurs at the same input combination, and therefore z(w, q) is unaffected by a
         common change in all input prices.49
      2. If the set {z: f(z) ≥ q} is strictly convex, then the firm’s demand correspondence z(w,
         q) is single valued. In addition, if the set {z: f(z) ≥ q} is weakly convex, then the
         demand correspondence z(w, q) is a convex set.
         These two properties are illustrated in figure 4.41. In the left panel, where set {z: f(z)
         ≥ q} is strictly convex, a unique combination of inputs is cost minimizing, and
         therefore the demand correspondence z(w, q) is single valued. However, where set

        This lemma is a direct application of the duality theorem described in previous
        chapters, where the cost function c(w, q) serves as the support function of the closed
        and convex set {z : wz = c(w, q)} of input combinations that are more costly than that
        solving the CMP, z(w, q).
      4. If z(w, q) is differentiable at w , then Dw2 c(w , q) = Dw z( w , q) is a symmetric and
         negative semidefinite (NSD) matrix, with Dw z( w , q) w = 0.
         First, matrix Dwz( w , q) represents how the firm’s demand for every input responds
         to changes in the price of such input (captured by the elements along the main di-
         agonal of the matrix), or in the price of other inputs (reflected by the elements away
         from the main diagonal). Therefore this matrix being negative semidefinite implies
         that the elements along the main diagonal must be negative (or zero). That is, own-
         substitution effects are weakly negative
                                    ∂z k ( w , q )
                                                   ≤0   for every input k.
                                        ∂wk

      Intuitively, an increase in the price of input k (e.g., higher wages) implies a reduction
      in the demand for this input (less workers being hired).
         Second, the fact that matrix Dwz( w , q) is symmetric implies that cross-substitution
      effects are symmetric. That is,

                                           ∂z k ( w , q ) ∂zl ( w , q )
                                                         =
                                               ∂wl           ∂w k
      for any two inputs k and l.

      4.8   Production Function, f(z)

      If the production set Y is closed and satisfies the free disposal, then the production
      function satisfies the following properties:
      1. If the production function f(z) is homogeneous of degree one (it exhibits constant
         returns to scale), then the cost function c(w, q) and the conditional factor demand
         correspondence, z(w, q), are both homogeneous of degree one in output, c(w, λq) =
         λc(w, q) and z(w, λq) = λz(w, q).
         Intuitively, if the production function exhibits constant returns to scale, an increase
         in the output level the firm seeks to reach induces an increase by the same propor-
         tion in the firm’s demand for inputs. Figure 4.42 illustrates this property. In particu-
         lar, an increase in the output level that the firm seeks to produce (e.g., from q = 10
         to q′ = 20 units) induces a similar increase in the amount of inputs that the firm
         needs to use from z(w, q) to z(w, q′), where z(w, q′) = 2z(w, q), because the produc-
         tion function exhibits constant returns to scale. This increase in input usage implies,
         in turn, a similar increase in the minimum cost that the firm must incur from c(w, q)
         to c(w, q′), where c(w, q′) =2c(w, q). Indeed, and c(w, q′) = w1z1(w, q′) + w2z2(w, q′).
         Using zi(w, q′) = 2zi(w, q) for every input i, we can rewrite c(w, q′) as

         which can be ultimately reduced to

                       increases output from q1 to q2. This implies that the firm must increase its minimal
                       cost from c(w, q2) to c(w, q3) when increasing output from q2 to q3, but only from
                       c(w, q1) to c(w, q2) when raising output from q1 to q2, where

                                                c(w, q3) – c(w, q2) > c(w, q2) – c(w, q1),
                       reflecting the convexity of the cost function c(w, q) with respect to q.

                    4.9   Alternative Representation of the PMP

                    We can alternatively represent the PMP using the cost function c(w, q) (i.e., the value
                    function of the CMP) as follows:
284                                                                                               Chapter 4




      Figure 4.43
      Convexity of the cost function


                                              max pq − c ( w , q ) .
                                               q ≥0

         In our previous discussion, the firm chose a cost-minimizing input combination,
      z(w, q), that guaranteed the production of a particular output level q (i.e., input vector
      z was the firm’s choice variable in the CMP). The firm now chooses an output vector
      q, given cost function c(w, q).52 Intuitively, this problem can be understand as a PMP
      in “two steps” (first, finding the cost function by solving the CMP, and then plugging
      the cost function in the above problem), rather than a PMP in “one step” (where the
      firm chooses input usage that yields an optimal output) as described in section 4.5. The
      PMP in “two steps” that we describe in this section is thus particularly useful if we
      have information about the cost function but do not observe the production function.
         The first-order conditions for q* to be profit maximizing in the PMP above are p
      −dc(w, q*) / dq ≤ 0; and in interior solutions, p =dc(w, q*) / dq. Intuitively, at an interior
      optimum q*, output price p equals the firm’s marginal cost of production, dc(w, q*) / dq.
      This is a common representation of the PMP in applications, which we next use to
      analyze the presence of external effects in the cost function.

        Recall that the cost function reflects the minimum cost that the firm must incur in order to produce

                    4.9.1    External Effects on Costs
                    Consider an industry with N firms facing a (exogenous) price p > 0 for each unit of
                    output. Every firm i ∈ N has cost function c(qi, q−i), where qi ≥ 0 denotes firm i’s own
                    output, while q−i = (q1, … , qi−1, qi+1, … , qN) represents the production vector of all firm
                    i’s rivals. In particular, costs are strictly increasing and weakly convex in
                    a firm’s own output, namely ∂c(qi, q−i) / ∂qi > 0 and ∂2c(qi, q−i) / ∂qi2 ≥ 0. In addition firm
                    i’s total and marginal costs increase in the output produced by its rivals, q−i (i.e., nega-
                    tive external effect on costs), that is,
                                  ∂c ( qi , q− i )                     ∂2 c ( qi , q− i )
                                                   >0   and                               ≥0    for every firm j ≠ i .
                                      ∂q j                                ∂qi ∂q j
                      Intuitively, firms may compete for a scarce input, such as qualified labor, or natural
                    resources, and thus every firm’s costs increase as its rivals produce a larger output. The
                    opposite argument applies when every firm’s costs decrease when its rivals produce
                    more units.53 (For the remainder of this section, we focus on negative external effects.)
                    For a parametric example of the cost function above, consider c(qi, q−i) = cqi(1 + αQ−i),
                    where c > 0, Q− i ≡ ∑ j ≠i q j denotes the aggregate output of firm i’s rivals, and parameter
                    α > 0 indicates the intensity of the negative external effect of Q−i on firm i’s costs. An-
                    other cost function that also exhibits external effects, and explored in exercise 16, is
                    c(qi, q−i) = (qi + Q−i)α qiβ, where α, β > 0.

                    In this context, every firm i’s PMP is

                    level of qi imposes on other firms’ costs, ∂c(qj, q−j) / ∂qi ≥ 0 for every firm j ≠ i.

                    53
                       This positive external effect on costs could be rationalized if a larger output from the industry we

                    of purchasing inputs by every firm in the industry. This positive effect on costs occurred, for instance,
                    in the cell phone and tablet industry, as their larger demand for memory chips trigger an increase in

                    a memory chip, and ultimately the price that a typical cell phone company had to pay for its inputs.

                    4.9.2    Firm’s Expansion Path
                    A firm’s expansion path represents the locus of cost-minimizing input combinations
                    (tangencies between the isocost and isoquant) as the firm reaches higher production
                    levels. We provide a graphical example of an expansion path in figure 4.44, in which
                    the firm increases its demand for both labor and capital when it raises its output from
                    q0 to q1, and then from q1 to q2.55 For instance, for the Cobb–Douglas production func-
                    tion in example 4.8, the firm’s expansion path was found in those input pairs for which
                    MRTS1,2 = w1 / w2 holds, that is, the combinations of z1 and z2 satisfying z2 = (β / α)
                    [(w1 / w2)z1].
                       Intuitively, figure 4.45a shows that, in order to increase output from q0 to q1 the firm
                    needs to hire more of all inputs, meaning more labor l1 > l0 and more capital k1 > k1 .
                    (For compactness, we use ki rather than k(w, qi) for any output level qi, and li rather
                    than l(w, qi).) Graphically, this implies that the firm’s expansion path is positively
                    sloped. Hence both inputs are regarded as “normal” inputs (as opposed to inferior in-
                    puts), since
                                                   ∂z1 ( w , q )              ∂z2 ( w , q )
                                                                 ≥0   and                   ≥ 0.
                                                       ∂q                         ∂q
                       If, instead, the firm uses fewer units of one input as output increases, that input
                    is denoted as inferior. Figure 4.45b illustrates one example in which both inputs are
                    normal when the firm increases production from q0 to q1, but labor becomes inferior
                    when output is further increased from q1 to q2. Such pattern in expansion paths might

         It is important to clarify a common confusion. At first glance, you might consider
      that our last result on the marginal cost function violates Euler’s theorem, since we
      show that both the cost function and its first-order derivative (the marginal cost func-
      tion) are homogeneous of degree one in input prices. Euler’s theorem would not pre-
      dict this result, but a different one: if the cost function is homogeneous of degree one
      in input prices, then its derivative with respect to input prices, ∂C(w, q) / ∂w= z(w, q), is
      homogeneous of degree zero in input prices. That is, the conditional factor
      demand correspondence z(w, q) (and not the marginal cost function) is homogeneous
      of degree zero in input prices, w.

      4.11   Aggregation in Production

      In this section we investigate under which conditions the “law of supply” holds at the
      aggregate level, and under which cases we can define a “representative producer” that

                    4.12     Efficient Production

                    4.12.1     First and Second Welfare Theorems
                    Let us continue our discussion of situations in which individual firms choose produc-
                    tion plans that maximize aggregate profits. In this regard let us define efficient

                       A simple example is that of oligopoly markets where firms compete in quantities (à la Cournot). In

298                                                                                                 Chapter 4



      production vectors. We say that a production vector y∈Y is efficient if there is no other
      production vector y′ ∈ Y such that y′ ≥ y and y′ ≠ y. That is, y is efficient if there is no
      other feasible production vector y′ producing more output with the same amount of
      inputs (or alternatively, producing the same amount of output with fewer inputs).
      Graphically, note that this definition of efficiency implies that, if a production plan is
      efficient it must lie on the boundary of the production set Y, as figure 4.50a illustrates.
      In particular, y is efficient, whereas y′ and y″ are inefficient (y′ is inefficient because it
      uses the same amount of inputs as y but produces less output; y″ is inefficient because
      it produces the same output as y but uses more inputs).

Production Theory                                                                                                         299



                       Hence every efficient production plan must lie on the frontier of the production set.
                    However, the converse argument (that every production plan lying on the boundary of
                    the production set must be efficient) is not necessarily true, as figure 4.50b indicates.
                    Specifically, production plan y′—despite lying on the boundary of production set Y—
                    is inefficient because it produces the same amount of output as y but uses more
                    inputs.67 After defining efficient production plans, we can now present the first and
                    second fundamental theorem of welfare economics (FTWE).


                         First FTWE If a production plan y ∈ Y is profit-maximizing for a price vector
                         p >> 0, then y must be efficient.


                    Proof Let us prove the first FTWE by contradiction. Suppose that production plan
                    y ∈ Y is profit maximizing, that is, py ≥ p y′ for any other y′ ∈ Y, y′ ≠ y; but y is not ef-
                    ficient. Then, there must be another production plan y′∈Y such that y′ ≥ y. That is, y′
                    produces more output using the same amount of inputs, or produces the same output
                    using fewer inputs. Multiplying both sides of this inequality by price vector p, we ob-
                    tain py′ ≥ py, since p >> 0. But then y cannot be profit maximizing (as the premise of
                    this proof established). We hence reached a contradiction, proving the first FTWE. ■

                    For this result we do not need the production set Y to be convex. (Indeed we did not
                    need to invoke convexity anywhere in the short proof above.) Figure 4.51 illustrates
                    convex and nonconvex production sets. In both cases, production plan y is profit max-
                    imizing, which implies that it must lie on a tangency point between the production
                    set Y and the isoprofit line, for both convex and nonconvex production sets, and it
                    is efficient because there is no other production plan that produces more output using
                    the same amount of inputs or produces the same output using fewer inputs.68
                       In addition note that the assumption p >> 0 on the price vector cannot be relaxed
                    to p ≥ 0. To see why, take a production set Y with an upper flat surface, such as that
                    depicted in figure 4.52. Hence any production plan y in the flat segment of the

                    67
                       This example illustrates that, in order to obtain the converse argument, we need production set Y

                    elaborate on this problem below.
                    68
                       In addition, production plan y′ in figure 4.51 is efficient because it lies on the boundary of produc-
                    tion set Y, but it is not profit-maximizing because there exists another production plan (in particular
                    y) that yields a larger profit, in that it lies on a higher isocost line. We comment on production plan y′
                    again in our discussion of the second welfare theorem below.

                    Second FTWE needs convex production set Y


                       The second FTWE states the converse of the first FTWE: if a production plan y is
                    efficient, then it must be profit maximizing. This result does not necessarily hold if we
                    do not impose further restrictions on the production set. Figure 4.53 illustrates that,
                    when the production set is convex, every efficient production plan (lying on the bound-
                    ary of the production set) must also be profit maximizing. When the production set is
                    nonconvex, however, the fact that a production plan is efficient does not imply that
                    such plan maximizes the firm’s profits. This is evident in production plan y′ in the right
                    panel, which lies on the boundary of the production set but is not profit maximizing.
                    Indeed production plan y is the profit-maximizing vector. The second FTWE is there-
                    fore restricted to convex production sets.

                         Second FTWE If production set Y is convex, then every efficient production
                         plan y ∈Y is a profit-maximizing production plan, for some nonzero price
                         vector p ≥ 0.

                    Proof In order to prove the second FTWE, let us use the following steps. First, take
                    an efficient production plan, such as y on the boundary of Y in figure 4.54. Let us now
                    define the set of production plans that are strictly more efficient than plan y, that is,

                                                    Py = { y ′ ∈ R L : y ′ >> y} .
                      As figure 4.54 depicts, this set contains all production plans producing more output
                    than production plan y while using the same amount of inputs, and those producing the
                    same amount of output using fewer inputs, graphically represented by all points to the
302                                                                                     Chapter 4




      Figure 4.54
      Py is an open and convex set to the northeast of production plan y


      northeast of y. In the figure, the boundaries of set Py are not included because we only
      consider production plans that are strictly more efficient than y. This implies that set Py
      is an open set, and hence there exists no intersection point between set Py and produc-
      tion set Y. In addition note that set Py is a convex set, since any convex combination of
      any two production plans in Py lies within the set.
         We can now apply the Separating Hyperplane Theorem. Specifically, we take
      two production plans, y′ ∈ Py and y″ ∈ y, which satisfy y′ > y″, and claim that
      there exists some price vector p ≠ 0 such that p y′ ≥ p y″. Since we can choose y′
      to be arbitrarily close to the efficient production plan y, we have py ≥ p y″ for every
      production plan y″ ∈ Y. Therefore the efficient production plan y must also be profit
      maximizing. ■

      One interesting property of the second FTWE is that we do not need all prices to be
      positive, p >> 0, but only that all must be weakly positive, p ≥ 0. Hence we just assume
      that the price vector is not zero at every single component, p ≠ (0, 0, …, 0). Note that
      this implies that the slope of the isoprofit line can be zero. Figure 4.55 illustrates this
      for the case in which the price of input z is zero but the output price is positive. Note
      in the figure that there is a set of profit-maximizing production plans (in the region
      where the isocost line is tangent to the production set). However, there is only one
      efficient production plan, y, located at the kink of production set Y. According to
      the second FTWE, such efficient production plan y must also be part of the set of
Production Theory                                                                                                       303




                    Figure 4.55
                    Second FTWE also holds when the price vector is weakly positive, p ≥ 0


                    profit-maximizing production plans, which indeed holds in this case. Hence the second
                    FTWE can be satisfied even if some input prices are zero.70
                       Despite allowing for some input prices to be zero, the second FTWE does not allow
                    for input prices to be negative. To see this, consider the case in which the price of input
                    l was negative, pl < 0. We would then have that p y′< py for any production plan y′ that

                    4.12.2   Objectives of the Firm
                    Thus far we assumed that profit maximization (or its dual, cost minimization) was a
                    natural objective for the firm. Since firms are controlled by managers, however, their
                    objectives in certain cases could be to maximize sales revenue, or the firm’s market
                    share. Second, we considered that firm owners (e.g., shareholders) can induce the
                    manager (e.g., CEO) to choose actions that would maximize the owner’s utility.

                    70
                      Recall, in contrast, that the first FTWE does not necessarily hold if some input prices are zero, as
                    described in figure 4.53.
                    71
                       Consider, for instance, a price vector p = (p1, p2) = (3, −5), and assume that the efficient
                    production plan is y = (1, 4), but a “more efficient” production plan (a production plan that is techno-
                    logically unfeasible) is y′ = (6, 25). Then the firm’s profits from these two production plans are
                    py = −$17 and py′ = −$107, respectively, implying that py > py′, the firm obtains a larger profit from
                    production plan y than from a technologically unfeasible production plan y′. This contradicts the
                    second FTWE.
304                                                                                     Chapter 4



      However, such a delegation often entails that the principal in the relationship (firm
      owner) needs to provide strong incentives, such as bonuses, to the agent (manager); for
      more details, see the principal–agent model in chapter 10. Third, we assumed that
      firm’s output decision did not affect market prices, but if prices are a function of its
      output, the objective of the firm owner may depend on that person’s tastes as a con-
      sumer (e.g., which good’s output should be increased the most). Last, if the firm faces
      uncertainty in its profits (e.g., how inputs transform into output), its production deci-
      sions could also be affected; as the next chapter examines.

      the individual incentives of entrepreneurs to create firms, see Daniel F. Spulber’s

      and contracts between firms, see the edited handbook by Robert Gibbons and John

      Appendix A: Graphical Representation of Cost Functions

      Let us now continue with our analysis of cost and supply curves in the single output
      case. For presentation purposes, we divide our analysis into three cases, depending on
      whether the production function exhibits: (1) decreasing, (2) constant, or (3) increas-
      ing returns to scale.72

      Case 1 (DRS)
      Figure A4.1 depicts a firm with a technology that exhibits strictly decreasing returns
      to scale (DRS). An increase in the use of inputs produces a less-than-proportional in-
      crease in output such that the firm’s production set is strictly convex, as the left panel
      of figure A4.1a illustrates. For simplicity, we normalize the price of input z to
      w = $1. Thus the use of z units of input implies a cost of z dollars. This normalization
      helps us represent the firm’s cost function in figure A4.1b as a 90-degree clockwise
      rotation of the production set, where the vertical axis in figure A4.1a (representing
      output) becomes the horizontal axis in figure A4.1b and the horizontal axis in figure
      A4.1a (representing units of input) becomes the firm’s total cost in figure A4.1b de-
      picted in the vertical axis. As a consequence the firm’s total cost function is convex
      (figure A4.1b). This, in turn, implies that marginal costs are increasing (as depicted in
      figure A4.1c), since the slope of the firm’s total cost function increases in q. Similarly

                    average costs are increasing in output (as represented in figure A4.1c). In particular,

                    Case 2 (CRS)
                    Figure A4.2 provides a similar analysis for technologies exhibiting constant returns to
                    scale (CRS). First, an increase in input usage produces a proportional increase in out-

                    we obtain a strictly linear total cost function. In addition this cost function yields con-

                    with the origin maintain the same slope for all q) and constant marginal cost curves
                    (since the slope of the total cost function is constant for all q). As in the case of strictly
                    convex production sets, the firm’s supply correspondence embodies output levels

      Case 3 (IRS)
      When the firm’s production set is nonconvex, an increase in input usage can lead to a
      more-than-proportional increase in output; as that depicted in the region of relatively
      low levels of input z in figure A4.3a. Additionally, if we rotate figure A4.3a 90 degrees
      in order to obtain the total cost curve in figure A4.3b, we observe that the total cost
      curve first increases very rapidly, becomes almost flat for intermediate levels of output,
      and then increases rapidly again for large scales of output. In this case, as described
      above, AC and MC start from the same height when q = 0 (see figure A4.3c), MC lies
      below AC for low levels of output, but MC is above AC for output levels above the
      minimum of the AC curve. That is, MC lies above AC for output levels q > q in figure
      A4.3c, where q identifies the minimum of the AC curve, AC(q ). Importantly, in this
      case the firm’s supply curve does not exactly coincide with the marginal cost curve, but
      rather, with only the portion of this curve that lies above AC. Indeed, for market prices
      below AC(q ), if the firm sells units at a price below AC, it would incur a loss of AC–
      MC per unit. As a consequence the firm sells no units for p < AC(q) (represented by
      the vertical spike at the vertical axis of figure A4.3c) but sells positive output levels at
      the locus of the MC curve for which p > AC(q ).
         Figure A4.4 examines the presence of nonconvexities in the production set Y arising
      from the existence of fixed setup costs, K, which are nonsunk. In particular, the firm’s
      cost function can be represented in this case as C(q) = K + Cv(q), where Cv(q) denotes
      variable costs. Let us next analyze how nonsunk fixed costs affect the total, average,
      and marginal cost curves.

                    Case 4 (Fixed Costs)
                    Figure A4.4a illustrates the case in which the firm incurs a fixed cost, and beyond that
                    input usage, its production set exhibits constant returns to scale. In figure A4.4b, we
                    rotate the production set 90 degrees, yielding a linear total cost curve. Importantly,
                    the firm’s costs in figure 4.54b are zero for q = 0, since the firm can recover its fixed
                    costs K if it shuts down its operations. If, however, q > 0, then the firm’s total costs
                    include K.
                      In addition, note that average costs are AC(q) = (K / q) + (Cv(q) / q). The second com-
                    ponent of AC(q), (Cv(q) / q), is a constant due to the linearity of the production function,
308                                                                                             Chapter 4



      that is, Cv(q) = c · q implying that Cv(q) / q = c. The first component of AC(q),which is
      K / q, is decreasing in q, implying that the overall expression of AC(q) declines in out-
      put, as depicted in figure A4.4c. However, the marginal costs are constant in output in
      this case, since total costs C(q) = K + Cv(q) = K + c · q entails a derivative of c, yielding a
      constant marginal cost curve, as depicted in figure A4.4c. In addition, since average
      costs are (K + q) + (Cv(q) / q) (or (K / q) + c), average costs, despite declining, lie above
      the firm’s marginal cost for all production levels, only approaching the marginal cost c
      as q goes to infinity. Last, regarding the firm’s supply curve, recall that the firm sup-
      plies positive amounts that satisfy p = MC(q) only if market prices are high enough to
      recover both variable and fixed costs, that is, if prices are above the average cost curve.
      However, since in this case average costs lie above marginal costs for all output levels,
      the firm’s supply curve is a vertical spike in the vertical axis, indicating that the firm
      does not produces positive amounts.

      Case 5 (Variable Costs)
      When the production of every additional unit is more costly for the firm, total costs are
      convex in output; as depicted in figure A4.5b. This is confirmed in figure A4.5c where
      marginal costs are positive and increasing in output (indicating that the slope of the
      total cost curve increases in output). As a practice, consider some parametric examples
      of total cost curves: (1) TC(q) = K + bq, where K, b > 0, is a linear cost function incur-
      ring fixed cost K > 0 as in case 4 above; (2) TC(q) = bq2, which represents the presence
      of convex production costs but without fixed costs (where marginal costs, 2bq, lie

                       Note that the average cost curve initially decreases and then increases in q. Intui-

5 Choice under Uncertainty



    Thus far we have analyzed preference relations, utility functions, and utility maximi-
    zation in deterministic settings. In the preceding chapters, the decision maker faced no
    uncertainty about the outcomes of his actions. However, we know that our daily choic-
    es are often surrounded by uncertainty: Will my pen stop working in the middle of a
    test? Will I find a traffic jam on my way to work? In our analysis of decision making
    under uncertainty, we start by considering simple lotteries, understood as a list of po-
    tential outcomes, each outcome with an associated probability of occurrence. We then
    analyze “lotteries of lotteries” (referred to as compound lotteries), where the decision
    maker faces a list of lotteries and plays each lottery with a specific probability. While
    this description of lotteries is useful in our representation of uncertainty, our ultimate
    goal is to describe individual’s preferences over lotteries, as we elaborate in section
    5.1. In particular, we seek to identify which properties are required on preference rela-
    tions over lotteries to guarantee that they can be represented by a utility function.1 We
    now require a new property that did not arise in deterministic contexts: the “indepen-
    dence axiom.” Essentially, this axiom states that if a decision maker prefers one lottery
    over another, then introducing a small perturbation on the probabilities of the two ini-
    tial lotteries does not entail a change in his preferences. In section 5.2 we examine this
    axiom and the controlled experiments in which participants violated the axiom. We
    also discuss the most important theoretical developments that, mainly in the last three
    decades, have been offered to account for this type of behavior. In section 5.3 we focus
    on a specific type of lottery for which outcomes are restricted to be monetary amounts,


    1
      Until now we have learned that in deterministic settings we only need preferences to satisfy mono-
    tonicity and continuity (or in alternative approaches, completeness, transitivity, local nonsatiation,
    and continuity) for them to be representable by a utility function. Most of these properties are also
    required in preferences over lotteries for them to be representable by a utility function, and in particu-
    lar, completeness, transitivity, and continuity.
324                                                                                              Chapter 5



      rather than any type of N-dimensional bundle. Section 5.4 then presents behavioral
      theories that modify or expand standard expected utility theory, such as “weighted util-
      ity theory” or “rank-dependent utility” and their properties.
         Section 5.5 examines how to measure an individual’s risk aversion by evaluating the
      curvature of his utility function, and discusses the Arrow–Pratt coefficient of absolute
      and relative risk aversion. Then section 5.6 compares payoff distributions in money
      lotteries, by which a decision maker chooses the lottery with the largest expected value
      (as captured by the notion of first-order stochastic dominance), and if two lotteries
      have the same mean, he chooses the lottery with the smallest variance (as represented
      by the concept of second-order stochastic dominance). We also present other common
      measures of stochastic dominance often used in the literature. Section 5.7 analyzes
      reference-dependent utility and prudence, section 5.8 examines prospect theory, and
      section 5.9 discusses common measures to compare payoff distributions. Section 5.10
      deals with subjective probability theory, whereby the probability of each event is not
      objectively observed but is instead inferred from individual choices, and thus prone to
      subjectivities. Section 5.11 explores three alternative theories to subjective probabil­
      ity: ambiguity aversion, smooth ambiguity aversion, and the theory of capacities (also
      known as Choquet expected utility). Last, the chapter provides an appendix that covers
      state-dependent utility, where the utility that the decision maker obtains in each state
      can differ.

      5.1   Simple and Compound Lotteries

      In contrast to our analysis in previous chapters where the individual or firm selects
      among a set of certain outcomes, we now examine choices under uncertain conditions.
      In this section we present the decision maker’s preferences over uncertain outcomes,
      and discuss how to represent his preference relation with an expected utility function.
         In particular, consider a set of possible outcomes (or consequences) C. This set
      might include, for instance, simple monetary payoffs (either positive or negative), im-
      plying that the set of consequences becomes C = ℝ. Alternatively, set could represent
      consumption bundles, in which case C = X (where X is a subset of ℝL, as in previous
      chapters). For simplicity, assume that there are only a finite number of outcomes; that
      is, the set of possible outcomes C contains N elements. Also the probabilities associ-
      ated to every possible outcome are objectively known,2 being p1 for outcome 1, p2 for
      outcome 2, and so on.

      2
        In section 5.11, we allow for situations where the decision maker does not perfectly know the prob-
      ability associated to every outcome.
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                   325

                   Lottery over two outcomes


                   5.1.1    Simple Lotteries
                   In this chapter we use the concept of lotteries to represent uncertain outcomes. In par-
                   ticular, a simple lottery is a list

                                                      L = (p1, p2, …, pN),

                   where pn is the probability of outcome n occurring, and satisfies pn ≥ 0 for every out-
                   come n, and ∑ nN=1 pn = 1. Therefore we can graphically represent a simple lottery with
                   two possible outcomes as a point along the line connecting the probability point (0, 1),
                   where outcome 2 happens with certainty, and (1, 0), where outcome 1 occurs with
                   certainty, as figure 5.1 depicts. This is known as the “simplex” of lotteries, Δ.
                      Intuitively, the horizontal (vertical) intercept represents a “degenerated” probability
                   distribution, where outcome 1 (outcome 2, respectively) is certain. Strictly positive
                   probability pairs (p1, p2) along the line p1 + p2 = 1, in contrast, describe a lottery where
                   none of the outcomes is certain, and therefore the individual faces some uncertainty.
                   We can easily extend this graphical representation of lotteries to the case of three pos-
                   sible outcomes with associated probabilities (p1, p2, p3), as figure 5.2 illustrates. First,
                   note that the intercepts also represent degenerated probabilities where one outcome is
                   certain. Second, points strictly inside the hyperplane connecting the three intercepts
                   denote a lottery where the individual faces uncertainty, such as the point depicted in
                   figure 5.2. This figure is usually referred as the probability simplex of lotteries with N
                   = 3 outcomes.
                      In order to simplify our graphical analysis, we can do a two-dimensional projection
                   of the hyperplane above, as figure 5.3 depicts. First, the vertices represent the inter-
                   cepts (where one outcome is certain). Second, a simple lottery (interior points in the
326                                                                                      Chapter 5




      Figure 5.2
      Simplex of a lottery with three outcomes


      triangle) represents settings where the individual faces uncertainty. Importantly, the
      distance from a given point to the side of the triangle measures the probability that
      the outcome represented at the opposite vertex occurs. In figure 5.3, for instance, the
      length of the segment x1 (from the strictly interior point to the side of the triangle con-
      necting the certain outcomes 2 and 3) measures the probability of outcome 1 occurring.
         Finally, as a practice, if a lottery lies on one of the boundaries of the triangle, then
      we can only construct segments connecting the lottery to two of the outcomes, entail-
      ing that the probability associated with the third outcome is zero. Figure 5.4 illustrates
      this case.

      5.1.2 Compound Lotteries
      We can use our previous notation to define compound lotteries. Specifically, we con-
      sider a list of K simple lotteries, where

                       Lk = ( p1k , p2k , …, pKk )   for every lottery k = 1, 2, …, K,
      with associated probabilities αk ≥ 0 for every lottery k, where ∑ kK=1 α k = 1. Then the
      compound lottery (L1, L2, …, LK; α1, α2, …, αK) yields the simple lottery Lk with
      probability αk.
        We can intuitively interpret a compound lottery as a “lottery of lotteries.” First, we
      face a probability α1 of playing lottery L1, and if lottery 1 occurs, then we face a
Choice under Uncertainty                                             327




                   Figure 5.3
                   Two-dimensional representation of a simplex




                   Figure 5.4
                   Lottery assigning zero probability to outcome 3
328                                                                                         Chapter 5




      probability p11 of outcome 1 occurring, probability p12 of outcome 2 occurring, and so
      on. In this context, the probability of outcome 1 is given by the probability that we play
      lottery L1 and outcome 1 occurs, α1 ⋅ p11, plus the probability that such outcome occurs
      in lottery L2, α 2 ⋅ p12, and similarly across all K lotteries. (Recall that p kj represents the
      probability that outcome j occurs when playing lottery k.) That is, we can write

                                    p1 = α1 ⋅ p11+ α 2 ⋅ p12 +…+ α K ⋅ p1K ,

      which describes the joint probability of outcome 1 occurring in lottery 1, 2, ..., K. Ex-
      tending the same argument to all possible outcomes in the compound lottery (L1, L2, …,
      LK; α1, α2, …, αK), we can calculate a corresponding reduced lottery as the simple lot-
      tery L = (p1, p2, …, pN) that generates the same ultimate probability distribution of
      outcomes as the compound lottery above. That is, the reduced lottery L of any com-
      pound lottery can be obtained by

                                   L = α1L1 + α2L2 + … + αKLK ∈ ∆.

      Example 5.1: Compound lotteries Let us consider two examples of reduced lotter-
      ies. In figure 5.5 all lotteries are equally likely (the probability of each lottery occur-
      ring is αi = 1/3 for every lottery i = 1, 2, 3). If lottery 1 occurs, we are guaranteed
      outcome 1, but if lottery 2 or 3 occurs, we face a positive probability of obtaining any
      of the three possible outcomes. The probability of outcome 1 in this compound lottery
      is therefore

                                         p1 = 1 + + = .

                   reduced lottery of the compound lottery represented in Figure 5.5 is therefore

                   Example 5.2: Finding the reduced lottery of a compound lottery Let us consider
                   another example (see figure 5.6b). Lotteries 4 and 5 are equally likely, meaning
                   α 4 = α 5 = 1 2 . While outcome 1 occurs with 50 percent probability on both lotteries,

                   originating from a different set of simple lotteries. ■

                   5.2     Preferences over Lotteries

                   Let us turn to the preferences of decision makers who face uncertain outcomes. We
                   assume that individuals only care about the compound lotteries that induce a given
                   reduced lottery, as in the previous example, where two different compound lotteries
                   produce the same reduced lottery. We refer to this assumption as “consequentialism,”
                   since only consequences (outcomes), and the probability associated with every conse-
                   quence, matter for the decision maker, rather than the process by which a given out-
                   come emerges.
                      In addition we consider the set of all simple lotteries over the set of outcomes, . We
                   assume that the decision maker has a complete and transitive preference relation over
                   lotteries in , allowing him to compare any pair of simple lotteries L and L′. That is,
                   1. Completeness Either L ≿ L′ or L′ ≿ L, or both, for every two lotteries L, L ′ ∈.
                   2. Transitivity If L ≿ L′ and L′ ≿ L″, then L ≿ L″ for every three lotteries L, L ′, L ′′ ∈.

                   Example 5.3: Four examples of preferences over lotteries Let us first consider
                   examples of preference relations over lotteries where the decision maker is only con-
                   cerned about the probability distribution over outcomes.
                   1. Extreme preference for certainty            The decision maker weakly prefers lottery L to
                      L′, meaning L ≿ L′, if and only if
                                                            max pn ≥ max pn′ .
                                                            n∈N        n∈N

                      Intuitively, this preference relation represents a decision maker who is only con-
                   cerned about the probability associated with the most likely outcome. That is, he first
                   considers the most likely outcome in lottery L and that in lottery L′, and afterward he
                   chooses the lottery in which such outcome is the most likely.3 For example, a decision
                   maker with these preferences would prefer lottery L = (70%, 30%), which assigns a
                   probability of 70 percent to the outcome $1 and 30 percent to an outcome of $100, to
                   lottery L′ = (40%, 60%), which assigns a probability of 40 percent to $1, and a proba-
                   bility of 60 percent to $100. Specifically, max{pn : pn ≥ 0} = 70 percent for lottery L,
                   but only 60 percent for lottery L′.

                   3
                     You might consider this preference relation to be reasonable. Note, however, that the most likely
                   outcome might differ from lottery L to lottery L′, making this preference relation over uncertain out-
                   comes not so sensible in certain settings.
332                                                                                     Chapter 5



      2. Smallest size of the support For two lotteries L and L′ over a finite number of ac-
         tions, the decision maker weakly prefers lottery L to L′, since L ≿ L′, if and only if

                                            supp( L) ≤ supp( L ′) ,
      where |supp(L)| denotes the cardinality of the support of lottery L, namely the number
      of outcomes receiving a strictly positive probability, where supp(L)={n ∈ N: pn > 0}.
      Intuitively, this decision maker prefers the lottery whose probability distribution is
      concentrated over the smallest set of possible outcomes. Note that this preference rela-
      tion only cares about the probability distribution. For example, an individual with this
      preferences would prefer a lottery L that assigns the same probability to $5 and $6 (a
      very small support of possible outcomes) than a lottery L′ assigning the same probabil-
      ity to all outcomes in a longer list of monetary outcomes that starts at $10, that is, in
      the list {$10, $11, …, $100}. In particular, |supp(L)| = 2 while |supp(L′)| = 90, entailing
      that L ≿ L′ for a decision maker with this type of preference over lotteries.
         Let us next examine preference relations over lotteries for which the decision maker
      cares not only about probability distributions but also about the lottery outcomes.
      3. Lexicographic preferences After ordering outcomes from most to least preferred,
         the decision maker weakly prefers lottery L to L′ so that L ≿ L′, if and only if
                                                   p1 > p1′     or

                                        p1 = p1′    and       p2 > p2′,   or

                            p1 = p1′,     p2 = p2′,     and p3 > p3′, and so on.
      Intuitively, the decision maker weakly prefers lottery L to L′ if outcome 1 (the most
      preferred outcome) is more likely to occur in lottery L than in lottery L′. If such out-
      come is equally likely in both lotteries, meaning p1 = p1′, then the decision maker pre-
      fers lottery L to L′ if outcome 2 (the second most preferred outcome) is more likely to
      occur in lottery L than in lottery L′, meaning p2 > p2′. As an example, for monetary
      outcomes ($3, $2, $−100) a decision maker with a lexicographic preference relation
      would prefer a lottery L = (2%, 0%, 98%) over L′= (1%, 99%, 0%), since p1= 2% >1%
      = p1′ , despite of the fact that L assigns a large probability to the lowest payoff $−100.
      4. Worst case scenario First, the decision maker attaches a real number to every
         outcome z ∈ C, v(z) ∈ ℝ, that can be interpreted as the utility from outcome z. Then,
         he weakly prefers lottery L to L′, that is, L ≿ L′, if and only if

                            min{v(z): p ( z ) > 0} > min{v(z): p′ ( z ) > 0}.
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                             333



                   Intuitively, this decision maker prefers lottery L if the lowest utility he can get from
                   playing lottery L, min v(z), is higher than the lowest utility he can obtain from playing
                   lottery L′, among all outcomes that can occur with a positive probability. For this rea-
                   son this preference relation is often regarded as that the decision maker first identifies
                   the “worst case scenario” of each lottery, and then prefers the lottery with the best
                   “worst case scenario.”4 ■

                   Let us next define continuity of preferences in this context. For completeness, we pre-
                   sent two equivalent definitions.


                       Continuity 1 For any three lotteries L, L′, and L″, sets

                       {α ∈[0, 1] : α L + (1 − α ) L′  L′′}     and     {α ∈[0, 1] : L′′  α L + (1 − α ) L′}
                       are closed.


                   In words, for a lottery L″, we can construct compound lotteries between L and L′ that
                   are weakly preferred to L″ (in the first set). Such a set of compound lotteries is closed
                   because it contains all its limiting points. That is, it contains the “limiting compound
                   lotteries” that the individual regards as indifferent to L″. A similar argument applies to
                   the set of compound lotteries for which the individual weakly prefers L″ to αL + (1 − α)L′.
                      The following definition of continuity is perhaps more intuitive. We elaborate on its
                   interpretation below.


                       Continuity 2 If lottery L is strictly preferred to L′, L ≻ L′, then there is a small
                       neighborhood around L and around L′, B(L) and B(L′), respectively, such that for
                       all lotteries La ∈B(L) and Lb ∈B(L′), we have that La ≻Lb.


                   Figure 5.8 illustrates the intuition behind this definition. In particular, small changes in
                   the probability distribution of lotteries L and L′ do not change the decision maker’s
                   preference over the two lotteries.
                      To better see this, let us consider an example from Mas-Colell et al. (1995). If a deci-
                   sion maker prefers a car trip to staying at home (both events occurring with certainty),
                   then he must still prefer the car trip (if we introduce a small probability of suffering a car

                   4
                     This preference ordering is sometimes observed in computer science, where one algorithm is pre-
                   ferred to another if it works better in the worst case scenario, independently of the probability that
                   such worst case scenario occurs (as long as it is positive).

      Continuity of preference over lotteries

      Continuity of preferences in the car trip example

                   accident) than staying at home. As figure 5.9 depicts, he slightly moves from the vertex
                   representing the certain event “car trip” (at the top of figure 5.9) to lottery La (which
                   represents a car trip with a small probability of a car accident) but still prefers lottery La
                   to lottery L′ (staying at home), or any lottery in its neighborhood, such as Lb.
                      The continuity assumption above, as in consumer theory, implies the existence of a
                   utility function from the set of all lotteries in  to the real numbers, U: →ℝ, such that
                   lottery L is weakly preferred to lottery L′, L ≿ L′, if and only if U(L) ≥ U(L′).
                      We must, however, impose an additional assumption on preferences over lotteries in
                   order to guarantee that the decision maker’s preferences satisfy “consequentialism” as
                   suggested above. We do so by imposing the following independence axiom (IA).

                      Independence axiom (IA) A preference relation over lotteries satisfies the IA
                      if, for any three lotteries L, L′, and L″, and for α ∈ (0, 1), we have that L ≿ L′ if
                      and only if the compound lottery αL + (1− α) L″satisfies
                                               α L + (1 − α ) L ′′  α L ′ + (1 − α ) L ′′ .


                      Intuitively, if we mix each of two lotteries, L and L′, with a third one, L″, the prefer-
                   ence ordering of the two resulting compound lotteries only depends on the preference
                   ordering of the two simple lotteries, L and L′. The preference ordering of the two re-
                   sulting compound lotteries does not depend on (is independent of) the particular third
                   lottery L″ that we use. We provide a graphical illustration of the IA below. Specifically,




                   Figure 5.10
                   Independence axiom (IA)
336                                                                                             Chapter 5



      in the left panel of figure 5.10 the individual prefers lottery L to L′. Hence it must be
      that, when we construct a convex combination of the first two lotteries with any third
      lottery L″ (right-hand panel of figure 5.10), the convex combination of L and L″,
      αL + (1 − α)L″, is still preferred to that of L′ and L″, αL + (1 − α)L″, meaning

                                      αL + (1 − α)L″ ≿ αL′ + (1 − α)L″.

         The following example illustrates the intuition behind the IA. Consider a
      decision maker who prefers lottery L to L′. We can construct a compound lottery
      where, after a coin toss, the decision maker plays lottery L when heads comes up
      and L″ when tails does, and another compound lottery where the decision maker plays
      lottery L′ when heads comes up and L″ when tails does. The IA tells us that this deci-
      sion maker, who preferred lottery L to L′, must still prefer the first to the second com-
      pound lottery.5

      Example 5.4: Testing the IA It is straightforward to show that not all preference
      relations satisfy the IA. For instance, the “extreme preference for certainty” prefer-

      Cardinality The expected utility property presented above is a cardinal property.
      That is, not only the ranking matters but also the particular number resulting from the
      expected utility function U: →  matters. Hence the expected utility form of an ini-
      tial utility function U(L) is preserved only under increasing linear transformations
      (also referred to as affine transformations), such as βU(L) + γ, where β > 0 and γ > 0,
      as the following result confirms.7

                   5.3     Violations of the IA

                   Despite the intuitive appeal of the independence axiom, individuals confronting choic-
                   es over lotteries in experimental settings seem to violate it, as we show in the next
                   examples.

                   Allais’s paradox Consider a lottery over three possible monetary outcomes: a first
                   prize of US$2.5 million, a second prize of half a million dollars, and a third prize of
                   zero dollars. The decision maker is initially asked to choose between lotteries L1 and
                   L1′, where

      selections in controlled experiments. Interestingly, more than 50 percent of the stu-

      result has been repeatedly observed in various countries, and among subjects with

      tions (as described by the IA) and people’s actual choices over lotteries has produced
      several reactions from the literature:
      1. Approximation to rationality One reaction to the Allais paradox considers that
         people might violate the IA the first time (or the first few times) they are confronted
         with choices among different lotteries. However, they are capable of adapting,
         and we should not expect subjects to continue violating the IA after a short period
         of time.
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                 343



                   2. Little economic significance Another reaction to the Allais paradox says that the
                      lotteries presented to subjects involve probabilities that are close to zero and one,
                      something that rarely occurs in real economic settings.
                   3. Regret theory Some subjects justify their choice of lottery L1 over L1′ claiming
                      they did not “want to regret a sure win of half a million dollars!” Such justification
                      has led to the development of regret theory regarding choices under uncertainty.
                      (See Exercise 5 for more details.)

                   Machina’s paradox Yet another setting where subjects in economic experiments
                   have repeatedly violated the IA is in their preferences over certain outcomes.

      prefer L2 to L1, violating as a consequence the IA. As in the Allais paradox, many sub-
      jects explain choosing L2 over L1 because of the disappointment they would experience
      in the case of losing the trip (to Barcelona, Venice, or any other tourist destination) and
      having to watch a movie about the city instead.
         In both lottery examples, the subjects’ behaviors are inconsistent with the IA. Can
      we still rely on the IA as a sensible assumption about individuals’ preferences among
      lotteries? One way to answer this question is instead by asking ourselves: What would
      happen to individuals whose behavior systematically violates the IA? As we describe
      next, such types of individuals would be weeded out of the market because they would
      be open to accepting so-called Dutch books, which would propel them to a sure loss of
      money.

      Example 5.5: Dutch books Say an individual prefers lottery L to L′and lottery L to
      L″, that is, L≻L′ and L ≻ L″. If his preferences satisfy the IA, he should prefer the
      compound lottery αL + (1 − α)L for every α ∈ (0, 1), which coincides with the simple
      lottery L, rather than the compound lottery αL + (1 − α)L′. However, in violation of the
      IA, he does prefer αL + (1 − α)L′ ≻ L.

         Hence, if we present the individual with the chance to trade lottery L for compound
      lottery αL + (1 − α)L′, which produces lottery L with probability α and lottery L′ with
      probability (1 − α), for a small fee (x dollars) he would accept such a trade. As soon as
      the first stage of the compound lottery is over, the individual will have either lottery L
      or L′ (i.e., the realization of the compound lottery gives him either L or L′). If the real-
      ization of the lottery is L′, we can again offer him to pay $y in order to trade L′ for L,
      which he accepts since L ≻ L′. If the realization is instead L, then we can offer him the
      compound lottery αL + (1 − α)L′ for a similar fee $y, which he will accept since
      αL + (1 − α)L′ ≻ L. Thus, after both trades, he has paid two fees (x + y dollars) and
      ended up exactly where he began. We could start the cycle again, extracting more
      money from this individual. Hence individuals who systematically violate the IA in
      their choices among risky lotteries can be exploited by heartless microeconomists, and
      they are ultimately weeded out of the marketplace. For this reason we assume that
      preferences satisfy the IA in most of our economic applications. ■

      Further reading If you are interested in more violations of the axioms in expected
      utility theory and the theories that have been proposed to account for such observed
      behavior, you will enjoy the next section in this chapter, where we briefly describe the
      most salient of these theories. For more details, see the review article by Chris Starmer
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                                      345



                   (2000) and the book Choices, Values and Frames (2000) by Nobel prize winners Dan-
                   iel Kahneman and Amos Tversky, Cambridge University Press. For a more detailed
                   examination of the theoretical axioms in choice under uncertainty, see Itzhak Gilboa’s
                   (2009) textbook.

                   5.4     Behavioral Theories That Modify Expected Utility Theory

                   Several theories have been advanced to account for the experimental anomalies that
                   standard expected utility theory cannot explain, as those in the Allais paradox. We
                   briefly list some of them below.

                   5.4.1    Weighted Utility
                   Initially developed by Chew and McCrimmon (1979) and extended by Fishburn
                   (1983), this theory assigns a weight function g(·)to each of the payoffs that the indi-
                   vidual can obtain in the lottery:

                                                             V ( L ) = ∑ wi ⋅ u( xi ) ,
                                                                        x ∈C


                   where

                                                       g ( xi ) p( xi )
                                              wi =                              and      g : C → .
                                                     ∑ x∈C g ( xi ) p( xi )
                     In words, the utility of outcome xi ∈ C, ui(xi), is weighted not only according to its
                   probability p(xi) but also according to the outcome xi itself through function g : C → ℝ.
                   For instance, in a gamble between two payoffs x1 and x2 with probabilities p and 1 − p,
                   respectively, the weighted utility is
                                                               V ( L ) = w1u ( x1 ) + w2 u ( x2 )
                                                  g ( x1 ) p                             g ( x2 ) (1 − p )
                                    =                                  u ( x1 ) +                                u ( x2 ) .
                                        g ( x1 ) p + g ( x2 ) (1 − p )            g ( x1 ) p + g ( x2 ) (1 − p )
                      Now, if g(xi) = g(xj) for any two payoffs xi ≠ xj, this function collapses to a standard
                   expected utility function V(L) = pu(x1) + (1 − p)u(x2). The weighted utility function re-
                   lies on the same axioms as expected utility, except for the IA, which is relaxed to the
                   following “weak independence axiom” due to Camerer (1989):
346                                                                                     Chapter 5



      Weak independent axiom If an individual is indifferent between lotteries L1 and L2,
      we can find a pair of probabilities α and α′ such that he is indifferent between the com-
      pound lotteries

                               αL1 + (1 − α)L3     and α′L2 + (1 − α′)L3

      for every probability α ∈ (0,1) and for every lottery L3.
        The standard IA becomes a special case of this axiom if probabilities α and α′ coin-
      cide; but otherwise, this weakened version of the axiom is more general.

      5.4.2   Rank-Dependent Utility
      An alternative theory that follows a similar approach to that of weighted utility theory
      by distorting probabilities so that they enter nonlinearly into the value function of the
      individual.
         However, the theory differs in two dimensions: first, it requires that we rank the
      outcomes x1, x2, … , xn from worst (x1) to best (xn) and, second, that we apply a probabil-
      ity weighting function wi to every outcome i, where
                               wi = π ( pi + … + pn ) − π ( pi +1 + … + pn )

                                            and wn = π ( pn ) .

      Here π(·) is a nondecreasing transformation of cumulative probabilities with π(0) = 0,
      and π(1) = 1. In addition, π(pi + … + pn) is the subjective weight that the individual
      assigns to receiving a payoff at least as good as xi, whereas π(pi+1 + … + pn) is the sub-
      jective weight that he assigns to receiving a payoff strictly better than xi. Hence wi
      represents the subjective probability weight on receiving a payoff of exactly xi. We just
      need to multiply the utility from each outcome xi times its associated weighted proba-
      bility wi, yielding a rank-dependent utility

                                          V ( L ) = ∑ wi ⋅ u( xi ) .
                                                    x ∈C


      In the special case of a simple gamble between two outcomes, x1 and x2, where x2 > x1,
      the rank-dependent utility becomes

                                V ( L) = w ( p)u( x1 ) + (1 − w ( p))u( x2 ) ,

      where p denotes the probability of outcome x1 and w(p) is the subjective probability
      weight that the individual assigns to this outcome.
         Intuitively, this model allows individual decision makers to attach a different weight
      to each outcome, depending on how good or bad it is relative to other outcomes—as
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                            347



                   opposed to expected utility theory models in which individuals attach the same weight
                   to all outcomes. As suggested by Quiggin (1993), a pessimistic individual can use a
                   concave transformation function π(·), yielding π(p) ≤ p for all p, thus assigning a high-
                   er (lower) probability weight on low (high) payoffs than p does. The opposite argu-
                   ment applies for an optimistic individual using a convex transformation function π(·),
                   which implies that π(p) ≥ p. Figure 5.14 depicts the transformation function for pessi-
                   mistic and optimistic individuals.
                      Empirical evidence nevertheless does show that individuals are not pessimistic or
                   optimistic for all values of p (as both panels in figure 5.14 would suggest); they instead
                   exhibit an S-shaped transformation function as the one in figure 5.15 (see Prelec 1998
                   for a survey of experimental results). For illustration purposes, the figure depicts
                   π ( p) = e ( − ln ( p )) , evaluated at α = 12 , but generally α can satisfy α ∈ (0, 1). Intuitively,
                                           α



                   individuals may be pessimistic in rare outcomes (those with a low probability, i.e.,
                   p < p in the figure) for which they do not have much previous experience, but be opti-
                   mistic for outcomes they frequently encounter. Interestingly, rank-dependent utility
                   theory relies on the same axioms as expected utility theory, except for the IA which is
                   replaced by co-monotonic independence (for more details on these axioms, see the
                   review by Machina and Sinischalci 2014).

                   5.6     Measuring Risk Preferences

                   In this section we evaluate individual preferences toward risky lotteries. We start with
                   the measure of risk aversion.

                   11

      5.6.1   Risk Aversion


         Risk aversion We say that an individual’s utility exhibits risk aversion if, for
         any money lottery F(·),

                                     ∫ u ( x ) dF ( x ) ≤ u ( ∫ xdF ( x )) .
         If this relationship holds with equality, we denote this individual as risk neutral.
         If, instead, the sign of the inequality is reversed (≥), we denote him as a risk
         lover.

         Intuitively, the utility that this individual obtains from receiving the expected mon-
      etary value of playing lottery F(·), at the right-hand side of the inequality above, is
      higher than the expected utility from playing such a lottery, as captured by the left-hand
      side, that is, u(EV) ≥ EU. Figure 5.19 illustrates this case. In particular, it considers a
      lottery with two possible outcomes: $1 and $3 that are equally likely. In the figure we
      depict the utility from outcomes $1 and $3, u(1) and u(3), respectively, by mapping the
      monetary amounts $1 and $3 into their utility values u(1) and u(3), on the vertical axis.
      We then find the expected value of the lottery ($2, i.e., 1 2 $1+ 1 2 $3) and map it into the
      utility function, obtaining u(2). This is what we refer to as the utility from the expected
      monetary value of the lottery, represented by u(EV).
         We can now analyze the expected utility from playing the lottery, which provides the
      individual with a utility of u(1), with probability 1 2, or a utility of u(3), with a

      5.6.2        Certainty Equivalent


            Certainty equivalent The certainty equivalent of money lottery F(·) for an
            individual with utility function u(·), c(F, u), is the amount of money for which
            the individual is indifferent between playing lottery F(·) and accepting a certain
            (sure) amount of money c(F, u).

      More compactly, the certainty equivalent can be expressed as the dollar amount c(F, u)
      that satisfies

                                                 u(c(F,u)) =∫ u ( x ) dF ( x ),

      where the left-hand side measures the utility from receiving the monetary amount c(F, u)
      with certainty, while the right-hand side denotes the expected utility that this individual
      obtains from playing lottery F(·). Figure 5.22 illustrates the certainty equivalent for a
      risk-averse individual. Specifically, c(F, u) is the amount of money that helps the indi-
      vidual to reach the same utility as if he played lottery F(·), given that his utility function
      is u(·). Because he is risk averse, the certainty equivalent c(F, u) is below the expected
      value of the lottery, $2. Graphically, c(F, u) is found by moving from the expected utility
      of the lottery in the vertical axis to the monetary amount that would yield this utility
      level in the horizontal axis (represented with arrows in Figure 5.22). In particular, for this
      numerical example, c(F, u) can be found by solving u(c(F, u))= 1 2u(1)+ 1 2 u(3).13

        Given these different measures of risk aversion, we next establish a connection be-
      tween them. In particular, the following properties are equivalent:16
      1. The decision maker is risk averse.
      2. The utility function is concave, u″(x) ≤ 0.
      3. The certainty equivalent is lower than the expected value of the lottery, written as
         c(F, u)) ≤ EV.
      4. The risk premium is positive, written as RP = EV – c(F, u) > 0, which implies that
         EV ≥ c(F, u).
      5. The probability premium is positive for all x and ε, π(x, ε, u) ≥ 0.

      5.7      Arrow–Pratt Coefficients of Absolute and Relative Risk Aversion

      5.7.1      Absolute Risk Aversion
      In this section we examine other forms of measuring risk aversion. In particular, we
      focus on the connection between risk aversion and the concavity of a decision maker’s
      utility function. We start by examining the Arrow–Pratt coefficient of absolute risk
      aversion, rA(x):
                                                                 u ′′( x )

         The equation tells us that, as the curvature of the utility function gets greater, captured
      by u″(x), the coefficient rA(x) gets larger.17 However, we cannot simply use u″(x) to mea-
      sure an individual’s risk aversion. In particular, such a measure is not invariant to
      positive linear transformations of the utility function. For instance, if we apply a linear
      transformation v(x) = βu(x), then the concavity of the transformed function, v″(x) = βu″(x),
      is affected by the linear transformation, whereas coefficient rA(x) is invariant, since

                   (CARA) utility function. ■

                   Coefficient rA(x) can, however, change in wealth. In particular, if rA(x) decreases as we
                   increase wealth x, we say that such utility function satisfies decreasing absolute risk
                   aversion (DARA), which we write as ∂rA(x) / ∂x < 0. Intuitively, this implies that
                   wealthier individuals are willing to bear more risk than poorer individuals.

      5.7.2   Relative Risk Aversion
