      5.7.3      Strong Risk Aversion
      Last we come to a more restrictive condition, often referred as “strong risk aversion.”
      Introduced by Ross (1981), a utility function uA(·) exhibits a stronger risk aversion
      than another utility function uB(·) if there is a constant λ > 0, such that
                                                     uA′′( x1 )     uA′ ( x2 )
                                                                ≥λ≥             .
                                                     uB′′( x1 )     u ′B ( x2 )
      If additionally x1 = x2, the condition above can be rewritten as
                                                        uA′′( x1 ) uB′′( x1 )
                                                                   ≥            ,
                                                        u ′A ( x1 ) u ′B ( x1 )
      which implies that, if a function uA(·) exhibits stronger risk aversion than uB(·), then it
      also exhibits more absolute risk aversion than uB(·).21

      5.7.4    Relationships

         becomes more concave, in that rA(x, u2) ≥ rA(x, u1).

      5.8     Prudence

      5.8.1    Absolute and Relative Prudence
      As suggested in the previous section, risk aversion measures the concavity of an
      individual’s utility function. An alternative interpretation of Arrow–Pratt’s coefficient
      of relatively risk aversion, rR(x), is that it takes the marginal utility of wealth, u′(x), and
      examines its elasticity, −xu″(x) / u′(x). A common criticism of this coefficient is that in
      standard applications in which risk enters linearly (i.e., with gains added to the initial
      wealth and losses subtracted), individuals do not necessarily choose to hold precau-
      tionary savings. More generally, the concept of risk aversion is not appropriate to ex-
      plain individual behavior when risks affect marginal rather than total utility.22 In order
      to consider the effect of these risks, Kimball (1990) suggested the notion of “pru-
      dence” (as an individual’s tendency to prepare for future risks), and provided two
      measures: absolute prudence,

      prudence finds the elasticity of its concavity. In this context, Kimball (1990) regarded
      an individual as “prudent” if the third derivative of his utility is positive, u‴(x) > 0.
      Arrow–Pratt’s coefficient of absolute risk aversion, rA(x), and the coefficient of relative
      prudence, KR(x), are closely related. In particular, differentiating rA(x) yields

      5.8.2    Cautioness and Temperance
      The literature has also analyzed the relationship between prudence and risk aversion
      that we explored in the examples above using the following ratio:
                                                            K R ( x)
                                              C (x) =                .
                                                            rR ( x )

      This ratio is often interpreted as measuring the “cautioness” of the individual, since a
      positive ratio C(x) > 0 implies KR(x) > rR(x), indicating that the individual wants to
      hedge against the downside risk of an investment. As suggested in the previous ex-
      amples, the CARA utility function yieldsC(x) = 1, whereas the CRRA entailsC(x) < 1.
      The literature has also developed the coefficient of “temperance,” T(x) = −u‴(x) / u‴(x),
      where an individual is deemed as “temperate” when the fourth derivative of his utility
      function is negative, u‴(x) ≤ 0, and describes his desire to totally reduce the exposure
      to risks. For a recent article unifying these approaches, see the review by Eeckhoudt
      (2012) and references therein.

      5.9     Prospect Theory and Reference-Dependent Utility

      5.9.1   Prospect Theory
      Kahneman and Tversky (1979, 1986) proposed a model of choice under uncertainty
      often referred as “prospect theory,” in which a decision maker’s total value from a list
      of possible outcomes x = (x1, x2, … , xn) with associated probabilities p = (p1, p2, … , pn) is
      given by
                                                      n
                                        v ( x, p ) = ∑ w ( pi ) v ( xi ).
                                                     i =1


         Hence prospect theory deviates from expected utility theory in three dimensions.
      First, probabilities are weighted with probability weighting function w(pi). At w(pi) = pi,
      this model would coincide with standard expected utility theory. However, at w(pi) > pi,
      the individuals overestimate the likelihood of outcome xi, and at w(pi) < pi, they
      underestimate it. (We assume, however, that over- or underestimation does not arise in
      outcomes occurring with certainty, i.e., w(0) = 0 and w(1) = 1.) Second, payoffs are
      evaluated relative to a reference point x0 with the so-called “value function” v(xi) de-
      scribing the utility that this individual obtains from outcome xi. As depicted in figure
      5.28, this value function is increasing and concave, v″(xi) < 0, for all outcomes that
      constitute a gain relative to reference point x0, xi > x0, meaning the decision maker is
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                             369




                   Figure 5.28
                   Utility function in prospect theory


                   risk averse toward gains but convex for losses, xi < x0, indicating that he is risk lover
                   toward losses.23 Third, the utility depicted in the figure has a kink at the reference
                   point, indicating that, as we decrease xi, the curve becomes steeper for losses (to the
                   left of x0). By this property, individuals exhibit loss aversion, in that a given loss of $a
                   relative to x0 produces a larger disutility than a gain of the same amount.

                   Example 5.12: Common functional forms in prospect theory For the case of lot-
                   teries over two possible outcomes, a probability weighting function commonly used in
                   the literature is

      sion alone consider β = 1 (no probability weighting) and α = 1, which yield a value
      function with two linear segments: one above the reference point x0 with slope 1, and
      another below x0 with slope –λ. ■

      5.9.2   Prospect Theory and Allais’s Paradox
      Let us now recall the lotteries in Allais’s paradox, in order to show that prospect theo-
      ry provides a rationale for subject choices among lotteries. In particular, all lotteries
      consider three outcomes: US2.5 million dollars, 0.5 million dollars, or zero dollars.
      The first pair of lotteries shown to the decision maker is
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                  371




                                                                           10 89 1 
                                          L1 = (0, 1, 0 ) and    L1′ =     ,   ,       ,
                                                                         100 100 100 

                   and the second pair of lotteries is
                                                  11 89                        10       90 
                                       L2 =  0,   ,           and   L2′ =      , 0,     .
                                              100 100                      100      100 
                   Recall that many subjects in controlled experiments report preferring L1 to L1′ , but
                   preferring L2′ to L2. If individuals exhibit preferences such as those in prospect theory,
                   the probabilities in lottery L1 will be unaffected, since the probability weighting
                   function w(p) satisfies w(0) = 0 and w(1) = 1. However, in lottery L1′ the probability of
                   winning 0.5 million dollars, 89 / 100, would be underweighted, making the lottery less
                   attractive than if the individual evaluated the lottery according to starndard EU theory;
                   which can help explain why he prefers L1 to L1′. In contrast, when confronted with
                   lotteries L2 and L2′ , both lotteries have the probability of the less likely outcome over-
                   weighted (0.5 million dollars in lottery L2, and 2.5 million dollars in lottery L2′), thus
                   making lottery L2′ more appealing than L2.

                   5.9.3   Prospect Theory and the “Endowment Effect”
                   Several experiments show that individuals’ willingness to pay for an object (e.g., a
                   coffee mug or an apple) is lower than their willingness to accept the same good. This
                   behavior cannot be rationalized with standard utility models, but prospect theory pro-
                   vides a simple explanation for such asymmetry: the loss aversion parameter λ > 1. In
                   particular, a subject would pay up to $x for a mug, where x solves
                                                                                      u( MUG )
                                  u ( MUG ) − u ( x ) = u ( MUG ) − λ x ≥ 0 ⇔ x ≤                ,
                                                                                             λ

                   implying that his willingness to pay is WTP = u(MUG) / λ. However, if the subject al-
                   ready has the mug (i.e., the mug was randomly given to some subjects at the beginning
                   of the experiment), then he needs to receive at least $x to give up the mug, where x solves

                                  u ( x ) − u ( MUG ) = x − λ u ( MUG ) ≥ 0 ⇔ x ≥ λ u ( MUG ) ,

                   indicating that his willingness to accept is WTA = λu(MUG). Since λ > 1 by definition,
                   WTA > WTP, as observed in controlled experiments. Last, note that if loss aversion was
                   absent, λ = 1, the individualʼs WTP = WTA.

                   Further reading For a detailed review of the now extense literature on prospect
                   theory, see Barberis (2013). The original model proposed by Tversky and Kahneman
372                                                                                           Chapter 5



      (1979 and 1986) was subsequently extended to the so-called cumulative prospect the-
      ory, which allows for the weighting function to shift the probability weight of the en-
      tire distribution function rather than to only shift the probability of specific outcomes
      (its density). For more details in cumulative prospect theory, see Luce and Fishburn
      (1991), Kahneman and Tversky (1992), and its axiomatization by Wakker and Tversky
      (1993). Finally, for an empirical test of prospect theory with data of the Deal or No
      Deal TV show, see Post et al. (2008).

      5.9.4   Reference-Dependent Preferences
      Koszegi and Rabin (2006) use a different approach to account for a similar regularity
      as prospect theory tries to explain, namely that individual preferences are affected by
      reference points, yielding gains and loses that can be differently evaluated. In particu-
      lar, they develop a model in which an individual’s consumption vector x ∈ ℝN is evalu-
      ated against a N-dimensional reference vector r ∈ ℝN, providing a utility
                                         u ( x|r ) = m ( x ) + n( x | r ),

      where u(xk | rk) = μ(mk(xk) − mk(rk)) measures the gain/loss of consuming xk units of good
      k relative to its reference amount rk. Function μ(·) is assumed to satisfy the properties
      of Kahneman and Tversky’s (1979) value function under prospect theory. Their model
      allows for deterministic consumption bundles x, also for lotteries over bundles
      with cumulative distribution function F(x), thus yielding U ( F |r ) = ∫ u ( x|r ) dF ( x ), and
      for lotteries over the set of reference points, which they express as
      u ( F |G ) = ∫∫ u ( x|r ) dG ( r )dF ( x ). Interestingly, Koszegi and Rabin (2006) show that ref-
      erence points can become endogenously determined as part of what they refer to as
      “personal equilibria,” and then they apply their results to shopping and labor supply
      decisions.

      Further reading Koszegi and Rabin’s (2006) model has been subsequently applied
      to dynamic settings by Koszegi and Rabin (2009) themselves. For an axiomatic char-
      acterization, see Masatlioglu and Ok (2005), Apesteguia and Ballester (2009) and ref-
      erences therein.

      5.10    Comparison of Payoff Distributions

      In previous sections we analyzed risk preferences for a given lottery and described
      different measures of riskiness. In this section we examine different distributions of
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                     373



                   payoffs, and how some payoffs might be more attractive than others to a risk-averse
                   decision maker. We use two main evaluation criteria:
                   1. If a lottery F(·) yields unambiguously higher returns than G(·), the first lottery
                      seems more attractive than the second lottery. We will explore this idea by the defi-
                      nition of first-order stochastic dominance (FOSD). This concept is connected with
                      the mean of the lottery.
                   2. If two lotteries F(·) and G(·) have the same mean, but lottery F(·) is unambiguously
                      less risky than G(·) (i.e., F(·) is distributed over a smaller support), then we can
                      anticipate that lottery F(·) would be preferred to lottery G(·). In this case the con-
                      cept developed to rank lotteries is related with the variance of a lottery, and we will
                      explore it in the definition of second-order stochastic dominance (SOSD).

                   5.10.1    First Order Stochastically Dominates (FOSD)


                      First order stochastic dominance Lottery F(·) first order stochastically domi-
                      nates (FOSD) lottery G(·) if and only if

                            1 − F(x) ≥ 1 − G(x)   for every payoff x, or alternatively     F(x) ≤ G(x).


                   First, recall that, for a given lottery F(.), 1 − F(x) intuitively represents the probability
                   of obtaining prizes above a given monetary outcome x. Hence FOSD implies that, at
                   any given outcome x, the probability of obtaining prizes above x is higher with lottery
                   F(·) than with lottery G(·), which is expressed as 1 − F(x) ≥ 1 − G(x). This intuition is
                   graphically represented in figure 5.30, where for a given outcome x , 1 − F(x ) ≥ 1 −
                   G(x ), or alternatively F( x ) ≤ G(x ). Graphically, this implies that the cdf of lottery F(·)
                   lies below that of G(·). Intuitively, lottery F(·) assigns a small probability weight to
                   low monetary outcomes but puts most of its probability weight on the highest payoffs
                   of the support. A converse argument applies to lottery G(·), which assigns most of the
                   probability weight to the lowest monetary outcomes.
                      Let us now take an example with lotteries over discrete outcomes (the examples
                   above considered that lotteries F(·) and G(·) were continuous cdfs). Figure 5.31a de-
                   picts lottery G(·) that assigns half probability to monetary outcome $1 and half to
                   outcome $4. Lottery F(·), in contrast, shifts the probability weight of outcome $1 to-
                   ward outcomes $2 and $3 equally (with a probability of 1/4 each), whereas the prob-
                   ability weight in outcome $4 is entirely shifted to $5. Figure 5.31b illustrates these cdfs

                   5.10.2   Second Order Stochastically Dominates (SOSD)
                   We now focus on the dispersion of monetary outcomes in a lottery, as opposed to the
                   higher/lower returns that FOSD analyzes. To focus on the dispersion of the lottery,
                   consider two lotteries F(·) and G(·) with the same mean (i.e., the same expected out-
                   come). We then say that lottery F(·) second-order stochastically dominates (SOSD)

                   24
                      Exercise 14 at the end of the chapter explores the relationship between FOSD and the (relatively
                   simpler) concept of dominance in means.
376                                                                                                          Chapter 5



      G(·) if, for every nondecreasing utility function u(x), u : ℝ → ℝ (mapping certain mon-
      etary outcomes into utility levels), we have that

                                            ∫ u ( x ) dF ( x ) ≥ ∫ u ( x ) dG ( x ).
      That is, lottery F(·) SOSD G(·) if the former generates a larger expected utility than the
      latter, where both of them yield the same mean, that is, ∫ xdF ( x ) = ∫ xdG ( x ).

      Example 5.14: Mean-preserving spread Let us first consider lottery F(·) which, as
      figure 5.33a illustrates, assigns an equal probability to outcomes $2 and $3 occurring.
      We then spread the probability weight of these two outcomes over the probability of
      these and other outcomes. In particular, we spread the probability weight of $2 (ini-
      tially occurring with probability 1/2) over outcome $1 and $2 equally (which now
      occur with probability 1/4 each), as figure 5.33a indicates. Similarly, we spread the
      probability weight of $3 (1/2) over outcomes $3 and $4 equally (1/4 each). First, note
      that the expected values of both lotteries coincide, being 5/2 for both F(·) and G(·).25
      Hence the mean is preserved across lotteries. However, lottery G(·) spreads the prob-
      ability weight of lottery F(·) over a larger set of monetary outcomes (larger support),
      making G(·) riskier than F(·) in the SOSD sense. ■

      Hence lottery F(·) SOSD G(·), since they both have the same mean, but the former
      concentrates its probability weight over a smaller support, in that F(·) is less dispersed
      than G(·). Note, however, that neither lottery FOSD the other. Indeed, as figure 5.33b
      indicates, F(·) is neither above G(·) for all values of x nor below G(·) for all x.

      Example 5.15: Elementary increase in risk We say that a cdf G(·) is an elementary
      increase in risk (EIR) of another cdf F(·) if G(·) takes all the probability weight of an
      interval [x′, x″] and transfers it to the endpoints of this interval, x′ and x″, such that the
      mean of the original lottery F(·) is preserved. Hence both cdfs F(·) and G(·) maintain
      the same mean but G(·) concentrates more probability at the end points of the interval
      [x′, x″] than the original distribution F(·). Figure 5.34 illustrates an EIR.
         Note that an EIR is a mean-preserving spread (MPS), but the converse is not neces-
      sarily true. In particular, this would be the case if the MPS shifts its probability weight
      toward points different than the endpoints x′ and x″ (e.g., evenly distributing probabil-
      ity over interior points of the interval [x′, x″]), thus satisfying the definition of a MPS

      25
         Indeed, the mean of F(x) is 1 2 2 + 1 2 3 = 5 2 , which coincides with that of G(x), 1 4 1 + 1 4 2 + 1 43 + 1 4
      4 = 5 2.

      but not that of an EIR. (The definition of the EIR would only hold if all probability
      weight is transferred to the endpoints of the interval.) Finally, if a lottery G(·) is a MPS
      of another lottery F(·), then we can claim that F(·) SOSD G(·), since both lotteries
      share the same mean but F(·) is less dispersed than G(·). As a consequence, if a lottery
      G(·) is an EIR from another lottery F(·), we can say that F(·) SOSD G(·).26 ■

                   5.11    Subjective Probability Theory

                   In previous sections we assumed that the probabilities of every possible outcome were
                   objective and observable by the decision maker. This might not be true in certain cases
                   where, instead, people hold probabilistic beliefs about the likelihood of a certain event.
                   We refer to these probabilistic beliefs as individual’s subjective probabilities. Because
                   of being subjective, one could ask whether we can infer a decision maker’s subjective
                   probabilities from his/her actual behavior. The answer to this question is yes: consider
                   a decision maker who prefers a gamble giving him $1 in state 1 and $0 in state 2 to
                   another gamble in which he gets $0 in state 1 and $1 in state 2. If the value of money
                   is the same across states, we can infer that this decision maker is assigning a higher
                   subjective probability to state 1 occurring than to state 2, meaning his beliefs about
                   state 1 occurring are higher.
                      In this section we want to extend the EU theorem with objective probabilities that
                   we described in previous parts of this chapter to a setting of subjective probabilities.30
                   Before stating this extension of the EU theorem we must, however, start defining an
                   individual’s preference over two lotteries in state s. In particular, we define state-s
                   preferences over lotteries by saying that an individual prefers lottery Fs(·) to Fs′(⋅) ,
                   both of them in state s, if and only if the expected utility from lottery Fs(·) is larger than
                   that from lottery Fs′(⋅). That is,

                               Fs (⋅)  Fs′(⋅)    if and only if      ∫ u ( x ) dF ( x ) ≥ ∫ u ( x ) dF ′( x ).
                                                                         s   s    s   s          s   s   s   s


                     Hence the state preferences ( ≿ 1, ≿ 2, … , ≿ s) on state lotteries (F1, F2, … , Fs) are state
                   uniform if
                                                  s ′= s ′′ for any two states s ′ and s ′′.

                   That is, preferences over lotteries are state uniform if, for any two states s′ an s″, the
                   ranking of any two lotteries Ft(·) and Ft ′(⋅) coincides when state is t = s′ and when it is
                   t = s″. More explicitly, either

                   Ft (⋅)  Ft ′(⋅) both when the state is t = s′ and when it is t = s′′ , or

                   Ft ′(⋅)  Ft (⋅) both when the state is t = s′ and when it is t = s′′ , or

                   Ft (⋅) ∼ Ft ′(⋅) both when the state is t = s′ and when it is t = s′′.

                   30
                      For more details on state dependent utility, see appendices A and B at the end of this chapter, and

382                                                                                         Chapter 5



         In words, the decision maker either prefers lottery F to F′ across all states, or F′ to
      F across all states, or he is indifferent between F and F′ across all states. By our defini-
      tion above of state uniform preferences, the Bernouilli utility function in state s and s′,
      us(·) and us′ (⋅) , can differ only up to an increasing linear transformation. That is, there
      is a utility function u(·) such that
                                               us (⋅) = π s u (⋅) + β s

      for every state s, where πs > 0 and βs (and similarly for us′ (⋅) , so that the ranking be-
      tween the expected utility in state s and s′ is unaffected).

      5.11.1   Subjective Probability EU Theorem
      We can now state the extension of the EU theorem to subjective probabilities; this
      extension is commonly referred to as subjective expected utility, or SEU.
        Let us allow for the possibility that the monetary payoff under state s, xs, is not a
      certain amount of money but a random amount itself, with associated distribution
      function Fs(·). Hence monetary outcomes arising from the S states of nature can be
      described as a lottery L for every state of nature, namely L = (F1, F2, …, FS). Given this
      “extended” definition of lotteries to account for state-dependence, we can then rewrite
      the IA as the “extended” IA, as follows.

      “Extended” IA The preference relation over lotteries satisfies the “extended” IA if,
      for any three lotteries L, L′ and L″ and α ∈ (0, 1), we have that
                     L L′ if and only if αL + (1 − α)L″  αL′ + (1 − α)L″.

      Hence this “extended” IA is a mere extension of the standard IA to the case of “ex-
      tended” lotteries L = (F1, F2, …, FS). We can now express the extended EU theorem.


         SEU theorem Suppose that a preference relation over lotteries satisfies conti-
         nuity and the extended IA. Suppose, in addition, that preferences over lotteries
         are state uniform. Then there are subjective probabilities (π1, π2, … , πS) ≫ 0 and
         a utility function u(·) on certain amounts of money, such that for any two lists
         of monetary amounts (x1, x2, … , xS) and ( x1′ , x2′ , … , xS′ ), the individual decision
         maker prefers (x1, x2, … , xS) to ( x1′, x2′ , … , xS′ ) if and only if,

                                 ∑ π ( x ) u ( x ) ≥ ∑ π ( x ) u ( x ′ ).
                                       s   s      s   s           s       s   s   S
                                   s                         s
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                        383



                      Intuitively, the last expression says that a decision maker prefers the first list of mon-
                   etary outcomes to the second if the “subjective” expected utility he obtains from the
                   first list is larger than that from the second. This result allows us to generalize much of
                   our previous methodology to the case of subjective probabilities (i.e., beliefs).
                      Nonetheless, the predictions of the SEU theorem are not necessarily satisfied in
                   some experimental settings. The Ellsberg’s paradox presents a behavioral pattern that
                   violates the SEU theorem, paralleling the “anomalies” we encountered in the IA under
                   objective probabilities, namely the Allais and the Machina paradoxes.

                   5.11.2   Ellsberg’s Paradox
                   Consider the following game. Your instructor shows up in the classroom with an urn
                   containing 300 balls. He informs you that, among the 300 balls, 100 are red, but the
                   remaining 200 can be either blue or green. Then he presents you the following two
                   gambles, asking you to choose only one of them. In all gambles you will be allowed to
                   insert your hand in the urn to extract one ball.
                   Gamble A: You win $1,000 if the ball you extract is red.
                   Gamble B: You win $1,000 if the ball you extract is blue.
                      Confronted with these two gambles, many subjects select gamble A, showing that
                    3 ⋅ u ($1, 000 ) > p ( Blue ) ⋅ u ($1, 000 ), The preceding condition implies the objective
                   1

                   probability that the ball is red ( 1 3 , a piece of information subjects have before selecting
                   a gamble) must be higher than the subjective probability (belief) that the individual
                   assigns to the ball being blue, 1 3 > p(Blue). Now your instructor offers you the choice
                   among two new gambles.
                   Gamble C: You win $1,000 if the ball you extract is not red.
                   Gamble D: You win $1,000 if the ball you extract is not blue.
                      In this situation, many subjects choose gamble C, indicating that
                    3 u ($1, 000 ) > p ( Not blue ) ⋅ u ($1, 000 ) , since the probability of extracting a ball that
                      ⋅
                   2

                   is not red is 2 3 . Therefore this condition implies that the objective probability that
                   the ball is not red ( 2 3 ) must be higher than the subjective probability the individual as-
                   signs to the ball not being blue, that is, 2 3 > p(Not blue). However, this selection is
                   contradictory with the previous choice (of gamble A over B) if the decision maker uses
                   subjective EU theory. In particular, from standard probability, we know that p(Blue) =
                   1 − p(Not blue). Therefore 2 3 > p(Not blue) implies 2 3 > p(Not blue) = 1 − p(Blue), or
                   p(Blue) > 1 − 2 3 = 1 3 . Hence either 1 3 > p(Blue) holds or the contrary p(Blue) > 1 3 is
                   satisfied, but not both conditions simultaneously.

      5.12 Alternatives to SEU: Ambiguity Aversion (MEU), Capacities (CEU), and
      Smooth Ambiguity Aversion (SAA)

      The observed behavior in the Ellsberg paradox led many scholars to suggest that indi-
      viduals have ambiguous (unclear) beliefs, rather than objective or subjective beliefs as
      previous theories considered. In order to allow for such ambiguity, and to explain the
      Ellsberg paradox, the literature has offered alternative theories. Given their importance
      and subsequent use in applications, we next present three of them: expected utility
      theory with multiple priors (also referred to as maxmin expected utility, MEU), rank-
      dependent expected utility (or Choquet expected utility, CEU), and smooth ambiguity
      aversion (SAA). In our discussion, we let F denote an act F : S → X from the set of
      states to the set of outcomes (which can be monetary payoffs or any other prize).

      5.12.1     Maxmin Expected Utility (MEU)
      Following Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989), consider a setting where subjects have too
      little information to form their priors, and allow the subjects to consider a set of priors.
      Now, if an individual is uncertainty averse (to be defined below), he will choose lottery
      F over another lotteryG if the former provides a higher expected utility than the latter
      according to a worst possible prior. In this context, Gilboa and Schmeidler replaced the
      IA with their “uncertainty aversion” axiom and their “certainty-independence” axiom,
      which we define next.


           Uncertainty Aversion Consider an individual who is indifferent between two
           lotteries F and G. Then he is uncertainty averse if he weakly prefers the com-
           pound lottery αF + (1 − α)G to lottery G, where α ∈ (0, 1).

        Intuitively, a decision maker who is uncertainty averse has a preference for mixing
      (or hedging), since the compound lottery becomes at least as valuable as either of the
      two lotteries alone.31 In particular, that may occur when the two acts have negatively
      correlated payoffs, so their mixture yields a more even payoff distribution across

      31
         The standard IA is actually a special case of the uncertainty aversion axiom if we restrict the decision
      maker to exhibit indifference between the compound lottery and the simple lotteries. Indeed, if F ∼ G,
      then by the IA we must have αF + (1 − α)G ∼ αG + (1 − α)G, or αF + (1 − α)G ∼ G; thus it becomes a
      special case of the definition of uncertainty aversion given above.
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                             385



                   states.32 Let us next define the second axiom, certainty independence, which weakens
                   the IA.


                        Certainty Independence For any two lotteries F and G and a constant act K
                        (i.e., a certain outcome or a lottery that remains constant across all states), the
                        decision maker weakly prefers lottery F to G if and only if he prefers αF + (1 − α)K
                        to αG + (1 − α)K, where α ∈ (0, 1).

                      The certainty-independence axiom relaxes the IA as it only requires that preferences
                   over two lotteries be unaffected when each lottery is mixed with a certain outcome K
                   (rather than when mixed with a third lottery, as required by the IA). In other words,
                   certainty independence can be understood as a special case of the IA, where the third
                   lottery yields the same outcome across all states (that is, it happens with certainty).
                      Importantly, when we replace the IA with uncertainty aversion and certainty indepen-
                   dence, we obtain a nice utility representation of preferences that allows for the possibility
                   of the individual decision maker sustaining multiple prior beliefs. In particular, a decision
                   maker weakly prefers lottery F to G if and only if (i.e., it is equivalent to)

                                            min ∫ u ( F ( s )) dp ( s ) ≥ min ∫ u (G ( s )) dp( s) .
                                            p∈C                           p∈C
                                                  S                             S


                      That is to say, the individual decision maker first evaluates the expected utility of lotter-
                   ies F and G according to each of his multiple priors p ∈ C; he then identifies the prior that
                   yields the lowest expected utility when playing lottery F, and similarly for lottery G; last,
                   he selects the lottery with the highest expected utility.33 Intuitively, he separately evaluates
                   each lottery at his worst possible prior and then chooses the lottery yielding the highest
                   expected utility, which explains why this approach is also referred to as “maxmin ex-
                   pected utility,” or MEU. (For a proof of this expected utility representation result, see
                   Gilboa and Schmeidler (1989, 145–49), or for a more didactic presentation see Ok (2007,
                   513–19).

      Next we will show that the Ellsberg paradox, despite not being rationalized by subjec-
      tive probability theory, can be explained if the decision maker exhibits MEU prefer-
      ences. Recall from the Ellsberg paradox that gamble A (B) rewards with $1,000 if the
      ball extracted is red (blue, respectively). While the proportion of red balls in the urn is
      known, 1/3, the decision maker does not receive any information about the number of
      blue balls. Hence an individual with MEU preferences finds

                   can occur. For instance, if the decision maker has two possible priors (pBlue,

                   while the lowest prior for pNot Blue is min pNot Blue = min{0.9,0.6} = 0.6, entailing that
                   min pBlue ≠ 1 − pNot Blue since 0.1 ≠ 0.6. Hence the Ellsberg paradox can be explained
                   according to MEU.

                   5.12.2   Choquet Expected Utility (CEU)
                   Schmeidler (1989) provided an alternate theory to account for the anomaly in the Ells-
                   berg paradox by defining beliefs with the use of capacities. Specifically, a capacity is
                   defined as a real-valued function v(·) from a subset of the state space S to [0, 1], with
                   the normalization v(∅) = 0 and v(S) = 1. In addition, we say that capacity v(·) satisfies
                   comonotonicity if v(A) ≥ v(B), where A is a superset of B; in words, the probability
                   weight assigned to the larger set A cannot be smaller than that assigned to its subset B.
                   While a probability distribution assigns weights that are additive across two mutually
                   exclusive events, such as a, b ∈ S (their probabilities are additive), their capacities al-
                   low for nonadditivity. For instance, if S = {a, b}, then a example of a capacity is
                   v(∅) = 0, v(a) = 0.4, v(b) = 0.5, and v(a, b) = 1, where v(a) + v(b) ≠ v(a, b).
                     In this context, we cannot simply use a standard integral over states, since capacity v(·)
                   does not correspond to our notion of beliefs. However, Choquet (1953) developed inte-
                   grals specifically for capacities, which Schmeidler (1989) used in his representation re-
                   sult. In particular, a decision maker weakly prefers F to G if the Choquet integrals satisfy

                                               ∫ u ( F ( S )) dv ( S ) ≥ ∫ u (G ( S )) dv(S ) .
                                               S                        S


                     Moreover the CEU and MEU models are connected if we impose the uncertainty
                   aversion axiom in this CEU context. In order to do that, we first need that capacity v(·)
388                                                                                                           Chapter 5



      satisfies supermodularity (also referred to as complementarity in this context), in the
      sense that the marginal contribution of a subset of events B is larger when it joins a
      large set of events A than when it joins a small set C. To see this, let us take two sets A
      and C, where C is a subset of A, that is, C ⊂ A. In this context, the marginal contribution
      of B to the large set A is larger than its marginal contribution to the small group C:

                                        v ( A ∪ B ) − v( A) ≥ v (C ∪ B ) − v( B) ,
      where A and B do not intersect, A ∩ B = ∅.34

      Example 5.17: Simple capacities While the use of Choquet integrals is involved, the
      literature often uses “simple” capacities. Intuitively, a simple capacity on state space S can
      be understood as a convex combination between two extreme capacities: (1) a standard
      probability weight on A, p(A) ∈ [0, 1], which is a capacity with additive probabilities; and
      (2) the “complete ignorance” capacity w, which assigns w(S) = 1 and w(A) = 0 for every
      A ⊆ S. (In other words, in w the decision maker assigns a zero probability weight to all
      events, except to the entire state space S.) Formally, simple capacities are then defined as

                                             v ( A) = λ p ( A) + (1 − λ )w( A)

      for every A ⊆ S and where λ ∈ [0, 1]. In this context, parameter λ denotes the individu-
      al’s degree of confidence on p(A), while 1 − λ captures his “degree of ambiguity” about
      p(A) (also referred to as his “degree of uncertainty aversion”). For applications of
      simple capacities to noncooperative games, see Haller (2000), and to common pool
      resources, see Aflaki (2013). ■

      5.12.3      Smooth Ambiguity Aversion (SAA)
      Klibanoff (2005) offered a framework that accounts for observed behavior in the Ells-
      berg paradox while achieving separation between ambiguity (defined as the decision
      maker considering multiple priors) and his ambiguity attitude (a reflection of the deci-
      sion maker’s taste).35 A decision maker weakly prefers F to G if and only if

                         p       S                                 p       S

                      That is to say, the individual decision maker, first, evaluates the expected utility of lottery
                   F for each prior p ∈ C; and second, he aggregates using prior μ over each of his multiple
                   priors p ∈ C given the increasing function ϕ(·). Performing a similar calculation for lottery
                   G, he can finally choose the lottery with the highest expected value. Intuitively, μ captures
                   the ambiguity the decision maker faces, as a more concentrated support of μ indicates that
                   he does not face much ambiguity on the possible priors p ∈ C. In the extreme, when μ is
                   degenerate on a single prior p, the SAA model reduces to the standard EU model. More-
                   over the shape of function ϕ(·) captures his attitude toward ambiguity. For example, if
                   ϕ(x) = −e−αx, parameter α describes the concavity of the function, as depicted in figure 5.35.
                   When α → 0, function ϕ(x) → −1 for all prior p, assigning a similar weight on all priors.
                   However, when α increases, so does the concavity of function ϕ(x), assigning a zero prob-
                   ability weight on a larger support of priors. In the limit, when α → ∞, function ϕ(x) → 0 for
                   all priors, expect for the lowest (i.e., the prior corresponding to the worst case scenario);
                   indicating that in such limiting case SAA collapses to the MEU model above.

      Further reading The preceding two models have been used in many applications.
      Dow and Werlang (1992) consider individuals with supermodular capacities in the
      CEU framework analyzed above to show that individuals do not have incentives to buy
      or sell assets for a potentially large range of prices. A similar finding emerged in varia-
      tions on the model developed by Epstein and Wang (1994) and Uppal and Wang (2003).
Choice under Uncertainty                                                                                    391



                   The multiple priors model in MEU has also been applied to labor economics by
                   Nishimura and Ozaki (2004), and to macroeconomic policy by Hansen et al. (1999) and
                   Hansen and Sargent (2001, 2008). For a detailed review of the different models pro-
                   posed in this literature that build on MEU and CEU, see Machina and Siniscalchi
                   (2014), and for an extensive survey of applications of these models to economics and
                   finance, see Mukenji and Tallon (2004). Last, the preceding models have been recently
                   tested in experimental labs, providing evidence of support for MEU and CEU in certain
                   contexts, but relatively more consistent evidence that supports prospect theory; see
                   Abdellaoui et al. (2014), Baillon, and Bleichrodt (2015), and Dimmock et al. (2015).

                   Appendix A: State-Dependent Utility

                   In our previous discussion, the decision maker only cared about the payoff arising
                   from every outcome of the lottery. In this appendix, we assume that the decision mak-
                   er cares not only about his monetary outcomes but also about the state of nature that
                   causes every outcome. Intuitively, this implies that, for a given outcome x, the decision
                   maker might experience a different utility if such outcome originates from state of
                   nature 1 occurring than from state of nature 2. In the following subsections we first
                   discuss how to describe uncertainty using states of nature, where states of nature are
                   allowed to be stochastic. Second, we analyze how these state-dependent preferences
                   can be used to obtain an “extended” expected utility representation.

                   Using States of Nature to Represent Utility
                   Let us assume that each of the possible monetary payoffs in a lottery is generated by
                   an underlying cause (an underlying state of nature). Consider the following two ex-
                   amples:
                   1. The monetary payoff of an insurance policy is generated by a car accident. In this
                      case, State of nature = {car accident, no car accident}.
                   2. The monetary payoff of a corporate stock is generated by the state of the economy.
                      In particular, State of nature = {economic growth, economic depression}.
                      Generally, let s ∈ S denote a state of nature, where S is a finite set containing all pos-
                   sible states of nature. Every state s has a well-defined probability of occurrence πs ≥ 0.
                   In this context, a random variable is a function g: S→ ℝ that maps states of nature in S
                   into monetary payoffs. Let us now extend our previous examples.
                   1. Car accident The random variable assigns a monetary value to the state of nature
                      “car accident” (e.g., −$1,000, with probability πacc) and to the state of nature “no
392                                                                                                                  Chapter 5



        accident” (e.g., −$50, since the driver only pays his insurance premium, with prob-
        ability (1 − πacc)). The following table summarizes the monetary payoff associated
        to every state of nature:
                           State of nature                                             Monetary payoff

                          πacc car accident                       –Damage + Deductible − Premium = −$1,000

                          πNoAcc no car accident                  Premium = −$50

      2. Corporate stock The random variable assigns a monetary value to the state of
         nature “economic growth” (e.g., $250 in increased value of the shares, with proba-
         bility πgrowth), and to the state of nature “economic depression” (e.g., −$125 in de-
         creased value of the shares, with probability (1 − πgrowth)).

                           State of nature                                                Monetary payoff

                      πgrowth economic growth                         Dividends, higher price of shares = $250

                      πdepression economic depression                 No dividends, loss if we sell shares = −$125

         Every random variable g(·), mapping states of nature into their corresponding mon-
      etary payoff, can also be represented as a monetary lottery F(·). In particular,

                                                        F(x) =       ∑ π,          s
                                                                 {s: g ( s )≤ x}

      where the set {s: g(s) ≤ x} represents all those states of nature s that generate a mone-
      tary payoff g(s) ∈ ℝ below a particular cutoff x. Hence the random variable g(·) gener-
      ates a monetary payoff for every state of nature s ∈ S, and since set S is finite, we can
      represent this list of monetary payoffs as

                                                    ( x1 , x2 , …, xS ) ∈  S+ ,
      where xs is the monetary payoff arising in state of nature s.

                   Appendix B: “Extended” Expected Utility Representation

                   We can now express a preference relation that ranks lists of monetary payoffs
                   ( x1 , x2 , …, xS ) ∈  S+ . (For simplicity, we restrict our attention to positive or zero
                   payoffs.)37

                   37
                     It is important to note the similarity of this setting with that in consumer theory. Recall that, in that
                   context, we described preferences over bundles, whereas now we analyze preferences over lists of
                   monetary payoffs. Since every list of monetary payoffs ( x1 , x2 , …, xS ) ∈  S+ specifies one payoff for
                   each state of nature (one for each contingency), this list is usually referred to as “contingent
                   commodities.”
394                                                                                                            Chapter 5



        We now expand our previous EU representation to this state-dependent utility. In
      particular, we say that a preference relation has an Extended EU representation if, for
      every state of nature s, there is a utility function us: ℝ+ → ℝ (mapping the monetary
      outcome in state s, xs, into a utility value us(xs) in R), such that for any two lists of
      monetary outcomes ( x1 , x2 , …, xS ) ∈  S+ and ( x ′1 , x ′ 2 , …, x ′ S ) ∈  S+ . Then
      ( x1, x2 , …, xS )  ( x ′1, x ′ 2 , …, x ′ S ) if and only if ∑ S π s ( xs )us ( xs ) ≥ ∑ S π s ( xs )us ( x ′ s ) .
         Interestingly, the main difference with previous sections is that now the Bernouilli
      utility function is state-dependent, us(·), whereas in previous sections it was state-
      independent, u(·).

      regardless of the state of nature, that is, x1 = x2 (along the 45-degree line). Second, all

                   6. Prospect theory and the equity premium puzzle An elderly economics pro-
                      fessor is planning to retire next year. He is evaulating risky investments relative to
                      the amount he invests (which we refer to as his reference point, r). Although he
                      never studied prospect theory, his preferences reveal that he compares investments
                      according to this theory. In particular, for a return x on his investment r, his utility
                      is 100 ( x − r ) − 12 ( x − r ) if his return exceeds his investment, x ≥ r, but becomes
                                                     2


                      400(x − r) + 2(x − r)2 if his return is smaller than his investment, x < r. Assume that
                      his expected utility is linear in the probabilities (even though aged faculty member
                      never studied prospect theory, he is good at vNM utility functions!). Intuitively,
                      note that this individual’s preferences exhibit loss aversion, since the term (x − r) is
                      more heavily weighted when x < r than otherwise.
                           a. Assume that this individual plans to invest $1,000 and faces two investment
                              options: (i) bonds that yield $1,022.54 next year and (ii) stocks that yield $900
                              with probability 0.12 and $1,100 with probability 0.88. Show that this individ-
                              ual is indifferent between both investment options, and he could thus opt for the
400                                                                                   Chapter 5



            riskless bonds. (This tendency toward bonds is referred to as the “equity pre-
            mium puzzle.”)
         b. Let us generalize our previous result. That is, assume that the professor has an
            initial investment I > 0, and faces two investment options: (i) bonds yielding
            outcome Ib with certainty and (ii) stocks, yielding ISL with probability p and ISH
            with probability 1 − p, where ISH > I > ILH > 0. Find under which values of p the
            equity premium puzzle emerges.
         c. Consider now an individual who does not use his initial investment as a refer-

      7. An introductory example on risk aversion Assume that your utility function
         over income, x, is given by u(x) = √x, that is, a Cobb–Douglas type of function.
         You have been offered two wage options.
         • In the first one you will receive a fixed salary of $54,000.
         • In the second one, you will only receive $4,000 as a fixed payment, plus a bonus
           of $100,000 if the firm is profitable. The probability that the firm goes profitable
           (and thus you get a total salary of $104,000) is 0.5, while the probability that the
           firm does not make enough profits is 0.5.
         a. Find the expected value of the lottery induced by accepting the second wage
            offer.
         b. Find the expected utility associated with the second offer.
         c. Draw an approximate figure where the following elements are illustrated:
           i. Utility function (concave, linear, or convex)
          ii. Utility level from the first wage offer
         iii. Utility level from each of the two possible outcomes of the second wage offer
          iv. Expected utility level from the second wage offer
         d. Using your answers from parts a and (b), find the risk premium associated with
            the second offer.
         e. What amount of money should the first wage offer propose in order to make you
            indifferent between accepting the first and the second wage offers?
         f. In your figure from part c include the risk premium and the certainty equivalent
            of the second wage offer.

                       tax. Assume that the taxpayer is risk averse, meaning her utility u(x) is increasing and

6 Partial and General Equilibrium



    In this chapter we study equilibrium allocations and prices in the market of a single
    good (partial equilibrium) or several goods (general equilibrium). In section 6.1 on
    partial equilibrium, we implicitly assume that (1) such a good represents a small pro-
    portion of the economy, which guarantees that changes in the price of that good do not
    significantly affect equilibrium conditions in markets for other goods, and (2) the bud-
    get share that individuals spend on the good we analyze is relatively minor, and thus
    its wealth effects are negligible (which allows us to use the change in consumer surplus
    as a relatively accurate measure of welfare change). In this context, we are particularly
    interested in identifying prices that guarantee that consumption and production deci-
    sions are compatible, so that the market clears, meaning no excess supply or excess
    demand exists in equilibrium. Last, we evaluate how equilibrium prices and quantities
    are affected by small changes in some parameters (section 6.2), and apply our results
    to the analysis of how the introduction of a sales tax impacts equilibrium prices and
    welfare (section 6.3).
       In section 6.4, we study the markets of several goods simultaneously, by first exam-
    ining, for simplicity, economies without production and later extending our results to
    economies with production. In the first type of economies (barter economies), indi-
    viduals are endowed with a set of goods that they can exchange with one another until
    reaching a satisfactory allocation for all parties. Mathematically, these simultaneous
    decision problems by different consumers are equivalent to solving several utility
    maximization problems (UMPs), one for each consumer, guaranteeing that their Wal-
    rasian demands are compatible. In economies with production, however, individuals
    must first determine how to allocate inputs in the production of different goods, and
    then market prices help consumption and production decisions to clear, so no excess
    supply or demand arises in any market. In section 6.5 we explore comparative statics
    results under a general equilibrium setting, where either the price of one good changes
    or the initial endowment of one of the inputs changes. Section 6.6 examines the effect
412                                                                                           Chapter 6



      of sale taxes and of taxes on inputs in a general equilibrium setting. Two appendixes
      describe large economies, and how equilibrium results naturally arise in this context.

      6.1     Partial Equilibrium Analysis

      In a competitive equilibrium allocation, all agents must select an optimal allocation
      given their resources: that is, firms choose their production plans to maximize profits
      given their technologies, and consumers choose bundles that maximize their utility
      levels given their budget constraints. A competitive equilibrium allocation will emerge
      at a price that makes consumers’ purchasing plans (as captured by the aggregate de-
      mand function) to coincide with the firms’ production decisions (as represented by the
      aggregate supply function). Let us analyze each of these agents starting with the firm.

      6.1.1  Firms
      For a given price p* ∈ ℝ+, every firm j’s equilibrium output level q*j must solve the
      PMP:
                                               max p*q j − c j ( q j ),
                                                q j ≥0


      which yields the necessary and sufficient condition

                                 p* ≤ c ’j ( q*j )       with equality if   q*j > 0 .
      In the case of interior solutions, this result states that every firm j operating in a per-
      fectly competitive market increases output until the point at which the marginal cost of
      producing such a unit equals its market price, as described in previous chapters.

      6.1.2    Consumers

      xi > 0, that is, each consumer obtains a positive but diminishing marginal utility from
      an additional unit of good xi. Examples of this utility function include ui ( m, xi ) = mi + xi
      and ui(mi, xi) = mi + ln xi.

                    exchanged.

      Intuitively, this condition indicates that the willingness to pay of the consumer most
      interested in the good is still lower than the marginal cost of producing this unit for the
      most efficient firm. As a consequence there is no room for a profitable exchange, and
      no units of the good are produced or consumed.
         Additionally, since the marginal utility v′i(xi) is downward sloping for every con-
      sumer, v″i(xi) < 0 for all i, and the marginal cost c′j(qj) is upward sloping in output for
      every firm j, c″j(qj) > 0 for all j, aggregate demand and supply cross at a unique point,
      implying that the CE allocation is unique.

      Example 6.1: Finding equilibrium conditions Suppose that a perfectly competi-
      tive industry consists of two types of firms: 100 firms of type A and 30 firms of type B.
      Each type A firm has a short-run supply curve sA(p) = 2p. Each type B firm has a short-
      run supply curve sB(p) = 10p. The Walrasian market demand curve is x(p) = 5000 − 500p.
      Assuming that no more firms enter the industry, we can obtain the short-run equilibri-
      um price as follows:
      First, we sum the individual supply curves of the 100 type-A firms and the 30 type-B
      firms, to obtain an aggregate supply curve of S(P) = 100(2p) + 30(10p) = 500p. The
      short-run equilibrium occurs at the price at which quantity supplied equals quantity
      demanded,
Partial and General Equilibrium                                                                            419




                                               5000 − 500 p = 500 p, or      p = 5.

                    At this price, each type-A firm supplies sA(p) = 2p = 2 × 5 = 10 units, and each type-B
                    firm supplies sB(p) = 10p = 2 × 5 = 50 units. ■


                    6.1.3    Experiments in Partial and General Equilibria
                    In the last decades, the sharp theoretical predictions of perfectly competitive markets
                    (mainly, that a precise equilibrium price and quantity are given by the crossing
                    point between demand and supply) were tested and confirmed in many controlled
                    experiments in different countries and subject pools. See, for instance, Smith (1991,
                    156) and his famous quote “I am still recovering from the shock of the experimental
                    results. The outcome was unbelievably consistent with competitive price theory.” The
                    results Smith alludes to were in reference to a “double auction” in which the experi-
                    menter assigns a reservation value to every buyer and a reservation price to every
                    seller, and then every seller is allowed to announce the price at which he is willing to
                    sell the good, and every buyer announces the price at which he is willing to buy. In this
                    setting, the experimenter then aggregates the reservation values (prices) for all buyers
                    (sellers, respectively) in order to construct the market demand curve (supply curve) and
                    find the point at which demand and supply cross each other. Such competitive equilib-
                    rium price and quantity (the theoretical prediction in this market) were then compared
                    with the experimental results in the lab. Interestingly, while every seller (buyer) in this
                    market only observed his reservation price (value), all sellers converged relatively fast
                    to the equilibrium outcomes. Subsequently Gode and Sunder (1993) experimentally
                    showed that behavior approaches the theoretical prediction even when some subjects
                    are “dumb.” The literature has also examined whether individuals in controlled ex-
                    periments behave as predicted by general equilibrium theory. While the implementa-
                    tion of these markets is more involved than perfectly competitive markets of a single
                    commodity, the results are generally positive as well. For references, see the seminal
                    work of Goodfellow and Plott (1990), the role of credit constraints in Bosch-Domènech
                    and Silvestre (1997), and the effect of money in Lian and Plott (1998) and Hey and Di
                    Cagno (1998).

        contrast, when γ → ∞ (supply is perfectly elastic), the price received by producers is
        unchanged and the price paid by consumers increases by the amount of the tax.

      6.4     General Equilibrium

      We now extend our discussion of equilibrium conditions from markets with a repre-
      sentative consumer to markets with multiple consumers (each consumer with poten-
      tially different preferences). We seek to evaluate under which price conditions the
      agents’ demands for different goods are compatible with one another given the initial
      endowment of goods in the economy. For simplicity, we start with equilibrium alloca-
      tions in economies without production (called “barter equilibrium,” since consumers
      exchange units of the goods they are initially endowed with), and subsequently ana-
      lyze economies with production. At the end of the chapter we test our equilibrium re-
      sults in large economies, and finally explore some comparative statics.

      6.4.1  Economies without Production
      Consider an economy with two goods and two consumers, i = {1, 2}, each initially en-
      dowed with ei ≡ (e1i , e2i ) units of good 1 and 2, respectively. Figure 6.12a depicts the
Partial and General Equilibrium                    429

      endowment e ≡ (e1, e2), while any other allocation x ≡ (x1, x2) could similarly be de-

         Hence a movement from the initial endowment e to allocation A (which lies outside
      the lens-shaped area) cannot be a barter equilibrium, since consumer 1 is worse off
      at A; thus he would oppose a proposal to exchange e for A. Does that imply that any
      point in the lens-shaped area is a barter equilibrium? Not necessarily. Consider bundle
      B in figure 6.13. Despite lying inside the lens-shaped area, and thus yielding a higher
      utility level than the initial endowment e for both consumers, individuals could still
      find other points, such as D, that would make both of them better off than at B. Gener-
      ally, any point on the CC curve depicted in figure 6.13 (often referred to as the “con-
      tract curve” in which indifference curves are tangent to one another) would be an
      equilibrium, since Pareto improvements are no longer possible. As we show in the next
      sections, while the contract curve depicts Pareto efficient allocations, only its portion
      lying inside the lens-shaped area constitutes a barter equilibrium.
         The graphical presentation in figure 6.13 helps us in our initial search of a definition
      of equilibrium allocations. Nonetheless, before providing such a definition, we first
      need to define some additional ingredients. In particular, since allocations can only be
      part of an equilibrium if they are feasible, we still need to clarify which allocations are
      feasible, as well as which allocations can be blocked by one or more individuals in the
      economy.

                    We are now ready to use these definitions in order to identify what we mean by an in-
                    dividual (or group of individuals) blocking a given allocation, that is, the formation of
                    a blocking coalition of S individuals in an economy with I individuals.


                       Blocking coalitions Let S ⊂ I denote a coalition of consumers. We say that S
                       blocks the feasible allocation x if there is an allocation y meeting two conditions:
                       1. Allocation y is feasible for S. The aggregate amount of goods that individuals
                          in S enjoy in allocation y coincides with their aggregate initial endowment,
                          ∑ i ∈S y i = ∑ i ∈S ei .
                       2. Allocation y is Pareto superior for S. Allocation y makes all individuals in
                          the coalition weakly better off than under x, yi ≿ xi where i ∈ S, and it makes at
                          least one individual i strictly better off, yi ≻ xi.

                      The following definitions form the “ building blocks” of our definition of equilibri-
                    um in a barter economy:
434                                                                                      Chapter 6




      Figure 6.14
      Contract curve x2A = 2 x1A



         Equilibrium A feasible allocation x is an equilibrium in the exchange econo-
         my with initial endowment e if x is not blocked by any coalition of consumers.

         Intuitively, we can claim that a feasible allocation x is an equilibrium if there is no
      group of individuals S that could form a blocking coalition against x by finding a fea-
      sible allocation y that makes at least one of its members strictly better without harming
      any of the other members in S. Hence we can group together all equilibrium allocations
      in what is called the “core” of an exchange economy.

         Core The core of an exchange economy with endowment e, denoted C(e), is
         the set of all unblocked feasible allocations (all equilibria).


      Intuitively, it represents those allocations that are unblocked: (1) they are mutually
      beneficial for all individuals (i.e., they lie in the lens-shaped area); and (2) they do not
      allow for further Pareto improvements (i.e., lie on the contract curve). As depicted in
      figure 6.15, the set of core allocations is therefore the segment of the contract curve
Partial and General Equilibrium                                                                           435




                    Figure 6.15
                    Core of an exchange economy


                    that lies within the lens-shaped area. Remarkably, these core allocations coincide with
                    those in equilibria, as we show next.

                    6.4.2    Competitive Markets
                    In the previous barter economy we did not require prices. Let us now explore the no-
                    tion of equilibrium in economies where we do allow prices to emerge. For presentation
                    purposes, we first describe consumers’ preferences, next the excess demand function
                    that results from comparing the aggregate demand under a specific market price against
                    the total endowment of each good. Then we define equilibrium allocations in competi-
                    tive markets (which we refer as “Walrasian equilibrium allocations”) and explore con-
                    ditions under which they exist.

                    Consumers We consider consumers’ utility functions to be continuous, strictly in-
                    creasing, and strictly quasi-concave in  N+ (recall that strictly quasi-concavity entails
                    strictly convex indifference curves).
436                                                                                          Chapter 6



      As a consequence the UMP of every consumer i, when facing a budget constraint

                              p ⋅ xi ≤ p ⋅ ei   for all price vectors p >> 0,
      yields a unique solution, denoted as the Walrasian demand x(p, p · ei). In addition,
      x(p, p · ei) is continuous in the price vector p. Intuitively, note that individual i’s in-
      come comes from selling his endowment ei at market prices p, earning
      p ⋅ ei = p1e1i + ... + pk eki dollars to be used in the purchase of allocation xi.
         We can add the Walrasian demand x(p, p · ei) for good k of every individual in the
      economy, obtaining the aggregate demand for good k, and compare it against the aggre-
      gate endowment of that good, which yields the excess demand of good k, as follows:

           Let us next explore existence and uniqueness of a Walrasian equilibrium.


           Existence of WEA A Walrasian equilibrium price vector p* ≫ 0, where
           z(p*) = 0, exists if the excess demand function z(p) satisfies continuity and Wal-
           ras’s law (and both of these properties hold given the initial assumptions we
           imposed on utility functions).11

      Uniqueness of WEA
      A desirable property of equilibrium prices is their uniqueness, as satisfied by the excess
      demand function in figure 6.17a but violated by that in figure 6.17b. As we next show, gross
      substitutability of all goods is a sufficient condition for an equilibrium price to be unique.

      Proof By contradiction, suppose that there is another equilibrium price vector p′, that
      is, p′ satisfies z(p′) = 0, where p′, p* ≫ 0. Let us define price vector p′ to be an increase
      in the price of all goods j ≠ k in vector p* (except for the price of good k) as follows:

                                           p’ = ( mp1* , …, pk* , …, mpL* ) ,
      where m > 1. Hence, since the price of all other goods increased, the excess demand of
      good k must be positive; as prescribed by gross substitutability (pj and xk must move in
      the same direction, and then so do pj and zk). But then zk(p′) > 0, implying that price
      vector p′ does not clear the market for good k. Since all markets are not in equilibrium
      at p′, price vector p′ is not a WEA. (A similar argument applies if, rather than

                    Equilibrium Allocations Must Be in the Core
                    Our previous discussion suggested that Walrasian equilibrium allocations (WEAs) are
                    mutually beneficial for all individuals. That is, an allocation cannot be blocked by any
                    coalition of individuals, or, in other words, must be in the core of the economy. Let us
                    next show that, if each consumer’s utility function is strictly increasing, then every
                    WEA is in the core, which we express as W(e) ⊂ C(e).

                    Proof Assume, by contradiction, a WEA, x(p*) with equilibrium price p*, that does

                    allocation is not part of the core, x(p*) ∉ C(e), we can find a coalition of S individuals
                    and another allocation y such that

      We can immediately infer two conclusions from the previous result. On one hand, the
      core C(e) will at least contain the WEA (or WEAs), implying that the core must be
      nonempty. On the other hand, since all core allocations are Pareto efficient, we cannot
      increase the welfare of one consumer without decreasing that of other consumers, im-
      plying that all WEAs (which are part of the core) are also Pareto efficient. This last
      result is often referred to as the first welfare theorem, as we compactly describe next.

           First welfare theorem Every WEA is Pareto efficient.


      As depicted in figure 6.19, the WEA lies on the core (the segment of the contract curve
      within the lens-shaped area), and the core is a subset of all PEAs (as illustrated in the
      contract curve). For a numerical example of the first welfare theorem, see example 6.6,
      where the WEA we found ( x1A,∗ , x2A,∗ ; x1B ,∗ , x2B ,∗ ; p1 p2 ) = (137.5, 275; 62.5,125; 2) , lies
      on the contract curve x2A = 2 x1A, and hence it is Pareto efficient.

      Consider the setting depicted in figure 6.20 and, starting from initial endowment e, as-
      sume that the WEA is x′, which also belongs to the set of core allocations C(e). How-
      ever, suppose that society would prefer allocations x to x′ according to some social
      welfare function that aggregates individual preferences over bundles.12 A natural

      agents cannot accurately observe—these two theorems do not necessarily apply, as we
      examine in subsequent chapters. Likewise our previous analysis assumed that consum-

      Equilibrium with Production—Welfare
      In this subsection we seek to extend the first and second welfare theorems to econo-
      mies with production, connecting WEA and PEAs. Before stating the first welfare
      theorem, let us define what we mean by a PEA in economies with production.

         Pareto efficiency A feasible allocation (x, y) is Pareto efficient if there is no
         other feasible allocation ( x, y ) such that

                                                               u i ( x i ) ≥ u i ( xi )
         for every consumer i ∈ I, with u i ( x i ) > u i ( xi ) for at least one consumer i.

      That is, a feasible allocation of bundles to consumers and production plans to firms is
      Pareto efficient if there is no other feasible allocation that makes at least one consumer
      strictly better off and no consumer worse off.
         As in section 6.4.1 analyzing barter economies, let us describe how to mathemati-
      cally find the set of PEAs. In particular, in an economy with two goods, two consum-

                       Indeed, if we move labor from firm 2 to firm 1, the production of good 2 increases by ∂F2 / ∂L while

      6.5   Comparative Statics

      In this section we briefly explore some comparative statics of our equilibrium results
      at the WEA in economies with production. Specifically, we analyze how equilibrium
      outcomes are affected by an increase in the price of one good, and then by an increase
      in the endowment of one input. For both questions, consider a setting with two goods,
      each being produced by two factors, 1 and 2, under constant returns to scale (CRS).
      Given CRS, a necessary condition for input prices ( w1∗ , w2∗ ) to be in equilibrium is that
      firms produce until their marginal costs equal the price of the good, that is,

                               c1 ( w1 , w2 ) = p1 and c2 ( w1 , w2 ) = p2 .
Partial and General Equilibrium                                                                                     461



                      For compactness, let z1j(w) denote firmj’s demand for factor 1, and z2j(w) be its de-
                    mand for factor 2.17 Hence we say that the production of good 1 is relatively more in-
                    tense in factor 1 than is the production of good 2 if
                                                             z11 ( w ) z12 ( w )
                                                                      >          ,
                                                             z21 ( w ) z22 ( w )

                    where z1j(w) / z2j(w) represents firm j’s demand for input 1 relative to that of input 2.

                    6.5.1     Changes in the Price of One Good pj (Stolper–Samuelson Theorem)18
                    Consider an economy with two consumers and two firms satisfying the factor intensity
                    assumption given above. If the price of good j, pj, increases, then (1) the equilibrium
                    price of the factor more intensively used in the production of good j increases, while
                    (2) the equilibrium price of the other factor decreases.

                    Proof Let us first take the equilibrium conditions about marginal costs being equal to
                    output prices:

                    Applying Shephard’s lemma, ∂ci(w1, w2) / ∂wj = zij(w) results in

                                                     z11 ( w )dw1 + z12 ( w )dw2 = dp1 ,

                                                     z21 ( w )dw1 + z22 ( w )dw2 = dp2 .
                      Hence, if only price p1 varies, then dp2 = 0. We can rewrite the second expression as

                    dw1 / dp1 yields
