      6.6     Introducing Taxes

      6.6.1    Tax on Goods
      Assume that as a result of a sales tax tk imposed on good k, the price paid by consum-
      ers, pkC , increases by pkC = (1 + t j ) pkP , where pkP is the price received by producers. In
      this circumstance, if the tax on goods 1 and 2 coincides (i.e., t1 = t2), the price ratio
      consumers and producers face is unaffected because
Partial and General Equilibrium                                                                                   467




                                                        p1C (1 + t1 ) p1P p1P
                                                           =              =    .
                                                        p2C (1 + t 2 ) p2P p2P

                       Hence the after-tax allocation is still Pareto efficient. However, if only good 1 is af-
                    fected by the tax (i.e., t1 > 0) while t2 = 0, or more generally, if each good is subject to a
                    different tax, (i.e., t1 ≠ t2), then the allocation will not be Pareto efficient. In this setting,
                    the MRTSL,K is still the same as before the introduction of the tax, since
                                                       ∂F1 ∂L w L ∂F2 ∂L
                                                             =   =
                                                       ∂F1 ∂K w K ∂F2 ∂K

                    is unaffected by the tax. Therefore the allocation of inputs still achieves efficiency in
                    production. Similarly the MRT1,2 still coincides with the price ratio of goods 1 and 2,
                    p1P p2P , where t1 > t2, that is,
                                                      ∂F2 ∂L p1P ∂F2 ∂K
                                                            =   =       ,
                                                      ∂F1 ∂L p2P ∂F1 ∂K

                    where recall that the price received by the producer, p1P , is the same before and after
                    introducing the tax. While the MRS1,2 coincides with the price ratio that consumers
                    face, which is p1C p2C or (1 + t1 ) p1P (1 + t 2 ) p2P , it now becomes larger than the price
                    ratio that producers face, p1P p2P , since t1 > t2. That is,
                                                             p1C (1 + t1 ) p1P   p1P
                                                  MRS1,2 =      =              >     .
                                                             p2C (1 + t 2 ) p2P p2P

                       Intuitively, the rate at which consumers are willing to substitute good 1 for 2 is
                    larger than the rate at which firms can transform good 1 for 2. As a consequence the
                    production of good 1 should decrease and that of good 2 increase.

                    6.6.2    Tax on Inputs
                    Similar arguments extend to the introduction of taxes on inputs, yielding a price paid
                    by producers (firms hiring the input) of wmP = (1 + t m )wmC for input m = {L, K}, where
                    wmC represents the price that input owners (consumers) receive. Specifically, if both
                    inputs are subject to the same tax, tL = tK = t, the input price ratio consumers and produc-
                    ers face coincides, yielding

                                                        w LP (1 + t )w LC w LC ,
                                                            =            =
                                                        w KP (1 + t )w KC w KC
468                                                                                         Chapter 6



      so the efficiency conditions remain unaffected. However, when they differ, tL ≠ tK
      (or, as a special case, when only one input is subject to taxes), such condition for
      productive efficiency no longer holds. Indeed, while input consumers satisfy
      w LC w KC = ( ∂F1 ∂L ) ( ∂F1 ∂K ) and input producers satisfy w LP w KP = ( ∂F2 ∂L ) ( ∂F2 ∂K ),
      the input price ratios they face do not coincide, that is,
                             ∂F1 ∂L w LC (1 + t L )w LC w LP ∂F2 ∂L
                                   =    ≠              =    =       .
                             ∂F1 ∂K w KC (1 + t K )w KC w KP ∂F2 ∂K

        For instance, if tL > tK, the MRTSL,K is larger for firm 1 than 2, implying that the al-
      location of inputs is inefficient, in that the marginal productivity of additional units of
      labor (relative to capital) is larger in firm 1 than in 2.

      Appendix A: Large Economies and the Core

      While we know that equilibrium allocations (WEAs) are part of the core, in this ap-
      pendix we seek to show that, as the economy becomes larger, the core shrinks until
      exactly coinciding with the set of WEAs.
         Let us first consider an economy with I consumers, each with utility function ui and
      endowment vector ei, and next consider this economy’s replica by doubling the num-
      ber of consumers to 2I, each of them still with utility function ui and endowment vector
      ei. Intuitively, there are now two consumers of each type, informally understood as
      “twins,” since they have identical preferences and endowments. We can now define an
      r-fold replica economy εr, having r consumers of each type, for a total of rI consumers.
      For any consumer type i ∈ I, all r consumers of that type share the common utility
      function ui and have identical endowments ei ≫ 0. As a consequence, when comparing
      two replica economies, the largest will be that having more of every type of consumer.
         In the context of replica economies, we need to adapt our notation from previous
      sections to keep track of consumer types and their number. In particular, allocation xiq
      indicates the vector of goods for the qth consumer of type i. Given this notation, we
      can rewrite feasibility in an r-fold replica economy as follows:
Partial and General Equilibrium                                                                                     469



                                                                I    r           I

                                                              ∑ ∑ xiq = r ∑ ei ,
                                                               i =1 q =1        i =1


                    since each of the r consumers of type i has a endowment vector ei.
                       Let us now examine the core of this replica economy εr. An important property of
                    the core in the r-fold replica economy, is that not only similar type of consumers start
                    with the same endowment vector ei, but they also end up with the same allocation at
                    the core; a property often referred to as “equal treatment at the core.”

                    Equal Treatment at the Core
                    If x is an allocation in the core of the r-fold replica economy εr, then every consumer
                    of type i must have the same bundle, xiq = xiq ′ , for every two “twins” q and q′ of type
                    i, q ≠ q′ ∈ {1, 2, … , r}, and for every type i ∈ I.

                    result can be easily generalized to r-fold replicas. Suppose that allocation

                    we are operating by contradiction, we need that when the premise of the claim is satis-

      The Core Shrinks as the Economy Enlarges
      Core set Cr weakly shrinks as the economy replicates (i.e., as r increases). That is, the
      core of the original (unreplicated) economy, C1, is a superset of that in the twofold
      replica economy, C2. Similarly the core in the twofold replica economy, C2, is a super-
      set of the threefold replica economy, C3; as depicted in figure A6.3.

      Proof Since we seek to show that C1 ⊇ C2 ⊇ C3 ⊇ … ⊇ Cr−1 ⊇ Cr ⊇ … it suffices to find
      that, for any r > 1, Cr−1 ⊇ Cr. First, suppose that allocation x = (x1, x2, … xI) ∈ Cr. Intui-
      tively, we cannot find any blocking coalition to x in the r-fold replica economy εr. We
      then need to show that x cannot be blocked by any coalition in the (r − 1)-fold replica
      economy εr−1 either. This is easy! If we could find a blocking coalition to x in εr−1, then
      we could also find a blocking coalition in εr (and we could not, as x is in the core Cr).
      Indeed, all members in εr−1 are also present in the larger economy εr and their endow-
      ments have not changed.
         While the result above shows that the core satisfies Cr−1 ⊇ Cr, it does not exclude the
      possibility that the core does not shrink (keeping its size unaffected as the economy is
      replicated). That is, we still need to show that, as r increases, the core strictly shrinks.
      We will do this by demonstrating that allocations at the frontier of C1 do not belong to
      the core of the twofold replica economy, C2. Consider figure A6.4, which depicts an

                    Appendix B: Marshall–Hicks Four Laws of Derived Demand

                    Consider a production function q = f(K, L), with positive marginal products, fL, fK > 0.
                    Assume that the supply of each input is positively sloped, w(L) where w′(L) > 0 and
                    r(K) where r′(K) > 0.Demand for output is given by q = g(p), which satisfies the law of
                    demand, g′(p) < 0 Total cost is then w(L)L + r(K)K. In addition assume that the capital
                    market is perfectly competitive, but let us allow for the labor and output market to not
                    necessarily be competitive.
                       In this context, define εq,p ≡ (∂q / ∂p)(p / q) as the price elasticity of output; sK,r ≡ (∂K / ∂r)
                    (r / K) as the elasticity of capital supply to a change in its price, r; sL,r ≡ (∂L / ∂r)(r / L) as
                    the elasticity of labor supply to a change in the price of capital, r; εL,w ≡ (∂L / ∂w)(w / L)
                    as the elasticity of labor supply to a change in its own price, w; and let σ be the elastic-
                    ity of substitution between inputs. We will use superscript i to refer to the elasticity that
                    an individual firm faces, for example, ε qi , p , while industry elasticities will not include
478                                                                                                Chapter 6



      superscripts, such as εq,p. Additionally let θL ≡ wL / pq and θK ≡ rK / pq be the cost of
      labor and capital, respectively, relative to total sales, which implies that θL = 1 − θK.
      Finally, for compactness, let us define A ≡ 1 − (1 ε qi , p ) and B ≡ 1 + (1 ε iL,w ) .
         In this setting, Marshall, Hicks, and Allen separately analyze how the input demand
      of a perfectly competitive input, such as capital, is affected by a marginal change in the
      price of capital r, finding the following expression21:
                                             θ K ε q, p A + (σε q, p sL,w ) A2 + θ L ABσ
                           sK , r = −                                                          .
                                        (θ K + θ L B )2 + θ K (σ sL,w ) A + θ L (σ sL,w ) AB
         Marshall–Hicks’s four laws of input demand (also known as “derived demand”)
      state that an input demand becomes more elastic, whereby sK,r decreases, in (1) the
      elasticity of substitution between inputs, σ; (2) the price-elasticity of output demand,
      εq,p; (3) the cost of the input relative to total sales, θK = (rK / pq); and (4) the elasticity
      of the other input’s supply to a change in its price, sL,w. For simplicity, we analyze these
      four comparative statics under two common market structures considered in the litera-
      ture: (1) the Marshall’s presentation, which assumes that ε qi , p = sLi ,w = ∞ and that inputs
      cannot be substituted in the production process, σ = 0, and (2) the Hick’s presentation,
      which assumes that ε qi , p = sLi ,w = ∞ but does not impose assumptions on the elasticity
      of substitution, σ.22

                    Exercises

                    1. Equilibrium number of firms in perfectly competitive markets Consider a
                       perfectly competitive industry with N symmetric firms, each with cost function
                       c(q) = F + cq, where F, c > 0. Assume that the inverse demand is given by p(Q) =
480                                                                                             Chapter 6



          a − bQ, where a > c, b > 0, and where Q denotes aggregate output. What is the
          short-run equilibrium price in this market?
          a. Short-run equilibrium If exit and entry are not possible in the industry, (as-
             suming N firms remain active), find the individual production level of each
             firm.
          b. Long-run equilibrium Consider now that firms have enough time to enter the
             industry (if economic profits can be made) or to exit (if they make losses by
             staying in the industry). Find the long-run equilibrium number of firms in this
             perfectly competitive market.
      2. Equilibrium allocations insensitive to a common shock in all prices Consider
         a competitive market with L goods, N consumers and J firms. In this setting, as-
         sume that we find an equilibrium price vector p* ∈  L+ and equilibrium allocation
         ( x1* , x2* , …, xN* ; y1* , y2* , …, y*J ), where xi* ∈ L for every consumer i and y*j ∈ L for
         every firm j. Show that, if we were to scale price vector p* to λp*, where λ > 0, then
         allocation ( x1* , x2* , …, xN* ; y1* , y2* , …, y *J ) is still the equilibrium allocation.
      3. Per unit taxes versus ad valorem taxes A tax is to be levied on a commodity
         bought and sold in a competitive market. Two possible forms of tax may be used.
         In one case, a specific tax is levied, where an amount t is paid per unit bought or
         sold. In the other case, an ad valorem tax is levied, where the government collects
         a tax equal to τ times the amount the seller receives from the buyer. Assume that a
         partial equilibrium approach is valid.
          a. Show that, with a specific tax, the ultimate cost of the good to consumers and

7 Monopoly



   In chapters 7 through 9 we explore three types of market failures: monopoly (i.e., in-
   dustries with a single seller), imperfect competition models (i.e., industries with a few
   sellers that retain some market power), and externalities and public goods. In this
   chapter we start by describing (in section 7.1) under which conditions monopolies ex-
   ist, that is, when barriers to entry in an industry are sufficiently high to deter further
   entry. For instance, a common entry barrier is the legal protection of patents, which is
   prevalent in some pharmaceutical industries and markets using advanced technologies.
   Next section 7.2 examines how the monopolistic firm chooses its profit-maximizing
   output by equating the revenue from additional units and its additional costs. As it
   turns out, the output in a monopolized industry is smaller than that in competitive in-
   dustries, giving rise to a welfare loss, which we analyze in section 7.3. In section 7.4
   we examine different comparative statics analysis, such as how monopoly output is
   affected by changes in production costs, which allows for a tractable application of the
   envelope theorem. Section 7.5 extends the initial analysis of monopoly to a setting in
   which the firm produces in several plants, each with different costs (i.e., the so-called
   multiplant monopolist). While the identification of aggregate output in this context is
   similar to that of standard monopolies with a single plant or with different plants with
   symmetric costs (i.e., marginal revenue must still equate total marginal costs), the
   multiplant monopolist needs now to optimally divide such aggregate output among its
   different plants. We provide numerical examples to facilitate the presentation of such
   optimal division of output.
      In section 7.6 we analyze whether the monopolist could increase its profits by prac-
   ticing price discrimination. In particular, we explore three forms: first-degree price
   discrimination (or perfect price discrimination, where the monopolist charges each
   consumer his maximum willingness to pay), second-degree price discrimination
   (where the monopolist cannot distinguish different types of potential customers, and
   offers a menu of price–quantity pairs so that each type of individual selects a pair, thus
490                                                                                       Chapter 7



      revealing his type), and third-degree price discrimination (where the monopolist faces
      different types of customers but can observe each type). Section 7.7 also examines a
      monopolist’s optimal expenditure on advertising. Like price discrimination, such a
      practice is also used by the monopolist to increase its profits but does not rely on set-
      ting different prices to different groups of customers. In section 7.8 we explore natural
      monopolies, that is, firms that exhibit diminishing average costs. In this context, a
      single firm could produce a given output level at a lower average cost than two or more
      firms would. As a consequence regulation does not seek to promote entry in the indus-
      try where the monopolist operates (as such entry would not be necessarily welfare
      improving) but instead focuses on inducing the monopolist to increase its output level.
      We also describe the advantages and disadvantages of such a regulation. Last, section
      7.9 analyzes the profit-maximizing behavior of a monopsony (unique buyer), and its
      similarities to that of a monopoly (unique seller).

      7.1   Barriers to Entry

      Entry barriers are understood as industry conditions that make the entry of potential
      competitors either impossible or very costly. The barriers can be legal, structural, or
      strategic. Legal barriers, such as patents, provide the incumbent firm in an industry
      with the legal right to be the only seller during the life of the patent (if no close substi-
      tutes to the patented product are available). Newly discovered drugs are often patented,
      and thus provided with the legal right to set monopoly prices during a number of years
      (20 years in the United States). While the prospect of future monopoly profits could
      induce firms to invest large amounts in research and development, many scholars ar-
      gue that the current duration of patents in most industrialized countries is socially ex-
      cessive; see, for instance, Boldrin and Levine (2010).
         The second set of entry barriers is structural, and arises when the incumbent has a
      cost or demand advantage relative to potential entrants. While cost differentials could
      be due to a superior technology of incumbent firms, demand advantages can emerge
      because the incumbent benefits from a loyal group of customers who would hesitate to
      switch to the product of a new (and potentially unknown) firm, or from the presence of
      positive network externalities, that is, goods that become more attractive as the number
      of users increases, such as social media websites (e.g., Facebook or Instagram) and
      Internet sellers (e.g., eBay). If network effects are significant, a new firm might find it
      extremely difficult to break into the market, as it would first need to reach a sufficient
      number of users who are, of course, difficult to attract if few users initially visit the
      website.
Monopoly                                                                                                        491



              The third set of entry barriers is strategic, and does not rely on legal protections (as
           patents) nor on differences in the cost or demand curves between incumbent and new-
           comers. Even if all firms are symmetric, the incumbent monopolist can still benefit
           from a strategic entry barrier if it builds a reputation of fighting off newcomers, ulti-
           mately driving them out of the market. For instance, it could start price wars against
           every firm that dares to enter the industry: despite lowering its profits for a few periods
           (relative to those of accommodating entry), its strategic behavior can deter future com-
           petitors considering entering the market.1

           7.2   Profit-Maximizing Output under Monopoly

           Let us start with a general demand function x(p) that is continuous and strictly decreas-
           ing in p, x′(p) < 0. As in our discussion of perfectly competitive markets, we assume
           that there is a price p < +∞, often referred as “choke price,” such that x(p) = 0 for all
           prices above it, p > p (as depicted in figure 7.1). Intuitively, this guarantees that if
           market prices are sufficiently high, no consumers buy positive amounts of the good.
             In addition, let us consider a general cost function c(q) that is increasing and convex
           in q.2 Hence the monopolist’s profit-maximization problem can be expressed as a
           choice of a price p that solves

           cost from such an increase in output. This implies that, at the profit-maximizing output

           from selling an additional unit equals the marginal costs from producing such unit.
           Figure 7.2 illustrates this result.

           7.2.1    Marginal Revenue
           Figure 7.2 also shows that market demand lies above the marginal revenue curve. In-
           deed, since p′(qm) < 0 (i.e., market price decreases in output), marginal revenue must
           lie below the demand curve, p(q).4 This result calls for a more elaborate interpretation
           of the MR(q):

                                              MR(q) = p(qm)+p′(qm) qm.

              Intuitively, an increase in output produces two effects on the monopolist’s total rev-
           enue. On one hand, it produces a direct (positive) effect, since the monopolist can sell
           a larger amount of units at a price p(qm), as captured by the first term in the MR(q)
           equation. On the other hand, it produces an indirect (negative) effect. In particular, the
           increased production entails a movement along the demand curve, lowering prices.
           Hence the monopolist must reduce the price it charges not only to the additional unit it
           produces (the marginal unit) but also to the units it was already producing (the “infra-
           marginal” units, i.e., those below the margin). Specifically, this indirect effect is em-
           bodied in the second term of the MR(q) expression, which shows the reduction in
           market price due to the increased production, p′(qm), times all the units the monopolist
           produces, qm.
              Furthermore, since p′(qm) < 0 in the preceding expression of MR(q), we have that
           p(qm)> c′(qm). In words, the price the monopolist sets is higher than its marginal costs
           from producing the last unit. In addition, since in perfectly competitive markets p(q*)
           = c′(q*), we can conclude that prices satisfy pm > p* and, given that the demand curve
           is negatively sloped, output levels satisfy qm < q*. Figure 7.2 compares market prices
           under monopoly and perfectly competitive industries, pm > p*, and total output, qm<q*.

           4
             Note that at q = 0 both MR(q) and p(q) coincide. This is also illustrated in the figure, where the
           vertical intercepts of both curves coincide. You can easily check that MR(q) ≤ p(q) for the case of a
           linear inverse demand p(q) = a − bq, where MR(q) = a − 2bq.
494                                                                                    Chapter 7



      7.2.2   Second-Order Conditions
      From the first-order conditions discussed above, the monopolist increases production
      until the point at which marginal revenue and marginal costs coincide. In order to show
      that this production level maximizes monopoly profits, we must check the second-
      order conditions associated with this profit-maximization problem. Differentiating
      with respect to q again, we obtain
                                 p′ ( q ) + p′ ( q ) + p′′ ( q ) q − c
                                                                      ′′ ( q ) ≤ 0 .
                                                    
                                               dMR                     dMC
                                                dq                      dq



         In words, this condition states that the slope of the marginal revenue curve must be
      (weakly) lower than the slope of the marginal cost function at the profit-maximizing
      output qm. This is satisfied at the optimum of figure 7.3. In particular, the slope of the
      marginal cost curve is positive while that of the marginal revenue curve is negative,
      which implies that the above second-order condition is satisfied. (Note that this condi-
      tion holds even if the marginal costs are constant in output, where the slope of the
      marginal cost is zero.) Alternatively, this condition can be understood as the MR(q)
      curve crossing the MC(q) curve from above.
         This property holds in a relatively extreme case such as that depicted in figure 7.4,
      at the point where the marginal cost curve is decreasing in output (e.g., this occurs
      when the firm exhibits a concave technology given the presence of increasing returns
      to scale). In this case the slopes of the marginal cost and marginal revenue curves are

           Second-order condition when MC(q) is decreasing in q


           both decreasing in q. Thus the previous second-order condition imposes the restriction
           that, at the optimum, the marginal revenue curve must be steeper than the marginal
           cost curve, as illustrated in figure 7.4 (or, alternatively, that the MR(q) curve crosses
           the MC(q) curve from above).

           7.2.3   Lerner Index
           The monopolist’s profit-maximizing condition found in the above first-order condi-
           tions can be alternatively expressed in terms of the markup that the monopolist charg-
           es over marginal costs. To see this, let us first rewrite the MR(q) function as MR = p(q)
           + p′(q)q = p + (∂p / ∂q)q. Multiplying by p / p, we obtain

                                                  p ∂p q        1
                                        MR = p     +      p= p+    p.
                                                  p ∂q p       εd
                                                      1/ ε d
498                                                                                               Chapter 7



         Given that the price elasticity of demand is εd = (∂q / ∂p)(p / q), its inverse is
      1 / εd = (∂p / ∂q)(q / p). In addition, since at the profit-maximizing output the monopolist
      sets MR(q) = MC(q), we can set the expression of MR(q) equal to MC(q) to obtain

                                                   1
                                             p+        p = MC ( q ) .
                                                  εd

          Rearranging yields

                                              p − MC ( q )   1
                                                           =− .
                                                   p         εd

         Intuitively, this index (called the Lerner index of market power) says that the
      price markup over marginal cost that a monopolist charges (as percentage of price)
      is inversely related to the elasticity of demand. That is to say, markets with more
      elastic demand curves have low price markups, whereas markets with more inelastic
      demands (e.g., because there are no close substitutes of the product sold by the
      monopolist) imply substantial price markups. In markets with perfectly elastic
      demand, εd → ∞, the Lerner index becomes (p − MC(q)) / p → 0, implying that p =
      MC(q), whereas for markets with perfectly inelastic demand, εd → 0, the Lerner index
      is (p − MC(q)) /p → ∞, hence suggesting that the monopolist can charge a substantial
      markup over marginal cost. Solving for p in the preceding expression, we can also
      rewrite the Lerner index as

                                                        MC ( q)
                                                 p=                 ,
                                                       1 + (1 ε d )

      which is usually referred to as the inverse elasticity pricing rule (IEPR), since it pro-
      vides us with the monopolist’s optimal price as a function of its marginal cost and
      elasticity of demand.
         Perloff (2013) provides two examples of the IEPR applied to different elasticities of
      demand. First, in the case of the heartburn medicine Prilosec OTC, the price elasticity
      of demand has been estimated at approximately −1.2. Using the Lerner index, we find
      that this implies p = 5.88MC, or that the price this drug company can charge is 5.88
      times higher than its marginal cost of production.7 The second example considers

      7

      elasticity of demand for this drug is now probably lower (more elastic), reducing as a consequence
      its price markup.
Monopoly                                                                                                    499



           designer jeans, with a slightly more elastic demand of −2. In this case the Lerner index
           is p = 0.6MC, showing a lower price markup than the previous example.8

           7.3    Welfare Loss of Monopoly

           Figure 7.7 illustrates the welfare loss associated with a monopoly. In the figure, con-
           sumer surplus in a perfectly competitive market is A + B + C, but consumer surplus
           decreases in B and C when we move to a monopoly. The producer surplus meanwhile
           increases from D + E to D + B (i.e., a net increase of B − E), since the producer gains
           area B due to higher prices but loses area E due to a lower output (fewer sales). There-
           fore area B simply represents a transfer from consumers to producers, whereas shaded
           areas C and E illustrate a net loss for the economy (the deadweight loss of monopoly),
           since they are not transferred from one economic agent to another.
              More generally, such a deadweight loss is given by the area below the inverse de-
           mand curve, p(q), and above the marginal cost curve, c′(q), lying between the mo-
           nopoly and the perfectly competitive outputs qm and q*. That is, the deadweight loss of
           monopoly, DWL, is measured by
                                                          q*
                                               DWL= ∫ m [ p ( s ) − c ′ ( s )] ds.
                                                         q



           8
             This chapter does not analyze the pricing decisions of monopolists that sell a durable good in dif-
           ferent periods (i.e., called the “Coase paradox”). For more details on the trade-off that monopolists
           face in this setting, see exercise 5 at the end of the chapter.
500                                                                                                 Chapter 7




      Figure 7.7
      Deadweight loss of monopoly

        Interestingly, note that this expression decreases as demand (and/or supply) becomes
      more elastic.9 If, for instance, demand becomes infinitely elastic, p′(q) = 0, the inverse
      demand curve becomes totally flat, as figure 7.8 represents. Since p′(q) = 0, then MR(q)
      = p(q) + (0 × q) = p(q). This explains why figure 7.8 does not show any marginal rev-
      enue curve: it coincides with the inverse demand curve.
        In this context the monopolist’s profit-maximizing rule, MR(q) = MC(q), becomes
      p(q) = MC(q), which exactly coincides with that of a firm operating in a perfectly
      competitive industry. As a consequence we observe that output levels coincide across
      market structures, qm = q*, leading to a nil deadweight loss of monopoly. More
      formally,
                                     q*                           qm
                         DWL = ∫ m [ p ( s ) − c ′ ( s )] ds = ∫ m [ p ( s ) − c ′ ( s )] ds = 0,
                                    q                             q


      where in the second equality we made use of the property that the profit-maximizing
      output under monopoly, qm, coincides with that in a perfectly competitive industry, q*,
      since MR(q) and p(q) are the same in this context. Exercise 3 at the end of the chapter
      examines the design of monopoly subsidies that induce a socially optimal output: first,
      considering general functional forms, namely p′(q) < 0 and c′(q) > 0; and second, for a
      linear inverse demand function p(q) = a − bq and constant marginal costs, c.

           Finally, note that the social costs of monopoly are not only evaluated by the DWL area
           defined above. There are a number of social costs due to monopoly.11 Here are some
           examples:
           1. Excessive R&D expenditure For instance, in a patent race, most of the R&D
              expenditure made by the firm that did not get the patent is a social cost.
           2. Persuasive advertising (when not informative)

           11
                For a more detailed discussion on these issues, see the textbook by Wolfstetter (1999, ch. 1).
504                                                                                     Chapter 7



      3. Lobbying costs (different from bribes) A bribe cannot be strictly considered a so-
         cial cost because it entails the transfer of money from the monopolist to politicians.
         Other type of lobbying costs, such as the time spent by lobbyists trying to convince
         politicians about the benefits of certain policies (e.g., a legal barrier of entry), can
         be considered a social cost associated with monopolies.
      4. Resources to avoid entry of potential firms in the industry For instance, the incum-
         bent (monopoly) overinvests in capacity that sits idle just to guarantee that any
         entry will be severely fought by flooding the market with products for a few
         periods.

      7.5   Multiplant Monopolist

      Let us briefly analyze the monopolist’s production decision when it operates more
      than one plant. Suppose that the monopolist produces in different countries (with
Monopoly                                                                                           507



           potentially different efficiency levels and salaries) but sells its global production to
           the international market. The monopolist’s decision about how much total output to
           produce resembles our previous analysis by equating marginal revenue and costs.
           However, its decision on how to distribute total output among its different plants
           requires a more detailed discussion. Suppose that the monopolist produces output q1,
           q2, …, qN across the N plants it operates, with total costs TCi(qi) at each plant i = {1, 2,
           …, N}. Hence this monopolist’s profit-maximization problem is

                                                  N
                                                        N      N
                                      max  a − b∑ qi  ∑ qi − ∑ TCi ( qi ) .
                                     q1 ,...,qN

           Taking first-order conditions with respect to the production level at each individual
           plant j, qj, we obtain
                            N
                    a − 2b∑ qi − MC j ( q j ) = 0 ⇔ MR(Q) = MCj(qj)        for every plant j.
                           i =1


              The last condition states that the monopolist must increase its production in plant j,
           qj, until the point at which the marginal cost of producing one more unit in that plant,
           MCj(qj), coincides with the marginal revenue that the monopolist obtains by selling
           this additional unit in the international market, MR(Q). Figure 7.12 illustrates this
           profit-maximizing condition for a multiplant monopolist operating two plants with
           marginal costs MC1 and MC2.
              Note that the monopolist total marginal costs, MCtotal, are given by the horizontal
           sum of its marginal costs across both plants, that is, MCtotal = MC1 + MC2. We can there-
           fore find the total production for this monopolist by setting its total marginal costs
           MCtotal equal to its marginal revenue curve, MR, which occurs at point A. Hence the
           monopolist produces Qtotal across both plants and sells this total output at a price pm. At
           this point we must distribute the total production Qtotal between the two plants. In order
           to do that, we must evaluate MR(Qtotal)—graphically represented by the height of point
           A in figure 7.12—and find the point of the MC1 for plant 1 that reaches the same height.
           This determines the output q1 that plant 1 produces where q1 solves MR(Qtotal) =
           MC1(q1). Similarly for plant 2, starting from the height of point A, which depicts
           MR(Qtotal), we extend a dotted line to the left crossing MC2 (point B in the figure). This
           determines q2 where MR(Qtotal) = MC2(q2). As a consequence the marginal cost of pro-
           ducing an additional unit coincides across both plants: the height of MC1(q1) coincides
           with that of MC2(q2) and, in turn, coincides with MR(Qtotal).

           Example 7.6: Multiplant monopolist (asymmetric plants) Consider a monopolist
           facing linear demand p(q) = 120 – 3Q and operating two plants with total costs TC1(q1)
           = F1 + 10q1 + 10q12 and TC2 ( q2 ) = F2 + 60q2 + ( 5 2 ) q2 2 , where F1 (F2) represents the
           fixed cost of plant 1 (2, respectively). The monopolist chooses the output pair (q1, q2)
           that maximizes its total profit by solving

              max ( q1 , q2 )(120 − 3 ( q1 + q2 )) ( q1 + q2 ) − ( F1 + 10q1 + 10q12 ) − ( F2 + 60q2 + ( 5 2 ) q2 2 )
           Taking first-order conditions with respect to q1 yields

                                               110 − 6(q1 + q2) − 20q1 = 0,

           and with respect to q2 yields

                                                 60 − 6(q1 + q2) − 5q2 = 0.

           Simultaneously solving for q1 and q2, we find the optimal output pair (q1, q2) = (3.4,
           3.6), for a total output of Q = 7 units. As a confirmation of our above discussion, note
           that marginal costs coincide across plants at these output levels since MC1(q1) = 10 +
           20q1, which entails MC1(3.4) = $78, and similarly MC2(q2) = 60 + 5q2, which produces
           MC2(3.6) = $78; as required. ■

           7.6   Price Discrimination

           Monopoly profits can be further increased by setting different prices for purchases of
           different quantities of the good (or different prices to different customers). Even though
510                                                                                    Chapter 7




      Figure 7.13
      Monopolist that further increases its profits


      the monopolist is making positive profits, it can still capture a larger surplus from two
      segments of customers, as figure 7.13 illustrates. On one hand, there are customers
      buying the product at pm who would be willing to pay more for the good, paying prices
      p > pm. On the other hand, there is a segment of customers who did not buy the good at
      pm but whose willingness to pay for the good, p, is still higher than the marginal cost of
      production, pm > p > c. When setting a uniform price pm for all units, however, the
      monopolist captures the surplus of neither of these segments. In fact, in order to cap-
      ture these additional surpluses, the monopolist must abandon uniform pricing and use
      some form of price discrimination.
         We will first discuss two types of price discrimination: first-degree (or perfect)
      price discrimination—where the monopolist charges every customer his/her maximum
      willingness to pay for the object—and third-degree price discrimination—where the
      monopolist charges different prices to two or more groups of customers, each with a
      different demand. We will then examine second-degree price discrimination, where the
      monopolist cannot observe the characteristics of every type of customer (e.g., his will-
      ingness to pay) and offers a menu (or plans) so that every type of customer self-selects
      the menu he finds most attractive.
Monopoly                                                                                          511



           7.6.1   First-Degree Price Discrimination
           Under first-degree (or perfect) price discrimination, the monopolist charges each buyer
           a different price (i.e., a “personalized” price). The first buyer pays p1 for the q1 units,
           the second pays p2 for q2 − q1 units, and similarly for all other buyers, as figure 7.14
           illustrates. Specifically, the monopolist continues doing so until the last buyer is will-
           ing to pay the marginal cost of production (increasing sales any further would entail
           losses for the monopolist).
              In the limit, by making the unit increments sufficiently small, the monopolist cap-
           tures all the area below the demand curve (representing consumers’ willingness to pay)
           and above the marginal cost, as depicted in figure 7.15.
              Let us prove this result more formally. Suppose that the monopolist can offer a com-
           bination of a fixed fee, F*, and an amount of the good, q*, that maximizes its profits.
           This implies choosing the pair (F*, q*) that solves the following PMP:
                                                    max F − cq
                                                     F ,q


                                                 subject to u(q) ≥ F,

           where the constraint indicates that, by acquiring q units, the consumer obtains a utility
           level u(q) weakly larger than the price the monopolist charges for the good, F; other-
           wise, he would not buy the good. First, note that the monopolist wants to raise the fee




           Figure 7.14
           First-degree price discrimination—I
512                                                                                     Chapter 7




      Figure 7.15
      First-degree price discrimination—II


      F until u(q) = F. (Otherwise, the monopolist could still increase its profits by further
      increasing fee F.) Inserting this result, u(q) = F, into the monopolist’s objective func-
      tion, F − cq, we obtain u(q) − cq, which helps us reduce the set of choice variables in
      the above maximization problem (from (F, q) to only q), as follows:

                                             max u ( q ) − cq.
                                              q


         Taking first-order conditions with respect to q, we obtain u′(q*) – c = 0, that is,
      u′(q*) = c. Intuitively, the monopolist practicing first-degree price discrimination in-
      creases output until the point in which the marginal utility that consumers obtain from
      additional units (graphically represented by the inverse demand curve) coincides with
      the marginal cost of production. Given this level of production q*, we can obtain the
      optimal fee, F*, by inserting q* into the individual’s utility function (i.e., F* = u(q*)).
      Thus the monopolist charges a fee F* that coincides with the utility that the consumer
      obtains from consuming q* units of output. Both of these results are graphically repre-
      sented in figure 7.16 where (1) fee F* is depicted by all the area below p(q) until q*
      units, and (2) monopoly profits are therefore F* − cq* (i.e., the area below the demand
      curve and above its marginal cost).

      Example 7.7: First-degree price discrimination Let us consider a numerical ex-
      ample. A monopolist faces inverse demand curve p(q) = 20 − q and constant marginal
      costs c = $2. When it practices uniform pricing, setting MR equal to MC, the monopo-
      list produces qm = 9 units at a price pm = $11 with associated profits of πm = $81. These
      profits are represented by the shaded area in figure 7.17.
Monopoly                                                            513




           Figure 7.16
           Profits under first-degree price discrimination




           Figure 7.17
           First-degree price discrimination: a numerical example
514                                                                                                Chapter 7



        If, instead, the monopolist practices first-degree price discrimination, it sets p(q) =
      MC, producing q = 18 units with corresponding profits of $162, graphically repre-
      sented by the area below the demand curve and above the marginal cost curve. As ex-
      pected, the practice of first-degree price discrimination increases the monopolist’s
      profits. ■

      Summarizing, under first-degree price discrimination, total output coincides with that
      in perfectly competitive markets, where p(q*) = c. Unlike perfectly competitive mar-
      kets, however, the consumer does not capture any surplus. In contrast, it is the pro-
      ducer who now captures all the surplus. Because this type of price discrimination
      requires an enormous amount of information, we do not see many examples of it in
      real applications. A case in which this type of price discrimination is partly observed is
      financial aid in undergraduate education, often cited as a form of “tuition discrimina-
      tion” practiced by many US colleges. Application forms, such as the Free Application
      for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA) form, ask many details about the student’s (and
      his/her family) finances in order to determine his/her financial need. This ultimately
      allows colleges to identify the student’s willingness to pay for higher education.
         Another imperfect form of first-degree price discrimination is two-block pricing, as
      described in the following example, whereby the first q1 units are sold at a price p1,
      while the remaining q2 − q1 units are sold at a lower price p2, showing that such a prac-
      tice helps the monopolist increase profits. The subsequent example then extends this
      setting to allow for N ≥ 2 blocks, illustrating that monopolists can obtain even larger
      profits eventually approaching those under first-degree price discrimination.

           7.6.2    Third-Degree Price Discrimination
           In this type of price-discrimination, the monopolist sells its product to two (or more)
           different types of customers that are easily identifiable by the monopolist (e.g., youth
           versus adult customers at the movies who can be distinguished by showing a valid
           ID).13 The monopolist’s profit-maximization problem hence becomes
                                        max p1 ( x1 ) x1 − cx1 + p2 ( x2 ) x2 − cx2 ,
                                         x1 , x2


           where the first two terms capture profits from customers in group 1, and the last two
           terms describe profits from customers in group 2. Taking first-order conditions with
           respect to x1 and x2, we obtain,

           13
              Recall that this easy identification of customers differentiates third-degree and second-degree
           price discrimination, where the monopolist cannot easily identify different groups of customers. In
           that case the monopolist must offer a menu in order to achieve self-separation, such as calling plans
           offered by a monopolistic phone company.
520                                                                                             Chapter 7




      Figure 7.19
      Third-degree price discrimination


                                p1(x1) + p1′(x1) x1 − c = 0 ⇒ MR1 = MC,

                                p2(x2) + p2′(x2) x2 − c = 0 ⇒ MR2 = MC.

         Interestingly, these first-order conditions coincide with those of a regular monopo-
      list who practices uniform pricing as if it was serving two completely separated mar-
      kets (i.e., MR1 = MC and MR2 = MC). Figure 7.19 illustrates this idea for the example
      of adults (market 1) and seniors (market 2) at the movies. In particular, p1(x1) = 38 − x1
      for adults, p2(x2) = 14 – 1/4x2 for seniors, and MC = $10 for both markets. Indeed it is
      easy to check that MR1(x1) = 38 – 2x1, which crosses MC = 10 at x1 = 14 units, implying
      a price for adults of p1 = $24. Similarly for seniors, MR2(x2) = 14 – 0.5x2, which cross-
      es MC = 10 at x2 = 8 units, implying a price for seniors of only p2 = $12.

           Example 7.10: Third-degree price discrimination A single airline operates the
           route Pullman–Seattle and considers charging different prices for their business class
           and economy seats, incurring the same marginal cost MC in each of them.14 Assume
           that, according to demand estimates, the price elasticity of demand for business-class
           seats is −1.15 while that for economy seats is −1.52, showing a larger sensitivity to
           price changes. From the first estimate, using the IEPR we can conclude that the price
           charged for every business-class seat must satisfy pB0.13 = MC. Similarly, using the
           IEPR, we obtain that the price charged for every economy-class seat must satisfy
           pE0.343 = MC. Therefore pB0.13 = pE0.343, or pB = 2.63pE. That is, the airline maxi-
           mizes its profits by charging business-class seats a price 2.63 times higher than that of
           economy-class seats.15

           7.6.3   Second-Degree Price Discrimination
           Consider a setting where the monopolist cannot observe the type of each consumer.
           Rather than offering a uniform price for all types of customers, the monopolist can
           design a menu of two-part tariffs, (FL, qL) and (FH, qH), with the property that the cus-
           tomer with type i = {L, H} is attracted to select the two-part tariff (Fi, qi) meant for him.
           In particular, assume that the utility function of type i’s customer is

                                              U i (qi , Fi ) = θi u ( qi ) − Fi ,
           where qi denotes the quantity he consumes, and Fi is the fixed fee he pays to the mo-
           nopolist for consuming qi units. Parameter θi measures the valuation he assigns to the
           good, where θH>θL with corresponding probabilities p and 1 − p. The monopolist’s con-
           stant marginal cost c satisfies θi > c for every type i = {L, H}.

           14
              If you have ever been in such a small plane, you would know that the airline’s marginal cost of
           offering business-class and economy-class seats is exactly the same!
           15
              Note that third-degree price discrimination might mean serving (not serving) some customers who
           might not be served (served, respectively) under uniform pricing. This implies that the practice of
           third-degree price discrimination can be welfare improving (or welfare reducing) under certain con-
           ditions. For a discussion on this topic, see Varian (1992, 250–53).
522                                                                                      Chapter 7



      Symmetric Information
      As a benchmark for comparison, consider a setting where the firm can perfectly
      observe every customer type, θi, for every i = {H, L}. The monopolist problem then
      coincides with that under first-degree price discrimination (section 7.6.1), whereby
      output qi is increased until θiu′(qi) = c. This output is regarded efficient, since the con-
      sumer’s marginal utility from further units of the good coincides with the firm’s mar-
      ginal cost. As we next show, the monopolist inability to recognize each type of buyer
      gives rise to output inefficiencies.

      Asymmetric Information
      In this setting the monopolist must guarantee two conditions: first, both types of cus-
      tomers must be willing to participate (i.e., the two-part tariff meant for each type of
      customer provides him with a weakly positive utility level) and; second, every type of
      consumer cannot have incentives to choose the two-part tariff meant for the other type
      of customer (i.e., type-i customer prefers (Fi, qi) over (Fj, qj) where j ≠ i). For compact-
      ness, the literature refers to the first condition as the “participation constraint,” as it
      guarantees the participation of all types of customers; whereas the second type of con-
      dition is referred to as the “incentive compatibility” condition. In particular, the par-
      ticipation constraints in this context are

                                                   θ L u ( qL ) − FL ≥ 0,                  (PCL)

                                                  θ H u ( qH ) − FH ≥ 0,                   (PCH)

      while the incentive compatibility conditions are

                                          θ L u ( qL ) − FL ≥ θ L u ( qH ) − FH ,           (ICL)

                                        θ H u ( qH ) − FH ≥ θ H u ( qL ) − FL .             (ICH)

       We can rearrange the four inequalities above and list them as constraints into the
      monopolist’s profit maximization problem, as follows:
                                  max            p [ FH − cqH ] + (1 − p )[ FL − cqL ]
                               FL ,qL , FH ,qH


      subject to

                                                     θ L u ( qL ) ≥ FL ,                   (PCL)

                                                     θ H u ( qH ) ≥ FH ,                   (PCH)

                                         θ L [ u ( qL ) − u ( qH )] + FH ≥ FL ,             (ICL)

                                         θ H [ u ( qH ) − u ( qL )] + FL ≥ FH .             (ICH)
Monopoly                                                                                         523




           Figure 7.20
           PC condition binds (upper panel) and IC condition binds (lower panel)


           Since both PCH and ICH are now expressed in terms of the fee FH, we can easily see
           that the monopolist increases FH until such a fee coincides with the lowest of θHu(qH)
           and θH[u(qH) − u(qL)] + FL, as depicted in figure 7.20, for all i = {L, H}. Otherwise, one
           (or both) constraints will be violated, leading the high-demand customer to not par-
           ticipate (or select the two-part tariff meant for the low-demand customer). A similar
           argument applies to the two constraints of the low-type buyer, since they are both ex-
           pressed in terms of FL. We examine this result more closely in the next discussion, by
           separately analyzing the constraints of each type of buyer. (Once we determine which
           constraints bind, we will reduce the program above to an unconstrained maximization
           problem.)

           High-Demand Customer
           Let us first focus on the high-demand consumer and show that ICH is binding (the
           lower panel of figure 7.20 arises for this type of customer).

           Proof An indirect way to show that ICH binds, whereby FH = θH[u(qH) − u(qL)] + FL, is
           to demonstrate that FH < θHu(qH) (i.e., as depicted be in the lower panel of figure 7.20).
           By contradiction, consider that FH = θHu(qH). If this condition holds, then ICH can be
           rewritten as

                                              FH − θ H u ( qL ) + FL ≥ FH ,
           which simplifies to FL ≥ θHu(qL). Additionally we can combine this result with the
           property that θH > θL to obtain
524                                                                                                           Chapter 7




                                               FL ≥ θ H u ( qL ) > θ L u ( qL ).
      That is, FL ≥ θLu(qL). This finding, however, violates the participation constraint of the
      low-demand customer, PCL, indicating that we have reached a contradiction and,
      therefore, FL < θHu(qH) (i.e., PCH is not binding). Thus ICH is binding but PCH is not,
      confirming that for the high-demand customer the lower panel of figure 7.20 applies
      (i.e., FH = θH[u(qH) − u(qL)] + FL). ■

      Low-Demand Customer
      We can use a similar approach to show that the top panel of figure 7.20 arises for the
      low-demand customer, that is, PCL binds since FL = θLu(qL).

      Proof As for high-demand customers, we can prove this result by showing instead
      that FL < θL[u(qL) − u(qH)] + FH holds. We prove this result by contradiction. Hence, we
      first assume that FL = θL[u(qL) − u(qH)] + FH. Plugging this expression into ICH (which
      binds, as shown in our discussion of the high-demand customer), we obtain

                             θ H [ u ( qH ) − u ( qL )] + θ L [ u ( qL ) − u ( qH )] + FH = FH .

      This expression simplifies to

                                    θ H [ u ( qH ) − u ( qL ) ] = θ L [ u ( qL ) − u ( qH ) ]

      and ultimately reduces to θH = θL, violating the initial assumption θH > θL. Therefore
      FL = θL[u(qL) − u(qH)] + FH cannot hold, and instead FL < θL[u(qL) − u(qH)] + FH must be
      true. As a consequence the top panel of figure 7.20 applies for the low-demand cus-
      tomer, implying that ultimately PCL binds and ICL does not. ■

           7.7   Advertising in Monopoly

           7.8   Regulation of Natural Monopolies

           Some monopolies exhibit decreasing cost structures, with the MC curve lying below
           the AC curve, as figure 7.22 depicts.18 For these industries, having a unique firm serve
           the entire market might seem better (more “natural”) than having multiple firms, since
           aggregate average costs for the entire industry would be lower in the former than in the
           latter case. For this reason monopolies with decreasing costs are usually referred to as
           “natural” monopolies.19 An unregulated natural monopoly, however, would maximize
           profits at the point where MR = MC, producing q1 units (see figure 7.22) and selling
           them at a price p1. If a regulatory agency forces the monopoly to charge marginal-cost
           pricing (as if the market structure was perfectly competitive), the monopoly will charge
           p2 (where demand crosses MC) and produce q2 units. This production level, however,
           implies a loss of p2 − c2 per unit as in figure 7.23.

           17
              Besides advertising, the monopolist can pursue other nonpricing strategies in order to further
           increase its profits, such as investing in cost-reducing technologies (as analyzed in exercise 9
           at the end of this chapter) or increasing production today in order to benefit from learning-by-doing
           effects in future periods (as explored in exercise 10). Finally, exercise 11 examines output and pricing
           decisions when the monopolist sells a good exhibiting intertemporal network effects in demand.
           18
              Consider, for instance, a total cost function TC(q) = F + c(qα), where F, c, α > 0. In this case, mar-
           ginal cost is MC(q) = αc/q1+α, whereas average cost is AC(q) = F/q + c/q1+α, where AC(q) > MC(q) for
           all fixed costs F, and all parameters c and α.
           19
              This type of cost function may arise in industries that require a large fixed investment in order to
           produce the first unit. Providing the good or service to further clients is, however, extremely cheap
           once that investment has been incurred. Examples might include water distribution and electric
           companies.
532                                                 Chapter 7




      Figure 7.22
      Regulation of natural monopoly




      Figure 7.23
      Price discrimination for natural monopolies
Monopoly                                                                                                  533



              Thus regulatory agencies face a dilemma when dealing with natural monopolies:
           either they abandon the policy of setting prices equal to marginal cost, or they apply
           marginal-cost pricing and forever subsidize natural monopolies for their losses (pro-
           viding p2 − c2 per unit of production). One way regulatory agencies can avoid this
           dilemma is through the implementation of a multiprice system that allows for price
           discrimination where the monopolist charges some users a high price while maintain-
           ing a low price (e.g., marginal-cost pricing) to other users. For instance, as figure 7.23
           illustrates, the regulatory commission could allow charging a high price p1 to some
           users while other users are offered a lower price p2. Specifically, this produces a ben-
           efit p1 − c1 per unit for the first segment of units in the interval from 0 to q1 (the shaded
           area in the light rectangle of figure 7.23) and a loss of c2 − p2 per unit for the additional
           q2 − q1 units sold to the second segment of customers, as depicted in the shaded area of
           the dark rectangle of figure 7.23. Then, in order to provide sufficient incentives to the
           monopolist to practice this price scheme, the profits from the first segment of custom-
           ers, (p1 − c1)q1, must exceed the losses from the second segment represented by the
           area, (c2 − p2)(q2 − q1). This approach is frequently used by utility companies (such as
           electricity and water supply) that set different prices to different types of customers
           (businesses and households).20
              An alternative regulation of natural monopolies is allowing the monopoly to charge
           a price above marginal cost that is sufficient to earn a “fair” rate of return on capital
           investments. This approach, however, presents two difficulties. First, it might be sub-
           ject to different interpretations about what is a “fair” rate of return. Second, it leads to
           overcapitalization, as we show more formally below.

           Example 7.12: Overcapitalization of natural monopolies (Averch–Johnson
           effect) Suppose that a regulated utility company has a production function of the
           form q = f(k, l). An unregulated monopoly with profit function pf(k, l) − wl − rk has a
           rate of return on capital, r. Assume that the rate of return on capital investments, r,
           constrained by a regulatory agency is equal to r0. The firm’s profit-maximization prob-
           lem (PMP) is represented by the following Lagrangian:

                                  L = pf(k, l) − wl − rk + λ [ wl − r0k − pf(k, l)],

      FOCs are

      Figure 7.25
      Alternative overcapitalization result


      isoquant). In other words, the overcapitalization result only captures the substitution
      effect of a cheaper input. However, from production theory we know that a cheaper
      input also gives rise to an output effect, since the firm seeks to produce a larger output
      when the price of an input decreases. If this output effect is sufficiently large, the regu-
      lator would need to compare the inefficiencies that arise from overcapitalization (as
      described in the Averch–Johnson effect) against the increase in welfare associated with
      a larger output.22

      7.9   Monopsony

      The analysis of a monopsony (single buyer) is analogous to that of a monopoly (single
      seller). In particular, a monopsony arises in markets where a single buyer of goods and
      services exercises its “buying power” by paying prices below those that would prevail
      in a perfectly competitive context. Standard examples of monopsonies are a coal mine,
      or more recently a Walmart superstore, in a small town, as the firm becomes the single
      (or most important) purchaser of labor services.
         For simplicity, consider that the monopsony faces competition in the product mar-
      ket, where prices are given at p > 0, but is a monopsony in the input market (e.g., labor

           Taking FOCs with respect to the amount of labor services that the monopsony hires,
           x, yields

                                        pf ′ ( x* ) − w ( x* ) − w′ ( x* ) x* = 0.
           After rearranging, we obtain

                                          pf ′ ( x* ) = w ( x* ) + w′ ( x* ) x* .
              Intuitively, the left-hand side represents the “marginal revenue product” of labor,
           whereby hiring an additional worker increases output by f ′(x*), which is sold at a
           given market price of p. The right-hand side, in contrast, measures the “marginal ex-
           penditure” on labor, which embodies two effects. First, the additional worker entails a
           monetary outlay of w(x*). Second, hiring more workers makes labor become more
           scarce, ultimately forcing the monopsony to raise the prevailing wage on all inframar-
           ginal workers, as captured by w′(x*)x*, that is, the increase in wages w′(x*) times all
           hired workers x*. Summarizing, in equilibrium, the marginal revenue product of hiring
           one more worker coincides with his marginal expenditure. (Otherwise, the monopsony
           would have incentives to hire more or less workers.)

           creasing in x given that pf ″(x) ≤ w0 by assumption; (2) the labor supply w(x), which is
           increasing in x, since w′(x)>0 by assumption; and (3) the marginal expenditure in la-
           bor, w(x) + w′(x)x. Note that the marginal expenditure on labor lies above the supply
           function w(x) since w′(x) > 0, thus entailing w(x) + w′(x)x > w(x).
              The figure illustrates that the monopsony hires x* workers at a salary of w(x*). If
           instead the labor market was perfectly competitive (e.g., having several potential em-
           ployers) more workers would be hired, xPC; and their salary, wPC, would be higher than
           under the monopsony. Such a difference gives rise to a deadweight loss from monop-
           sony, namely the area below the marginal revenue product and above the supply curve,
           between x* and xPC workers. That is,

           Sufficiency The equilibrium condition found above is also sufficient as long as

                                      pf ′′ ( x* ) − 2w′ ( x* ) − w′′ ( x* ) x* < 0.
           Since f ″(x*) < 0 and w′(x*) > 0 by assumption, we only need that either (1) the supply

                                        pf ′′ ( x* ) − 2w′ ( x* ) < w′′ ( x* ) x*.

           Example 7.13: Optimal output in a monopsony Consider a monopsonist with
           production function f(x) = ax, where a > 0, and facing a given market price p > 0 per unit
           of output. Labor supply is w(x) = bx where b > 0. In this context, the marginal revenue
           product of hiring an additional worker is pf ′(x) = pa, whereas the marginal expenditure
           on labor is

                                        w ( x ) + w′ ( x ) x = bx + bx = 2bx .
           Setting the marginal revenue and marginal expenditure equal to each other, pa = 2bx*,
           yields a profit-maximizing labor of

           which increases in the price of output, p, and in the marginal productivity of labor, a,
           but decreases in the slope of labor supply, b. Intuitively, parameter b represents to
           which extent additional hires force the monopsonist to raise wages to all workers.
           (Last, you can check that sufficiency holds in this setting because pf ″(x*) − 2w′(x*) =
           p0 − 2a < 0 = w″(x*)x*.) ■

8 Game Theory and Imperfect Competition



    The industry structure we studied in the previous chapter, monopoly markets, served
    as an extreme setting in which a single firm determines output and prices. However,
    less extreme industry structures, involving the interaction of a limited number of firms
    (oligopolies) are actually prevalent in most markets.1 Section 8.1 presents some ba-
    sic game theory that will be used in the models of this chapter. We use game theory
    to study firm competition, first analyzing static models in which firms produce ho-
    mogeneous products and independently select either their prices (Bertrand model of
    price competition in section 8.2) or output levels (Cournot model of quantity com-
    petition in section 8.3). In addition we demonstrate that, when allowing for a large
    number of firms, the equilibrium predictions in these models embody our results in
    perfectly competitive and monopoly markets as special cases. Section 8.4 examines
    firms’ incentives to coordinate their actions (i.e., collude in a cartel), and how their
    equilibrium profits are affected if some of the firms in the industry merge. Section
    8.5 then extends the Bertrand and Cournot models to settings in which firms produce
    heterogeneous goods. Given the radically different equilibrium predictions in the Ber-
    trand model (where even the presence of only two firms drives profits to zero) and
    the Cournot model (where firms generally obtain positive profits), section 8.6 pre-
    sents a tractable model by Kreps and Scheinkman (1983) reconciling these extreme
    results.
       Next, to explore firms’ competition when they act sequentially rather than simulta-
    neously, we study the Stackelberg model of sequential quantity competition. With this
    model we can consider settings in which one of the firms acts first (the leader) by
    choosing its output level. Its rival (the follower), observing the leader’s output choice,

    1
      A widely used market concentration measurement is the Herfindahl–Hirschman index. Information
    on market concentration for US firms can be found at https://www.census.gov/econ/concentration.html.
548                                                                                                        Chapter 8



      decides its own production level in order to optimally respond to the leader’s output.
      We show that the leader obtains, in this context, larger profits than when both firms act
      simultaneously in the Cournot model; what we refer to as the “leader’s advantage.”
      However, when we consider a sequential-move version of the Bertrand model of price
      competition (where the leader chooses its price first, and the follower responds with its
      price afterward), the follower is the firm benefiting from the sequential nature of the
      interaction and, hence, a “follower’s advantage” emerges.
         While the beginning of this chapter considers an exogenously given number of
      firms, section 8.7 analyzes the number of firms that enter an industry in an unregulated
      equilibrium. Additionally we compare this equilibrium result with the number of
      firms that a benevolent social planner would select in order to maximize social welfare.
      Section 8.8 examines how firms’ competition can be ameliorated when firms repeat-
      edly interact with one another, which under certain conditions allows for the emer-
      gence of collusive practices. In particular, we first consider a setting in which firms
      compete in prices, and then one in which they compete in quantities. Along these lines,
      we provide some extensions of the models of repeated interaction, such as allowing for
      imperfect monitoring or temporary punishments. Each of these extensions is explored
      in an exercise.

      8.1   Game Theory Tools

      Consider a setting with I players (e.g., firms, individuals, or countries), each choosing
      a strategy si from a strategy set Si, whereby si ∈ Si and i ∈ I, such as an output level, a
      price, or an advertising expenditure; and let (si, s−i) denote a strategy profile where s−i
      represents the strategies selected by all firms i ≠ j, whereby s− i = ( s1 , …, si −1 , si +1 , …, sI ).


         Dominated strategy Strategy si* strictly dominates another strategy si′ ≠ si*
         where si′ ∈ Si , for player i if si* yields a strictly higher payoff than si′ does, regard-
         less of the strategy profile s−i selected by player i’s rivals, that is
                               π i ( si* , s− i ) > π i ( si′, s− i ) for every si′ ≠ si* and all s− i .


         In the payoff matrix in table 8.1, where firm A chooses rows and firm B chooses
      columns, “low prices” is a strictly dominant strategy for both firms, since “low prices”
      yields a higher payoff than “high prices,” both when a firm’s rival chooses “low pric-
      es,” where 5 > 1, and when its rival selects “high prices,” given that 9 > 7.
         In the definition above, strategy si′ (i.e., “high prices”) is, however, a strategy that
      firm i would never choose regardless of the specific strategy chosen by its rival. This
