                  is why si′ is referred to as a strictly dominated strategy. This type of strategy can be
                  removed from the set of strategies a rational player would use, helping us reduce the
                  number of strategies to consider as optimal for each player. In the preceding example,
                  if we delete all strictly dominated strategies for both firms, we are left with “low pric-
                  es” as the only undominated strategy for each firm. We can thus claim that both firms
                  will select “low prices” in the unique equilibrium of that game. That is, if we itera-
                  tively delete all strictly dominated strategies for every player, we are left with strategy
                  profile(s) that can be understood as the equilibrium of the game. For this reason this
                  solution concept is often referred to as equilibria surviving the “iterative deletion of
                  strictly dominated strategies” or IDSDS.
                     Often, games do not allow us to eliminate all but one strategy for each player, or
                  have no strictly dominated strategies whatsoever. The matrix in table 8.2a depicts a
                  technology adoption game with no strictly dominated strategy for either player. Note
                  that Adopt yields a higher payoff than Not adopt for firm A if its opponent selects
                  Adopt, but yields a lower payoff than Not adopt when its opponent chooses Not adopt.
                  A similar argument applies for firm B. What is the equilibrium of the game then?
                  In games without strictly dominated strategies, we can rely on the Nash equilibrium
                  solution concept we next present.


                     Nash equilibrium A strategy profile ( si* , s−* i ) is a Nash equilibrium (NE) if, for
                     every player i, π i ( si* , s−* i ) ≥ π i ( si , s−* i ) for every si ≠ si* .
550                                                                                                Chapter 8




         That is, si* is player i’s best response to his opponents choosing s−* i , as si* yields a
      higher payoff than any of his other available strategies si ≠ si*. In the game depicted
      in table 8.2a, firm A’s best response to firm B’s playing Adopt (in the left column) is
      BRA(Adopt) = Adopt, and to firm B playing Not adopt (in the right column) is BRA(Not
      adopt) = Not adopt. Likewise firm B’s best response to firm A choosing Adopt (in the
      top row) is BRB(Adopt) = Adopt, and to firm A selecting Not adopt (in the bottom row)
      is BRB(Not adopt) = Not adopt. Hence strategy profiles (Adopt, Adopt) and (Not adopt,
      Not adopt) are mutual best responses, which is to say, each player chooses a best re-
      sponse to his opponent’s strategy, and these profiles constitute the two NEs of the game.

      8.1.1   Mixed-Strategy Nash Equilibrium
      In the preceding discussion we restricted players to use one of their available strategies
      100 percent of the time (commonly known as “pure strategies”), but generally
      they could randomize (mix) their choices, for example, by choosing strategy A
      with probability p and strategy B with probability 1 − p. Allowing for the strategy of
      every player i to be defined as a probability distribution σi over his strategy space Si,
      we can extend this definition of NE to the following mixed strategy Nash equilibrium
      (msNE):


         Mixed-strategy Nash equilibrium Consider a strategy profile σ = (σ1, σ2, … ,
         σn), where σi is a mixed strategy for player i. Strategy profile σ is an msNE if and
         only if

                         π i (σ i , σ − i ) ≥ π i ( si′, σ − i ) for all si′ ∈ Si and for all i.

         That is, σi is a best response of player i to the strategy profile σ−i of the other N − 1
         players, whereby σi ∈ BRi(σ−i).


         Three points are noteworthy about the definition above. First, in an msNE, players
      must be indifferent among all (or at least some) of their pure strategies. That is, if a
      player randomizes over all his pure strategies (or over a subset of them), then he must
      receive the same expected payoff from each of those pure strategies. Otherwise, he
      would prefer one strategy over another, and thus choose such strategy with 100 per-
      cent probability, playing a pure strategy. We provide examples of players’ incentives
      to randomize below. Second, since players never use strictly dominated strategies, we
      can conclude that a NE assigns a zero probability to dominated strategies. For in-
      stance, in the game of table 8.1, the strategy “high prices” is strictly dominated,
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                            551



                  implying that it receives no probability of being played. A similar argument applies
                  to games with K > 2 strategies where, if one of the strategies is strictly dominated, it
                  can be removed from the payoff matrix, restricting the pool of strategies that can re-
                  ceive a positive probability in the msNE to K − 1. Finally, in games with a finite set of
                  players and a finite set of available actions, we will generally find an odd number of
                  equilibria (e.g., three equilibria in our example above, two pure and one mixed, or
                  one equilibrium in the game of table 8.1).2
                     As a practice, let us consider an example of a game with no NE in pure strategies,
                  but one msNE when players randomize. Table 8.2b shows a variation on the “Technol-
                  ogy Adoption Game” of table 8.2a in which firm A prefers to choose the same action
                  as its rival (adopt if firm B adopts, but not adopt otherwise). However, firm B’s prefers
                  to choose technology opposite to that of firm A (not adopt when firm A adopts, in the
                  top row, and adopt otherwise). After underlining best-response payoffs, we find that
                  there is no cell of the matrix in which players select mutual best responses, and thus we
                  cannot find a NE in pure strategies. Intuitively, firm A (B) seeks to coordinate (misco-
                  ordinate) its decision with that of firm B (A, respectively).
                     Given their opposed incentives, firm A would like to make its choice difficult to
                  anticipate. If firm A chooses a specific action with certainty, firm B will be driven to
                  select the opposite action. (An analogous argument applies to firm B, which does not
                  want firm A to select the same action as firm B chooses.) As a consequence, players
                  have incentives to randomize their actions. Let p (q) denote the probability with which
                  firm A (B, respectively) adopts the technology. Then, if firm A is indifferent between
                  adopting and not adopting the technology, its expected utility must satisfy

                                                    EU A ( Adopt ) = EU A ( Not adopt ) ,

                                                   3q + ( −4 ) (1 − q ) = ( −3) q + 2 (1 − q ) ,

                                                          6q = 6 (1 − q ) ⇒ q = 12 .

                  Table 8.2b
                  Payoff matrix with no NE in pure strategies

                                                                      Firm B
                                                           Adopt                Not adopt

                  Firm A         Adopt                      3, −3                 −4, 0

                                 Not adopt                  −3, 1                 2, −2



                  2
                    This property is due to the number of fixed points of a player’s best-response correspondence, as
                  described in the mathematical appendix at the end of this book.
552                                                                                 Chapter 8




      Hence firm A adopts the technology with probability q = 12 . Similarly firm B must be
      indifferent between adopting and not adopting the technology:

                                EU B ( Adopt ) = EU B ( Not adopt ) ,
                                  −3p + 1(1 − p) = 0p − 2(1 − p),
                                       1 − p = 3 p ⇒ p = 12 .

      which yields p = 12 , implying that firm B adopts the technology with probability
      p = 14 . Combining our results, we obtain the msNE

                          ( 12 Adopt 12 Not adopt , 12 Adopt 12 Not adopt ) ,
      where the firm term of the parenthesis describes the randomization of firm A, while the
      second term indicates that of firm B.
         Let us consider again the Technology Adoption Game of table 8.2a in which we
      already found two NEs in pure strategies, to check if there are any msNE.

      Example 8.1: msNE in the Technology Adoption Game As previously discussed,
      the game in table 8.2a has two Nash equilibria in pure strategies: (Adopt, Adopt) and
      (Not adopt, Not adopt). There is, however, a third Nash equilibria in which both firms
      use a mixed strategy. This strategy can be found by allowing each firm to randomize.
      We denote p (q) as the probability that firm A (B, respectively) adopts the technology.
      Each firm must be indifferent between adopting and not adopting the technology, as

                       8.1.2    Sequential-Move Games
                       When players choose their strategies sequentially, rather than simultaneously, the defi-
                       nition of strategy becomes more involved. In particular, a strategy must now be under-
                       stood as a complete contingent plan describing what action player i chooses at each
                       point at which he is called on to move, given the previous history of play. In some
                       games such history can be observable by player i (i.e., he can observe all moves by all




                       Figure 8.1
                       Best responses
554                                                                                     Chapter 8



      players acting before him), or not observable if player i cannot observe at least one past
      move from one of his opponents. We explore both types of sequential-move games in
      the following sections.
         We often represent sequential-move games using game trees, as that depicted in
      figure 8.2, rather than with matrices. The “root” of the tree, where the game starts, is
      referred to as the initial node, and the last nodes of the tree, where no more branches
      originate, are the terminal nodes.
         In particular, game trees must satisfy a few basic rules: First, a tree must have only
      one initial node, as opposed to the tree in figure 8.2. Second, every node of the tree has
      exactly one immediate predecessor except the initial node, which has no predecessor.
      Otherwise, nodes could have two predecessors. Third, multiple branches extending
      from the same node must have different action labels. The left panel of figure 8.4 de-
      picts a game tree satisfying this property while the right panel violates it, as label A is
      on two branches for player 1.
         Let information sets denote a group of nodes among which a player cannot distin-
      guish, a common feature of trees representing games of incomplete information as
      described in subsequent sections. Information sets arise when a player does not

      observe the action that his predecessor chose. For instance, in the left panel of figure
      8.5 the second mover does not know whether the first mover selected A or B, and
      thus the second mover has both nodes connected with a dashed line that emphasizes
      his lack of information (player 2 does not know which node he is at). The fourth
      property on game trees states that every information set contains decision nodes for
      only one of the players in the game. Figure 8.5 depicts a game tree that satisfies this
      property (left panel) and one that violates it (right panel).
         Fifth, all nodes in a given information set have the same immediate successors; oth-
      erwise, the player who is called on to move on that information set would be able to
      infer in which node he is located by just looking at the number of immediate succes-
      sors he faces and their labels. Figure 8.6 depicts a game tree violating this property. In
      this case player 2 would know whether he is located in the top node of the information
      set (if only actions A and B are available to him) or in the bottom node (if A, B, and C
      are available).
         At this point, you might wonder whether we can simply use the NE solution concept
      defined above in order to find equilibrium predictions in sequential-move games. We
      can, but as the next example shows, some of the NE predictions are not very sensible
      (or credible, to be precise).

      Example 8.2: Nash equilibria in the Entry and Predation Game Consider the
      game tree in figure 8.7 illustrating an entrant’s decision on whether to enter into an
      industry where an incumbent firm operates or to stay out. If the entrant stays out, it

                  entrant, which results in losses of 1 million USD for each firm.

      that the incumbent’s best response is to accommodate once it goes in. As a conse-

      enter, as in the NE (Out, Fight)—but rather it believes that its entry will always be
      accommodated. In other words, only the NE (In, Accommodate) is credible. ■

      The preceding example indicates the need to require a notion of credibility in sequential-
      move games that did not exist in the NE solution concept, a requirement commonly
      known as “sequential rationality.” In particular, we say that player i’s strategy is se-
      quentially rational if it specifies an optimal action for player i at any node (or informa-
      tion set) of the game where he is called on to move, even those information sets that
      player i does not believe will be reached in the equilibrium of the game. That is, play-
      er i behaves optimally at every node (or information set), both nodes that belong to the
      equilibrium path of the game tree and those that lie off-the-equilibrium path.
         How can we guarantee that it holds when finding equilibria in sequential-move
      games? Using backward induction, which essentially requires that, starting from every
      terminal node, each player uses optimal actions at every subgame of the game tree.
      Before applying backward induction to find equilibria in different game trees, let us
      first define what we mean by a subgame. A subgame can be identified by drawing a
      rectangle around a section of the game tree without “breaking” any information set.3
      The two panels of figure 8.8 depict subgames in two game trees. Note that in the right
      panel we cannot draw a circle breaking player 2’s information set, and thus the small-
      est subgame must include a larger portion of the tree, starting at player 1’s choice be-
      tween A and B.
         Therefore the application of backward induction requires us to find the strategy that
      every player i finds optimal when he is called to move at every subgame along the
      game tree. That is, we start by identifying the optimal behavior of the player who acts
      last (in the last subgame of the tree). Then, taking the optimal action of this player into

      Example 8.4: Applying backward induction in three steps Let us apply back-
      ward induction in the game tree of figure 8.10 in order to find SPNE. After identifying
      subgames (circled in the figure for easier reference), we start with the last mover (play-
      er 1), who chooses E as it yields a higher payoff than F (i.e., 3 > 2). We can now move
      to player 2 in his bottom node who, anticipating that player 1 will respond with E, can
      compare his payoff from C (3) against that from D (2). Hence player 2 selects C if he
      is called on to move at the bottom node of the tree. If instead player 2 is called on to
      move at the top node, then he chooses A as it yields a higher payoff than B (i.e., 4 > 2).
      Finally, we examine the first mover (player 1) who can anticipate how the game will
      ensue if he chooses Up (i.e., player 2 will respond with A, yielding a payoff of only
      1 for player 1) and if he chooses Down (i.e., player 2 will respond with C and player 1
      will subsequently respond with E, entailing a payoff of 3). As a consequence player 1
      chooses Down since his payoff (3) is higher than from Up (1). ■

                  8.1.3    Simultaneous-Move Games of Incomplete Information
                  While the strategic settings that we previously analyzed assume that all players are
                  perfectly informed about all relevant details of the game, there are often real-life situ-
                  ations where players operate without such information. In particular, players act under
                  “incomplete information” if at least one player cannot observe a piece of information,
                  such as the marginal costs of rival firms, or the private valuation for the object of other
                  bidders in an auction.4 For compactness, we often refer to this piece of private informa-
                  tion as player i’s “type” and denote it as θi. While player j might not observe player
                  i’s type (e.g., its marginal costs), he knows the probability distribution of each type,
                  namely its frequency in the population. For instance, if marginal costs can be either
                  high or low, whereby Θi = {H, L}, the probability of firm i’s costs being high is
                  p(θi = H) = p and the probability of its costs being low is p(θi = L) = 1 − p, where
                  p ∈ (0, 1). We can graphically represent the presence of incomplete information by
                  adding, at the beginning of the game, a first move of nature determining the precise

                  4
                   The literature refers to these incomplete information games in which players act simultaneously as
                  Bayesian games.
564                                                                                                Chapter 8




      Figure 8.13
      Investment game under incomplete information


      type of θi. Figure 8.13 introduces incomplete information in the technology adoption
      game, allowing for firm A to have two possible types, either high or low costs from
      investing in the new technology, with associated probabilities 2/3 and 1/3. While firm
      A observes its own type, firm B cannot observe it; graphically implying that firm A
      knows which payoff matrix firms are playing, while firm B can only assign a probabil-
      ity 2/3 (1/3) to playing the right-hand (left-hand) matrix.
         Before describing the equilibrium solution concept in this setting, note that every
      player i’s strategy in an incomplete information context needs to be a function of its
      privately observed type θi (e.g., its benefit from investing in a new technology), imply-
      ing that si is a function si(θi). Importantly, player i’s strategy is not conditioned on
      other players’ types,

                                      θ − i = (θ1 , θ 2 , …, θ i −1 , θ i +1 , …, θ n ).

         That is, we do not write si(θi, θ−i) because player i cannot observe the types of all
      other players.5 Finally, and for simplicity, we assume that types are independently dis-
      tributed, which entails that every player i cannot infer additional information about
      his rivals’ types θ−i after observing his own type θi. We are now ready to define the
      Bayesian Nash equilibrium solution concept.

      5
        In fact, if all players could observe the types of all of their rivals, we would be describing a com-
      plete information game, as those in previous sections of the chapter.
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                                                 565




                     Bayesian Nash equilibrium A strategy profile ( s1* (θ1 ) , s2* (θ 2 ) , …, sN* (θ N ))is a
                     Bayesian Nash equilibrium (BNE) of a game of incomplete information if

                                 EU i ( si* (θi ) , s−* i (θ − i ) ; θi , θ − i ) ≥ EU i ( si (θi ) , s−* i (θ − i ) ; θi , θ − i )
                     for every strategy si(θi) ∈ Si, every type θi ∈ Θi, and every player i.

                     In words, when all other players select equilibrium strategies, the expected utility
                  that player i obtains from selecting si* (θi ) when his type is θi is larger than that of de-
                  viating to any other strategy si(θi). This must be true for all possible types of player i,
                  θi ∈ Θi, and for all players i ∈ N in the game. Intuitively, this definition entails that
                  player i does not deviate from his strategy function si* (⋅) to a different function si′ (⋅),
                  nor does he evaluate his equilibrium strategy function si* (⋅) at a different type θi′ ≠ θi ;
                  in other words, he does not have incentives to “lie” about his type.
                     Let us next apply this solution concept to the incomplete information version of the
                  technology adoption game depicted in figure 8.13. A useful approach for finding all
                  BNEs in simultaneous-move games of incomplete information is illustrated in the next
                  four steps:
                  1. Strategy sets Identify the strategy set for each player, which can be a function of
                     his privately observed type.
                     In the context of the technology adoption game, Firm A’s strategy is conditional
                     on its type being high or low, yielding a strategy set with four possible elements
                     S1 = {IHIL, IHNIL, NIHIL, NIHNIL}. Here the first component of every pair indicates
                     what firm A does when its type is high, and the second component describes its

                     regardless of its type. In contrast, firm B does not have a privately observed type
                     in which it could condition its strategy, and as a consequence its strategy set is
                     S2 = {I, NI}.

                  8.1.4   Sequential-Move Games under Incomplete Information
                  The BNE solution concept helps us find equilibrium outcomes in settings where
                  players interact under incomplete information. While the applications in the previous
                  section considered that players act simultaneously, we can also find the BNEs of
                  incomplete information games in which players act sequentially, such as in the game
                  depicted in figure 8.15. In particular, player 1 decides to make an investment offer (O)
                  or not make the offer (N) to player 2. Player 1 is privately informed about whether the
                  investment will be Beneficial for player 2 or Not beneficial. Player 2, however, does

        In order to find the set of BNEs, we first represent the Bayesian normal-form repre-
      sentation of the game tree, as depicted in table 8.9. Recall that this matrix includes
      expected payoffs for each player, and that the uninformed player 2 has only two avail-
      able strategies (two columns), whereas the informed player 1 has four different strate-
      gies (four rows) as he can condition his strategy on his privately observed type.
        Expected payoffs are underlined in order to identify each player’s best response. We
      can conclude that there are two BNEs in this game: (OBONB, A) and (NBNNB, R).
        The first BNE is rather sensible: player 1 makes the offer regardless of his type, and
      thus the uninformed player 2 chooses to accept the offer if he receives one. The sec-
      ond BNE, however, is more difficult to rationalize as an equilibrium prediction in this
      sequential-move game. In particular, no type of sender makes an offer in equilibrium,
      and the responder rejects any offer presented to him. If an offer was ever observed (a
      surprising event only happening off-the-equilibrium path), the receiver should com-
      pare the expected utility of accepting and rejecting the offer, based on the off-the-
      equilibrium belief μ, which denotes the probability that player 2 assigns to such a
      surprising offer originating from a beneficial type, that is, the probability of being in
      the top right-hand node of the game tree. In particular, the receiver finds that

                                      EU 2 ( A) = 3.5 ⋅ µ + 0 ⋅ (1 − µ ) = 3.5µ,

                                    EU 2 ( R ) = 2 ⋅ µ + ( −3) ⋅ (1 − µ ) = −3 + µ.
        Hence player 2 accepts the offer, since 3.5μ > −3 + μ simplifies to 2.5μ > −3, which
      holds for all μ ∈ (0, 1). Importantly, this acceptance holds for any arbitrary off-the-
      equilibrium belief, μ, that player 2 might sustain upon observing an offer. Therefore
      the offer rejection that the BNE (NFNE, R) prescribes cannot be sequentially rational
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                                      571



                  because the responder’s optimal reaction is to accept an offer if it is ever made by
                  the sender.7
                    In order to avoid identifying equilibrium predictions that are not sequentially ratio-
                  nal (as described earlier in this section), rather than use BNE, we can apply a solution
                  concept called the Perfect Bayesian Equilibrium (PBE) that can deal with sequential-
                  move games with incomplete information.


                      Perfect Bayesian equilibrium A strategy profile (s1, s2, … , sN) and beliefs μ
                      over the nodes at all information sets are a PBE if:
                      1. each player’s strategies specify optimal actions, given the strategies of the
                         other players, and given his beliefs, and
                      2. beliefs are consistent with Bayes’s rule, whenever possible.


                    Intuitively, the first condition resembles the definition of BNE, as it requires players’
                  actions to be optimal under an incomplete information setting, that is, given the beliefs
                  that each of them sustains about other players’ types. The second condition, however,
                  was not present in the definition of BNE, as it states that beliefs must be consistent with
                  Bayes’s rule whenever possible. Applying Bayes’s rule in the previous investment
                  game, we can express player 2’s probability that the investment is beneficial after re-
                  ceiving an offer as

                                          p ( B ) ⋅ p (Offer|B )                   p ( B ) ⋅ p (Offer|B )
                        p ( B|Offer ) =                          =                                                     .
                                                p (Offer )         p ( B ) ⋅ p (Offer|B ) + p ( NB ) ⋅ p (Offer | NB )
                     In words, p(B|Offer) describes the the probability that, upon receiving an offer, the
                  investment is beneficial. This probability is equal to the probability of the investment
                  being beneficial and an offer being made by player 1, p(B) · p(Offer|B), conditional on
                  an offer being received, p(Offer). Player 2’s belief that the investment is beneficial,
                  conditional on receiving an offer, is often referred to as player 2’s “posterior probabil-
                  ity,” since it takes the initial (prior) probability of the investment being beneficial,
                  p(B), and updates it after receiving an offer to obtain p(B|Offer). Denoting for com-
                  pactness, μ = p(B|Offer), αi = p(Offer|i), where i = {B, NB}, p = p(B), and thus 1 − p =
                  p(NB), we can express player 2’s belief as

                                                                      pα B
                                                          µ=                        .
                                                               pα B + (1 − p ) α NB

                  7
                    Recall that sequential rationality requires that every player chooses optimal actions at every point
                  of the game at which the player is called on to move, either a node or an information set, given the
                  available information at that point.
572                                                                                       Chapter 8




        If in the previous investment game, player 2 assigns a probability 18 to player 1 mak-
      ing an offer when the investment is beneficial, and a probability 116 making an offer
      when the investment is not beneficial, his posterior probability μ that an offer is made
      when the investment is beneficial becomes

                                         pα B                   1 ⋅1       2
                             µ=                        =         2 8
                                                                          = .
                                  pα B + (1 − p ) α NB   1
                                                           2 ⋅ 8 + 2 ⋅ 16
                                                              1     1 1    3

         In words, if an offer is made, it is twice as likely to originate from player 1 when the
      investment is beneficial than when the investment is not beneficial. The last compo-
      nent of condition 2 in the definition of PBE, “beliefs must be consistent with Bayes’s
      rule whenever possible,” might well seem obscure. It allows for the possibility of off-
      the-equilibrium messages and beliefs. Indeed it is possible to specify beliefs that are
      consistent with Bayes’s rule only when we deal with information sets that are reached
      in equilibrium. However, when we are in information sets that have not been reached
      in equilibrium, Bayes’s rule cannot be applied. For instance, if player 2’s information
      set is not reached (what can only happen if no type of player 1 makes an offer), the
      denominator in Bayes’s rule is zero (i.e., the probability of receiving an offer from any
      type of player 1 is zero, since αF = 0 and αE = 0). This makes μ indeterminate because it
      becomes 0/0. In these instances we leave μ unrestricted at μ ∈ [0, 1].
         Therefore we refer to μ as off-the-equilibrium beliefs: the probability of being in a
      node of an information set that is actually not reached in equilibrium. You might be
      wondering why we should care about off-the-equilibrium beliefs. The reason why
      these beliefs are important in our identification of equilibrium strategies is that they
      determine what player 2 does in the event of receiving an investment offer. This can
      induce player 1 to make offers (or deter him from doing so), ultimately affecting our
      equilibrium results.

      8.1.5   Procedure to Find PBEs
      Let us next describe how to test if a specific strategy profile satisfies the definition of a
      PBE. The following five-step procedure (based on Muñoz-García 2012) may help in
      this endeavor:
      1. Specify a strategy profile for the privately informed player. In our example, there
         are only four possible strategy profiles for the privately informed player 1: two
         separating strategy profiles (which specify a different action for player 1 depending
         on his type), OBNNB and NBONB, and two pooling strategy profiles (which prescribe
         the same action for all types of player 1), OBONB and NBNNB. (For future reference,
         we will shade the branches corresponding to the strategy profile that we test.)
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                                573



                  2. Update the uninformed player’s beliefs using Bayes’s rule at all information sets,
                     whenever possible.
                  3. Given the uninformed player’s updated beliefs, find his optimal response. In our
                     example, we need to determine the optimal response of player 2 upon receiving
                     an offer from player 1 given his updated belief. (Also for future reference, it might
                     be helpful to shade the branch corresponding to the optimal responses we just
                     found.)
                  4. Given the optimal response of the uninformed player obtained in step 3, find the
                     optimal action (message) for each type of informed player. In our previous example,
                     we first check if player 1 makes offers when the investment is beneficial (given
                     player 2’s optimal response after receiving an offer that we found in step 3). We then
                     proceed similarly when the investment is not beneficial, checking whether player 1
                     prefers to make an offer.
                  5. Last we check if the strategy profile for the informed player found in step 4
                     coincides with the profile suggested in step 1:
                      a. If it coincides, then this strategy profile, updated beliefs, and optimal responses
                         can be supported as a PBE of the incomplete information game.
                      b. Otherwise, we say that this strategy profile cannot be sustained as a PBE of the
                         game.
                    We will next apply this five-step procedure using a simplified version of Spence’s
                  (1973) famous labor market signaling game.

                  Example 8.6: Labor market signaling game In the sequential game with incom-
                  plete information shown in figure 8.16, a worker privately observes whether he has a
                  high productivity or a low productivity. The worker then decides whether to pursue
                  more education (e.g., an MBA) that he might use as a signal about his productivity
                  level.8 The firm can either hire him as a manager (M) or as a cashier (C), observing
                  whether the worker acquired an additional college degree, butnot observing the work-
                  er’s real productivity.
                    We next examine whether the separating strategy profile (EH, NEL), in which only
                  the high-productivity worker acquires education, and whether the pooling strategy

      8.2     Bertrand Model of Price Competition with Homogeneous Products10

      Consider an industry with two firms, 1 and 2, selling a homogeneous product, such as

                     price anywhere on or above that of firm k, whereby pj ≥ pk. That is, firm j does not
                     undercut firm k because that would entail negative profits. Graphically, the segment
                     of best-response function pj(pk) in figure 8.22 that lies to the left of pk = c must be

      has a positive slope for all pk between c and pm, where firm j charges a price slightly
      below firm k’s.
         A symmetric argument applies to the construction of firm k’s best-response function,
      pk(pj), depicted in figure 8.23. Combining both firms’ best-response functions, we see
      that the only pair of prices ( p1* , p2* ) that constitutes a mutual best response for both
      firms is that in which their best-response functions cross each other, which only occurs
      at ( p1* , p2* ) = (c, c) . That is, at the Nash equilibrium of the Bertrand model, all firms
      charge a price equal to their common marginal cost of production, thus making no
      economic profits. A similar result extends to settings with N > 2 firms, whereby all of
      them charge a price equal to their common marginal cost.
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                       583




                  Figure 8.23
                  Equilibrium in the Bertrand model


                     This is often interpreted as a surprising result, as it essentially says that, even when
                  only two firms sell a homogeneous product, as long as their competition is in prices,
                  competitive pressures will be strong enough to lead them toward the same outcome
                  as in perfectly competitive industries, where firms set prices equal to marginal cost.
                  In our construction of the demand curve, the reason why such a result emerges in a
                  Bertrand duopoly is that, when firms compete in prices, every firm j faces an infinitely
                  elastic demand curve at its rival’s price, pk. Intuitively, any increase (decrease) from
                  pk infinitely reduces (increases, respectively) firm j’s demand. In addition, this implies
                  that firm j can serve all market demand when its price is lower than k’s, thus not fac-
                  ing any capacity constraint. As a consequence this equilibrium result hinges into our
                  assumptions. For instance, the competitive pressures we just described are amelio-
                  rated if we instead consider that firms sell heterogeneous, rather than homogeneous,
                  products (i.e., we allow for product differentiation as we do in subsequent sections
                  of this chapter), or if firms compete in quantities (rather than prices) even if their
                  product is undifferentiated as shown in the Cournot model of quantity competition we
                  explore next.

                  Remark A natural question at this point is how our results would be affected if we
                  consider firms to face different production costs, that is, 0 < c1 < c2. In such a setting the
                  most efficient firm sets a price equal to the marginal cost of the least efficient firm
584                                                                                                  Chapter 8



      p1 = c2 (or marginally below that), while other firms will set a random price in the inter-
      val [c2, c2 + η] where η > 0.14

      Application Morrison and Winston (1996) studied the intense price competition
      between airlines in different routes after an important deregulation during 1977, which
      led to 20 percent price reductions in less than a quarter for several routes.

      8.3     Cournot Model of Quantity Competition15

      When two firms compete in quantities, they bring their output q1 and q2 to the market,
      the market clears and the price is determined from the inverse demand function p(q),
      where q = q1 + q2 represents aggregate demand. Like in previous sections, we consider
      that p(q) satisfies p′(q) < 0 at all output levels q ≥ 0, and that both firms face a common
      cost function c(qj ), where c′(qj ) > 0 and c″(qj ) ≥ 0, thus facing increasing and weakly
      convex cost in output, for every firm j = {1, 2} (later on we relax this assumption by
      allowing firms to be asymmetric in their costs).16
         Following an approach similar to the Bertrand model of price competition, let us
      first identify every firm j’s best-response function in order to find the pair of output
      levels ( q1* , q2* ) that constitutes an equilibrium in the Cournot model. In order to do
      so, we set up firm 1’s profit maximization problem for a given output level of its
      rival, q2,

                                            max p ( q1 + q2 ) q1 − c ( q1 )
                                            q1 ≥0                     .

         Importantly, when solving this profit-maximization problem (PMP), firm 1 treats
      firm 2’s production, q2 , as a parameter, since firm 1 cannot vary its level. Taking first-
      order conditions with respect to q1 (the only choice variable for firm 1), yields

                      p′ ( q1 + q2 ) q1 + p ( q1 + q2 ) − c ′ ( q1 ) ≤ 0, with equality if q1 > 0.

                  c′(0). As a result we must have that both q1* and q2* are positive.18

      20
        Recall that in perfectly competitive markets, p(q) = c, which in this context entails a − bq = c.

                  prices under the Bertrand model, whereby firms’ behavior mimics that in perfectly
                  competitive markets. The difference in the models’ prediction arises because, unlike in
                  the Bertrand model, the demand that every firm faces in the Cournot game is not infi-
                  nitely elastic. Indeed a reduction in output does not produce an infinite increase in
                  market price, but instead an increase of −p′(q1 + q2). As a result, if firms produce the
                  same output as under marginal cost pricing, which is half of (a − c) / 2, each firm would
                  have incentives to deviate from such a high output level by marginally reducing its
                  output. In this setting the increase in market price that such smaller output entails
                  would offset the loss in sales that the deviating firm suffers (as it now sells fewer
                  units), yielding an overall increase in its profits.
                     In fact equilibrium outcomes do not coincide with the monopoly output either. The
                  reason why this result emerges is because every firm i, individually increasing its out-
                  put level qi, takes into account how the reduction in market price affects its own profits
                  but ignores the profit loss that its rival suffers from such a lower price, that is, it pro-
                  duces a negative external effect. Since every firm does not take into account this exter-
                  nal effect, aggregate output is too large, relative to the output that would maximize
                  firms’ joint profits, which is the output that firms would select when acting as a cartel
                  (and which coincides with the monopoly output, as the next example shows).

      8.3.2   Cournot Pricing Rule
      The market power firms sustain in the Cournot model of quantity competition can be
      compactly expressed using a variation of the Lerner index of market power we en-
      countered in our discussion on monopoly. In particular, from the first-order conditions
      found for every firm j in the Cournot model, we know that
                           p′ ( q ) q j + p( q) − c = 0, or p( q) − c = − p′ ( q ) q j .

      Multiplying both sides by q, and dividing them by p(q), yields

                                             p (q ) − c − p′ (q ) q j
                                         q             =              q.
                                               p( q )      p( q )

      And from the definition of price-elasticity of demand, ε = (∂q(p) / ∂p) · (p / q), we can
      use its inverse, 1 / ε = (∂p(q) / ∂q) · (q / p(q)), or more compactly, 1 / ε = p′(q) · (q / p(q)),
      which coincides with the first term on the right-hand side of the expression above. As
      a consequence such expression can be rewritten as

                                                  p (q) − c    1
                                              q             = − q j.
                                                    p( q )     ε
      Finally, defining αj ≡ qj / q as firm j’s market share, we obtain

                                                  p (q) − c   αj
                                                            =− ,
                                                    p( q )    ε
      which, given its similarity with the inverse elasticity pricing rule (IEPR) under mo-
      nopoly, is often referred to as the “Cournot pricing rule.” In fact, when αj = 1, implying
      that firm j is a monopoly, the IEPR becomes a special case of the Cournot price rule
      that we just found. When firms are symmetric, αi = αj for all firms i and j, entailing a
      market share of αj = 1/n for every firm j. In this case, the right-hand side of the
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                       591



                  Cournot pricing rule simplifies to 1/nε. Moreover note that the larger the market share
                  αj of a given firm is, the larger the price markup over marginal cost that firm j can
                  charge. A similar argument applies to a more inelastic demand (ε close to zero), intui-
                  tively indicating that the good might not have close substitutes.

      8.4     Product Differentiation

      We have thus far considered that firms sell homogeneous products, but firms often try
      to differentiate their products from those of their rivals. In this section we explore how
      our previous results in the Cournot and Bertrand model are affected by the presence of
      product differentiation.21

      8.4.1  Bertrand Model with Heterogeneous Products
      Consider the case in which every firm i, where i = {1, 2}, competing in prices, faces
      demand curve
                         qi ( pi , p j ) = a − bpi + cp j , where a, b, c > 0 and j ≠ i.

      Intuitively, if firm i increases its price, it reduces its own demand, but if its rival
      (firm j) increases its price, firm i’s demand increases. Additionally some applications
      assume that b > c, which indicates that the firm i’s demand, qi(pi, pj), is more sensitive
      (in absolute value) to changes in its own price pi, than to its rival’s price pj. In short,
      own-price effects dominate cross-price effects.
         Hence firm i’s PMP (for simplicity, we assume no costs) is

                                           max ( a − bpi + cp j ) pi .
                                            pi ≥ 0


      Taking first-order conditions with respect to pi we obtain a − 2bpi + cpj = 0, and solving
      for pi we find firm i’s best-response function

                                                               a + cp j
                                                pi ( p j ) =            ,
                                                                 2b
      with firm j also having a symmetric best-response function. Figure 8.27 depicts the fact
      that best-response functions are now positively sloped. Intuitively, an increase in firm
      j’s price leads firm i to increase his, and vice versa. We say that, in this case, firms’

                        8.4.2    Cournot Model with Heterogeneous Products
                        What if products are (exogenously) differentiated, but firms compete in quantities
                        rather than prices? Consider two firms with the following inverse demand curves
596                                                                                           Chapter 8




                                 p1 ( q1, q2 ) = α − β q1 − γ q2   for firm 1,

                                 p2 ( q1, q2 ) = α − γ q1 − β q2   for firm 2,
      where we assume that β > 0 and β > γ. Note that more units of either firm’s products
      reduce market prices, but the effect of firm 1’s increasing its output, q1, is larger on its
      own price, p1, than on its rival’s price, p2 (and similarly for q2). Intuitively, the price of
      a particular brand is more sensitive to changes in its own output than to changes in its
      rival’s output.22
         Hence firm i’s PMP is (again, assuming no costs)

                                          max (α − β qi − γ q j ) qi .
                                           qi ≥ 0

                                              α − 2β qi − γ q j = 0 ,

      and solving for qi, we find the best-response function of firm i, qi(qj) = (α / 2β) − (γ / 2β)qj,
      as depicted in figure 8.28.

                  Clearly, as γ increases (products become more homogeneous), individual and aggre-

                  its upper bound, that is, γ→β (indicating completely homogeneous products), indi-
                  vidual output becomes qi* = α ( 2β + β ) = α 3β as in standard Cournot models of
                  homogeneous products. In the other extreme, when γ→0 (completely differentiated
                  products), then qi* = α ( 2β + 0) = α 2β , as in monopoly.

                  8.4.3   Experimental Tests
                  Huck et al. (2000) test whether the theoretical predictions in the Bertrand and Cournot
                  models with product differentiation approach actual behavior of individuals participat-
                  ing in controlled laboratory experiments. In particular, they considered four firms
                  facing a linear inverse demand function

                                                                2
                                                 p1 = 300 − q1 − ( q2 + q3 + q4 )
                                                                3
                  and a common marginal cost c = 2 for all firms. Their results show that the average
                  output level when experimental subjects competed in quantities, 74.2, was close to the
                  equilibrium prediction of the Cournot model, 74.5. Similarly the average price when
                  individuals were asked to compete in prices, $41.9, was also close to the equilibrium
                  prediction of $39.25. In addition a series of recent articles experimentally tested the
                  impact of information on subjects’ behavior in Cournot and Bertrand settings, which
                  include Huck et al. (2000), Davis (2002), and Altavilla, Luini, and Sbriglia (2006).
598                                                                                           Chapter 8



      Suetens and Potters (2007) analyze data from these experiments and argue that collu-
      sion seems stronger when subjects compete à la Bertrand than à la Cournot.

      8.5     Dynamic Competition

      Let us now examine how our equilibrium results in the Bertrand (Cournot) model
      are affected if firms select their prices (output levels) sequentially rather than
      simultaneously.

      8.5.1    Sequential Bertrand Model with Homogeneous Products
      Consider first the Bertrand model with homogeneous products, but now assume
      that firm 1 chooses its price p1 first, whereas firm 2 observes that price and responds
      with its own price p2. Since in equilibrium firms must be making positive or zero
      profits, we restrict our search to prices satisfying pi ≥ c for every firm i = {1, 2}. In this
      setting, results are rather obvious, since firm 2 (the follower) has a best response
      given by

                                                  p1 − ε   if p1 > c, or
                                     p2 ( p1 ) = 
                                                 c         if p1 = c.
         Intuitively, the follower undercuts the leader’s price p1 by a small ε > 0 (e.g., one
      cent) if p1 > c, or keeps it at p2 = c if the leader already practiced marginal cost pricing
      (i.e., p1 = c). The leader anticipates such a best response from the follower. In particu-
      lar, the leader expects that its price will be undercut by the follower when p1 > c
      (leaving the leader with no sales and zero profits), but its price is mimicked by the
      follower when p1 = c (leaving the leader with half of the market share). The leader then
      has (weak) incentives to set a price p1 = c. As a consequence the equilibrium price
      pair remains at ( p1* , p2* ) = (c, c) , as in the simultaneous-move version of the Bertrand
      model we explored in previous sections.

      effects. In this context, the follower (firm 2) faces the following PMP:

         Interestingly, this first-order condition coincides with that we found in the standard
      Cournot model with simultaneous output decisions, except for the strategic effect,
      p′(Q)(∂q2(q1) / ∂q1)q1. Moreover such an effect is positive given that p′(Q) < 0 and

      simultaneous model. Intuitively, by overproducing, the leader forces the follower to
      reduce its output q2 by the amount ∂q2(q1) / ∂q1, which helps the leader sell its produc-
      tion at a higher price, as reflected by p′(Q), and ultimately earning a larger profit than
      in the Cournot model. The leader’s ability to force the follower into reducing its own
      output (and thus obtain more profits than the follower) is referred to as the “leader’s
      advantage.”24

      8.6     Reconciling Cournot and Bertrand: Introducing Capacity Constraints

      How come the results in the standard Bertrand and Cournot models with homogeneous
      products are so different, predicting a fierce competition in the former but a softer in
      the latter? Kreps and Scheinkman (1983) investigated the difference between the two
      models by asking another question: Do firms really compete in prices without facing
      capacity constraints? Recall that, in our discussion of the Bertrand model of price com-
      petition, we allowed every firm to satisfy all existing demand if its price is lower than
      that of its rivals. Kreps and Scheinkman (1983) considered this assumption was rather
      restrictive, and proposed an extension of the Bertrand model in which, in the first
      stage, firms set capacities, q1 and q2 , with a cost of every unit of capacity given by
      c > 0; then, in the second stage, firms observe each other’s capacities and compete in
      prices, simultaneously setting p1 and p2. For simplicity, let us consider that production
      costs are zero, and inverse demand is p(q) = a − q.

      8.6.1  Role of Capacity Constraints
      Before finding equilibrium behavior in this model, let us briefly analyze the role of
      capacity constraints. When a firm’s price is lower than its capacity, not all consumers
      can be served. In the event this happens, sales must be rationed, which we assume
      to be done through efficient rationing, meaning the customers with the highest
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                          607




                  Figure 8.32
                  Rationing of demand


                  willingness-to-pay get the product first. (Note that this is not a restrictive assumption
                  if there is arbitrage.) Hence, if p1 < p2 and the quantity demanded at p1 is so large that
                  Q( p1 ) > q1, the first q1 units are served to the customers with the highest willingness-
                  to-pay (i.e., the upper segment of the demand curve), while the remaining customers
                  are left as residual demand to firm 2. Figure 8.32 depicts this rationing: first, at p1 the
                  quantity demanded is Q(p1), but only q1 units can be served, implying that the remain-
                  ing Q( p1 ) − q1 units are left as residual demand (see shaded segment in the horizontal
                  axis). Since firm 2 sets a price of p2, its demand will be Q(p2), and thus only a portion
                  of the residual demand, namely Q( p2 ) − q1 , is captured as units sold by firm 2.
                     Firm 2’s residual demand can thus be expressed as Q ( p2 ) − q1 if Q ( p2 ) − q1 > 0, and
                  0 otherwise. Before finding equilibrium behavior in this sequential-move game, we
                  must restrict q1 and q2 in order to discard capacity levels so high that lead firms to
                  negative profits, independently of the decision of its competitor. In particular, since
                  the maximal revenue of a firm under monopoly is max q ( a − q)q , which is maximized
                  at q = a / 2, yielding profits of a2 / 4, we can claim that maximal revenues are larger than
                  costs if a2 4 ≥ cq j , or solving for q j , a2 4c ≥ q j . Intuitively, the capacity cannot be too
608                                                                                         Chapter 8



      large; otherwise, the firm would not obtain positive profits regardless of the opponent’s
      decision.

      8.6.2    Second Stage
      We can now start our search for equilibrium behavior. As in other sequential-move
      games, we first obtain first-order conditions on the second stage (pricing game) where
      firms simultaneously choose prices p1 and p2 as a function of the capacity choices
      q1 and q2. In particular, we want to show that, both firms set a common price
       p1 = p2 = p* = a − q1 − q2 , where demand equals supply, total capacity. That is,
       p* = a − Q , where Q ≡ q1 + q2.
         To prove this result, we first assume that firm 1 sets a price p1 = p*. We need to show
      that firm 2 also has an incentive to set p2 = p* rather than deviating from the common
      price p*. If firm 2 does not deviate, p1 = p2 = p*, then firm 2 sells up to its capacity q2 .
      Firm 2 could thus deviate by charging a price lower or higher than p*. If it reduces its
      price below p*, demand would exceed its capacity q2 . As a consequence firm 2 would
      sell the same units as before, q2 , but at a lower margin, and thus a price reduction from
      p* is not a profitable deviation. If instead firm 2 charges a price above p*, then p1 = p* < p2,
      and its revenues become

      rival, ultimately raising its revenues after increasing its price. We can now find the
      maximum of this revenue function. Taking first-order conditions with respect to p2
      yields

      8.7     Endogenous Entry

      with inverse demand function p(q), where q denotes aggregate output. Every firm j

      8.8   Repeated Interaction

      In all previous models we considered firms interacting during only one period. In real-
      ity, firms compete over several periods and, in some cases, over many generations.
      Therefore a firm’s action during one period might affect its rivals’ behavior in future
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                                615



                  periods. More important, we can show that under certain conditions, the strong com-
                  petitive results in the Bertrand model (and, to some extent, in the Cournot model)
                  are lessened when firms interact repeatedly. In particular, we can demonstrate that
                  collusion can be sustained in the repeated game even if it cannot in the one-shot (unre-
                  peated) version of the game.26 For simplicity, all subsequent discussion considers
                  that firms face a decreasing and linear inverse demand function p(Q) = a − bQ, where
                  a, b > 0.

                  8.8.1    Price Competition
                  For simplicity, let us start with the Bertrand model of price competition with two firms
                  selling homogeneous products. In particular, let ptj denote firm j’s price at period t,
                  which is a function of the history of all price choices by the two firms, H t −1 = { p1t , p2t }
                  for every period t = 1 … t − 1, based on the sequence of price pairs chosen by both firms
                  from the first period of their interaction until period t−1. Conditioning ptj into the full
                  history of play allows for a wide array of pricing strategies, such as (1) setting the same
                  price ptj = d regardless of previous history where d > 0; (2) setting a price p1j in the first
                  round of interaction and continue to do so in subsequent rounds t > 1 but retaliate by
                  setting a price ptj , where ptj < p1j , if firm k (the competitor) lowers its price below a
                  threshold level pkt = e during any previous period, where e > 0; and (3) start with a
                  relatively low price p1j and practice one dollar increments in each period during subse-
                  quent rounds until reaching the monopoly price pm as long as both firms respected this
                  pricing strategy in all previous periods; or any other combination.

                  Finitely Repeated Game
                  A natural question is whether we can sustain collusion in the Bertrand model when
                  firms interact for a finite number of T ≥ 2 rounds. Unfortunately, the answer is nega-
                  tive. To see why, note that this is a sequential-move game of complete information,
                  which we solve by backward induction, thus starting from the last period of the re-
                  peated game (period T). Regardless of previous pricing strategies, the optimal pricing
                  strategy of every firm at this stage is to set a price pi*,T = c . Thus each firm behaves as
                  in the one-shot (unrepeated) Bertrand game, using marginal cost pricing. Anticipating
                  such a behavior in the last round of interaction, firms in the previous to the last period
                  (T − 1) expect to select a price pi*,T = c in period T, and that such pricing strategy will

                  26
                    The presentation of repeated interaction in this section is based on folk theorem results in repeated
                  games. For more details, see the seminal work by Friedman (1971), the survey of the literature by
                  Mertens (1987), and the textbook on this type of games by Mailath and Samuelson (2006).
616                                                                                                      Chapter 8



      not be affected by how they behave during period T − 1. Hence it is optimal for both
      firms to select a price pi*,T −1 = c in period T − 1 as well.27 We can now move to period
      T − 2 where both firms, anticipating their behavior in periods T − 1 and T (and, impor-
      tantly, knowing that such behavior is unaffected by their pricing strategies in T − 2),
      select a price pi*,T − 2 = c as well. The same argument extends to all previous periods,
      including the first round of play t = 1, ultimately implying that both firms behave as
      prescribed by the unrepeated Bertrand game of price competition during all periods of
      interaction t = 1, 2, … , T, hindering their attempts to sustain a more cooperative out-
      come in the finitely repeated game.

      Infinitely Repeated Game
      A more positive result emerges when the game is repeated for infinite periods or,
      equivalently, when firms expect their interaction to continue with a positive probabil-
      ity in the next period.28 In particular, selecting prices above the marginal cost (and
      thus allowing both firms to earn larger profits than in the unrepeated Bertrand model)
      can indeed be sustained using different pricing strategies. For simplicity, consider a
      pricing strategy that prescribes every firm j to initially set the monopoly price pm
      in period 1. Then, in each subsequent period t > 1, every firm j keeps setting pm if both
      firms charged pm in all previous rounds of play; otherwise, firm j charges a price equal
      to marginal cost.

                                           pm   if all elements in H t −1 are ( p m , p m ) or t = 1,
                      p j, t ( H t −1 ) = 
                                          c     otherwise.

         The two firms cooperate until one of them deviates, in which case both firms revert
      to the Nash equilibrium of the unrepeated game; this type of strategy is usually re-
      ferred to as “Nash reversion strategy” (NRS). In order to show that NRS can be sus-
      tained in the equilibrium of the infinitely repeated game, we need to demonstrate that
      the firms do not have incentives to deviate from it, during any period t > 1 and regard-
      less of their previous history of play. While such a requirement seems rather general

         When the future loss in profits is larger than the instantaneous gain from deviating

         Thus far we analyzed the conditions under which firms behave as prescribed by NRS
      after a history of play, in which both firms cooperated. We turn now to histories of play
      in which one (or both) firms deviated from NRS. Since the NRS prescribes that both
      firms will punish such deviation by reverting to the Nash equilibrium of the unrepeated
      game, what we need to check now is whether every firm, upon detecting a deviation,
      will carry out the punishment embodied in NRS. On one hand, by sticking to the NRS
      (which calls for a punishment), its discounted stream of payoffs is 0 + δ0 + … = 0. On
      the other hand, by deviating from NRS (setting a price pj,t = pm while its opponent sets a
      punishing price pk,t = c), its profits are zero in all periods. Firm j therefore has incentives
      to carry out the threat of setting a punishing price pj,t = c upon observing a deviation in
      any previous period. Note that the argument above applies for every firm j both when
      such a firm cheated in the past and when it was being cheated by firm k. Hence the NRS
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                       619



                  can be sustained in equilibrium, since both firms have incentives to use it at any period
                  t > 1 and regardless of the previous history of play (when only cooperation prevailed in
                  the past, but also when some deviations flared up).

                  Example 8.14: Collusion in prices Firm A and B face a demand curve of
                  Q = 5000 − 100p, and both firms have constant marginal and average costs of c = $10.
                  Competing à la Bertrand, both A and B would charge a price that coincides with their
                  common marginal cost, p = c = $10, thus selling a total quantity of Q = 4,000 units and
                  earning zero economic profits. Firm A decides to contact the manager of B and see if
                  they could collude to fix prices at the monopoly price. Can this kind of collusion be
                  sustained?
                     First, we need to determine the monopoly price. This can be done by solving the
                  firms’ joint PMP, but given symmetry, such program is equivalent to the PMP of a
                  monopolist, which we can express as

                                    max ( p − 10 ) ⋅ Q = p (5000 − 100 p ) − 10(5000 − 100 p)
                                        p


                  with the first-order condition
                                                   5000 − 200 p + 1000 = 0.

                  Solving for p, the monopoly price is pm = 30 with corresponding aggregate quantity of
                  Q = 2000 (i.e., 1000 units per firm) and corresponding profits of πm = $40,000 ($20,000
                  per firm).
                     Collusion will only be sustainable if the value of discounted future profits exceeds
                  that of the instantaneous gain by deviating. As discussed above, the optimal deviation
                  in a Bertrand model is for one of the firms to slightly undercut the monopoly price pm
                  of its rival, that is, to charge a price of pd = pm − ε, capturing the entire profit stream of
                  $40,000 for that period. Such a deviation entails no profits after the deviation period
                  because, according to NRS, the betrayed party will revert back to the Nash equilibrium
                  of the unrepeated game thereafter (i.e., pricing at marginal cost forever). Hence collu-
                  sion can be sustained if

                                                    πm  1           δ
                                                            ≥ πm +      ⋅ 0.
                                                     2 1− δ        1− δ
                  Since πm = $40,000, this inequality entails

                                                          1                1
                                                 20000        ≥ 40000 ⇔ δ ≥ .
                                                         1− δ              2
620                                                                                     Chapter 8



        As an extension, what would happen if there were n firms? In this case each firm’s
      share of the monopoly profit stream under collusion would be πm / n = 40,000 / n, and
      collusion would only be able to be sustained as long as
                                  40000 1                   1
                                           ≥ 40000 ⇔ δ ≥ 1 − ≡ δ .
                                    n 1− δ                  n

      Thus, as the number of the firms in the industry increases, it is more difficult to sustain
      collusion since the one-period payoff from deviating, 40,000, becomes much larger
      relative to the per-period payoff from colluding, 40000 / n. Figure 8.38 depicts the
      minimal discount factor sustaining collusion, δ = 1 − (1 n), as a function of the number
      of firms. For instance, when n = 100, the discount factor needs to exceed 1 − (1 / 100) =
      0.99 for cooperation to be sustained. ■

      8.8.2   Extensions
      The models presented in this section can be easily extended in several dimensions.
      (Each of the following extensions are explored by one of the exercises at the end of
      this chapter.) First, we have only considered permanent reversions to the equilibrium
      of the unrepeated game. Cooperation could still be sustained if firms temporarily re-
      vert to such an equilibrium (e.g., during four periods) and then return to the coopera-
      tive outcome. In this setting, however, cooperation is more difficult to support (i.e., it
      only arises for higher discount factors) because firms are not as severely threatened
      by future punishments as they are under permanent reversions. Second, we assumed
      that as a punishment firms use equilibrium play in the unrepeated version of the game.
      However, they could use a punishment that yields even lower payoffs, and perhaps
      apply it temporarily as a short but “nasty” punishment. In this context, one can sustain
      cooperation under lower discount factors, thus making cooperation easier to arise than
      in the NRS we considered in this chapter. Third, we considered a “pure” form of co-
      operation, in which both firms set the monopoly price pm (the same price they would
      set should they form a cartel). Other less “pure” forms of cooperation are nonetheless
      sustainable, where firms set intermediate prices in the range p ∈ (c, pm). Finally, we
      allowed for perfect monitoring, since firms could immediately detect deviations from
      the NRS. In real life, however, monitoring might be imperfect, as firms only detect
      their rivals’ deviations after a few periods. In such a model, firms earn deviation profits
      during more than one period, making deviation more attractive, hinders the chances of
      cooperation in equilibrium (i.e., to only arise under extremely high discount factors).

      Further reading For an excellent review of the literature on cartel formation, their
      sustainability over time, and cartel monitoring by regulatory authorities (e.g., the US
      Federal Trade Comission or the EU Competition Directorate), see Harrington (2006).
      For more recent advances on cartel analysis and its regulation, see the edited book by
      Harrington and Katsoulacos (2012).
Game Theory and Imperfect Competition                                                                         625
