      Appendix: More General Policy Mechanisms

      Sections 9.7–9.9 showed that, in the presence of incomplete information about the
      firms’ marginal profit function and the consumers’ marginal damage function, standard
      policy tools (quotas and emission fees) entail welfare losses. Let us now examine more
      general policy mechanisms that attempt to maximize social surplus in the context of
      incomplete information. In particular, we consider mechanisms in which we ask agents
      to self-report their types. That is, we ask the firm: What is your benefit from increasing
Externalities and Public Goods                                                                                        719



                    the externality level from x = 0 to x = x , b = b(θ), given your private observation of θ?
                    And we ask the consumer: What is your damage from the externality c = c(η) given
                    your private observation of η? At first glance, this type of mechanisms may seem to
                    induce firms to underreport their benefits, stating a benefit b̂ below their true benefit b,
                    b̂ < b , in order to reduce the compensation that they have to provide to the consumers
                    affected by the externality. Similarly one might anticipate these mechanisms to pro-
                    vide incentives to consumers to overestimate their damages, stating a cost ĉ > c, in
                    order to guarantee that the externality is not allowed by the regulator or, if allowed, that
                    they are substantially compensated for the cost they suffer (beyond the true damage
                    they experience from the externality).
                       The mechanisms we are interested in, instead, focus on providing incentives to all
                    parties to guarantee that a truth-telling equilibrium emerges, that is, on achieving that
                    the firm report chat coincides with its true benefit from increasing the externality from
                    x = 0 to x = x , whereby b̂=b; and the consumer reports the costs he experiences from
                    the externality, ĉ=c. One such mechanism is the so-called Groves–Clark–Vickrey
                    mechanism (GCV),47 in which the regulator declares that it will set the level of the
                    externality at x = x if the reports received from the firm and the consumers satisfy b̂ >
                    ĉ. (Otherwise, the regulator keeps the level of the externality at x = 0.) If this is the
                    case, the government pays b̂ to the consumer and charges ĉ to the firm. Let us next
                    demonstrate that this simple mechanism induces truth-telling from both parties, by
                    separately analyzing the incentives of every agent.48

                    Consumer
                    Consumer. Consider a consumer with real cost c = c(η). Let us first examine her opti-
                    mal announcement, ĉ, given a firm’s announcement of a benefit b̂ > c; as depicted in
                    figure A9.1.
                       Note first that this consumer does not have incentives to overreport her cost, ĉ > c
                    (as indicated by the arrow at the right-hand side of figure A9.1 illustrating a deviation

                    47
                       See the seminal articles of Groves (1973) and Clarke (1971). Moulin (1988) and Green and Laffont
                    (1979) provide a detailed presentation of this mechanism.
                    48
                       Though the GCV mechanism induces truth-telling as a weakly dominant strategy, it does not nec-
                    essarily entail a balanced budget for the authority implementing the public project. In particular, if
                    the profile of marginal benefits and costs satisfies b > c, then the GCV mechanism predicts that the
                    regulator implements the public project, requiring the firm to compensate with c dollars the con-
                    sumer, but paying b dollars to the consumer and ultimately leading to a b − c budget deficit since b >
                    c. Some extensions of the GCV mechanism avoid this problem, but only under certain conditions.
                    For more details about this type of mechanisms, see chapter 23 in Mas-Colell et al. (1995).

      from reporting c = c(η) to ĉ > c); or underreport it, ĉ < c (left-hand arrow), since in both
      cases the compensation she receives is b̂. Intuitively, the compensation that the con-
      sumer receives is unaffected by her report, inducing the consumer to truthfully reveal
      her cost c = c(η). If, instead, the consumer overreports her costs, reporting a level of ĉ

      from the firm.
         A similar argument is applicable to the case where b̂ < c, as depicted in figure A9.2.
      In particular, overreporting the cost (right-hand side arrow) implies that the govern-

      ĉ (see figure A9.2), the externality is still not allowed by the regulator, given that re-
      ports satisfy ĉ > b̂. Finally, an extreme underreport of her costs to values below b̂ is not

        The government official would indeed consider that the damage that the externality imposes on the

                    sensible either: while the externality is now allowed (given that reports satisfy b̂ > ĉ),
                    the consumer receives a subsidy b̂ below her true cost c, and thus a negative utility
                    level.
                       In summary, the consumer has incentives to truthfully reveal the damage she suffers
                    from the externality, ĉ = c(η), regardless of the precise report b̂ that the firm makes,
                    such that truthfully reporting her cost is a weakly dominant strategy for the consumer
                    because it yields a weakly larger payoff than reporting a different cost, ĉ ≠ c, regardless
                    of the firm’s report b̂.

                    Firm
                    Let us now analyze the firm with a benefit from the externality given by b = b(θ). Fol-
                    lowing a similar approach to that for the consumer, let us first consider the case in
                    which the consumer’s report, ĉ, lies below the firm’s true benefit from the externality,
                    b, as figure A9.3 illustrates.
                       The firm has no incentives to overreport its true benefit b, thus making a report b̂
                    such that b̂ > b, as indicated by the right-hand arrow of figure A9.3. In particular, the
                    firm would have to pay the same compensation to the consumer, ĉ, and the externality
                    would still be allowed since reports satisfy b̂ > ĉ. Likewise the firm has no incentives
                    to underreport its true benefit by declaring a value of b̂ in the interval between ĉ and b
                    (see figure A9.3). Indeed the compensation that the firm has to pay is still ĉ and the
                    externality is allowed, since reports still satisfy b̂ > ĉ. Finally, the firm has no incen-
                    tives to extremely underreport its true benefit to values below ĉ, since in this case the
                    externality would not be allowed by the government given that reports satisfy b̂ < ĉ.
                    Let us now consider the case in which, in contrast, the consumer’s report ĉ lies above
                    the firm’s true benefit b, as depicted in figure A9.4.
                       First, note that the firm would not like the externality to be allowed, since the true
                    benefit that the firm obtains from the externality lies below the cost ĉ that the
                    consumer declared to experience (which, in this mechanism, also represents the




                    Figure A9.3
                    GCV mechanism—Firm’s reports when ĉ < b
722                                                                                         Chapter 9




      Figure A9.4
      GCV mechanism—Firm’s reports when ĉ > b


      compensation that the firm must pay consumers). If, rather than truthfully revealing its
      benefit b from the externality, the firm overreports values above ĉ, the externality
      would be allowed, since reports would satisfy b̂ > ĉ. In this case, the government
      would require the firm to pay a compensation ĉ to the consumer, which is higher than
      the real benefit the firm obtains from the externality, ĉ > b = b(θ). Similarly, overre-
      porting values of b̂ between b and ĉ is insensible as well, given that the externality
      would be allowed (since reports satisfy b̂ > ĉ), and the firm would still have to pay a
      compensation to the consumer, ĉ, above its true benefit, ĉ > b = b(θ). Finally, under-
      reporting (any report b̂ such that b̂ < b) is not strictly profitable for the firm either, since
      in this case the externality will not be allowed (given that reports would now satisfy
      bˆ < cˆ ), yielding the same payoff for the firm that it obtains from truthfully revealing
      its benefit, b̂ = b = b(θ). As a consequence the firm has no incentives to deviate from a
      truthful revelation of the benefits it obtains from the externality, b̂ = b(θ) regardless of
      the precise report from the consumer, ĉ. Hence truthfully reporting its benefit from the
      externality is a weakly dominant strategy for the firm.

10 Contract Theory



      In this chapter we explore contexts in which agents interact under asymmetric informa-
      tion. We focus on two main contexts: (1) settings in which an agent does not observe
      the actions of the other individual(s), and (2) settings in which an agent does not observe
      the payoff of the other individual(s). The first type of information problem is referred
      to as “hidden action,” since the uninformed individual (e.g., a manager in a firm) cannot
      observe the action that another individual exerts (e.g., the effort of employees in the
      firm) even if the manager is perfectly informed about the type of worker he deals with
      (e.g., the worker’s ability or productivity). In this context the worker might have incen-
      tives to slack from exerting a costly effort, thus giving rise to moral hazard problems.
      (That is why these settings are also known as “hidden action” or “moral hazard” prob-
      lems). In this context the manager can offer contracts that provide incentives to the
      worker to work hard, such as paying a higher salary (bonus) if the worker’s output is
      high but a low salary otherwise. Providing incentives to work hard is thus costly for the
      manager, giving rise to a trade-off: higher salaries induce high effort (increasing the
      firm’s output) but are more expensive to implement than a low effort level. As a con-
      sequence the manager only induces a high effort if the firm’s expected profits are high-
      er than those of inducing a low effort. Another context in which moral hazard problems
      abound is insurance markets, since an insurance company does not observe how care-
      ful the insured party is (e.g., the driver’s carefulness is a hidden action for the company)
      but seeks to give incentives to its clients so that they are as careful as possible.1
         The second type of information problem is referred to as “hidden information,”
      since in this case one party does not observe another party’s payoff function. Continu-
      ing with the example above, the manager might not observe the worker’s ability.

      1
        In recent years insurance companies, such as Progressive in the United States, have started to partly
      observe their clients’ driving patterns with electronic devices such as Snapshot by Progressive. This
      information is, however, relatively limited as it only records how many miles the client drives each
      day, when he slams the brakes in sudden stops, and how often he drives between midnight and 4 am,
      but does not record the client’s driving speed or sudden accelerations.
736                                                                                  Chapter 10



      This information setting is also labeled as “adverse selection,” since the manager could
      err in its selection of candidates for a job if he does not observe their ability. Other
      examples include contracting problems between a bank lending money to a client (e.g.,
      entrepreneur) without observing the client’s probability of success in his project. In
      this context we study menus of contracts that induce each type of worker to select only
      one contract, so that by their choice they reveal their unobserved type (hidden charac-
      teristic) to the manager. For instance, the firm could offer two contracts, one with a
      high salary but involving a high effort level and another with low salary and low effort,
      achieving self-selection by each type of worker, whereby the worker with high (low)
      productivity would select the first (second) type of contract.
         In section 10.1, we discuss moral hazard problems, and how their results are af-
      fected by the principal’s and agent’s risk attitudes. We analyze discrete and continuous
      choices, and allow for one or multiple signals of effort. In section 10.2, we examine the
      “lemons” problem, and show the market inefficiencies that can arise when buyers and
      sellers have access to different amounts of information. Last, in section 10.3, we ex-
      plore the adverse selection problem when a principal contracts an agent whose produc-
      tivity the former cannot observe.

      10.1     Moral Hazard

      In this section we consider optimal contracts that a principal (e.g., firm) offers to an
      agent (e.g., worker) in order to induce him to exert a profit-maximizing effort level. We
      first discuss the basic setup of the model, then we analyze the optimal contract when
      the principal perfectly observes the effort that the agent exerts, and finally examine
      how such a contract varies when the principal cannot observe the agent’s effort.

      10.1.1    The Model
      Consider a principal with benefit function B(π − w), where π represents the profit that
      arises from the agent’s effort (e.g., output or sales), and w denotes the salary that the
      principal pays to the agent. The benefit function is assumed to be increasing and con-
      cave, whereby B′ ≥ 0 and B″ ≤ 0. The agent’s utility function is, for simplicity, assumed
      to be quasi-linear,

                                      U ( w , e ) = u ( w ) − g (e),
      where u(w) represents the utility that the agent derives from the salary he receives,
      which is increasing and concave, u′ > 0 and u″ ≤ 0; while g(e) denotes his disutility
      from effort, which is increasing and convex, g′ > 0 and g″ ≥ 0.
Contract Theory                                                                                                          737



                    Importantly, the effort level that the agent exerts affects the probability that a certain
                  profit occurs. In particular, for a given effort e (e.g., 10 hours of work) the conditional
                  probability that a profit of exactly π = πi happens (e.g., $1 million), is

                                     f( π i|e) = Prob{π = π i|e} ≥ 0          for every profit level π i

                  where i = {1, 2, … , N} denotes the profits that can emerge for a given effort e. Hence
                  the property above entails that a high profit could arise even if the worker slacks (ex-
                  erts low effort). In other words, a given profit level π = πi can arise from every effort
                  level. We next explore the principal’s optimal contract if it could perfectly observe the
                  agent’s effort, e.

      offers a contract to the risk-averse agent that guarantees the latter a fixed salary of
      w*regardless of the specific profit realization that emerges.2 Additionally, since the

      we do not need to take the expectation of profit levels πi as they do not affect the
      agent’s salary (which is fixed in this case). Rearranging the PC expression above yields
      u (we* ) = u + g (e ), and applying the inverse u−1 on both sides, we obtain a salary of

                                                we* = u −1 (u + g (e )) .

      as depicted in the figure 10.2. For instance, in order to induce eH, we need to evaluate
      the utility function at a height of u + g (eH ) , and the inverse u −1 (u + g (eH ) ) is graphi-
      cally represented by the point in the horizontal axis that yields a height of u + g (eH ) on
      the vertical axis, which we find by mapping u + g (eH ) from the vertical to the horizon-
      tal axis. That is, inducing a higher effort implies offering a higher salary.

      10.1.4    Asymmetric Information
      When the principal cannot observe the agent’s effort level, he needs to offer to the
      agent enough incentives to exert the profit-maximizing effort level, rather than slaking
      (which can be really tempting when his effort is not being observed!). How can the
      principal achieve this objective? He could do this by making the salary an increasing
      function of the realized profit. As we examine below, this is optimal even if the agent
      is risk averse. In particular, the principal’s problem now becomes

748                                                                                      Chapter 10



      the agent the lowest salary that induces the latter to exert a high effort. Next note that
      f(π|eL) < f(π|eH), which entails the probability of obtaining a given profit level π is high-
      er when the agent exerts a high effort eH than when he exerts a low effort eL. As a
      consequence f(π|eL) / f(π|eH) < 1 and ultimately 1 − [f(π|eL) / f(π|eH)] must be a number in

      Figure 10.4 depicts the FOC of this principal–agent problem under symmetric infor-
      mation, from expression (10.2), and under asymmetric information, from expression
      (10.7). Since u″ < 0 (and thus 1 / u′ is increasing inw), function 1 / u′ is evaluated at a
      higher height under asymmetric than symmetric information (see vertical axis of figure
      10.4), implying that the salary the principal needs to offer when effort is not observ-
      able, weH , is more generous than that when effort is observable, w(π).
         When deciding which effort to implement, the principal compares the effects of in-
      ducing a high effort level eH. On one hand, effort eH yields a positive effect on profits,
      since it increases the likelihood of higher profits, given that expected profits increase
      in effort. Importantly, this positive effect emerges under both symmetric and asym-
      metric information. On the other hand, inducing effort eH also entails a negative effect,
      since the salary that induces such effort is higher under asymmetric than under




      Figure 10.4
      Principal–agent problem
Contract Theory                                                                                           749




                  symmetric information, that is, weH > w(π). In summary, since the positive effect of
                  effort eH arises under both information contexts, but its associated cost is larger when
                  effort is unobservable, the principal is less willing to induce eH when the agent’s effort
                  is unobservable than when it is observable.

                  10.1.5     Comparative Statics
                  How does the salary above change as a function of the profit realization? For that to
                  happen, we need the left-hand side of the FOC in (10.7) to increase in π, which can
                  only occur if the likelihood ratio f(π|eL) / f(π|eH) decreases inπ. In words, as profits in-
                  crease, the likelihood of obtaining a profit level of π from effort eH increases faster than
                  the probability of obtaining such a profit level from eL. (This probability is commonly
                  known as the monotone likelihood ratio property, MLRP; described in chapter 4.)
                  Graphically, since λ + μ[1 − (f(π|eL) / f(π|eH))] is evaluated at higher profit levels, the
                  MLRP guarantees that f(π|eL) / f(π|eH) declines, which produces an upward shift in the
                  flat line of the figure 10.5, ultimately increasing the agent’s wage from w(π1) to w(π2).
                  In summary, if the likelihood ratio is monotone (i.e., it satisfies the MLRP), the princi-
                  pal will offer a wage compensation w(πi) that increases in the profit realization, πi,
                  since such higher observed profit makes it more likely that the agent exerted effort eH
                  than eL.

                  Comparative statics and MLRP

      agent’s IC condition becomes more difficult to sustain when e increases, unless the
      principal offers a more generous salary.

                  10.3   Moral Hazard with Multiple Signals

                  Consider a setting in which the principal, still not observing effort e, observes not only
                  the profits π of the firm but also a signal s, based on a middle management report about
                  the agent’s performance. Such a signal provides no intrinsic economic value (i.e., s
                  does not affect profits), but it does provide information about effort e. In earlier prob-
                  lems, the probability density function had only one argument, π. In this problem, the
                  probability density function has two observables, π and s. Setting up the problem the
                  same way as in the asymmetric information section, yielding equation (10.7), we ob-
                  tain the condition

                                                      1            f (π , s eL ) 
                                                            =γ + µ               .
                                                   u ′( w )        f (π , s eH ) 

                     Hence variations in s affect wages only if f(π, s|e) ≠ f(π|e), that is, if π is not a suffi-
                  cient statistic of e. Intuitively, the pair (π, s) contains more information about the man-
                  ager’s exerted effort e than π alone. If f(π, s|e) = f(π|e), then the observation of signal s
                  becomes uninformative (provides no more information than π alone), and the problem
                  of asymmetric information, and its results in equation (10.7) would coincide with those
                  in the current case.
                     As in the comparative statics section above, where we analyzed whether salary w
                  was increasing in the observed profits π, we can now apply a similar approach to ex-
                  amine under which conditions w increases in signal s. Specifically, for two signals s1
                  and s2 where s2 > s1, if salary increases in the signal, w(π, s2) > w(π, |s1), we would have
                  that u′(w) decreases (by concavity), which in turn increases 1 / u′(w), on the left-hand
                  side of the FOC above. Hence the right-hand side must also increase in s, that is,

                                                  f (π , s2 eL )               f (π , s1 eL ) 
                                      γ + µ 1 −                     > γ + µ 1 −                   .
                                                  f (π , s2 eH )              f (π , s1 eH ) 
                    As depicted in figure 10.7, this inequality ultimately requires that
760                                                                                    Chapter 10




      Figure 10.7
      Moral hazard with multiple signals


                                           f (π , s2 eL ) f (π , s1 eL )
                                                         <               ,
                                           f (π , s2 eH ) f (π , s1 eH )

      or, after cross-multiplying,

                                           f (π , s1 eH ) f (π , s2 eH )
                                                         <               .
                                           f (π , s1 eL ) f (π , s2 eL )

         In words, for the salary to increase in the intermediate signal s that the principal re-
      ceives, we need such a signal to have a decreasing likelihood ratio. That is, a high ef-
      fort is relatively more likely to originate from a high than from a low signal (i.e., more
      likely to come from s2 than from s1).

      Extensions The moral hazard model we analyzed in this section can be extended in
      many dimensions: (1) allowing for the firm manager to have a team of employees (not
      observing the effort exerted by any of them), as analyzed by Holstrom (1982),
      Mookherjee (1984), and Itoh (1991), and examined in exercise 9; (2) permitting the
      agent to exert effort on different, rather than a single, tasks (e.g., producing goods and
      commercializing them), as described by Holstrom and Milgrom (1991); and (3) allow-
      ing dynamic contracts lasting for several periods, as in Bolton and Dewatripont (2005,
      ch. 10) and references therein. Finally, for empirical work testing the presence of mor-
      al hazard in different markets, see Salanié (1997, ch. 8).
Contract Theory                                                                                          761



                  10.4     Adverse Selection—The “Lemons” Problem

                  As described in previous chapters, under symmetric information markets often work
                  well, and allow buyers interested in a particular good to find sellers offering that good,
                  ultimately purchasing it at a mutually agreeable price. Under asymmetric information,
                  however, markets do not necessarily work well (as we next show, they might even fail
                  to exist!) even when both buyers and sellers would benefit from their existence.
                     Following the original model of Akerloff (1970), consider a market of used cars,
                  whose quality is denoted by q, where q ~ U[0, Q] and Q ∈ (1, 2). A car of quality q is
                  valued as such by the buyer, and as q / Q by the seller. Since q / Q < q, the buyer assigns
                  a higher value to the car than the seller, thus allowing both parties to exchange the car
                  at a price p between q / Q and q and make a profit (for the seller) and a surplus (for
                  the buyer). In particular, if car of quality q is exchanged at price p the buyer obtains
                  a utility

                                                         u(p, q) = q − p ,

                  while the seller makes a profit of
                                                                          q
                                                       π(p, q, Q) = p −     .
                                                                          Q

                     Assume that there are a sufficient number of buyers prompting all gains from trade
                  to be appropriated by the seller.

                  10.4.1    Symmetric Information
                  When the buyer can perfectly observe the car quality q, he buys at a price p if and only
                  if his utility from such a trade is positive, q − p ≥ 0, or p ≤ q. Anticipating such a re-
                  sponse from the buyer, a seller with a car of quality q sets a price that solves
                                                                     q
                                                           max p −
                                                            p≥ 0     Q

                                                        subject to p ≤ q,                              (PC)

                  where p ≤ q can be interpreted as the buyer’s participation constraint (PC), meaning
                  that for prices p > q he would reject the price, and the trade would not take place. Con-
                  dition (PC) must bind; otherwise, the seller could increase the price p and extract a
                  larger profit from the buyer. We thus have p = q, which can be plugged into the seller’s
                  objective function (second term) to yield the following unconstrained problem:
762                                                                                                  Chapter 10




                                                               p
                                                   max p −       .
                                                     p≥ 0      Q

         Taking the FOC with respect to p yields 1 − (1 / Q), or (Q − 1) / Q > 0. Since Q > 1 by
      definition, a corner solution exists whereby the seller raises the price p as much as pos-
      sible (as long as it is accepted by the buyer). Hence the price under symmetric informa-
      tion is pSI = q for every quality q.

      10.4.2     Asymmetric Information
      When the buyer is unable to observe the car’s true quality q, he forms an expectation
      E[q]. Hence the buyer accepts a trade if the car’s asking price p satisfies p ≤ E[q]. In
      this context the seller anticipates such an acceptance rule by the buyer and sets a price
      p that solves

                                                                p
                                                    max p −
                                                     p≥ 0       Q

                                              subject to p ≤ E [ q ].                                      (PC)

       By the same argument as under symmetric information, PC binds entailing p = E[q],
      which becomes the price that the seller sets as long as his profits are positive, that is,
                                        q          q
                                   p−     = E [q] − ≥ 0 ⇔ q ≤ Q ⋅ E [q] ,
                                        Q          Q

      as depicted in figure 10.8, where cars with quality to the left of Q · E[q] are offered by
      the seller, while those exceeding this quality level are not profitably offered (and its
      market ceases to exist).
        For instance, when quality q is uniformly distributed, that is, q ~ U[0, Q], its ex-
      pected value becomes

                                                            Q−0 Q
                                               E[q] =          = ,
                                                             2  2

      and Q · E[q] is then Q2/2.7 Hence all cars with relatively low quality q ≤ Q2 / 2 are of-
      fered by the seller at a price p = E[q] = Q / 2, yielding a profit of Q / 2 − q / 2 for the seller,

      7
        For instance, if Q = 3 / 2 since Q ∈ (1, 2), then the buyer’s expected value is (3 / 2)2 / 2 = 3 / 4, and
      cutoff Q · E[q] of cars offered by the seller becomes (3 / 2) · 3 / 4 = 9 / 8, leaving cars in the interval
      (9 / 8, 3 / 2) not offered by the seller.
Contract Theory                                                                                             763




                  Figure 10.8
                  Lemons problem


                  and a zero (expected) utility for the buyer since p = E[q]. However, cars with relatively
                  high quality, q > Q2 / 2, are not offered by the seller since the highest price he can charge
                  to the uninformed buyer, p = E[q], does not compensate the seller’s costs. This is prob-
                  lematic because, as stated above in the symmetric information model, seller and buyer
                  could make a positive margin from exchanging cars of all quality levels if they could
                  both observe their quality. In other words, the buyer’s inability to observe q leads to
                  the non-existence of the market for good cars (“peaches”), whereas only bad cars
                  (“lemons”) exist in the market.

                  10.4.3   Further Iterations
                  The previous result assumes that the buyer forms his expectation of the average car
                  quality, E[q], and the seller, anticipating such a lack of information, sets a price p = E[q].
                  However, one could argue that a fully rational buyer would anticipate such a pricing
                  decision by the seller and, hence, that the seller finds it worthy to only offer low-
                  quality cars, namely those with p ≤ Q2 / 2. In that case, the buyer anticipates that only
                  cars of quality q ∈ [0, Q2 / 2] are offered, and if quality is uniformly distributed
                  q ~ U[0, Q], buyers can compute the expected quality of those offered cars as

                                                       Q 2  (Q 2 2 ) − 0 Q 2
                                               E q q ≤      =            =    .
                                                       2        2        4

                  Therefore the buyer would only buy cars whose price satisfies p ≤ Q2 / 4. The seller
                  would then set the price at p = Q2/4, yielding a profit of p – q/Q = Q2/4 – q/Q which is
                  positive only if quality q satisfies q ≤ Q3/4.

         Figure 10.9 illustrates that the seller now further restricts the set of cars that he of-
      fers, moving toward cars of worse average quality (note that Q3 / 4 < Q2 / 4 < Q2 / 2 given
      that Q ∈ (1, 2) by assumption).
         The argument above can, of course, be extended since now a rational buyer would
      update its expected car quality (among those offered by the seller) to those satisfying
      q ≤ Q3 / 4, yielding an expected quality of only

                                           Q 3  (Q 3 4 ) − 0 Q 3

      leading the seller to offer cars that yield a positive profit, that is, those with quality q
      satisfying Q3 / 8 − q / Q ≥ 0, or q ≤ Q4 / 8, which lies closer to zero than cutoff Q3 / 4 in
      figure 10.9. In summary, the seller would shift the set of offered cars even more to the
      left of the quality line toward worse cars (closer to zero). Repeating the same argument
      enough times, we find that the market “unravels,” as it only offers cars of the worse
      possible quality, q = 0, and the buyer is only willing to pay a price of p = 0, leaving all
      other types of cars unsold.

      Example 10.5: Lemons problem Consider a market of used cars with maximum
      available quality Q = 1.9, and that q is uniformly distributed in [0, Q]. Recall that
      Q ∈ (1, 2), so our example illustrates the availability of several cars of relatively good
      quality. In this context, the buyer’s expected value is 1.9 / 2 = 0.95, and the cutoff
      Q · E[q] of cars offered by the seller becomes 1.9 · 0.95 = 1.805, leaving cars in the in-
      terval (1.805, 1.9) unoffered. Under a context of complete information, these cars
      would have been bought by the buyer who values them at q, and sold by the seller
      who values them at only q / 1.9 = 0.52q, but the presence of asymmetric information
      between buyer and seller prevents mutually beneficial trades from occurring.
Contract Theory                                                                                                       765



                  Additionally a rational buyer will anticipate that only cars in the interval (0, 1.805) are
                  offered by the seller, and thus update his expected value of offered cars to E[q|q ≤ 1.80
                  5] = (1.805 − 0) / 2 = 0.9, which leads the seller to only offer those cars with quality
                  q ≤ Q3 / 4 = 1.71. The set of offered cars is thus restricted from (0, 1.805) to (0, 1.71). A
                  similar argument applies to further iterations in the buyer’s expected car quality. ■

                  Application to Labor Markets
                  We can extend a similar argument to other markets where buyers have access to less
                  information than sellers. For instance, consider a competitive labor market with many
                  firms seeking to hire a worker for a specific position. The worker (seller of labor ser-
                  vices) privately observes his own productivity θ, but firms (the buyer of labor in this
                  context) cannot observe it. In this setting, firms would offer a wage according to the
                  worker’s expected productivity, which is E [θ ] = 12 in the case that θ ~ U[0, 1]. For this
                  salary, only workers with a productivity lower than 1 2 would be interested in accepting
                  the position, while those with θ > 1 2 will be left unemployed. The argument continues
                  since a fully rational manager will only offer a salary of w = E [θ θ ≤ 1 2 ] = 14 , which is
                  the expected productivity of the subset of workers accepting the job, entailing that only
                  those workers with productivity θ ≤ 1 4 accept the job. Extending the argument infinite
                  times, we find that workers with lowest productivity level θ = 0 are employed, while
                  the labor market for all other worker types θ > 0 unravels (i.e., it ceases to exist due to
                  the firm’s asymmetric information).

                  Solutions to the Adverse Selection Problem
                  The market failure described above can be overcome by a number of tools. First, sell-
                  ers can offer warranties for their cars in order to signal their quality. In that setting we
                  seek to find under which conditions a separating equilibrium exists, whereby lemons
                  are sold without warranty while peaches are sold with warranty, and all cars are ex-
                  changed at their symmetric information price.8 We explore this type of separating equi-
                  librium in the exercises at the end of the chapter. Specifically, we show that, if offering
                  a warranty is more costly for the seller of lemons than for the one selling peaches, a
                  separating equilibrium emerges where warranties serve as signals that sellers use to
                  convey their private information to uninformed buyers, who can now easily infer the
                  car’s quality. A second solution to the lemons problem is screening, whereby the

                  8
                    Rather than offering warranties, the seller could sell the car as a certified pre-owned (CPO) vehicle,
                  which go through a more thorough inspection and repair service at the dealership than used cars do.
                  Customers seem to interpret these cars have a better expected quality than similar used cars, since
                  casual observation indicates CPOs are often sold at higher prices.
766                                                                                    Chapter 10



      principal (in this case the buyer) offers a menu of contracts to the agent (the seller), to
      induce each type of agent to voluntarily choose the contract meant for his type, where-
      by the contracts induce self-selection. Screening is often easier to interpret in the stan-
      dard principal–agent relationship between a firm manager and a worker. In the next
      section we present the principal–agent model, and then examine how to design screen-
      ing contracts in that setting.

      10.5   Adverse Selection—The Principal–Agent Problem

      Consider a setting where a firm (the principal) seeks to hire a worker (an agent) but
      cannot observe the worker’s cost of effort, which ultimately affects the amount of ef-
      fort that the worker exerts and thus the firm’s profits. Hence the firm’s manager would
      like to know the worker’s cost of effort in order to design his salary. In particular, the
      firm’s profit function is

                                          π ( e, w ) = x ( e ) − w ,

      where function x(e) represents the benefit that the manager obtains when the worker
      supplies e units of effort, which is increasing and concave in effort, x′(e) ≥ 0 and
      x″(e) ≤ 0. Now the worker’s utility function is

                                      v ( w, e θ ) = u( w ) − c ( e, θ ),
      where u(w) denotes the value he assigns to salary w, u′(w) > 0, u″(w) ≤ 0; and c(e, θ)
      represents the worker’s cost of exerting e units (e.g., hours) of effort when his type is
      θ. For simplicity, we assume that the worker can only be of two types, θL and θH, where
      θL< θH. Intuitively, a high-type worker faces a higher total and marginal cost of effort,
      expressed as c(e, θL) < c(e, θH) and c′(e, θL) < c′(e, θH), respectively, for every e > 0.
         For comparison purposes, we first analyze a symmetric information setting in which
      the principal can observe the agent’s type, and evaluate the optimal contract of salary
      and exerted effort (wi, ei), where i = (H, L) denotes the worker’s type. In the following
      subsection we examine a more realistic setting where the principal cannot observe the
      agent’s type but knows that the relative frequency of low-type workers in the popula-
      tion is p ∈ (0, 1) while that of the high-type workers is 1 − p. In such circumstances the
      principal will need to design a contract different from that under symmetric informa-
      tion. Otherwise, workers with a low cost of effort could lie about their true type in or-
      der to benefit from the contract meant for the worker with a high cost of effort. We
      show that the principal designs a menu of contracts, (wL, eL) for the low type and
      (wH, eH) for the high type, which induces each type of worker to choose the contract
      meant for him (self-selection of contracts).

                  10.5.2     Asymmetric Information
                  When the firm cannot observe the worker’s type, it seeks to maximize the expected
                  profits by designing a pair of contracts, (wH, eH) and (wL, eL), that satisfy four con-
                  straints: (1) voluntary participation of the high-type worker; (2) voluntary participation
                  of the low-type worker; (3) that the high-type worker prefers the contract meant for
                  him, (wH, eH) rather than that for the low-type, (wL, eL); and (4) that the low-type work-
                  er prefers contract (wL, eL) rather than that for the high-type worker (wH, eH). Since
                  every type of worker has an incentive to select the contract meant for him, we say that
                  these contracts induce “self-selection.” Hence the firm solves the following profit-
                  maximization problem

                                          max             p [ x (eL ) − w L ] + (1 − p )[ x (eH ) − w H ]
                                      w L ,eL , w H ,eH


                                                  subject to u ( wH ) − c ( eH , θ H ) ≥ 0                  ( PC H ),
                                                            u ( w L ) − c ( eL , θ L ) ≥ 0                  ( PC L ) ,
                                             u ( w H ) − c ( e H , θ H ) ≥ u ( w L ) − c( e L , θ H )       ( IC H ),
                                              u ( w L ) − c ( e L , θ L ) ≥ u ( w H ) − c( e H , θ L )       ( IC L ) ,
                  where the first constraint, PCH, represents the participation constraint for the high-type
                  worker; the second constraint, PCL, denotes that for the low-type worker; the third
                  constraint, ICH, is the incentive compatibility condition for the high-type worker so he
                  does not have incentives to choose the contract meant for the low-type worker; and the
                  fourth constraint, ICL, is the incentive compatibility condition for the low-type worker
                  so that he prefers the contract meant for him rather than that of the high-type worker.
                  As described above, the PC constraints guarantee voluntary participation of all types
                  of workers, while the IC constraints ensure self-selection.

      Monotonicity in Effort
      Another property to consider is that effort levels satisfy eL ≥ eH, that is, the worker with
      the lowest cost of effort exerts a larger effort level than the worker with a high cost of
      effort. In order to show this property, let us combine ICL and ICH to obtain

         u ( w L ) − c ( e L , θ L ) ≥ u ( w H ) − c ( e H , θ L ) > u ( w H ) − c ( e H , θ H ) ≥ u ( w L ) − c( e L , θ H ) ,
      where the first inequality originates from ICL, the second inequality is due to the cost
      of effort satisfying c(eH, θH) < c(eH, θH), and the third inequality is due to ICH. Hence the
      triple inequality above can be rearranged as

                     c ( eH , θ L ) − c ( eL , θ L ) ≥ u ( wH ) − u ( wL ) > c ( eH , θ H ) − c(eL , θ H ).
      Multiplying this expression by −1, and using the first and last terms, yields

                                   c ( eL , θ L ) − c ( eH , θ L ) < c ( eL , θ H ) − c ( eH , θ H ) .
        This condition indicates that the marginal cost of increasing effort from eH to eL is
      higher for the high-type than for the low-type worker. Therefore the worker with the
      low (absolute and marginal) cost of effort exerts a larger effort level than the high-type
Contract Theory                                                                                                         775



                  worker.9 We can evaluate this condition in the cost of effort function c(e, θ) = θc(e),
                  which yields

                                                       θ L [ c ( eL ) − c ( eH )] < θ H [ c ( eL ) − c ( eH )].

                     Since θL < θH by definition, we must have that c(eL) > c(eH); otherwise, the sign of
                  the above inequality would be switched. Therefore, since the cost of effort function
                  increases in e, c(eL) > c(eH), effort is larger for the worker with the low cost of effort,
                  eL > eH. ■

                    In a context with continuous effort, this condition can be expressed as ∂c(e, θL) / ∂e < ∂c(e, θH) / ∂e,
                  and it is commonly known as the “single-crossing property” since it guarantees that the indifference
                  curve of a θL-type worker and a θH-type worker cross each other only once.

         From example 10.6, we can see that the introduction of asymmetric information
      entails no changes in effort for the worker with low cost of effort, eLSI = eLAI = 0.707
      (i.e., “no distortion at the top” for the most efficient worker), but a lower effort for the
      high-cost worker than under symmetric information, eHAI = 0.408 < 0.5 = eHSI . Salaries
      are, in contrast, higher for the low-cost worker under asymmetric than symmetric in-
      formation, namely w LAI = 0.667 > 0.5 = w LSI ; but lower for the high-cost worker, namely
      w HAI = 0.333 > 0.5 = w HSI . Overall, the net utility that each type of worker obtains under
      asymmetric information is

                                         uHAI = w H − 2eH2 = 0,

                                      uLAI = w L − eL2 =     ≅ 0.167,
                                                           6
      which entails that the worker with a low cost of effort captures an information rent of
      uLAI − uLSI = 0.167 − 0 = 0.167 > 0 , while the worker with a high cost of effort does not,
      uHAI = uHSI = 0. Intuitively, the firm must compensate the low-cost worker above sym-
      metric information terms in order for him to reveal his type (i.e., to choose the contract
      meant for him), while the worker with a high cost of effort is not compensated above
      his symmetric information utility level. Additionally we can compare the effort levels
      and wages between both information contexts as follows:

                                      eLAI = 0.707 = 0.707 = eLSI ,

                                      eHAI = 0.408 < 0.500 = eHSI ,

                                      w LAI = 0.667 > 0.500 = w LSI ,

                                      w HAI = 0.333 < 0.500 = w HSI .

      Extensions The principal–agent problem considered above can be extended in many
      dimensions. We next provide some examples commonly examined in the literature: (1)
      allowing for several principals to compete for the labor services of one common agent
      (as described in Stole 1990 and Martimort 1996); (2) allowing for the agent’s privately
      observed type θ to be multidimensional (i.e., a vector), such as his productivity in dif-
      ferent tasks (see Laffont et al. 1987; Rochet 1996); (3) allowing for the principal to
      assign different tasks to the agent (where at least one of the tasks can be done by either
      the principal or the agent) in order to identify conditions under which the principal
      profitably delegates the task, or instead prefers to carry it out himself (as in Riordan
Contract Theory                                                                                                       777



                  and Sappington 1987); (4) considering a principal–agent relationship that lasts for
                  more than one period (i.e., repeated adverse selection), and how the agent’s incentives
                  to conceal his type from the principal can increase with and without commitment (see
                  Baron and Besanko 1984; Laffont and Tirole 1988, 1990); (5) allowing the principal to
                  incorrectly observe realized profits (as analyzed by Caillaud et al. 1992); or (6) permit-
                  ting the contract between the principal and the agent to be dynamic, thus spanning
                  several periods (see Bolton and Dewatripont 2005, chapter 9, and references therein).

                  10.6    Application of Adverse Selection—Regulation

                  There are several contexts in which regulatory agencies cannot observe some charac-
                  teristic of the regulated firm or of individual. Examples include a firm’s production
                  costs (in the case of setting production subsidies), its costs from pollution abatement
                  (when regulators set emission fees or quotas seeking to curb pollution), and a con-
                  sumer’s willingness to pay for certain products (e.g., when governments design tax
                  rebates for the purchase of solar panels or home insulating materials). In these sce-
                  narios the privately informed party (e.g., firm) has the incentives to overstate its costs
                  and, as a consequence, the regulator cannot directly ask firms about their production
                  costs since responses would be unreliable. As we next show, the above-mentioned re-
                  sults in adverse selection models offer an alternative contracting tool for regulators to
                  use in order to extract information from firms (or consumers) that are privately in-
                  formed about a relevant characteristic, such as their production costs, that the govern-
                  ment can use to design public policies.
                     Consider a government regulating a monopoly with cost function c(q) = C + cq,
                  where C denotes its fixed costs and c > 0 its marginal costs. The consumer pays F for
                  the bulk of q units consumed, and the monopolist may receive a lump-sum subsidy
                  from the government of S. Assume that the shadow cost of raising public funds is
                  g ∈ (0, 1), thus implying that the total cost of providing a subsidy S to the monopolist
                  is (1 + g)S.10 For completeness, we first analyze the first-best outcome, which arises
                  when the government has symmetric information about the monopolist’s costs, and
                  then we will move to different regulatory context in which the government does not
                  accurately observe monopolist’s costs.

                  10
                     The shadow cost of raising public funds can be understood as the deadweight loss that arises from
                  setting a sales tax (or a payroll tax). Recall from previous chapters that a deadweight loss arises from
                  these taxes unless individuals and firms are completely unresponsive to the tax (inelastic demand and
                  supply).
778                                                                                                 Chapter 10



      10.6.1    Symmetric Information
      If the government can perfectly observe the monopolist’s marginal cost of production,
      c, it solves the following welfare-maximization problem subject to the voluntary par-
      ticipation of both the monopolist and the consumer:

                              max [ u ( q ) − F ] + [ F + S − C − cq ] − (1 + g ) S
                              F ,S ,q


                                          subject to F + S − C − cq ≥ 0,                           ( PCmonop. )

                                                     u ( q ) − F ≥ 0,                             ( PCconsumer )
      where u(q) − F represents consumer utility after paying F for the bulk of q units; and
      F + S − C − cq denotes the monopolist’s profits after receiving F from consumers, the
      subsidy S from the government, and incurring total costs of C + cq when producing q
      units.
        The Lagrangian of this program is

           = [u ( q ) − F + F + S − C − cq − (1 + g ) S ] + λ1 [ F + S − C − cq ] + λ2 [u ( q ) − F ].

      Taking FOCs with respect to government’s three choice variables F, S, and q yields

                                           ∂
                                              = λ1 − λ2 = 0 → λ1 = λ2 ,
                                           ∂F

                                        ∂
                                           = 1 − (1 + g ) + λ1 = 0 → λ1 = g ,
                                        ∂S

                                        ∂
                                           = u ′ ( q ) − c − λ1c + λ 2 u ′ ( q ) = 0,
                                        ∂q

                          λ1 ( F + S − C − cq ) = 0 ,          and      λ2 (u ( q ) − F ) = 0 .

         Combining the first and second FOC, we obtain that λ1 = λ2 = g. Plugging this result
      into the third FOC yields

                                            u ′ ( q ) − c − gc + gu ′ ( q ) = 0,

      or, on rearranging,

                                    (1 + g ) u ′ (q) = (1 + g ) c ⇔ u ′ (q ) = c .

                  Figure 10.12
                  Monopoly regulation—Symmetric information


                     That is, under symmetric information, the monopolist’s production is efficient since
                  q is increased until the point where marginal utility from further units coincides with
                  its marginal cost. Figure 10.12 depicts the result by separately plotting the left- and
                  right-hand sides of u′(q) = c.

                  10.6.2   Asymmetric Information
                  Consider now that the government cannot observe the monopolist’s marginal cost,
                  which can be low or high c = {cL, cH}, where cL < cH, with associated probabilities p and
                  1 − p, respectively. In this context, the government offers two menus (FL, SL, qL) and
                  (FH, SH, qH) that seek to maximize the expected social welfare, subject to the voluntary
                  participation of the monopolist and consumers (PC constraints), and to the monopo-
                  list’s self-selection (IC constraints), as follows:

                                       max                    p [ u ( qL ) − FL + FL + S L − C − cL qL − (1 + g ) S L ]
                             ( FL ,SL ,qL ), ( FH ,SH ,qH )

                                           + (1 − p )[ u ( qH ) − FH + FH + S H − C − cH qH − (1 + g ) S H ]

                                                          subject to FL + S L − C − cL qL ≥ 0                                (PCL),

                                                                 FH + S H − C − cH qH ≥ 0                                 (PCH, λ1),
780                                                                                                  Chapter 10




                               FL + S L − C − cL qL ≥ FH + S H − C − cL qH                            (ICL, λ2 ),

                               FH + S H − C − cH qH ≥ FL + S L − C − cH qL                           (ICH, λ3 ),

                                               u ( qL ) − FL ≥ 0                             (PCconsumer-L, λ4 ),

                                               u ( qH ) − FH ≥ 0                             (PCconsumer-H, λ5 ).

      Note that the PC constraints for each consumer do not include probabilities, indicating
      that he is the last mover in this game: first, the government offers contracts, then the
      monopolist chooses one of them, and finally the K-type monopolist offers qK units to
      the consumer at a lump-sum price of FK where K = {L, H), which the consumer can ac-
      cept or reject.
        In this program, PCL does not bind (and thus becomes redundant), as it is implied by
      ICH. Indeed

                  FH + S H − C − cH qH ≥ FL + S L − C − cH qL > FL + S L − C − cL qL .

      The first inequality holds by ICH, and the second is obvious since cH > cL. Hence, PCL
      holds with strict inequality, and we can solve the above maximization problem ignor-
      ing PCL. In particular, we assign Lagrange multipliers λ1 to PCH, λ2 to ICL, λ3 to ICH,
      λ4 to PCcons-L, and λ5 to PCcons-H. Taking FOCs, we obtain

         Overall, the government distorts the contract of the high-cost firm to make it less
      attractive for the low-cost firm, and thus achieves self-selection. Specifically, since
      PCH binds, the high-cost firm obtains zero profits both under symmetric and asymmet-
      ric information. Since qHAI < qHSI , its subsidy must also be lower S HAI < S HSI , so its
      profits are unaffected. In contrast, the low-cost firm obtains positive profits under
      asymmetric information (since PCL does not bind, as shown at the beginning of this
      section), but its profits where zero under symmetric information. However, since
      its output is not distorted, qLAI = qLSI , this type of firm must receive a more generous
      subsidy under asymmetric than under symmetric information, giving rise to its
Contract Theory                                                                                           785



                  information rent (the difference between its profits in asymmetric and symmetric infor-
                  mation), which in this setting are given by SL.

                  Example 10.8: Monopoly regulation Consider consumers with utility function
                   u ( q ) = q , a monopoly with cost function c ( q ) = 1 4 + cq, where marginal costs can be
                  high, cH = 18 , or low, cL = 116 . The shadow cost of raising public funds is g = 1 24 . In
                  this context symmetric information entails an output level that solves 1 2 q = cK ,
                  which yields output levels of qHSI = 16 and qLSI = 64 for the firm with high and low cost,
                  respectively. Under asymmetric information, the low-cost firm produces the same
                  amount as under symmetric information, qLSI = qLAI = 64, but the high-cost firm pro-
                  duces a lower output, qHAI = 15.38 , as depicted in figure 10.14. ■

                  Extensions A recent branch of the literature has considered the effect of changing
                  behavioral assumptions on different contractual settings, commonly referred to as “be-
                  havioral contract theory.” In the context of moral hazard, examples include (1) the ef-
                  fect of inequity aversion when the agent compares his payoff with that of the principal;
                  (2) the agent’s intrinsic motivation for exerting effort (other than the explicit, mone-
                  tary, reward); and (3) overconfidence on the probability distribution of outcomes; that
                  is, agents sustaining overestimated beliefs (relative to those of the principal) about
                  how likely effort transforms into profit. In the case of adverse selection and screening,
                  examples of behavioral extensions include (1) the effect of an agent’s present bias, and
                  the ability to commit to a long-term contract rather than allow for a flexible contract;
                  (2) overconfident agents, in the sense that they incorrectly assess their own type (e.g.,
                  thinking that their productivity for the task that the principal assigns is high, when it is
                  actually low, which they learn during the task, and after signing the contract); and (3)
                  agents who exhibit inequity aversion, or loss aversion, relative to a reference point,
                  which can lead to certain types of agents being exploited by the principal, or not being
                  hired at all. For a detailed literature review of these models, see Koszegi (2014) and
                  references therein.

             not observe the latter’s effort. In this context the banks needs to first anticipate

Mathematical Appendix




This mathematical appendix briefly covers basic concepts, such as intervals in the real
line, sequences, functions, limits, continuity (in functions and correspondences), dif-
ferentiation and integration, optimization, a brief introduction to topology, fixed point
theorems, comparative statics, and examples of mathematical proofs. It is assumed that
the reader is familiarized with standard topics in undergrad mathematics for econo-
mists, such as those in commonly used textbooks by Klein (2001) and Chiang and
Wainwright (2004). Several examples are presented that apply the main definitions to
standard real-valued functions in economics in order to enhance the understanding of
mathematical properties.
   The reader is, of course, recommended to refer to more advanced textbooks usually
assigned in graduate-level courses, such as Simon and Blume (1994), Sundaran (1996),
de la Fuente (2000), Ok (2007), Corbae et al. (2009), and Hoy et al. (2011), as well as
those commonly recommended as introductions to real analysis, such as Rudin (2006)
and Bartle and Sherbert (2011).

A.1   Sets

We understand a set S as a collection of objects, and use x ∈ S to denote that “element
x belongs to set S.” A subset S′ of S is denoted as S′ ⊆ S. Let us analyze some common
set operators:
1. The intersection of two sets A and B, which describes to elements that belong to
   both sets A and B, is represented as A ∩ B.
2. The union of two sets A and B, which lists all the elements that belong to either A or
   B or both, is denoted as A ∪ B.
804                                                                          Mathematical Appendix



      3. The complement of B relative to A, represented by A \ B, is the set of all elements
         that belong to A but do not belong to B. (This is also denoted as the set difference
         A − B, since we remove from A all elements that are also elements of B.)
      4. The Cartesian product of sets A and B, A × B, is the set of all ordered pairs (a, b),
         where a ∈ A and b ∈ B.
      5. We say that sets A and A are disjoint if their intersection is empty, A ∩ B = ∅.
         For instance, if A = {a, a′} and B = {b, b′}, its Cartesian product A × B is
      (a, b), (a, b′), (a′, b) and (a′, b′), that is, all the combinations of pairs where the first
      component originates from set A and the second component from set B. Moreover the
      union of sets A and B in this example is A ∪ B = {a, a′, b, b′}, and the complement is
      empty, A \ B = ∅, since A and B do not share any elements.
         We can extend the property of union and intersection to combinations of three
      sets. In that setting, the following de Morgan’s laws provide us with two useful
      relationships:
      1. Union: A(B ∪ C) = (A \ B) ∩ (A \ C)
      2. Intersection: A(B ∩ C) = (A \ B) ∪ (A \ C)
      For a standard, yet readable, proof, see Bartle and Sherbert (2011).

         Relations A binary relation between two sets X and Y is a set of ordered pairs
         (x, y) ∈ X × Y.


      For instance, if X, Y ⊆ ℝ, the binary relation “larger or equal than,” ≥, is defined for
      every pair x ∈ X and y ∈ Y. In this example, for any two real numbers x ∈ X and y ∈ Y,
      either x ≥ y, or y ≥ x, or both (which would only happen if x and y are the same number,
      x = y). Below we include properties that a binary relation R can satisfy:
      1. Reflexivity For all x ∈ X, xRx.
      2. Symmetry For all two elements x, x′ ∈ X, xRx′ implies that x′Rx.
      3. Transitivity For all three elements x, x′, x″ ∈ X, xRx′ and x′Rx″ implies xRx″.
      4. Completeness For all two elements x, x′ ∈ X, either xRx′ or x′Rx, or both.
      5. Antisymmetry For all two elements x, x′ ∈ X, if xRx′ and x′Rx then it must be that x
         and x′ are the same element, x = x′.
        Continuing with the example of binary relation ≥, note that it is reflexive, transitive,
      complete, and antisymmetric. If instead we define the relation > (“strictly larger than”),
      we can see that it is complete, transitive, and antisymmetric. In a different context, if
      we consider to relation “be the brother of” in a group of people X, it is easy to show
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                      805



                  that it is not reflexive (I am not the brother of myself!), it is not symmetric (unless all
                  elements are brothers of each other), and not transitive (Bob can be the brother of Tom,
                  and Tom the brother of Alex, yet Bob does not need to be the brother of Alex but half-
                  brother).

                  A.2   Intervals of Real Numbers

                  We denote open intervals as (a, b) where a, b ∈ ℝ, indicating that numbers a and b are
                  not contained within the interval. In contrast, a closed interval [a, b] includes its bound-
                  ary points a and b. For a given set S of real numbers (e.g., those in an interval),
                  if we can find a real number u such that u ≥ x for all x ∈ S, we then say that u is the
                  upper bound of set S, and that set S is bounded above. (Alternatively, the upper
                  bound is represented as u = max S.) Similarly, if we can find a real number l ≤ x for all
                  x ∈ S, we say that l is a lower bound of set S, and that set S is bounded below. (Alterna-
                  tively, l = min S.)

                  Example A.1: Lower and upper bounds Interval S = (a, b) has a as one of its lower
                  bounds (along with any other number smaller than a) and b as one of its upper bounds
                  (along with any other number higher than b). However, neither of these belongs to set
                  S, implying that set S has no maximal or minimal element. In contrast, set S = [a, ∞) has
                  l = a as one of its lower bounds, which is also its minimal element, but such a set is
                  unbounded above. ■

                  Hence, as example A.1 indicates, for a number to be the maximum (minimum) of a set,
                  it needs to be an upper (lower) bound of such a set and also belong to the set. Alterna-
                  tively, if a set has a maximum (minimum), that number must be an upper (lower)
                  bound of the set. While sets such as S = (a, b) have no maxima or minima, we can still
                  use the definition of upper and lower bounds to define some “virtual boundaries” on
                  the set. In particular, the supremum of a set (written as sup S) is the least upper bound
                  of that set, meaning the smallest upper bound we can find for S. Similarly the infimum
                  of a set (inf S) is the greatest lower bound of the set, meaning the highest lower bound
                  we can find for S. When considering sets of real numbers, the supremum and infimum
                  will exist and be unique (which is referred to as the completeness axiom). For instance,
                  if S = (a, b) then inf S = a and sup S = b; a similar argument applies to S = [a, b] with the
                  difference that min S = a and max S = b exist when S = [a, b] but do not exist when
                  S = (a, b). Finally, if set S is unbounded above (below), its supremum (infimum) is
                  sup S = +∞ (inf S = −∞, respectively).
806                                                                              Mathematical Appendix



        Let us finish this section with a few more properties of the real numbers. (All the
      following properties are equivalent. For a proof of these results, see Gordon 2002.)
      1. (Archimedean property) If a, b ∈ ℝ+, we can then find an integer n such that na > b.
         Intuitively, if a and b differ, we can double a into 2a, triple it into 3a, and so on,
         until we can guarantee that na > b. For instance, if a = 2 and b = 8, we can find that
         for integer n = 5, we obtain 5*2 > 8.
      2. For each real number a ∈ ℝ, we can find an integer n such that a lies between n and
         the next integer n + 1, namely a ∈ [n, n + 1]. For instance, if a = 3 2 , we can find n = 1
         such that 3 2 ∈[1, 2]
      3. For each positive real number a ∈ ℝ+, we can find a positive integer n such that
         na > 1, or a > 1 n . For instance, if a = 1 2 , we can find a positive integer n = 3 such that
         3 × 1 2 = 1.5 > 1, or 1 2 > 1 n = 1 3 .
