      A.4   Sequences

      Sequences are ordered lists of objects, and they are denoted as {xn}, where n is a posi-
      tive integer, or alternatively as {xi }i =1, and each of the numbers x1, x2, … , xn represents
                                             ∞


      a term of the sequence. For instance, the sequence { 1 n} starts at 1 when n = 1, and then
      decreases to 1 2 when n = 2, 1 3 when n = 3, and so on, as depicted in figure A.3.
         A similar argument applies to sequence {n/(1 + 2n)}, which starts at 1 3 when n = 1,
      and then increases to 2 5 when n = 2, 3 7 when n = 3, and so on, as depicted in figure A.4.
         As the previous examples illustrate, sequences can be increasing if xn+1 ≥ xn for all n,
      as in the case of {n/(1 + 2n)}, or sequences can be decreasing if xn+1 ≤ xn for all n, as in
      the case of { 1 n}. (If we refer to a sequence as monotone, we are just saying that it is
      either increasing or decreasing.) Another interesting property of the sequences in both
      of the previous examples is that, as n increase, they converge to a specific value in the




      Figure A.3
      Decreasing sequence
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                    809




                  Figure A.4
                  Increasing sequence


                  vertical axis. Indeed { 1 n} converged to zero and {n/(1 + 2n)} converged to 1 2 . We de-
                  fine convergent sequences next.


                        Convergent sequences A sequence {xn} converges to a real number p if, for
                        every ε > 0, there exists a positive integer N such that the distance |xn − p| < ε
                        for all n ≥ N.


                    A sequence that converges to p is denoted as

                                                         lim {xi }i =1 = p,
                                                                  ∞
                                                         n→∞


                  or simply xn → p. Intuitively, the definition above states that, for a sequence to be re-
                  garded as convergent, we need, for every number ε > 0 to move forward in the se-
                  quence and, eventually, find that for all positions n ≥ N in the sequence, the distance
                  between xn and p is smaller than the number ε > 0. Since we can choose our ε > 0 to be
                  arbitrarily small, we need to find a sufficiently big term N that guarantees a difference
                  |xn − p| satisfying |xn − p| < ε for all n ≥ N. A common trick in identifying whether a se-
                  quence is convergent or divergent is to express the term N as a function of the measure-
                  ment error ε, that is, N(ε), as the following example illustrates.
810                                                                           Mathematical Appendix



      Example A.2: Convergent sequence In order to show that the decreasing
      sequence { 1 n} converges to zero (this sequence is depicted in figure A.3), let us choose
      an Nth term N(ε) = 1/ε. Then the difference xn − p = 1 n − 0 = 1 n is smaller than
      ε > 0 for all n > N(ε) = 1/ε. Indeed, in the Nth term, the difference becomes
       xN ( ε ) − p = (1 N (ε )) − 0 = (1 1ε ) − 0 = ε , but it is smaller than ε for any n > N(ε). ■


         Cauchy sequences A sequence {xn} of real numbers is called a Cauchy se-
         quence if, for every positive real number ε, there exists a positive integer N such
         that, for all natural numbers m, n > N, we have |xm − xn| < ε.


      In the case of sequences of real numbers, the definition of convergent sequences and
      Cauchy sequences are equivalent.
         While both sequences in the previous examples were convergent, other sequences
      can be divergent. This is the case of sequence {(−1)n+1} depicted in figure A.5, which
      starts at 1 when n = 1, and then alternates between −1 when n = 2, and 1 when n = 3, and
      so on, without ever approaching a limiting point. (For a formal proof of this result, see
      Chartrand et al. 2003, 219.)




      Figure A.5
      A nonconvergent sequence
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                   811



                     Moreover all the previous sequences (including the divergent sequence {(−1)n+1})
                  took values in a bounded range of the vertical axis, for instance, values smaller than 1
                  for {1/n}, between 0 and 1 3 for {n/(1 + 2n}, and either −1 or 1 for {(−1)n+1}. That is,
                  all sequences were bounded. We next define this property.

                        Bounded sequences A sequence {xn} is bounded above (below) if we can
                        find an upper bound U (lower bound L) for which xn ≤ U (or xn ≥ L, respectively)
                        for all n.


                  While all previous sequences were bounded above and below, often sequences are not.
                  For instance, sequence {n2} = {1, 4, 9, 16, …} is not bounded above, as it converges to
                  +∞. Interestingly, this result leads us to the following result, describing the convergent
                  properties of sequences that monotonically increase, as in the example of {n2}; or
                  decrease, as in the case of {1/n}.

                        Monotonic convergence If a sequence {xn} is monotonic, it converges to a
                        limiting real number p.


                  As a corollary of the two definitions above, if a series is both monotonic (either
                  increasing or decreasing) and bounded, then it must converge to a finite real number p.
                  This is an interesting result, as we can claim that a sequence converges (without the
                  need to find its limit) if we can demonstrate that it is bounded and monotonic. The fol-
                  lowing two theorems about the convergence properties of subsequences are very often
                  used in analysis. (For proofs, see Bartle and Sherbert 2011, 72.)


                        Monotonic subsequence theorem Every sequence {xn} has a monotonic sub-
                        sequence, that is, a subsequence that monotonically increases or decreases.


                     Furthermore, if sequence {xn} is bounded, it has a monotonic subsequence that must
                  also be bounded, given that the original sequence {xn} was itself bounded. Then such
                  a subsequence must be convergent. This result is called the Bolzano–Weierstrass
                  theorem, as presented below.

                        Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem Every bounded sequence has a convergent
                        subsequence.
812                                                                         Mathematical Appendix



      While the Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem states that we can find a subsequence of
      {xn} that converges, it does not say that all subsequences of {xn} converge to the same
      point. For instance, the sequence {xn} = {(−1)n+1} that we considered in the previous
      sections can produce two subsequences: one grouping all +1’s in the original sequence,
      that is, {(−1)2n} converging to 1, and another with all the −1’s, that is,{(−1)2n+1} con-
      verging to −1.

      A.5   Functions

      Let f : ℝN → ℝN denote a real-valued function. When the domain of the function is re-
      stricted to a subset of vectors of real numbers A ⊂ ℝN and its range to subset B ⊂ ℝN, we
      have f : A → B.


         One-to-one function Function f : A → B is one to one (or injective) if any two
         points of its domain yield a different image. That is to say, for every x ≠ y where-
         by x, y ∈ A, their images f(x) and f(y) satisfy f(x) ≠ f(y).


         Therefore a function f is not one-to-one if we can find two elements of its domain
      x ≠ y yielding the same image, f(x) = f(y). For instance, U-shaped and inverted U-shaped
      functions are not one-to-one, as figure A.6 describes.
         In contrast, functions that increase or decrease for all the points in its domain (i.e.,
      monotonically increasing or decreasing) are one-to-one, such as f(x) = ax + b, where
      a, b ∈ ℝ and a ≠ 0 are constants (but b is not necessarily positive), as figure A.7 depicts.




      Figure A.6
      Not one-to-one functions
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                                813




                  Figure A.7
                  One-to-one functions


                      We next consider a property that is regarded as the converse of one-to-one.


                        Onto functions Function f : A → B is onto (or surjective) if every element in B
                        is the image of an element in the domain A. That is, for every b ∈ B, there exists
                        an element in the domain a ∈ A such that f(a) = b.


                    The previous examples f(x) = ax + b are onto functions since, for every image in the
                  vertical axis, we can find the point in the horizontal and that produces such an image.
                  However, some real-valued functions are not onto, such as f(x) = 2x, which is one-to-
                  one but not onto; or f(x) = x2, which is neither one-to-one nor onto, as depicted in figure
                  A.8. (Unless otherwise stated, we assume x ∈ ℝ throughout the appendix.1)
                    Note that a function can be onto despite not being one-to-one, thus making both
                  properties independent. For instance, f(x) = xsin(x), depicted in figure A.9, is onto but
                  not one-to-one. In words, for every point in the range we can find a point in the domain
                  producing such an image; but the same image can be obtained from more than one
                  point in the domain (such as x and y in the figure, which both yield a height of 1).


                        Bijective functions     If a function f is both one-to-one and onto, we say it is
                        bijective.

                  Composite Functions
                  We often need to work with “functions of functions.” In particular, if a function
                  f : A → B is the argument of another function g : B → C, their composition is g(f(x)),
                  where x ∈ A. (This composition is alternatively denoted as (g ∘ f)(x), where g ∘ f : A → C.)
                  For instance, if f(x) = x2 and g(x) = sin x, then their composition is g(f(x)) = g(x2) = sin x2.
                  Some of the properties of functions described above (one-to-one and onto) extend to
                  the composition of functions with the following characteristics:
                  1. If both f and g are one-to-one, then their composition f(g(x)) is also one-to-one.
                  2. If both f and g are onto, then their composition f(g(x)) is also onto.
                  3. If both f and g are bijective, then their composition f(g(x)) is also bijective.
                  4. If the composition g(f(x)) is one-to-one, then f must be one-to-one, but g need not be.
                  5. If the composition g(f(x)) is onto, then g must be onto, but f need not be.

                  Example A.3: Composite functions Consider functions f ( x ) = x and g(x) = ax2

                  is one-to-one since, for any two elements x ≠ y, their image differs, that is,
                   ( x ) + b ≠ a ( y ) + b. Similarly, if f ( x ) = x and g(x) = log(x), where only g(x) is
                         2              2

                  It is convenient to find the point in the domain producing a certain point in the range.
                  With this goal we use the inverse of a function. That is, for f : A → B, meaning f(a) = b,
                  where a ∈ A and b ∈ B, its inverse function is f−1 : B → A, where f−1(b) = a. For instance,
                  if f(x) = a − bx, where a, b > 0, then its inverse can be found by solving for x, that is,

      A function and its inverse


      and f(y) can be traced back into different points x and y. That is, f−1(f(x)) = x while
      f−1(f(y)) = y. This requirement is, however, easy to circumvent if we restrict the domain
      of the inverse function. For instance, f(x) = sin x is not one-to-one. However, if we re-
      strict its domain to values of x for which sin x is one-to-one, such as one of the cycles
      from −π/2 to π/2 as depicted in figure A.11, the inverse function f−1(x) = arcsin x exists.

      A.6    Limits

      Consider a real-valued function f(x), f : A → B, where A, B ⊆ ℝ. We say that function f(x)
      has a limit p ∈ B at c ∈ A if, for every ε > 0 such that |f(x) − p| < ε, there exists a real
      number δ > 0 such that x is δ-close to c, meaning |x − c| < δ. More compactly,

                                            lim f ( x ) = p .
                                             x →c


         As for sequences, we seek to find that, as x is sufficiently close to c, as defined by
      |x − c| < δ or x → c, the difference between f(x) and p becomes so small that |f(x) − p| < ε
      holds for any arbitrary value of ε > 0. Figure A.12 depicts the interpretation of the
      limit definition for two functions.

                   Limits of two functions

        We can use these limits to state what is called the “squeeze theorem” (also referred
      to as the “sandwich theorem”) as follows. (For a proof, see, for instance, Gordon
      2002.)


         Squeeze theorem for functions Consider three real-valued functions f(x),
         g(x), and h(x), satisfying f(x) ≤ g(x) ≤ h(x) for all x. If the limit of functions f(x)
         and h(x) at point c coincide, meaning lim x→c f ( x ) = lim x→c h( x ) = p , then the
         limit of function g(x) at c is also p, that is, lim x→c g ( x ) = p .


         Figure A.13 provides a graphical representation of this theorem. In particular, func-
      tion g(x) lies between h(x) and f(x) for all x, where these two functions can be thought
      of as making a “sandwich” or “squeezing” function g(x). Then, if h(x) and f(x) share a
      common limiting point p at x = c, function g(x) must also share this limiting point.

      A.7   Continuity

      We say that a real-valued function f(x) is continuous if it does not have breaks or
      “jumps” as we increase x. In particular, f(x) is continuous at a point x if its limit at that
      point satisfies lim x→ x f ( x ) = f ( x ) . An alternative presentation of this definition uses
      the notation of δ and ε in limits.


         Continuity A real-value function f(x) is continuous at x if f(x) and f ( x ) are
         ε-close, whereby f ( x ) − f ( x ) < ε for any arbitrary ε > 0 when x − x < δ .


         Note that the preceding definition can be adapted to express the continuity of a
      function f(x) at the endpoints of its domain [a, b], namely lim x→a f ( x ) = f ( a) and
      lim x→b f ( x ) = f (b) . Moreover, if a function is continuous in all points of its domain A,
      we just say that lim x→ x0 f ( x ) = f ( x0 ) for all x0 ∈ A. Further, since continuity is defined
      using limits, and limits satisfy usual arithmetic operations, continuity is preserved after
      applying these manipulations. That is, if f(x) and g(x) are continuous on an interval of
      their domain A′ ⊆ A, then functions f(x) + g(x), f(x) − g(x), kf(x), and kg(x) (where k ∈ ℝ
      is a constant), and f(x)/g(x) (if g(x) ≠ 0) are also all continuous in interval A′.
Mathematical Appendix                                                   819




                  Figure A.13
                  “Squeeze” (or “sandwich”) theorem for function g(x)

                  A continuous and a discontinuous function

      Bolzano’s intermediate value theorem



          Bolzano’s intermediate value theorem Consider a function f : [a, b] → ℝ
          that is continuous in all points of its domain [a, b]. Then, for every y between f(a)
          and f(b), f(b) > y > f(a) or f(b) < y < f(a), a corresponding point x can be found in
          the domain yielding f(x) = y.

        This result is depicted in the left panel of figure A.15. Intuitively, for every y in the
      vertical axis between f(a) and f(b), we can recover the point in the horizontal axis, x,
      that produces f(x) = y by using the inverse f−1(y) = x. Note that, if function f(x) was not
      continuous, we could not guarantee such a result, as depicted in the right panel.2


          Extreme value theorem Consider a function f : [a, b] → ℝ being continuous in
          all points of its domain [a, b]. The range of function f is therefore bounded, and
          includes its maximum and minimum points, M = f(d) and m = f(e), where M ≥ f(x)
          for all x ∈ [a, b] and m ≤ f(x) for all x ∈ [a, b].


      2
        In addition, when function f(·) is monotonically increasing in x, point y satisfies f(b) > y > f(a), as in
      the left panel of the figure; but when f(·) is monotonically decreasing, point y satisfies f(b) < y < f(a).
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                          821




                  Figure A.16
                  Extreme value theorem


                     While in figure A.15 the minimum and maximum are actually the endpoints of
                  the domain, M = f(b) and m = f(a), in other functions this need not be the case, as
                  figure A.16 depicts.
                     The examples about functions satisfying continuity at the beginning of the section
                  emphasized the fact that, as images of the function grow close to each other,
                  |f(x) − f(p)| < ε, the number δ that satisfies |x − c| < δ might vary. In other words, δ can be
                  a function of the “closedness” parameter ε but also of the point c itself. A usual
                  example of such a result is the function f(x) = 1/x. In particular, for a given value of
                  ε > 0, the value of δ decreases as c increases.
                     If, in contrast, δ is only a function of ε, but remains constant (i.e., uniform) for all
                  points in the domain, we say that the function f(x) is uniformly continuous, as defined
                  below.


                        Uniform continuity Consider a real-valued function f : A → ℝ, where A ⊂ ℝ.
                        Function f(·) is uniformly continuous if for every two points x, x ∈ A satisfying
                         f ( x ) − f ( x ) < ε for any arbitrary ε > 0, we can find an associated δ(ε) such that
                        x − x < δ (ε ).
822                                                                        Mathematical Appendix




      Figure A.17
      A continuous function


         That is, the value of δ depends on ε but becomes independent on x. This property is
      satisfied if small variations in x produce a similar change in f(x), regardless of the spe-
      cific value of x at which we initially evaluated the function. In contrast, functions that
      change in x very rapidly for small values of x but slowly for high values of x would
      violate uniform continuity, even if they can satisfy continuity. Hence uniform continu-
      ity implies continuity, but the converse is not necessarily true. Linear functions, such
      as f(x) = ax + b are uniformly continuous. Indeed, if |x − c| < δ, then |f(x) − f(c)| is

                               ( ax + b) − ( ac + b) = a x − c < aδ = ε.

      Functions of Several Variables
      The previous definitions of continuity and uniform continuity can be extended from
      functions with unidimensional domains x ∈ ℝ to functions where x ∈ ℝN by making use
      of the Euclidean distance x − p, which must be smaller than δ. (For two points x and p,
      the difference f(x) − f(p) is a real number, and therefore the distance |f(x) − f(p)| must
      still satisfy |f(x) − f(p)| < ε for any arbitrary ε > 0.)

                  Continuity in Correspondences
                  We can extend the definition of continuity from functions to correspondences. Corre-
                  spondences are often used in consumer theory when a given price vector and income
                  yields a continuum of utility-maximizing bundles rather than a unique bundle. In that
                  setting we talk about a Walrasian correspondence rather than a Walrasian demand
                  function. Correspondences are also used in game theory when an agent is indifferent
                  among different strategies that yield the same payoff against a given strategy of his
                  opponent; for instance, player i is indifferent between si1 and si2, where si1 , si2 ∈ Si when
                  his opponent j selects sj. In that case, we say that player i’s best-response correspon-
                  dence to sj is si ( s j ) = {si1 , si2 }. We first define correspondences, and its relationship with
                  functions, and then present a notion of continuity for correspondences.


                        Correspondence A correspondence F assigns a set of points in the range to at
                        least one point in the domain, that is, F : A → 2B, where A, B ⊆ ℝn and F(x) ∈ 2B.


                  Correspondences are also known as set-valued mappings since at least one point of the
                  domain x ∈ A can be mapped into a set of points in the range F(x) ∈ 2B, as opposed to
                  functions where f(x) is just a point in the range for every x ∈ A. Figure A.18 depicts a
                  function (left panel) and a correspondence (right panel).
                     While the interpretation of correspondences shares many features with that of
                  functions, defining continuity in correspondences is more involved. Figure A.19 illus-
                  trates how a small change in x leads to changes in the image of the function where we




                  Figure A.18
                  A function (left panel) and a correspondence (right panel)
824                                                                                 Mathematical Appendix




      Figure A.19
      A small change in x in a function (left panel) and in a correspondence (right panel)


      only need to compare f(x1) and f(x2) as we move from x1 to x2 (left panel). The same
      change in x in the correspondence (right panel) leads to a change in sets F(x1) and
      F(x2). How can we compare these two sets in a meaningful way to ultimately obtain a
      definition of continuity for correspondences? Intuitively, we look for a definition of
      continuity that requires small changes in x to produce small changes in the set of
      images F(x). In order to provide such a definition we first need to adapt the notion
      of continuity from above and from below in functions to the context of correspon-
      dences: upper and lower hemicontinuity.


         Upper hemicontinuity (in correspondences) A correspondence F : A → 2B is
         upper hemicontinuous at x0 if, for every open set V containing F(x0), F(x0) ⊆ V,
         there is an open set N containing x0, x0 ∈ N (a neighborhood of points around x0
         that include x0) such that, for every point on that set, x′ ∈ U, their images are also
         part of set V, that is,

                                      F ( x′) ⊆ V     for every x ′ ∈U .

         A correspondence is upper hemicontinuous (UHC) if it is UHC at every x ∈ X,
         that is, at every point of its domain.

         Lower hemicontinuity (in correspondences) A correspondence F : A → 2B
         is lower hemicontinuous at x0 if, for every open set V in which F(x0) lies,
         F(x0) ∩ V ≠ ∅, there is an open set N containing x0, x0 ∈ N (a neighborhood of
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                         825




                  Figure A.20
                  LHC and UHC



                        points around x0 that include x0) such that, for every point on that set, x′ ∈ U, their
                        images are also part of set V, that is,

                                                 F ( x0 ) ∩ V ≠ ∅   for every x ′ ∈U .


                  A correspondence is lower hemicontinuous (LHC) if it is LHC at every x ∈ X, that is,
                  at every point of its domain.
                     The left panel of figure A.20 depicts a correspondence satisfying LHC. Intuitively,
                  LHC implies that “downward jumps” are allowed. Graphically, if we move from point
                  x0 rightward, we allow for sudden expansions of the range of images that the corre-
                  spondence produces. In contrast, leftward movements from x0 do not produce sudden
                  contractions in the correspondence. The right-hand panel depicts a correspondence
                  satisfying UHC, since a rightward jump from point x0 (in which the correspondence
                  “expands”) is allowed. Finally, we say that a correspondence F is continuous if it is
                  both LHC and UHC.
                     As you may suspect, if F is single valued (thus becoming a function), the definition
                  of continuity is equivalent to LHC and UHC. Figure A.21 depicts functions either sat-
                  isfying or violating LHC and UHC at point x0.

                  are differentiable. The following theorem states the condition that such extremum
                  points satisfy in terms of the derivative f ′(·)

         Rolle’s theorem Consider a continuous function f : [a, b] → ℝ that is differen-
         tiable at all points of (a, b), that is, potentially not at the endpoints of its domain.
         If the image of the function at the endpoints coincides, whereby f(a) = f(b), we
         can then find a point c between points a and b where the derivative of f satisfies
         f ′(c) = 0.

                        Mean value theorem Consider a function f : [a, b] → ℝ, which is differentiable

                  f(a), and b and its image f(b). The line connecting f(a) and f(b) has a slope of (f(b) − f(a))/

                  the mean value theorem states that we can find a point c in between a and b such that
                  the tangent of function f(·) at that point, f ′(c), is parallel to the slope (f(b) − f(a))/(b − a)
                  we obtained before.

              A.9     Integration

              Integration helps us measure the area under the curve of a function. One common
              method is a numerical technique known as the Riemann integral.

              Riemann Integral
              This method uses rectangles to approximate the area underneath a curve by slicing it
              into pieces of width w. The height of the function depends on several factors but can
              be any point between f(x) and f(x + w). Examples of two different methods of approxi-
              mating the area under a curve can be seen in figure A.28.
                  The area under the curves is then found by summing the areas of the rectangles
              ∑ ba w ∗ f ( x + i ), where i ∈ [0, w]. As can be seen by the figures, where the height is
              measured can lead to completely different results. This disparity can be resolved by
              shrinking the size of the slice, which will increase the accuracy of the calculation. The
              process here is similar to differentiation, where we find slices that are infinitesimal in
              width to get the most accurate sum possible. In fact this process can complement the
              differentiation process, in which case it then becomes the fundamental theorem of
              calculus. Intuitively, this theorem states that the definite integration of a function is
              related to its antiderivative, and can be reversed by differentiation.
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                          833

                  The point f(c) is thus called the average value of f(x) on the interval [a, b]. This is
                  known as the mean value theorem for integrals.

                  A.10   Introduction to Topology

                  Metric Space
                  In contexts where we seek to measure the difference between two vectors (e.g., two
                  consumption bundles) x and y, where x, y ∈ X ⊆ ℝN, it is convenient to define a metric
                  (or distance) d(x, y), that is, d : X × X → ℝ, which provides us with a numerical measure
                  of the distance between x and y. We can then define a metric space (X, d), where in the
                  parentheses we just list the set X that we consider (e.g., a set of feasible consumption
                  bundles in ℝN) and the distance function, or metric, that we use to measure the differ-
                  ence between two points on that set, x, y ∈ X. The standard metric used in ℝN is the
                  Euclidean distance

                                 d ( x, y ) = x − y = ( x1 − y1 )2 + ( x2 − y2 ) + … + ( xn − yn )
                                                                                       2             2



                  where x, y ∈ X ⊆ ℝN. Note that if x and y are unidimensional, meaning x, y ∈ ℝ, the dis-
                  tance above collapses to

                                                 d ( x, y ) = ( x − y ) = x − y .
                                                                               2
836                                                                               Mathematical Appendix



         In particular, a metric between two points x, y ∈ X, d(x, y) must satisfy the following
      three properties:
      1. d(x, y) ≥ 0, which says that the distance between two points is zero or positive.
      2. d(x, y) = d(y, x), which says that the distance between x and y coincides with the dis-
         tance between y and x.4
      3. d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z), which says that the distance between two points x and z is
         smaller than a “detour” in which we first go from x to another point y, and then from
         y to z (our final destination). This third property is often referred to as the “triangular
         inequality.” Figure A.29 depicts the triangular inequality in the case of X ⊂  2+.
        We next present a series of examples of metrics. As a practice, the reader can check
      that they all satisfy these three properties (while the first two are rather straightforward,
      the third can become a bit challenging to prove in some cases).




      Figure A.29
      Triangular inequality and distances

      4
        Otherwise, a distance would provide us with a number that is sensitive to whether we start measur-
      ing from point x or from y.
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                           837



                  Example A.4: Examples of metric spaces While the Euclidean distance is a com-
                  mon example of a metric, d(x, y) = |x − y|, other metrics are used in economic applica-
                  tions, such as the discrete distance

                                                                       0 if x = y,
                                                          d ( x, y ) = 
                                                                       1 if x ≠ y.
                     As a practice, note that the discrete distance function satisfies all three properties of
                  a metric: (1) the distance is d(x, y) = 1 (and thus positive) if points x ≠ y, and is zero if
                  both points coincide; (2) for any two points x and y, the distance between them satisfies
                  d(x, y) = 1 =d(y, x) when the two points differ x ≠ y, and d(x, y) = 0 =d(y, x) when the two
                  points coincide, x = y; and (3) the triangular inequality holds since, for any three points
                  x ≠ y ≠ z,

                                       d ( x , z ) ≤ d ( x , y ) + d ( y , z ),   that is, 1 ≤ 2 = 1 + 1.

                  The triangular inequality also holds if x = y ≠ z, whereby d(x, z) = 1, d(x, y) = 0
                  and d(y, z) = 1, entailing that 1 ≤ 0 + 1; it is also satisfied if x ≠ y = z, whereby d(x, z) = 1,
                  d(x, y) = 1 and d(y, z) = 0, which yields 1 ≤ 1 + 0; as well as when x = y = z, whereby
                  d(x, z) = d(x, y) = d(y, z) = 0. ■

                  A different example of metric simply considers the sum of the absolute value between
                  each component of two vectors x and y:
                                                                            n
                                                            d ( x, y ) = ∑ xi − yi .
                                                                           i =1


                  The left panel of figure A.30 depicts this metric, where x, y ∈  2+ , and where the dis-
                  tances between x and y and between x and z coincide according to this metric, meaning
                  d(x, y) = d(x, z), although they would not coincide if we measure their distance by using
                  the Euclidian distance. (To see this, imagine a circle with center at x passing through z,
                  thus yielding that d(x, z) > d(x, y) as depicted in the right panel of the figure.)
                    Yet, a different metric, for instance, measuring how different two consumption bun-
                  dles are for an individual in terms of the utility they provide, could solely focus on the
                  good with the largest unit difference between the two bundles. That is,

                                                           d ( x, y ) = max xi − yi
                                                                            i
838                                                                              Mathematical Appendix




      Figure A.30
      Examples of two metrics


      For instance, if x = (10, 11) and y = (9, 2), their distance measured by the metric above
      would be max{10 − 9, 11 − 2} = max{1, 9} = 9. ■

      Interestingly, we can extend the definition of a metric space to measure the distance
      between functions (rather than vectors, as we did in the previous examples). For ex-
      ample, if we consider all continuous functions in a domain A ∈ ℝ, a metric between any
      two functions f and g could focus on the largest distance between their images,
      d ( f , g ) = max x f ( x ) − g ( x ) , as shown in the left panel of figure A.31; or the smallest
      distance, d ( f , g ) = min x f ( x ) − g ( x ) , as shown in the center panel. Each of these
      metrics are depicted below, for the interval [0, 1].
         Last, note that, while we could define different metrics on the same space, such as
      A ∈ ℝN in all our previous examples, some metrics are actually equivalent. Since the
      properties of convergence, openness, and continuity depend on the metric space, they
      are preserved if we move from one metric to an equivalent metric. In particular, we say
      that two metrics d1(x, y) and d2(x, y) are equivalent if we can find two numbers m, M ∈ ℝ+
      such that, for all points x, y ∈ X, distances satisfy

                                    md1 ( x, y ) ≤ d2 ( x, y ) ≤ Md1 ( x, y ).

      Open Ball
      We can now use the distance function d(x, y) to construct a ball around a given point y.
      In particular, taking a radius r around point y, we obtain the open ball {x ∈ X : d(x, y) < r}.
      That is, all points x ∈ X whose distance from y, d(x, y), is strictly smaller than r. As
      depicted in figure A.32, in a two-dimensional context the open ball around point y does
      not contain its boundary points.

      Closed Ball
      In contrast, a closed ball includes all its boundary points. That is, it is described by the
      set {x ∈ X : d(x, y) ≤ r}. A closed ball in ℝ2 and ℝ are depicted in the right-hand panel of




      Figure A.32
      Open balls (left panel) and closed balls (right panel)
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                     841




                  Figure A.33
                  Open set (left panel) and close set (right panel)


                  figure A.33. In the case of open (closed) balls in ℝ3, we would depict them as spheres
                  that do not include (or do include) their boundary points.


                        Open set Set A is an open set if, for every point x ∈ A, there is an open ball with
                        center at x that is contained in A.


                  That is, a set is open if, for all of its points, we can draw open balls around them that
                  completely lie inside the set. The left-hand panel of figure A.33 depicts an open set A.
                  Graphically, for every point x (even if we select a point that lies infinitesimally close
                  to the boundary of set A, such as that on the left-hand side of the figure), we can define
                  a sufficiently small open ball (with radius r → 0) that lies completely inside set A. Such
                  a property does not hold in the set depicted in the right panel of the figure, which il-
                  lustrates a closed set. In particular, there are points in set A, such as the boundary point
                  x, for which not even an open ball with radius r → 0 would completely belong to set A.
                  Let us more formally define closed sets.

                        Closed set   Set A is closed if its complement, Ac, is an open set.


                  In the right-hand panel of figure A.33, note that for all points in Ac, such as y, we can
                  define a sufficiently small ball that lies entirely in Ac, implying that set Ac is open. In
                  the context of ℝ, sets can be more intuitively interpreted as intervals, and we can
842                                                                         Mathematical Appendix




      Figure A.34
      Open set (left panel) with its closed set complement (right panel)


      easily think about open sets, such as (a, b); closed sets, such as [a, b]; and sets that are
      neither open nor closed, (a, b]. In ℝ2, the set {(x, y) = x2 + y2 < 1} is open, whereas
      {(x, y) = x2 + y2 ≥ 1} is closed. Figure A.34 depicts these two sets.

      A.11    Compactness

      Compactness is commonly presented as follows: set A is compact if every sequence in
      A has a subsequence that converges to a point in A. Since this definition implies that set
      A must then be closed and bounded, some textbooks identify a set as compact if and
      only if it is closed and bounded. In fact, in ℝN, both lines of implication hold, thus mak-
      ing both properties equivalent:

                           Set A is compact ⇔ Set A is closed and bounded.

      For generality, we provide next a common definition of compactness based on the no-
      tion of the “cover” of a set. Let us start by defining this concept.

         Cover A collection of sets S covers a set A if their union contains A, that is,

                                                   A ⊆ ∪ si .
                                                        i ∈
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                      843




                  Figure A.35
                  Different covers of the [0, 500] interval


                  Moreover, if S is a collection of open sets, S is said to be an open cover of A. We can
                  graphically think about an open cover as a collection of open sets (i.e., whose bound-
                  ary points are not included) that we lay on top of a given set A, ultimately covering
                  set A with this collection of open sets. As these sets are open, they will need to
                  overlap if we seek to cover all the points of original set A. In the context of a set such
                  as A = [0, 500], we can have different covers. For instance, consider a collection of sets
                  {si} = {(0, n) : n ∈ ℕ}, which is depicted as successively longer intervals, (0, 1), (0, 2)
                  (0, 3), …, with successively longer overlaps, as figure A.35 illustrates in the left panel.
                  Set A can be similarly covered by {si} = {(n − 1, n + 1) : n ∈ ℕ}, which is illustrated as
                  intervals of equal length in the real line (length 2) and with the same overlap across
                  intervals; see right panel of figure A.35. Finally, the collection of sets {si} = {(0, n) : n
                  ∈ ℕ, n ≥ 100} also covers set A = [0, 500], but does it using fewer intervals than
                  {si} = {(0, n) : n ∈ ℕ}, as depicted in figure A.36.
                     When we restrict the sets in the original cover and still cover set A, we refer to such
                  smaller collections of sets as a subcover. In particular, if a subcollection S ′ of the sets
                  in cover S also covers set A, we say that S′ is a subcover of S. Furthermore, if S ′ consist
                  of finitely many sets, we say that S ′ is a finite subcover. We are now ready to define
                  compact sets.


                        Compact set A set A ⊆ ℝN is compact if every cover S of A has a finite sub-
                        cover S′.
844                                                                       Mathematical Appendix




      Figure A.36
      Other covers of the [0, 500] interval


      Given this definition of a compact set, it is easy to show that every compact set A ⊆ ℝn
      must be closed and bounded. Then the Heine–Borel theorem states the converse,
      namely that every closed and bounded set must be compact, ultimately making both
      sets of properties equivalent. This is actually the origin of the standard definitions of
      compactness in several textbooks. (For a proof of these two results, see Bartle and
      Sherbert 2011, 320–22.)
        The compactness of a set provides us with two useful results: the Bolzano–
      Weierstrass theorem and the Weierstrass theorem about extremum points, which we
      separately present next.

         Bolzano–Weierstrass theorem Every sequence {xn} in a compact set has a
         convergent subsequence.



         (Weierstrass’s) Extreme value theorem Let f : A → ℝ be a continuous func-
         tion where A ⊆ ℝn. Then, for every compact subset X of A, X ⊂ A, function f
         attains a maximum and a minimum in A. That is, f(xmin) ≥ f(x) and f(xmax) ≤ f(x)
         for all x ∈ X.
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                      845



                     This is an existence theorem: as long as the subset of the domain that our optimiza-
                  tion problem considers is compact and the objective function f(x) is continuous, a
                  maximum and minimum exist. This is a piece of good news, as many economic ap-
                  plications consider a feasible set that is compact (e.g., budget set for the consumer, or
                  production set for the firm are often closed and bounded, and thus compact), and their
                  objective functions (e.g., utility function for the consumer, or profit function for the
                  firm, respectively) are continuous. Under these conditions we can run optimization
                  problems, such as the utility-maximization problem or the cost-minimization problem,
                  anticipating that a maximum or minimum exists.

                  A.12    Fixed Point Theorems

                  In different economic models, we seek to guarantee existence of equilibria. In particu-
                  lar, in many settings, the function we optimize, f(x), has the property that f(x) = x for
                  some point of its domain x ∈ A. If x ∈ ℝ, the property f(x) = x entails that f(x) crosses the
                  45-degree line at x, either from above or from below, as depicted in the left panel of
                  figure A.37. Points such as x, which satisfy f(x) = x, are labeled fixed points of a func-
                  tion (or correspondence) f(x).




                  Figure A.37
                  Fixed point of a function
846                                                                             Mathematical Appendix



        A natural question is, therefore: Under which conditions of function f(x) does a fixed
      point exist? The fixed point theorems we next explore provide us with an answer. In all
      our subsequent discussions, we assume that domain A ⊂ ℝn is nonempty, compact and
      convex.


         Brouwer’s fixed point theorem If f : A → A is a continuous function, then
         there is at least one fixed point, that is, a point x ∈ A such that f(x) = x.


         In the case in which A ⊂ ℝ, as in figure A.38, we can prove this theorem by defining
      function g(x) = f(x) − x, which measures the vertical distance from f(x) to the 45-degree
      line, and then applying the intermediate value theorem. In particular, at the lowest
      bound of A, x = 0, function g(x) becomes g(0) = f(0) − 0 ≥ 0, since f(0) must be in the
      range [0, 1], meaning f(0) ≥ 0, which graphically implies that f(x) originates weakly
      above the 45-degree line. In the other extreme, where x = 1, we instead have that f(1) ≤ 1
      as f(1) must be in the range [0, 1]. That is, function f(x) must lie weakly below the
      45-degree line at x = 1, in which case g(1) = f(1) − 1≤ 0. Note that if f(x) did not have an
      image at x = 1, function f(x) would not be continuous in its entire domain. If, instead,
      function f(x) is continuous, as in figure A.38, we can finally invoke the intermediate
      value theorem to say that if the distance function g(x) satisfies g(0) ≥ 0 and g(1) ≤ 1,
      there must be an intermediate value of x between 0 and 1 (or more than one) that satis-
      fies g(x) = 0, implying g(x) = f(x) − x = 0, or f(x) = x, as required for a fixed point to exist.




      Figure A.38
      Using the distance function to depict fixed point of f(x)
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                                     847



                    Note that the distance function g(x) = f(x) − x resembles the excess demand function
                  z(p, w) = x(p, w) − e introduced in the chapter on partial and general equilibrium (chapter
                  6), measuring the difference between a consumer’s Walrasian demand and his initial
                  endowment. Therefore in the fixed point the equilibrium is achieved, as there is no
                  excess demand at given market prices, x(p, w) > e implying z(p, w) > e; nor excess supply,
                  x(p, w) < e entailing z(p, w) < 0. Another example of the application of fixed point theo-
                  rems is to players’ best-response functions in game theory. Interestingly, in figure A.37,
                  we see that, f(0) ≥ 0 and f(1) ≤ 1, implying that function f(x) can cross the 45-degree line
                  once (and thus yield a unique fixed point, which in this context entails a unique Nash
                  equilibrium), cross it three times (first from above, then from below, and then from
                  above; yielding three Nash equilibria), and more generally, an odd number of times.
                    The following theorem generalizes Brouwer’s fixed point theorem to correspon-
                  dences.


                        Kakutani’s fixed point theorem If F : A → A is an upper-semicontinuous and
                        convex correspondence, then there is at least one fixed point, that is, a point x ∈ A
                        such that F(x) = x.


                    A particular class of functions always have fixed points. In particular, functions that
                  are a contraction, as defined below, have images f(x) and f(y) that are closer than their
                  corresponding points in the domain x and y.

                  Contraction
                  Consider a real-valued function f : A → A, where A ⊂ ℝ. Function f(·) is a contraction if,
                  for every two points x, y ∈ A, there exists a constant α ∈ (0, 1) such that

                                                          f ( y) − f ( x) ≤ α y − x .

                  Interestingly, if a function is a contraction, then it must have a fixed point. Intuitively,
                  as we move along the points of the domain, their images get closer and closer, eventu-
                  ally not changing at all, |f(y) − f(x)| → 0.5 For instance, function f(x) = x / 2 defines a con-
                  traction mapping for all x ∈ ℝ. In particular,

                                                                        y x 1
                                                    f ( y) − f (x) =     − = y−x ,
                                                                        2 2 2

                  which is weakly smaller than α|y − x| for all α ≤ 1 2 .
                  5
                    This definition can be extended to metric spaces by using the metric distance rather than the abso-
                  lute value. In particular, for a metric space (X, d), a function f : X → X is a contraction if, for every two
                  points in the domain x, y ∈ X, there exists a constant α ∈ (0, 1) such that d(f(x), f(y)) ≤ αd(x, y).
848                                                                                      Mathematical Appendix



      A.13    Optimization

      Consider a maximization problem such as the utility maximization problem in con-
      sumer theory or the profit maximization problem in production theory (the analysis of
      minimization problems is analogous). We seek to maximize an objective function
      f(x; θ) subject to a list of k constraints g1(x; θ) ≤ b1, … , gk(x; θ) ≤ bk. For generality, we
      write the constraints as a function of parameter θ (which can be a vector), and x. Now
      assume, for simplicity, that all functions are continuously differentiable. Then the La-
      grangian function of this constrained maximization problem is
                                                            K
                                 ( x; λ ) = f ( x; θ ) + ∑ λ k [bk − gk ( x : θ )].
                                                            k =1


        Taking first-order conditions with respect to x yields

                                         ∂f ( x; θ ) K     ∂g ( x; θ )
                                                    = ∑ λk k           ,                                (A.1)
                                            ∂x        k =1    ∂x

      and with respect to the Lagrange multipliers (λ1, λ2, … , λk) we obtain

                                 bk − g k ( x; θ ) ≥ 0 for all k = 1, 2, …, k ,                         (A.2)

      which can be rewritten as gk(x; θ) ≤ bk, thus coinciding with the original constraints. In
      addition we need

                              λk [ bk − g k ( x; θ )] = 0     for all k = 1, 2, …, k .                  (A.3)

         Intuitively, either λk = 0 and then the constraint slacks, whereby gk(x; θ) < bk with
      strict inequality, or λk > 0 and the constraint binds, whereby gk(x; θ) = bk. Any pair of
      (x, λ) simultaneously solving conditions (A.1) to (A.3), often referred to as the Kuhn–
      Tucker conditions, is a solution to this constrained maximization problem.

      While Kuhn–Tucker conditions are necessary for a solution, they are not sufficient.
      For them to be sufficient, we need that the objective function be quasi-concave, that is,
      the upper contour sets f(x; θ) ≥ c are convex, and the constraints gk(x; θ) be quasi-
      convex, that is, the feasible set defined by the intersection of all constraints is convex.
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                   851



                  For instance, in a standard utility-maximization problem, the utility function we seek
                  to maximize is concave, and thus quasi-concave, and the budget and resource con-
                  straints define a set of feasible allocations that is convex. If these conditions on
                  objective functions and constraints hold, we can guarantee that the Kuhn–Tucker
                  conditions are not only necessary but also sufficient. Alternatively, we could test
                  whether the candidate for a maximum we obtained from the Kuhn–Tucker first-order

                     While for functions with only one argument such a test is straightforward, for func-
                  tions with several arguments one needs to compute the Hessian matrix. For instance,
                  for x = (x1, x2), we would need to check if the matrix

                                                             ∂2 f ( x; θ )      ∂2 f ( x; θ ) 
                                                             ∂x 2                ∂x1∂x2 
                                           D 2 f ( x; θ ) =  2                                
                                                                     1

                                                             ∂ f ( x; θ )       ∂2 f ( x; θ ) 
                                                             ∂x ∂x
                                                                  2    1           ∂x22 

                  is negative semidefinite (which would show concavity everywhere) or when the matrix
                  is evaluated at the candidate for maximum x*(θ) (which would show concavity of
                  the objective function at that point, i.e., local concavity). Analogously, we would need
                  to check if the matrix above is positive semidefinite (implying a convex function)
                  when solving minimization problems, such as the cost-minimization problem in pro-
                  duction theory.
                     Finally, a natural question is whether one can simplify our constraints from gk(x;
                  θ) ≤ bk to gk(x; θ) = bk. This actually happens in many of the economic applications dis-
                  cussed throughout the book. For instance, consumer j exhausts his income when solv-
                  ing his utility-maximization problem, which is to say, his budget constraint holds
                  with equality ∑ k pk xk = w j , or for the manager solving the profit-maximization prob-
                  lem, where his production plan y achieves production efficiency, i.e., f(z) = y holds with
                  equality. Interestingly, when the constraints hold with equality, we can substitute them
                  into the original constrained maximization problem and transform it into an uncon-
                  strained maximization problem, which is often easier to manipulate and solve. Fortu-
                  nately, as long as the objective function is quasi-concave and the constraints are
                  quasi-convex, we can treat the constraints as holding with equality.

                  A.14      Comparative Statics

                  If we have explicit functional forms for f(x; θ) and gk(x; θ) ≤ bk we can find a
                  reduced-form solution for x*(θ). In this case, comparative statics analysis are rather
                  straightforward, as ∂x*(θ)/∂θ would provide us with a measure of whether x*(θ)
                  increases/decreases in parameter θ and by how much. In some applications, however,
                  a reduced form solution for x*(θ) might be difficult to find. In other settings, we might
                  not even have explicit functional forms for the objective function f(x; θ) and constraints
                  gk(x; θ) ≤ bk but instead know the properties that these functions satisfy by assumption.
                  Fortunately, we can still obtain some comparative statics about x*(θ). In particular,
                  the implicit function theorem, the envelope theorem, and the more advanced theory
                  of monotone comparative statics and supermodularity come to our rescue, as we
                  discuss next.

                        Implicit function theorem Consider a maximization problem with a continu-
                        ously differentiable objective function f(x; θ) and solution x*(θ). Then the effect
                        of parameter θ on the solution of the problem is given by

                                                      ∂x* (θ )    f xθ ( x* (θ ) , θ )
                                                               =−                      ,
                                                        ∂θ        f xx ( x* (θ ) , θ )

                        where the second derivatives fxθ(x*(θ), θ) and fxx(x*(θ), θ) are evaluated at the
                        optimum (of course, fxx ≠ 0).
854                                                                                           Mathematical Appendix



      In order to prove these results, consider, for simplicity, an unconstrained maximization
      problem where the first-order condition of f(x; θ) with respect to x yields fx(x*(θ), θ) = 0.
      Differentiating the FOC with respect to parameter θ, we obtain

                                                      ∂x* (θ )
                               f xx ( x* (θ ) , θ )            + f xθ ( x* (θ ) , θ ) = 0 .
                                                        ∂θ

      Solving for ∂x*(θ)/∂θ yields the above formula of the implicit function theorem.
         In the case of constrained maximization problems, the implicit function
      theorem applies by taking into account that the first-order conditions not only include
      fx(x*(θ), θ) but can generally include terms from the constraints, and that some Kuhn–
      Tucker first-order conditions are actually the constraints themselves. In particular, if
      h(x*(θ), θ) = 0 is the first-order condition that emerges from a constrained maximiza-
      tion problem, we can then apply the implicit function theorem to obtain

                                          ∂x* (θ )   h ( x* (θ ) , θ )
                                                   =− θ *              .
                                            ∂θ       hx ( x (θ ) , θ )

                  The envelope theorem helps us measure how the value function (e.g., the maximal util-

                        continuously differentiable. Then we can take the value function v(θ) = f(x*(θ), θ)

                  affects the value of the objective function. However, by the definition of a maximum,
                  the first term must be zero at x*(θ), that is, ∂f(x*(θ), θ)/∂x = 0. Therefore the expression

      A.15   Monotone Comparative Statics: An Introduction

      While the implicit function theorem and the envelope theorem are widely used in
      economics, they can be subject to some problems as they critically depend on the con-
      tinuity, differentiability, and concavity/convexity of the objective function f(x; θ). In
      particular, any increasing transformation T of f, despite producing the same solution
      x*(θ), can generate discontinuities in the new objective function T(f), points of nondif-
      ferentiability (kinks), and convexities. A natural question is, then, whether we can
      make comparative statics about x*(θ) without the need to check whether the objective
      function (or its increasing transformation) still satisfies continuity, differentiability,
      and concavity/convexity assumptions. Supermodularity and monotone comparative
      statics address our concerns.


        Topkis’s monotonicity theorem                 If the objective function f(x; θ) is supermodu-
        lar, that is,

                               f ( x ′, θ ′ ) − f ( x, θ ′ ) ≥ f ( x ′, θ ) − f ( x, θ )

        for all x′ > x and θ′ > θ, then the solution x*(θ) is weakly increasing in θ.


      Intuitively, supermodularity implies that the marginal effect of increasing x on f is
      weakly increasing in parameter θ; that is, it is larger when the objective function is
      evaluated at θ′ (left-hand side) than when it is evaluated at θ (right-hand side of the
      inequality). If function f is continuously differentiable, then supermodularity simplifies
Mathematical Appendix                                                                                     857



                  to the cross-partial derivative fxθ ≥ 0. In words, the marginal effect of increasing x, fx,
                  increases in parameter θ. However, supermodularity, and its effect on the increasing
                  pattern of x*(θ), is defined irrespective of the continuity or differentiability property of
                  f(x; θ).

                  Further reading For an introductory presentation of complementarity and super-
                  modularity with applications to economics, see Van Zandt (2002) and Vives (2000,
                  ch. 2). For more advanced treatments, see Milgrom and Shannon (1994) and Topkis
                  (1998).

                  A.16   Introduction to Mathematical Proofs

                  In this section we list three common approaches to mathematical proofs in economics.

                  Direct Proof
                  This is perhaps the simplest type of proof, since we use some piece of information to
                  conclude another property or new information. We illustrate this type of proof with a
                  simple example.

                  If m and n are two odd integers, its product mn must also be odd.

                  Proof Since m and n are odd integers, they can be expressed as m = 2a + 1 and
                  n = 2b + 1, where a, b ∈ N. Then their product is

                                 mn = ( 2a + 1) ( 2b + 1) = 4 ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 2 ( 2ab + a + b ) + 1,

                  which simplifies to 2c + 1, where c ≡ 2ab + a + b. Since c is also an integer, whereby
                  c ∈ N, then the product mn = 2c + 1 is also odd. ■

                  Proof by Contrapositive
                  Direct proofs show that p ⇒ q, that is, assuming that p is true, then q follows; proof by
                  contrapositive shows the equivalent statement ¬q ⇒ ¬p, where ¬ denotes the negation
                  of the next clause. That is, “if q does not hold, then p does not hold either.” This result
                  might be easier to show in certain cases, but this also helps us conclude that p ⇒ q.
                  Let’s consider a simple example.

                  If 5x − 7 is an even number, where x is an integer, then x must be odd.

                  Proof The statement can be expressed as “5x − 7 is even ⇒ x is odd.” Then in order
                  to construct ¬q ⇒ ¬p, we use the negation of “x is odd,” that is, “x is even.” (Note that
858                                                                               Mathematical Appendix



      we now seek to prove ¬p, i.e., that “5x − 7 is an odd number.”) Since we started by as-
      suming that x is even, we now have that x = 2a for some other integer a. As a conse-
      quence we can rewrite 5x − 7 as

                       5 x − 7 = 5 ( 2a ) − 7 = 10a − 7 = 10a − 8 + 1 = 2 (5a − 4 ) + 1,

      that is, 5x − 7 can be expressed as 2b + 1 where integer b = 5a − 4. Hence 5x − 7 must be
      odd, as required. ■

      Proof by Contradiction
      This technique is often used in economics, such as to show the uniqueness of the equi-
      librium price vector in chapter 6, and in several end-of-chapter exercises. In order to
      prove that p ⇒ q, we start by assuming that p is true, as in direct proofs. However, we
      now assume that q is false and seek to find a contradiction, namely a violation of the
      initial premise p.

      If m2 is an odd number, then m is also odd.

      Proof Since m2 is odd, it can be expressed as 2a + 1. Our assumption that q is false
      implies that m must be even, being able to be expressed as 2b. As a consequence we
      can write

                                       m 2 = m ⋅ m = 2b ⋅ 2b = 2( 2b 2 ) ,

      that is, m2 can be expressed as 2c where c ≡ 2b2, and thus m2 must be even. This result
      contradicts the premise of m2 being odd, as required. Thus m must be odd. ■
